title: State showering grants to grow clean energy workforce - State House News Service
description: The state will send nearly $20 million across 77 grant awards to help more than 5,500 people get skills and hands-on training necessary for a career in the clean energy
text:
The state will send nearly $20 million across 77 grant awards to help more than 5,500 people get skills and hands-on training necessary for a career in the clean energy field.

The workforce development grants announced Wednesday through the Mass. Clean Energy Center span five programs, funding job training, equipment and facility upgrades, career exposure for students and young adults, and business support for underrepresented firms. Gov. Maura Healey’s administration announced the awards during an event at Roxbury Community College.

"Clean energy and climatetech reduces energy costs and emissions. To build those solutions, we need a workforce that is ready to deliver. Our role is to strengthen the foundation of our workforce training system so that the residents and businesses it serves can grow together,” Clean Energy Center CEO Ben Downing said. "These grants do that by helping organizations expand their reach, strengthen their programs, and open doors for more people to take part in Massachusetts’ clean energy industry."

The largest single awards include $800,000 for a business support hub in southeastern Massachusetts run by the New England Business Growth Collective, and $750,000 each for a northeast business hub led by Roads Consulting Group and for EV training equipment at Essex North Shore Agricultural and Technical School. Roxbury Community College received $350,000 to train people involved in the criminal justice system, starting with education before release.

Helfrich Bros. Boiler Works, a Merrimack Valley company, landed about $964,000 across three grants for its welding academy, and Upper Cape Cod Regional Technical School received $900,000 across three awards for electric vehicle technician training.

"We want more residents to benefit from the jobs and opportunities this growing industry is creating," Healey said.

In its 2025 annual jobs report, MassCEC said the state was home to 162,940 climatetech workers, including more than 118,000 jobs dedicated to clean energy. The report said the climatetech industry (which includes jobs related to clean energy, greenhouse gas mitigation, and climate impact prevention and repair) contributes $17.3 billion to the Massachusetts economy.

text:
Ford has started shipping its first lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery cells from a new Michigan factory, marking the automaker’s entry into battery manufacturing and a step toward producing more affordable electric vehicles in the US.

The first prismatic cells have rolled off the production line at BlueOval Battery Park Michigan in Marshall. They are heading to Ford’s Louisville Assembly Plant in Kentucky, where they will power prototypes of the upcoming Fathom electric pickup.

Ford says it will become the first company to deliver LFP batteries in the US for mainstream consumer automotive use. The milestone follows years of work to establish domestic production of a battery chemistry widely used by Chinese manufacturers.

The Michigan facility is owned and operated by Ford, but its manufacturing technology is licensed from China’s Contemporary Amperex Technology Co. Limited (CATL), the world’s largest electric vehicle battery maker.

Lower-cost batteries for EVs

Ford selected LFP chemistry for its Universal Electric Vehicle Platform because it can help reduce battery costs without relying on nickel or cobalt. The chemistry also offers durability over years of charging and use, making it suitable for vehicles expected to support additional functions such as bidirectional home power.

The automaker chose rectangular prismatic cells because they can fit directly into the vehicle’s chassis. Ford is also designing the battery pack as a structural component of the vehicle rather than simply housing it inside the frame.

This approach is intended to reduce the number of parts, weight, and manufacturing complexity. Ford says the combination of cell design and vehicle architecture will help make its next generation of electric vehicles more affordable.

The Fathom pickup will be the first vehicle built on the Universal Electric Vehicle Platform. Its prototypes will use the initial battery shipments from Michigan as engineers continue development.

Production scales in Michigan

BlueOval Battery Park Michigan’s assembly lines can produce 40 cells per minute, according to Ford, placing the facility among the fastest LFP prismatic battery production lines outside China. The company says the plant has additional capacity to increase output.

Manufacturing speed is only part of the challenge. Ford is also using automated inspection systems, including image-recognition tools, to identify defects during production. The company aims to reduce defects to levels measured per billion cells rather than per million.

The plant’s production expertise will also support Ford Energy’s planned battery energy storage business in Glendale, Kentucky. The company is preparing to manufacture battery storage systems for applications beyond electric vehicles.

Ford plans to bring a separate battery pack facility in Marshall online in 2027, ahead of the Fathom’s launch. The first cells will help inform prototype development and the next stages of production preparation.

The launch comes as automakers seek lower-cost battery technologies to make electric vehicles more competitive. LFP batteries have gained ground because they avoid expensive nickel and cobalt while offering long service life.

For Ford, the Michigan operation also represents an effort to build domestic manufacturing expertise while relying on licensed technology from an established Chinese supplier. The first shipments mark a shift from factory construction and trial production to supplying cells for vehicle development.

description: U.S. SENATE News:
text:
By LINDA DALY, President, Los Alamos Community Foundation Bo…





U.S. SENATE News:

WASHINGTON, D.C. — In an op-ed published by The Economist, U.S. Sen. Martin Heinrich (D-N.M.), Ranking Member of the U.S. Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee, highlighted the need for the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA), explaining how the legislation will speed up the federal approval process for energy projects to get more power onto the grid, lowering electricity bills for Americans and creating more jobs – while codifying into law Tribal consultation, maintaining key environmental protections, and holding data centers accountable for their costs.

“In June, the largest clean-energy-infrastructure project in the western hemisphere came online in New Mexico. “The [SunZia] project took 17 years to permit and build—and SunZia isn’t alone. Across America, energy-infrastructure projects take far too long to permit… Indeed, permitting might be the economy’s most expensive bottleneck,” began Heinrich.

“America’s ability to meet the energy demands of the 21st century depends on its ability to build a modern, clean energy economy… That process is now standing in the way of getting new clean energy online and unlocking important economic investment,” continued Heinrich. “The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act—which the Senate voted to advance on November 9th and which I co-sponsor with another Democrat and two Republicans—does not remove environmental considerations, the ability to litigate projects or the ability for local communities to comment… But it does make these reviews a standardized part of a predictable process.”

“Modelling by Resources For the Future suggests that BAAJA could cause a decline in cumulative CO2 of about 1.8 gigatons—more than if the entire light-duty vehicle fleet was taken off America’s roads for a year—between now and 2041. Similarly, the Solar Energy Industries Association, a trade body, estimates that BAAJA’s adoption would mean solar and wind would provide 37.4% of America’s electricity generation in 2035, against 19.6% if the current permitting regime remains in place. These forecasts starkly illustrate the heavy drag America’s permitting regime places on the economy. For the nation’s future prosperity and security, it must be reformed,” concluded Heinrich.

text:
Both parties agree the current permitting framework, a decades-old tangle of overlapping laws, needs an overhaul.

The US electric grid in particular faces growing strain from AI data centers, electric cars, heat pumps and extreme weather.

In September, Democratic Senator Sheldon Whitehouse of Rhode Island, Republican Senator Shelley Moore Capito of West Virginia and others introduced the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026 (BAAJA).

It advanced in the Senate on Wednesday and could get a floor vote Thursday, ahead of the Thanksgiving recess, before moving on to the House.

"It's time to pass BAAJA so we can lower costs, juice the clean energy economy, build big things again in America, reduce pollution, and create new union jobs," Whitehouse, viewed widely as a climate champion in Congress, wrote recently on X.

- Upgrades vital to green transition -

BAAJA aims to speed up energy, infrastructure, and industrial projects by limiting challenges under existing laws such as the National Environmental Policy Act, the Clean Water Act, the National Historic Preservation Act and the Endangered Species Act.

The bill would update the nation's aging power grid -- requiring utilities to upgrade existing transmission lines and deploy advanced technologies, while limiting a state's ability to scupper projects.

A source familiar with the talks and in favor of the bill said such upgrades were vital for getting electricity from desert solar farms and offshore wind projects to high-demand areas.

President Donald Trump's administration moved last week to advance some wind projects, seen as a way to win Democratic support.

Permitting reform "has been talked about forever, and meanwhile we continue pumping carbon into the atmosphere, so we don't have any time to lose," the source told AFP.

The bill limits the president's ability to discriminate among energy sources, which could bar Trump from blocking renewables but also stop a future Democratic president from revoking oil and gas pipelines.

Its Democratic backers believe that in a market-based shootout, clean energy will beat fossil fuels.

It also requires data centers to pay for their impact on the grid, a major demand as residential electricity rates have surged -- but does not address their air pollution or water consumption.

- Environmental rollbacks -

Even groups backing the bill's grid measures object to its weakening of environmental safeguards.

"Our position is that as the bill is currently written, we oppose it," Erik Olson, an attorney at the Natural Resources Defense Council, told AFP.

One key objection, according to the Environmental Working Group (EWG), is that it could lock in toxic water pollution.

Jared Hayes, a senior policy analyst for EWG, said one provision gives industry more power to challenge the scientific benchmarks that define pollutant levels in water -- giving chemical companies new ways to delay or sue over limits on PFAS "forever chemicals."

Another section doubles the maximum term for discharge permits from five to 10 years, which "doesn't align with science," Hayes said, because it would make it hard to act if a new contaminant is identified.

That is "an incredible concern for us," Emily Donovan, co-founder of Clean Cape Fear, told AFP from Wilmington, North Carolina, which is grappling with a massive PFAS crisis linked to the chemical GenX.

Tap water at her children's elementary school showed the highest PFAS levels ever recorded, she said, and her husband recently overcame a brain tumor the family links to PFAS exposure.

Native American groups are also staunchly opposed.

"Congress must reject BAAJA in its entirety. Native sovereignty, sacred places, and cultural heritage are not negotiable," the National Congress of American Indians said in a statement.

Some Democrats have floated writing a better bill once their party takes control of Congress next year following a sweeping midterms victory.

The source familiar with discussions disagreed, telling AFP: "The president for the next two years will be Donald Trump. The idea that there is some better bill to be had in the next Congress, I think, is entirely illusory."

text:
General Motors Company (GM) is a U.S.-based multinational automotive manufacturer that designs, builds, and sells vehicles, vehicle parts, and mobility solutions. The company operates primarily in the global automotive industry, with activities spanning electric vehicles (EVs), autonomous driving technologies, financing services, software-enabled vehicle platforms, and commercial fleet solutions. GM’s core automotive brands include Chevrolet, GMC, Cadillac, and Buick, while its financing operations are conducted through GM Financial. The company generates revenue primarily from vehicle sales, financing and leasing activities, aftermarket parts, software and connected services, and commercial fleet operations. GM serves retail consumers, commercial fleets, government entities, and dealership networks across multiple global markets.

GM traces its origins to 1908 when William C. Durant founded General Motors in Flint, Michigan. Over the twentieth century, the company became one of the world’s largest automakers through acquisitions and global expansion. Following financial distress during the 2008–2009 global financial crisis, GM underwent a government-supported restructuring and emerged as the current General Motors Company in 2009. In recent years, GM has repositioned its strategy toward electrification, software-defined vehicles, and autonomous mobility. The company’s competitive advantages include large-scale manufacturing capabilities, extensive dealer and distribution networks, established automotive brands, vertically integrated EV battery development through strategic partnerships, and broad North American market share in trucks and SUVs.

Business Operations

GM organizes its operations primarily into the segments GM North America (GMNA), GM International (GMI), Cruise, and GM Financial. GMNA represents the company’s largest revenue and profit contributor, driven largely by full-size pickup trucks, SUVs, and commercial vehicles sold under the Chevrolet and GMC brands. GMI oversees operations outside North America, including activities in China, South America, and select international markets. GM Financial provides automotive financing, leasing, insurance, and commercial lending services to dealers and consumers, contributing recurring financial-services income. The company also operates BrightDrop, focused on electric commercial delivery solutions, and connected vehicle software businesses tied to subscription services and telematics platforms such as OnStar.

GM maintains extensive manufacturing, engineering, and supply-chain operations across North America, South America, Asia, and other international regions. The company has invested heavily in EV technologies through its proprietary Ultium battery platform and electric propulsion systems. GM has maintained strategic relationships and joint ventures with battery and manufacturing partners, including collaborations with LG Energy Solution through battery cell manufacturing ventures in the United States. The company has also historically maintained strategic operations in China through joint ventures with local manufacturers, including SAIC-GM and SAIC-GM-Wuling, which remain important contributors to GM’s international vehicle volumes.

Strategic Position & Investments

GM’s current strategy centers on vehicle electrification, advanced driver-assistance systems, software-enabled recurring revenue, and autonomous mobility technologies. The company has committed substantial capital expenditures toward expanding EV production capacity, battery manufacturing, and digital vehicle platforms. Major investments include dedicated EV assembly plants, battery cell facilities, and software architecture designed to support over-the-air updates and connected services. GM has also invested in hydrogen fuel-cell technologies through its Hydrotec platform and has pursued commercial opportunities in defense, logistics, and industrial applications.

The company has made notable investments and acquisitions to strengthen its technology portfolio. Cruise, GM’s autonomous vehicle subsidiary, has been a major focus of investment, although operational expansion has faced regulatory and safety-related scrutiny in recent years. GM also acquired software and technology assets over time to support autonomous driving, artificial intelligence integration, and vehicle connectivity initiatives. In the commercial sector, BrightDrop was established to target electric delivery and logistics markets. GM continues to prioritize scalable EV production, North American battery supply-chain localization, and software monetization as long-term growth drivers.

Geographic Footprint

GM is headquartered in Detroit, Michigan, and maintains operations across North America, South America, Asia-Pacific, the Middle East, and other international markets. The company’s strongest market position is in the United States, where it remains one of the largest automotive manufacturers by vehicle sales. North America contributes the majority of GM’s earnings, particularly through high-margin truck and SUV sales. The company also maintains manufacturing plants, engineering centers, proving grounds, and distribution operations across Canada and Mexico.

Internationally, GM has maintained a significant presence in China through joint ventures and localized production partnerships, although competitive pressures and changing market dynamics have affected market share in recent years. The company also operates in countries across South America, including Brazil and Argentina, and maintains selective operations in additional global regions through exports, partnerships, and regional subsidiaries. GM’s global footprint supports both manufacturing scale and access to key automotive growth markets, particularly in EV adoption and commercial mobility solutions.

Leadership & Governance

GM is led by Mary Barra, who serves as Chair and Chief Executive Officer. Barra has emphasized a long-term strategic vision centered on an “all-electric future,” software-enabled vehicle ecosystems, disciplined capital allocation, and autonomous mobility development. Under her leadership, GM has accelerated investments in EV manufacturing, battery technologies, and connected services while reshaping the company’s global operating structure following its post-bankruptcy transformation.

Key executives include:

Mary Barra – Chair and Chief Executive Officer

Paul Jacobson – Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer

Mark Reuss – President

Rory Harvey – Executive Vice President and President, Global Markets

Marissa West – Executive Vice President and President, GM North America

Kurt Kelty – Vice President, Batteries, Propulsion, and Sustainability

Jill Dougherty – Chief Communications Officer

Craig Glidden – Executive Vice President and President, GM Insurance and Strategic Growth Initiatives

GM’s governance framework is overseen by its board of directors and supported through public disclosures including annual reports, investor presentations, and filings such as the Form 10-K submitted to the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC). Company operational, financial, and strategic information is consistently disclosed through regulatory filings, shareholder communications, and investor relations materials.

Key Takeaways

Ford Motor's (NYSE: F) plant in Michigan has rolled out its first lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery cells using technology licensed from CATL (HKEX: 3750), marking the US auto giant's official entry into battery manufacturing.

The prismatic LFP cells, produced at BlueOval Battery Park Michigan in Marshall, Michigan, are headed to the Louisville Assembly Plant to power prototypes of the Fathom electric pickup truck, Charles Poon, vice president of hardware engineering at Ford, said in a statement on Wednesday.

With commercial-scale deliveries from the wholly owned and operated plant, Ford will become the first automaker to introduce LFP batteries for the mainstream US consumer automotive market, helping push pure electric vehicle (EV) prices lower.

To significantly reduce vehicle cost and weight, Ford chose proven technology from CATL, the world's largest battery maker, and integrated the prismatic LFP battery pack directly into the vehicle design as a structural chassis component.

The plant's assembly lines can produce 40 cells per minute, making them among the fastest prismatic LFP battery lines outside China, and use AI image recognition technology to pursue a low defect rate at the parts-per-billion level.

Following the shipment of the first cells, Ford plans to bring a supporting battery pack plant into operation in Marshall in 2027 to prepare for the official launch of the Fathom electric pickup.

Manufacturing experience gained from the on-schedule launch of the Michigan plant is helping a battery energy storage system plant in Glendale, Kentucky, prepare for its start of production in 2027, Ford Energy president David Carroll said on Thursday.

The bumpy partnership began in February 2023, when Ford initially announced a $3.5 billion investment to build a plant with an annual capacity of 35 gigawatt-hours (GWh), with CATL providing technology licensing and operational support.

After US Republican lawmakers questioned whether federal subsidies could indirectly flow to CATL, the project was temporarily halted in 2023 before restarting in November of the same year with investment and annual capacity cut to $2 billion and 20 GWh, respectively.

Facing policy headwinds such as the early termination of US federal EV tax credits in September 2025, Ford recorded $19.5 billion in related asset impairment charges in December 2025, but kept the LFP project and decided to expand into the energy storage business.

text:
Tesla has opened its first Semi-only Megacharger in Texas, but the pace of expanding its public charging network is falling well short of its original target. As mass production and customer deliveries of the Semi gather pace, building charging infrastructure to support long-haul operations has emerged as a task.

On Nov. 18 local time, electric vehicle outlet Electrek reported that Tesla opened an eight-stall Semi Megacharger in Mesquite, east of Dallas, Texas. That brings public Megacharger sites available to general customers in the United States to seven across four states, with 44 chargers in total.

The new site is on South Town East Boulevard in Mesquite. Each of the eight chargers supports up to 1.2 megawatts of power. Tesla's charging business posted news of the opening and on-site photos on X, formerly Twitter.

Still, the network rollout is not keeping up with the plan. In its 2025 fourth-quarter shareholder report, Tesla set a goal of securing about 37 Megacharger sites during 2026. Dan Priestley, head of the Semi programme, has also said he wants to build 46 sites by early 2027.

Seven publicly operated sites currently fall short of even one-fifth of the annual target. With about six weeks left in the year, meeting the goal would require opening 30 additional sites over the next 43 days. Given the recent pace of about one new site every two weeks, achieving the target will not be easy.

In February, Tesla added 64 Megacharger candidate sites to its charging map, expanding planned locations to 66. Of these, Texas was assigned the most candidates at 19, but Mesquite is the first to actually begin operations. Other candidates in the Dallas-Fort Worth area remain listed as coming soon.

Expansion of cooperation with charging infrastructure company Pilot also has not progressed as much as planned. Pilot opened its first Megacharger in Georgia in October and mentioned Flying J in Fort Stockton, Texas, as one of the next candidates. But the site is still not shown as an operating location on Tesla's map. Pilot said in October that nine additional sites were under construction, but large-scale openings would need to continue over the remaining period to come close to the year-end goal.

Tesla's public Megachargers are currently operating in Bloomington, Vernon and Tulare in California; Conley and Ellabell in Georgia; Hodgkins in Illinois; and Mesquite in Texas. In early October, customer sites numbered four with 26 chargers, but Tulare, Hodgkins and Mesquite were added in turn, expanding the network to its current size.

Rivals are also entering the large electric truck charging market. Greenlane, a joint venture of Daimler Truck, NextEra and BlackRock, announced in May it would build high-power truck charging hubs in Dallas and Houston. The stations are to be open to all electric trucks using the CCS and MCS connector standards. Tesla began operating first with Mesquite, but competition over charging infrastructure around the Texas logistics market is already intensifying.

Expanding the public charging network is also tied to the Semi mass-production schedule. Tesla began mass production of the Semi at its Nevada plant in September and said it plans to have annual capacity of 50,000 units. Last week it also disclosed it had delivered 50 Semis for the first time to the Chicago area.

Large transport operators can build charging facilities at their own depots, but public Megachargers are core infrastructure for the Semi to leave company bases and undertake long-haul transport. Even if vehicle production and deliveries increase, routes and the range of use could be limited if the public charging network is not sufficiently built out.

Tesla also operates private Megachargers for its own vehicles at the Nevada Gigafactory and in Carson, California. It is also running a business programme that sells Megachargers to transport operators and depot operators. Earlier this month, Forum Mobility began operating two Megachargers at the Port of Long Beach. Such self-operated and customer-only facilities are separate from the public charging network available to general Semi buyers.

Ultimately, for the Semi's full commercialisation, it has become important not only to expand vehicle production but also to accelerate the buildout of public charging infrastructure. How close Tesla can get to its annual goal by speeding up site openings over the remaining period is expected to be a key point to watch for the Semi business.

title: Curing EV range anxiety: An update - Brookings Institution
authors: Omar Isaac Asensio, Elaine Buckberg, Cassandra Cole, Luke Heeney, Christopher R. Knittel, Ben Swedberg, Adie Tomer, Tommy Wan
description:
Range anxiety—the fear that an EV driver won’t find a working charger along the highway on a long drive—is holding back EV sales, surveys show.
Real-time data enables EV drivers to confidently and reliably navigate to a working charger.
On top of wanting chargers to work, EV drivers want to avoid price surprises.
Nationally, over 1,300 fast charging stations with scheduled pricing have a high-low range of more than $0.20.
Fast charging providers would also benefit if real-time data helped the EV market grow faster—and we estimate it would.
text:
Range anxiety—the fear that an EV driver won’t find a working charger along the highway on a long drive—is holding back EV sales, surveys show.

Several colleagues and I published a paper at the Hutchins Center and the American Enterprise Institute in 2025 proposing that states enact laws requiring fast chargers report real-time status and pricing that any EV mapping app can access and make available to drivers. We’re talking information like whether the charger is working or broken, and how much it costs to charge—the electric equivalent of dollars per gallon. The 2021 Bipartisan Infrastructure Law set that requirement for chargers it funded on major interstates—$5 billion designated to create a highway network any EV driver could use. We proposed to broaden the requirement.

When our paper was published in September 2025, only Massachusetts required real-time data, and only for new chargers receiving public funding.

Since then, California and Vermont have put in place real-time data requirements. California did it by regulations; Vermont did it by law.

Real-time data enables EV drivers to confidently and reliably navigate to a working charger. This is particularly important in Vermont, with a state average 86.9 reliability rating from Paren based on charging success on the first and second try, failed attempts, and downtime. Of the 50 states, only Oklahoma had a worse rating. Reliability scores are generally rising over time. But the trend is not straight up. Paren reports that reliability fell in 29 of 52 states and territories over the past year.

On top of wanting chargers to work, EV drivers want to avoid price surprises.

Gas stations are very clear about their pricing. They post pricing on big signs that you can easily read as you’re approaching on the road—and in some cases, tall signs enable drivers to read prices from the highway before deciding whether to exit. Prominent gas station signs are a standard practice by convention, not by law. While gas stations often change their prices daily, they’re not more expensive at rush hour.

Contrast that with charging stations. In June 2026, 32% of fast charging stations nationally had prices that varied by time of day, based on our analysis of Paren data. Because those tended to be larger stations, the rates at 52% of charging ports nationally changed throughout the day.

At most stations where charging rates vary, they do so according to a pre-set schedule—cheaper overnight, most expensive during the business day. So, in theory, local users could learn the schedule at a station they visit repeatedly. Price-sensitive road trippers, though, would want to check pricing before deciding where to exit and charge.

The variation can be big; for example, at one Los Angeles station with scheduled pricing, prices ranged from $0.48 to $0.72 per kWh—a $0.24 gap. Depending on how you look at it, that’s a 50% daytime hike over the overnight rate, or a one-third overnight discount off the daytime rate. Nationally, over 1,300 fast charging stations with scheduled pricing have a high-low range of more than $0.20.

Another 4% of stations and 13% of ports nationally have Uber- and Lyft-style dynamic pricing. That means local and road-tripping users want to check the current price before deciding where to fast charge.

Data transparency can help the charging station companies as well.

Fast charging providers would also benefit if real-time data helped the EV market grow faster—and we estimate it would. By 2030, the policy we recommend, if adopted nationally, would put 3.5 million more EVs on the road, 15% more than without real-time data, as our paper found. More EVs means more charging sessions, enabling charging providers to pay off their investments faster.

State action matters and can lead to transparency behind their boundaries. Weeks after California approved its regulations, both Tesla and Electrify America, the two largest fast-charger networks, made their status data available for free via Google Maps. That’s progress, but the job is not done. That’s only one app, albeit a very widely used one; Google Maps lacks pricing information; and without rules in place, the companies could withdraw that status information.

The case for state action is straightforward. Left alone, the market won’t do this. Requiring EV charging companies to provide more information is not only a convenience to EV drivers, but it removes an obstacle to the spread of EVs, which are an essential element of any response to the threat posed by climate change. title: Ford bets on CATL know-how to bring cheap LFP batteries to U.S. EVs
description:
Ford has started making lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery cells in the United States with technology licensed from CATL, China’s battery giant.
Ford said its first LFP prismatic cells have come off the line at BlueOval Battery Park Michigan in Marshall.
Ford says the milestone puts it “in the battery business” and claims it will be the first company to deliver LFP batteries in the U.S. for mainstream consumer vehicles.
Why LFP, and why CATL LFP cells contain no nickel or cobalt, which keeps costs down, and they hold up well over many years of charging, according to Ford.
A timeline of the Ford–CATL partnership
text:
Ford has started making lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery cells in the United States with technology licensed from CATL, China’s battery giant. The Detroit automaker hopes the cells will help it build cheaper electric vehicles and challenge Chinese rivals.

Ford said its first LFP prismatic cells have come off the line at BlueOval Battery Park Michigan in Marshall. They are headed to Louisville Assembly Plant in Kentucky to power prototypes of the Fathom, Ford’s upcoming midsize electric pickup. Ford says the milestone puts it “in the battery business” and claims it will be the first company to deliver LFP batteries in the U.S. for mainstream consumer vehicles.

Cell production at the roughly 3 billion USD plant, about 100 miles west of Detroit, began last month. CATL supplies the technology and manufacturing support, but Ford owns and runs the plant.

Why LFP, and why CATL

LFP cells contain no nickel or cobalt, which keeps costs down, and they hold up well over many years of charging, according to Ford. The company picked rectangular prismatic cells because they fit directly into the chassis, allowing the battery pack to act as part of the vehicle’s structure and cutting structural costs.

Ford said it spoke with battery makers around the world before choosing CATL. It wanted a technology that was “proven in the field, ready to manufacture at scale”, and CATL’s batteries power some 30 million vehicles worldwide.

“If we want to get to being able to produce affordable EVs in the United States, we need to also do it the fastest way possible,” Alan Clarke, Ford’s vice president of advanced development projects, said during a tour of the plant. “CATL being the biggest in the world means that they’re the best supplier to get us that technology and help us learn ourselves how to produce LFP cells.”

LFP chemistry was invented in the U.S. but commercialised mostly in China. CATL staff helped Ford ramp up the Marshall plant by providing training and manufacturing expertise.

Capacity and timeline

Ford says the Marshall lines can turn out 40 cells per minute, which it calls among the fastest LFP prismatic lines outside China, and that the site has room to expand. Workers use AI-powered image recognition to catch defects, with a goal of measuring the defect rate per billion cells rather than per million.

That pace works out to about 20 gigawatt-hours a year for EVs and Ford’s energy storage business. The original plan was up to 40 GWh, but Ford scaled back as it and the broader industry slowed their EV push. Ford says it is still early in certifying its processes. It plans to increase cell output next year, ahead of the Fathom’s expected launch in the fourth quarter of 2027. A battery pack plant in Marshall is due to open in 2027.

The Fathom will start at 28,350 USD for the standard-range model, and Ford plans to open preorders in early 2027. What Ford learns in Marshall is also feeding into Ford Energy’s plans for battery energy storage production in Glendale, Kentucky.

Political headwinds

The project has drawn criticism in Washington. Some lawmakers and Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy have objected to Ford’s ties with CATL. In September, Duffy wrote to Ford CEO Jim Farley expressing “profound concern” about the company’s links to Chinese firms. The White House praised Ford’s U.S. jobs and manufacturing the next day.

In January, Rep. John Moolenaar, a Michigan Republican who chairs a House committee, asked Ford whether its CATL licensing terms had been “updated, expanded, or otherwise altered” to fit its new focus on energy storage and data centre batteries. Ford replied that expanding domestic LFP production is “an investment in American workers” and said it is confident the batteries meet tax credit requirements.

The start of shipments comes the same week President Donald Trump is meeting Chinese leader Xi Jinping at the APEC summit in Shenzhen.

The U.S. Department of Energy has issued Grid United a $2.8 billion conditional loan commitment to finance a 1.8-GW, high-voltage, direct current transmission line in Wyoming — the latest in a series of funding decisions that could add about 7 GW of transfer capacity between the Western and Eastern interconnections.

In 2021, the DOE said a collection of back-to-back converter stations enabled just 1,320 MW of electricity to flow between the two networks. Increasing transfer capacity could save money and boost grid reliability and resilience, it says.

The Wyoming Intertie project would run about 106 miles between a converter station in Wyoming’s Platte County and an existing substation in Carbon County, linking the Southwest Power Pool and the Western Electricity Coordinating Council. The area around the project is rich in wind resources.

Also, that part of Wyoming “sits at the confluence of major grid expansion projects in WECC and SPP, which makes it a particularly advantageous location for a grid-to-grid connection,” Ashley Kang, a Grid United spokesperson, said in an email.

Grid United expects to complete the permitting for the project in 2029 and begin construction in 2030. The company plans to bring the project online in 2032 or 2033, depending on its procurement of needed HVDC equipment, according to a company fact sheet.

The Houston-based transmission company is developing three other projects that would also add lines between the Eastern and Western interconnections. They include the 3-GW North Plains Connector project between North Dakota and Montana; the 1.8-GW Three Corners Connector between Oklahoma and Colorado; and the 1.5-GW Pecos West project between SPP’s footprint in Texas and WECC in New Mexico.

In separate funding decisions, DOE has recently agreed to help finance the Three Corners and North Plains connector projects. Taken together, the department has agreed to help fund about 6.6 GW of East-West transmission infrastructure by Grid United.

DOE has also agreed to help fund a 490-MW expansion project between Colorado and Texas. The project, planned by Xcel Energy, could be expanded to a total of 2 GW.

Keep up with the story. Subscribe to the Utility Dive free daily newsletter

The DOE’s draft 2026 National Transmission Needs Study found that average price differentials along the seam between SPP’s eastern footprint and the Western Interconnection ranged from $18/MWh to $33/MWh from 2012 to 2023.

The Wyoming Intertie project could produce $39 billion in cost savings for ratepayers, help meet growing demand and improve grid resilience during periods of high electric use and extreme weather, DOE said Tuesday. Closing conditions on the loan include Grid United obtaining full project right-of-way, contracts for capacity on the line, and federal, state and local permits.

The conditional, 30-year DOE loan would finance 80% of the project’s construction costs, reducing interest expenses by about $500 million compared with typical financing sources, according to Grid United.

The low-cost, federal loan can be assigned to utilities that may buy capacity on the transmission line, translating into savings for ratepayers, Grid United said.

text:
Tesla is gearing up Cybercab, its all-electric and fully autonomous ride-hailing vehicle, for a very public debut as it plans to start customer deliveries in December. However, the units that rolled out of Gigafactory Texas this morning seem to differ from what we have seen previously.

Explore Auto Tech

Aerial images captured by drone photographer Joe Tegtmeyer at Giga Texas on November 18 reveal a noticeable update to the appearance of Tesla’s Cybercabs equipped with Starlink. Rows of gold production vehicles sit in the outbound lot, each carrying a flush-mounted Starlink V5 terminal on the rear hatch that looks more refined than the version first shown months earlier.

When Tesla first unveiled the integration in July and displayed a physical example in August, the Starlink hardware appeared as a relatively distinct rectangular panel on the hatch. Later September footage of large numbers of Cybercabs leaving the factory still showed a lighter, more obvious rectangular cover that roughly matched the vehicle’s gold paint:

The newest batch stands out for how cleanly the cover blends into the roof’s character lines. Observers and replies to Tegtmeyer’s post describe the result as tighter and more intentional, sitting flush and following the body contours rather than reading as an added panel.

All of the Cybercabs in the latest images also wear prominent “Cybercab” logos on the doors and rear hatch, confirming these are finished production units rather than early prototypes. They are staged near the factory building, end-of-line areas, and covered transport trailers, with some already lined up for shipment.

Explore Auto Tech

The scale and consistency of the installation point to factory tooling rather than retrofit work.

A secondary detail noted in related sightings is a darker tone to the Starlink cover compared with earlier lighter panels. Tegtmeyer himself left open whether the darker finish is deliberate. There are a variety of explanations for it: perhaps for thermal performance, signal characteristics, or simple visual identification—or simply a batch variation still being refined.

Either way, the overall effect is a more integrated, production-ready appearance. For a Robotaxi that relies on Starlink for fleet connectivity, passenger services, and backup data links in areas with weak cellular coverage, the cleaner hatch design is more than cosmetic.

It signals that Tesla is polishing the final visual and hardware details as Cybercab volumes continue to climb at Giga Texas ahead of broader Robotaxi deployment. The vehicles now look to be built with Starlink instead of it being added afterward.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy has responded to Elon Musk’s claim that the Federal Aviation Administration turned down free Starlink terminals before last week’s nationwide ground stop, saying the department chose a ground-based network after running into problems with an earlier version of the satellite service. Musk’s reply was a single emoji: “ .”

Speaking at a press conference, Duffy said Starlink had been useful in some parts of the system. “I’ve worked well with Elon, and he, Starlink was a great solution for some of our assets in Alaska, but we sent Starlink, in one of its prior iterations, to our tech lab, and, there was some issues that we had to navigate, and we thought that the best method is to have a network that’s based on the ground,” Duffy said, according to a transcript published by ZeroHedge. “Now, I think what he’s doing with Starlink and the speed is remarkable, but, our airspace is very big. We have assets everywhere. And so, again, we used him for different parts of the airspace.”

Duffy did not dispute that the offer was made. He also did not say what problems the FAA found during testing.

The exchange started Monday, when Musk wrote on X, “Free Starlinks for FAA were offered to Sec Duffy, but he said they were not needed. As it turns out, they were,” as Teslarati reported. That post came three days after the FAA grounded departures nationwide on November 13, when its legacy equipment became unstable as data flooded its telecommunications network at 1,000 connection attempts every four to five seconds. The FAA traced the flood to a radar site in Amarillo, Texas, and a radio site in El Dorado, Arkansas, where L3Harris had been installing a new router. Roughly 12,462 flights were canceled that day.

Duffy has also signaled frustration with L3Harris, which runs the FAA’s current network. “I want to get away from L3Harris and get to a new one, but they own the network,” he said. “I can’t cancel the network that they own.” He has asked Congress for $50 billion to modernize air traffic control, arguing against “a patchwork, a fix to a system that’s critical for every single family.”

The FAA’s position on satellite links predates this week. In a July 2025 letter to lawmakers, FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford said the agency “would not use Starlink (or any satellite service) as the sole communications technology” for safety-critical air traffic services. Reuters reported at the time that the FAA was not considering replacing its L3Harris and Verizon contracts with Starlink. Verizon’s FAA Enterprise Network Services contract, awarded in 2023, is valued at up to $2.4 billion over 15 years.

Musk first pressed the issue in February 2025, while he was leading the Department of Government Efficiency, writing that “the Verizon system is not working and so is putting air travelers at serious risk” before correcting himself days later to blame L3Harris. SpaceX said at the time it was supplying Starlink kits to the FAA at no cost and had no intent to take over any existing contract.

Tesla has unveiled Powercore, a solid-state medium voltage transformer that also handles the jobs of an inverter and a circuit breaker in a single unit. “Solid state medium voltage transformer, inverter and breaker – reliable, safe and secure,” the company’s Tesla Megapack account posted on X Tuesday, adding that the product is “Made in America” and will be “Operating 2027.” Elon Musk followed with his own post: “Advanced solid state transformers at scale from Tesla.”

Tesla rates Powercore at 7.4 MW, or 9 MVA, of continuous output at 34.5 kV AC, with grid-forming support for 10 MVA of peak power. Specs shared by Sawyer Merritt list a peak efficiency of 98.86 percent, a DC range of 800 to 2,000 volts and a built-in solid-state breaker that clears faults in about 100 microseconds. Tesla has not announced pricing, a factory location or a first customer.

The product fills a gap Tesla left open last year. When it introduced Megapack 3 and Megablock in September 2025, Tesla said it would build its own transformers, but shared almost nothing about them. Megablock groups four Megapack 3 units with a transformer and switchgear into a single medium voltage block, as Teslarati reported. Powercore appears to be that missing piece.

A typical battery or solar project today uses low voltage inverters to turn DC into AC, then a large oil-filled transformer to step that power up to grid voltage. A solid-state unit handles both steps with power electronics, which means less equipment, a smaller footprint and no flammable oil. Grid-forming capability lets it actively help hold voltage and frequency steady rather than simply following the grid.

Advertisement

-

Timing is a big part of the pitch. Lead times for conventional transformers have stretched into years as AI data centers and renewable projects crowd utility interconnection queues. Tesla energy executive Max de Zegher pointed to the problem in a post Musk shared, noting that “transformers have barely changed since the 1890s: copper coils in a tank of oil,” while batteries, solar and compute all run on DC. Powercore, he wrote, delivers “one conversion and about half the losses.” Tesla has also said its Megapack supply for 2027 is nearly sold out.

Tesla deployed 13.7 GWh of energy storage in the third quarter, its second best quarter on record. On Tuesday, the company also said customer solar systems deployed by Tesla Energy now generate more than twice the electricity its global operations consume each year.

Tesla tuner Unplugged Performance, the company pleading to save the Cybertruck, detailed in a new phase of its plan to rescue manufacturing lines from Gigafactory Texas that it would also build a three-row CyberSUV.

UP has already navigated a lot of the difficult thought work, including how it will woo Tesla to turn over the all-electric pickup’s production lines at no cost or risk to them. Tesla has signaled it will wind down Cybertruck output at Gigafactory Texas sometime around the middle of next year.

Tesla upfitter offers to keep Cybertruck alive

Unplugged, the Hawthorne-based aftermarket specialist that has tuned Teslas since 2013, first floated an open offer on November 10 and followed with a more specific “Phase 3” outline on November 15. Under the structure, outside investors would fund the new company.

The line would leave Giga Texas on Tesla’s schedule, supplier contracts would transfer, and Unplugged would hire its own staff, drawing from interested Tesla alumni, without pulling current Tesla employees or engineering resources.

Tesla would retain intellectual-property ownership, final say on specifications and brand, a quality veto, and an option to reclaim the line. In return, Tesla would collect a license fee on every vehicle plus margin on parts it continues to supply, Full Self-Driving and Robotaxi revenue, and a no-cost equity stake in the new entity.

If Unplugged cannot meet demand or capital targets Tesla sets, it would withdraw.

UP looked at the overwhelming demand for a full-size SUV, something that Tesla has had a lot of demand for but has not developed internally. A poll put out by the tuner that surveyed 892 responses showed 82 percent of voters favored a CyberSUV. There is a substantially deeper market for three-row SUVs priced above $80,000 compared to pickups.

Not to mention, the new body tooling plus limiting other changes from the Cybertruck line would enable the company to use the existing platform to produce an all-terrain family vehicle while continuing to produce Cybertruck builds at a modest incremental cost.

Tesla has already shown interest in a CyberSUV, as it hid Cybertruck-inspired clay models of what appeared to be a full-size SUV in a video last year:

Tesla appears to be mulling a Cyber SUV design

The proposal from UP also contemplates multiple configurations that would enable owners to utilize a full-fledged Robotaxi in the form of a CyberSUV, aiming to build one with conventional controls for private buyers while a no-wheel/pedal version would be available for the Robotaxi fleet.

Tesla has made it clear that its manufacturing space and cell capacity is set aside for Cybercab, but UP already has soft commitments from a conglomeration of investors, but it all hinges on Tesla’s willingness to engage.

description:
A Madison-based nuclear fusion energy company will receive up to $15 million in state tax incentives to support its new headquarters and research facility at the former Oscar Mayer plant.

text:
A Madison-based nuclear fusion energy company will receive up to $15 million in state tax incentives to support its new headquarters and research facility at the former Oscar Mayer plant.

The Wisconsin Economic Development Corporation voted Nov. 17 to approve up to $15 million in Enterprise Zone tax credits for Realta Fusion's $800 million project, dubbed "The Realta Forge."

The facility, announced in July, will allow Realta to further its goal of achieving commercial fusion energy in the 2030s, according to CEO Kieran Furlong. It will span 200,000 square feet at OM Station, the site of the Oscar Mayer plant that shuttered in 2017.

The number of credits Realta receives will be tied to the number of jobs the project creates and the amount of capital invested. The company is expected to break ground on the new facility by the end of the year.

Realta Fusion, founded in 2022, grew out of the University of Wisconsin-Madison and employs around 50 people. The new facility will create an additional 500 jobs, the company said.

Proponents of nuclear fusion say it will completely upend the energy landscape – if it can achieve commercial viability. Fusion could provide reliable carbon-free energy without producing the large amounts of radioactive waste present in tradition nuclear fission.

"We don’t have to choose between a clean energy future and supporting good-paying jobs and a strong economy; we can and should do both, and that’s exactly what this partnership will do," Gov. Tony Evers said in a Nov. 18 statement.

WEDC's incentive package represent its largest investment in fusion energy and another step in Wisconsin's plan to become a fusion hub. Earlier this year, Evers signed a sales and use tax exemption for capital expenditures on fusion energy projects. The WEDC also provided grant money to help the Wisconsin Fusion Energy Coalition boost the state's position as a national fusion hub.

In addition to state incentives, the city of Madison approve a $2.8 million tax increment financing loan for The Realta Forge.

Dominick Bindl, Realta's chief operating officer, said the WEDC's tax incentive package "was a critical factor in selecting OM Station as the best location within the most supportive business environment for us to build The Realta Forge."

"Formalizing this agreement allows us to continue moving at the speed required to bring commercial fusion energy to the world as fast as humanly possible," Bindl said.

Realta is currently conducting research with UW-Madison's Wisconsin HDS Axisymmetric Mirror, or "WHAM," a small-scale experimental machine that uses magnets to superheat and fuse hydrogen into helium, releasing energy in the process.

The eight-meter-long machine traps an amount of plasma about the size of a dinner plate, according to Furlong said. Realta plans to build a fusion machine five times the size of WHAM to eventually be housed in the new facility.

The company hopes this machine can demonstrate the conditions required for commercial fusion energy, which include stabilizing plasma for longer periods of time and producing more energy than it takes to power the fusion process.

Realta's ultimate goal is to build reactors that can power heat-intensive manufacturing industries, like plastics and fertilizer, that need reliable around-the-clock energy.

Francesca Pica can be reached at fpica@usatodayco.com.

name: Clean Energy
title: China and the U.S. are still the biggest polluters, but only China is doing better
description:
The rise of electric vehicles means China is also reducing its oil use.
But last year, U.S. emissions went in a different direction.
U.S. greenhouse gas emissions rose in 2025, as the country burned more coal for power and oil and gas for heating.
Two-thirds of passenger vehicle sales in China are now electric vehicles, according to recent data from the China Passenger Car Association.
China will be promoting trade of its clean tech technologies at the conference, says Li Shuo, director of the China Climate Hub at the Asia Society Policy Institute.
text:
As more than 200 countries meet in Turkey for the annual United Nations climate talks, COP31, the two largest emitters of greenhouse gases remain China and the United States. Now the countries' stories are diverging.

For years, China's climate pollution was growing, driven by increased coal use. But for the past two and a half years, China's emissions have been flat or falling.

"And that is a remarkable change," says Lauri Myllyvirta, lead analyst at the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air.

China is driving down emissions by increasing renewable energy and batteries, which is displacing coal. The rise of electric vehicles means China is also reducing its oil use.

"Those are bigger reductions than we expected," Myllyvirta says, "and I think anyone expected."

But last year, U.S. emissions went in a different direction. U.S. greenhouse gas emissions rose in 2025, as the country burned more coal for power and oil and gas for heating. A recent report from United Nations scientists notes that the U.S. sticks out as the only major economy where planet-warming pollution increased significantly last year.

This year, emissions in the U.S. are projected to fall slightly. The country will likely burn less coal than last year. But the U.S. could reduce its emissions more if it were deploying large-scale renewable energy and batteries like China, says Alex Wang, a professor at UCLA Law and an expert on Chinese climate policy.

The problem, Wang says, is the U.S. hasn't had long-term policy support for these climate technologies. The Biden administration increased funding for solar, wind, batteries and electric vehicles. The Trump administration reduced that funding and created regulatory hurdles for those industries.

" What we're suffering through these days is the policy whiplash that comes with the political divisions in the U.S.," Wang says.

Here are the four things you need to know about U.S. and Chinese emissions.

China had long-term planning

China started building the infrastructure that is allowing it to reduce emissions about twenty years ago. Back then, China was still known as a manufacturer of low-cost items. Air pollution in major Chinese cities was also reaching record levels.

Chinese leadership made policies to tackle both the country's economic identity and its air quality. Five-year plans from the central government helped provinces pivot into the clean energy sector.

"Because the policy direction was so consistent and clear," Wang says, "they used that to drive the development of all of these industries that really didn't exist before."

The government set up nationwide supply chains for technologies like solar panels, batteries, wind turbines and electric vehicle manufacturing. Today, China is the unparalleled global leader in producing, deploying and exporting these clean energy technologies.

"On the electrification front, they're going gangbusters," Wang says.

These technologies are helping China reduce its emissions, Myllyvirta says. His research group found that last quarter China's emissions dropped 3% – the largest decline since the COVID-19 pandemic.

In the power sector, emissions are falling as coal use decreases and solar, wind, and nuclear energy increase. China has built many new coal plants in recent years, but they often don't run at full capacity and instead are used for backup generation.

Industries like cement and steel manufacturing are also reducing climate pollution. In the transportation sector, electric vehicles are displacing demand for gasoline and diesel. Two-thirds of passenger vehicle sales in China are now electric vehicles, according to recent data from the China Passenger Car Association.

The U.S. has flip-flopped, experts say

While China has consistently invested in clean technologies, that hasn't been the case in the U.S. The U.S. has struggled to scale up climate tech industries that reduce emissions because of flip-flopping by the federal government, Wang says.

Under the Biden administration, Congress passed new financial incentives for renewable energy and electric vehicles, and policies that cut greenhouse gas emissions in sectors like the oil and gas industry. The Trump administration has reversed those policies, putting up roadblocks for solar and wind projects, canceling tax breaks for home solar and electric vehicles, and proposing to cut regulations on methane — a super planet-heating gas.

The Trump administration frequently cites its "energy dominance agenda," which prioritizes keeping coal plants running.

Asked about increased U.S. greenhouse gas emissions last year, White House spokesperson Taylor Rodgers wrote in an email to NPR, "The United States is in a position of strength thanks to the President's energy dominance agenda which has unleashed affordable, reliable, secure energy sources. America is the world's leading producer and exporter of oil and gas, and many nations rely on the United States for their energy supply."

This is a growing problem as the country builds more energy-hungry data centers, says Ben Haley at consulting firm Evolved Energy Research. Most of those data centers are now being powered by fossil fuels like natural gas and coal.

"The pace and scale at which they come online tends to increase emissions," Haley says. "You can't really match that with clean energy deployment at scale, currently."

A new study finds that carbon dioxide emissions from about 400 large U.S. data centers equal almost as much as an entire country like Denmark.

Chinese exports equal emissions reductions

Wang says it's great that China's emissions seem to be plateauing. But he says, "We shouldn't forget the fact that their emissions really are outsized compared to the rest of the world."

Still, the country is exporting clean technologies like solar, batteries and electric vehicles to countries including Pakistan, Nepal and the Philippines. That's helping these countries reduce their dependency on fossil fuels.

Chinese clean tech exports have only increased since the beginning of the U.S. war with Iran, says Kingsmill Bond, an analyst at the energy think tank Ember.

The ongoing U.N. climate talks in Turkey will have a large emphasis on getting countries to commit to increasing electrification. China will be promoting trade of its clean tech technologies at the conference, says Li Shuo, director of the China Climate Hub at the Asia Society Policy Institute.

As China gets a bigger share of the global clean tech trade, it will be harder for the U.S. to compete, he says.

"This dominating position will not go away, and if anything, it will be further consolidated in the coming years," Li Shuo says. "The U.S., I think, will struggle."

Ocean, Science, & Coastal Resilience SEEC Members participated in events related to ocean, science, and coastal resilience to highlight how the climate crisis is transforming marine ecosystems and coastal livelihoods.

text:
Washington, D.C. – This week, 18 members of the House of Representatives, including House Sustainable Energy and Environment Coalition (SEEC) Vice Chairs Reps. Don Beyer (VA-08), Suzanne Bonamici (OR-01), Sean Casten (IL-06), and Mike Levin (CA-49), as well as Reps. Jared Huffman (CA-02), Yassamin Ansari (AZ-03), Ami Bera (CA-06), Kathy Castor (FL-14), Salud Carbajal (CA-24), Adriano Espaillat (NY-13), Maxine Dexter (OR-03), Jonathan Jackson (IL-01), Teresa Leger Fernández (NM-03), Lucy McBath (GA-06), Dave Min (CA-47), Emily Randall (WA-06), Raul Ruiz (CA-25), and Nikema Williams (GA-05), joined the international climate community at the 31st Conference of Parties (COP31) in Antalya, Türkiye to renew and strengthen U.S. engagement on climate leadership on the global stage. The member delegation reaffirmed partnerships and highlighted shared challenges, including topics ranging from energy affordability and clean electrification to food security and disaster resilience. Members returned to Congress with new relationships and new ideas to build a more affordable, clean, and healthy future for our nation and the world.

SEEC members participated in events across 8 themes.

Forests, Nature, and Natural-Capital Resilience

SEEC members highlighted how protecting and restoring ecosystems can preserve nature’s capacity to absorb and sequester carbon, while bolstering climate resilience for our planet.

“For millions of people around the world, forests sustain their livelihoods, provide clean water, and store the carbon we desperately need to keep out of the atmosphere,” said House Natural Resources Committee Ranking Member Jared Huffman (CA-02). “As climate change fuels more destructive wildfires and floods, protecting the forests we still have and restoring those we’ve lost is essential to protecting communities, supporting local economies, and giving people a say in the future of the lands they depend on. We’ll fight to keep public lands in public hands, restore the lands and waters our communities depend on, and cut the pollution that’s making these disasters worse.”

Adaptation, Disaster Resilience, & Community Preparedness

SEEC members joined panels and discussions on adaptation, disaster resilience, and community preparedness to highlight how adaptation must be a central pillar of climate action.

“Extreme weather threatens our critical infrastructure and makes life more expensive – something my neighbors in Tampa Bay know too well,” said Congresswoman Kathy Castor (FL-14). “At COP, we showed up to work with and learn from our international partners to address these shared challenges together. We’re ready to put SEEC Institute’s Thriving Economy Project into action – our blueprint to lower costs, strengthen American leadership, and make our communities safer.”

Clean Electrification, Climate Finance,and Private-Sector Competitiveness SEEC Members engaged with experts in the clean electrification and climate finance space, and engaged with private sector voices from around the world.

“Anyone who can access electricity, heat, and transportation without burning fossil fuels not only lowers their costs, but also cuts down on pollution and helps provide a livable planet to our children and grandchildren,” said Congressman Sean Casten (IL-06). “Clean electrification is the moral and economically smart path forward for anyone interested in helping both their pocketbooks and our future. It's an imperative next step in addressing both the cost-of-living crisis and climate crisis."

Ocean, Science, & Coastal Resilience SEEC Members participated in events related to ocean, science, and coastal resilience to highlight how the climate crisis is transforming marine ecosystems and coastal livelihoods.

“The ocean has given us time we did not earn,” said Congresswoman Suzanne Bonamici (OR-01). “It has absorbed our emissions, buffered our climate, and fed our communities. The challenge now is whether we will answer that generosity with responsibility. If we get the science right, and we get the trust right, ocean carbon removal will have a fair chance to prove itself and we will have the evidence to decide wisely. The ocean, and the communities that depend on it, deserve our best evidence and our full partnership.”

Transatlantic Industrial, Trade, and Energy Policy SEEC Members highlighted how the U.S. and Europe must work together to transition away from fossil fuel dependence.

“The United States and Europe have a shared responsibility to lead the global transition away from fossil fuels,” said Congressman Mike Levin (CA-49). “That means working together to accelerate clean energy deployment, strengthen our economies, and reduce our dependence on fossil fuel markets. Our transatlantic partnership is essential to building a cleaner, more secure, and more affordable energy future.”

Climate Equity, Mobility, and Community Leadership

SEEC Members highlighted how the climate challenge exacerbates existing social inequities and climate solutions must expand economic opportunity, while giving communities agency in shaping their futures.

“The families with the least wealth, insurance, and political voice are hit first and recover last, from Chicago to the Horn of Africa to the Caribbean. Congress’ job is to help people stay home safely where they can, and move with dignity when they can’t,” said Congressman Jonathan Jackson (IL-01). “I am proud to lead the Congressional Diversity, Equity, and Inclusion Caucus in the House of Representatives. Equity should not be a controversial topic, and I am proud to be here with you today to discuss how we can work together on equitable solutions to the climate crisis.”

Climate, Energy, and National Security SEEC Members joined discussions on how climate resilience, clean energy deployment, and international cooperation are essential to our collective security.

“Now more than ever – it’s important to show the world that Democrats in Congress are committed to engaging with the global community to ensure that we are living up to our obligations to protect our planet and our future,” said Congresswoman Emily Randall (WA-06). “I’m grateful to bring the stories and experiences of my neighbors in Washington’s 6th district who face climate threats like coastal erosion and wildfires, and hear from other leaders and organizations that are both domestically and globally situated to help our communities achieve a climate-secure future.”

Food Security, Agricultural Innovation, and Trade SEEC Members participated in events related to food security, agricultural innovation, and trade that spoke to solutions to help farmers adapt to the climate crisis, build more resilient food systems on a global level, and ensure that feeding the world and protecting the planet go hand in hand.

name: Indiana American Energy
title: Guest Column: Utility regulation: Too much or not fast enough?
description: In 2022, America’s utilities planned for about 24 gigawatts of new peak electricity demand over the following five years. By 2025, according to the consulting firm Grid Strategies, their forecasts
text:
Ober

In 2022, America’s utilities planned for about 24 gigawatts of new peak electricity demand over the following five years. By 2025, according to the consulting firm Grid Strategies, their forecasts called for 166 gigawatts, more than six times as much. Data centers account for more than half of that growth, and manufacturing is the next largest driver.

Those forecasts describe a different industry from the one I helped regulate. During my years on the Indiana Utility Regulatory Commission, the question before us was usually whether a utility was building too much. Today’s question is how quickly a growing economy can get the power it needs, and on what terms, and the public-interest standard that answers both has held steady.

When I joined the commission in 2018, American electricity demand had grown at well under 1% a year for two decades. Indiana’s coal fleet, which had supplied 90% of the state’s electricity as recently as 2010, was aging, and by 2020 its share had fallen to about 53%. Our work was to pace that transition: how quickly old plants should close and what should replace them.

The clearest test of that era came from Evansville. Vectren (now CenterPoint) had coal units scheduled to retire in 2023, so the issue was how much to build in their place and in what form. Its own forecast showed customers’ demand on the hottest summer days growing by fewer than 100 megawatts over 17 years, yet it proposed a single plant of roughly 850 megawatts, enough for about three-quarters of that peak, at a cost of $781 million. In 2019, the commission denied the request, and our order explained why. It found that the request for bids had been “unduly restrictive,” ruling out combinations of smaller resources; that one facility would have carried most of the utility’s baseload; and that the plant’s economics depended on wholesale market sales with no firm contracts behind them, a revenue stream the order called “a speculative influence that we find must be materially discounted.”

That caution followed from how utilities earn money. A regulated utility earns an return on what it builds and owns, while power it buys from others under contract generally earns it nothing. The arrangement attracts the long-term investment the industry needs and inclines a utility toward building. Our job was to check that inclination before customers paid for a plant they might never use.

When we decided the Evansville case, we believed we were serving through the most consequential period in the industry’s history, which we called the energy transition. Our order considered how a changing industry might leave customers with an uneconomic plant, yet every change we imagined pointed toward the plant becoming unnecessary. Our decision fit the record before us, but within seven years, a short time for plants built to run 40, the outlook reversed, and a forecast like today’s would have made for a very different record.

Today the pressure runs toward building, and talk of transition has given way to talk of abundance. Data centers and new manufacturing are the kind of investment states compete hard to attract, and available power has become the first filter in choosing a site.

Under that pressure, the commission’s job is to test need on the record. A faster pace does not lower the utility’s burden of proof or the duty to keep rates fair for Hoosier households and businesses. Cost causation protects both: Large new customers carry the cost of serving them, backed by long-term commitments, so households are not left holding the bill if that demand never arrives.

Expectations of regulators have also risen with their audience. Utility cases that once drew mainly lawyers and analysts now draw public comment and press coverage. That attention is healthy, because customers pay for every decision, and it rewards decisions that can be explained plainly and defended on the evidence.

Whether the question is how much to build or how fast, the answer has to come from the record, built through sworn testimony and cross-examination, with the state’s consumer advocate at the table for customers and the utility required to prove its case. That design weighed flat demand in 2019 and suits the growth Indiana is pursuing now. Forecasts will keep changing, and a public, evidence-based process remains the surest way for a state to build quickly and build well.

David Ober is an Albion native who represented northeast Indiana in the Indiana House from 2012 to 2018 and chaired the House Committee on Utilities, Energy and Telecommunications. He served on the Indiana Utility Regulatory Commission from 2018 to 2022. Find this and other commen tary at indianacapitalchronicle.com .
