title: After the Blue Wave, Climate Policy Flows to the Statehouses - Capital & Main
description:
Almost no one ran on climate change this fall, but the election may reshape climate policy all the same.
Across the 21 states where the nonprofit Environmental Voter Project works, 49.3% of its identified climate voters cast early ballots, said Nathaniel Stinnett, the group’s founder.
“Even if politicians weren’t talking about climate, climate voters were sure thinking about politics, because they ran to the polls to vote as soon as possible,” Stinnett said.
Local: The data center revolt Closer to home, the story was almost entirely data centers.
Newly elected local officials in states such as in Pennsylvania and Virginia campaigned on the same promise — reining in data centers.
text:
Almost no one ran on climate change this fall, but the election may reshape climate policy all the same.

Democrats won both houses of Congress, a majority of governorships and — as projected by the National Conference of State Legislatures — control of 25 state legislatures by talking about prices: gasoline, diesel, home heating and above all — electricity. Geoff Garin, a Democratic pollster who works with the advocacy group Climate Power, told Capital & Main that nearly three-quarters of Democratic candidates in battleground-state races ran at least one ad about energy costs.

“The old Republican mantras of ‘drill, baby, drill’ and American energy dominance were and are wholly irrelevant to the current energy debate,” Garin said. “Instead, the energy debate now is focused on [President Donald] Trump’s ill-conceived war, on data centers, on price gouging by oil companies and on Trump’s war on clean energy.”

Indeed, in a NBC News exit poll, 74% of voters pointed to the war in Iran as a major factor in their vote and 86% said they were concerned about utility costs. In Garin’s polling, 53% said producing more wind and solar power would make energy more affordable — with one in five saying renewables would make it much more affordable.

Voters who rank climate first in their priorities, meanwhile, showed up early. Across the 21 states where the nonprofit Environmental Voter Project works, 49.3% of its identified climate voters cast early ballots, said Nathaniel Stinnett, the group’s founder. That was up from 41% in the 2024 presidential election and 32.5% in the 2022 midterms, he told Capital & Main.

“Even if politicians weren’t talking about climate, climate voters were sure thinking about politics, because they ran to the polls to vote as soon as possible,” Stinnett said. “I think we can safely say that the climate crisis is already impacting our political choices and behavior in a profound way.”

In Washington, the answer over the next two years is oversight and leverage but little new law. In state capitals and town halls, it could be a great deal more.

Washington: Subpoenas, spending and one live bill

Neither Democratic majority approaches the two-thirds needed to override a veto, and Trump has promised to use his freely. David Victor, a professor of public policy at the University of California, San Diego, predicted a stalemate at the federal level. That leaves three tools.

The first is the gavel. Starting in January, Democratic chairs in the House reportedly plan to use subpoena power to investigate budget cuts, staff reductions and pollution-limit reversals at the Environmental Protection Agency under Administrator Lee Zeldin. They also plan to examine deals in which energy companies traded offshore wind leases for fossil fuel development or won exemptions from Clean Air Act requirements.

The second is the purse. Democrats intend to use must-pass spending bills — broad budget bills required to finance federal agencies, military operations, national parks and public services — to restore money for climate research, disaster resilience and clean energy grants. They also may try to revive clean energy tax credits repealed in the 2025 reconciliation law, framing them as a way to cut utility bills. A Senate majority can also block nominees to the EPA, the Energy Department and the federal bench.

The third is the one major bill that’s actually already moving. The Senate voted 73-25 on Nov. 9 to advance the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, designed to speed reviews of power plants, transmission lines and data centers. Democrats are split. Sen. Jeff Merkley (D-Ore.), in line to chair the Environment and Public Works Committee, voted no, and House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries has voiced his opposition. Rep. Jared Huffman (D-Calif.), in line to chair the House Committee on Natural Resources, wants amendments that would shield clean energy projects from agency discrimination, end federal buyouts of offshore wind leases and make data centers pay for their own power needs.

“Voters sent a clear message last week that they want better deals than the ones they’ve gotten under unified Republican leadership,” said Sen. Ed Markey (D-Mass.), a member of the environment committee who won reelection in the midterms. Democrats, he said, owe voters a deal “that delivers clean energy megawatts and jobs, near- and long-term savings on energy bills, and real climate benefits without leaving so many important members of our community on the losing side of the ledger.”

The oil and gas industry has a different take on the election results. Mike Sommers, chief executive of the American Petroleum Institute, said the affordability message was unmistakable and called the permitting bill the place for bipartisan cooperation to start. The White House said Trump remained committed to reliable, affordable and secure energy.

However, the incoming class of Democrats is not of one mind. U.S. Sen.-elect James Talarico of Texas promised to protect oil and gas jobs. Rep.-elect Cait Conley (D-N.Y.) framed climate change as a “national security crisis” and called for federal investment in solar, wind and geothermal power and a return to the Paris climate agreement. Rep.-elect Will Lawrence, a 36-year-old co-founder of the climate advocacy group Sunrise Movement who won a swing seat in Michigan, campaigned for state and federal moratoriums on hyperscale data centers — and, as Grist reported, has moved away from the Green New Deal’s massive build-out toward the politics of community control over projects and clean energy.

The states: Six new trifectas

The most immediate changes are expected where Democrats won the governor’s office and both legislative chambers: Arizona, Michigan, Minnesota, Nevada, Pennsylvania and Wisconsin. The party also broke Republican trifectas in Georgia, Iowa, New Hampshire, Ohio and Texas.

Pennsylvania has the biggest runway. Democrats flipped the state Senate to cement the first trifecta since 1993, and lawmakers plan to pass long-stalled bills streamlining community solar, warehouse solar and battery storage while barring local governments from banning renewable projects. Gov. Josh Shapiro, who has presidential aspirations, has also proposed a carbon cap-and-trade program, which sets a hard cap on emissions, similar to what California and other states have on the books.

In Michigan and Minnesota, restored trifectas are likely to protect laws requiring 100% clean electricity by 2040 from repeal and open the door to grid modernization bills. In Arizona and Wisconsin, new majorities could pursue the renewable standards and decarbonization targets that Republican legislatures blocked for years.

Utility regulators are shifting too. Democrats won both open seats on the Georgia Public Service Commission for a 3-2 majority, their first majority in decades, and new appointments in Michigan and Arizona are expected to bring tougher scrutiny of utility spending on fossil fuels.

Michigan voters went further, approving a measure that bars state-regulated utilities such as DTE Energy from contributing to the campaigns of officials who oversee them. The bill was backed by U.S. Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed. A separate measure to replace DTE Energy with a public utility was narrowly defeated.

Local: The data center revolt

Closer to home, the story was almost entirely data centers. Voters in 10 states decided 41 local measures, 21 of them in Ohio, and 32 with reported results favoring limits. Pataskala and Granville, Ohio, approved bans on facilities above 25 megawatts with 74% and 82% of the vote.

Newly elected local officials in states such as in Pennsylvania and Virginia campaigned on the same promise — reining in data centers. They are expected to tighten zoning, require new facilities to procure their own renewable power and keep utilities from passing grid upgrade costs on to residential ratepayers.

Not every local measure said no. Voters in Eugene, Oregon, approved a Clean Energy Fund that places a 2% license fee on large retailers such as Amazon and Walmart to pay for renewable energy and job training. It is expected to raise at least $15 million a year by 2030 and was modeled on Portland’s 2018 fund, which has invested $1.7 billion.

The local votes set up the next fight. Pennsylvania Democrats want to stop towns from banning solar farms even as towns across the Midwest vote to ban data centers — and legislatures weighing statewide rules will have to decide whether to codify those bans or override them.

Garin, the Democratic pollster, said the politics favored his side. Each of those issues, he said, “gave Democrats the high ground in the energy debate, and I think that that will continue to be the case as we move from elections into legislating and policymaking.”

text:
New hires bring Dechert to 60+ lateral partner hires in 2026, continuing firm’s strategic growth

Dechert LLP announced today that Nandan Nelivigi and Michael (Mike) Sykes have joined as partners in its corporate and tax practices, based in New York and Washington, D.C., respectively. Their arrivals strengthen the firm’s project development, financing and tax capabilities, bringing additional experience to support clients in the power, renewable energy and related infrastructure sectors.

With these new hires, Dechert has welcomed 61 lateral partners in 2026 as the firm continues to execute on its strategy of focused deliberate growth. The new partners have deepened capabilities across the firm’s steeples of excellence and strengthened Dechert’s position in key markets in the United States and internationally.

“Energy is a natural extension of our steeples of excellence and an increasingly important part of our clients’ business and investment strategies,” said Mark Thierfelder, co-chair of Dechert. “Nandan and Mike bring Dechert to 60+ lateral partner hires this year, reflecting the focused strategic growth underway across the firm. Their experience in energy and infrastructure transactions will be valuable to clients in these sectors, and their collaborative approach makes them a strong fit for Dechert.”

“Our clients’ investments often require closely coordinated advice across corporate, finance and tax matters,” said Mike Poulos, vice chairman and global head of strategy. “That is particularly true of build-to-suit data centers and the power infrastructure that supports them. Nandan and Mike bring complementary experience that will help clients navigate these complexities, from an investment thesis to an executable project.”

Mr. Nelivigi focuses on the development, financing, acquisition and sale of major energy and infrastructure projects, representing private equity investors, corporates, lenders, developers and sponsors across the U.S. and internationally. Throughout his more than 30-year career, he has advised on transactions involving renewable and conventional power, solar, geothermal, carbon capture, nuclear, hydrogen and ammonia projects. His practice includes debt and preferred equity financing and tax credit-related transactions, advising on both the lending and borrowing sides. His international experience spans the Middle East, Asia and Latin America, including some of the largest renewable energy projects in those markets and the United States. He is recognized for Project Finance by Chambers USA.

“Structuring a project requires thinking ahead about construction and commercial risks, financing challenges, regulatory changes and exit options,” said Mr. Nelivigi. “Dechert offers the opportunity to bring together lawyers with relevant skills to assist clients from the outset. I look forward to working with colleagues across the firm to help clients build structures that meet their immediate financing needs and support their longer-term plans.”

Mr. Sykes advises developers, sponsors, investors and lenders on tax incentives and related financing strategies for energy projects. His experience spans more than 25 gigawatts of deals, project portfolios and developer pipelines across solar, wind, energy storage, manufacturing, carbon capture, green and blue hydrogen, geothermal, nuclear, clean fuels and sustainable aviation fuel. He brings significant experience in tax credit structuring, tax equity financing and navigating the evolving federal tax and regulatory landscape. He also advises on tax credit transfers, tax credit insurance and requirements relating to prevailing wage and apprenticeship, domestic content and energy community adders, as well as evolving eligibility and compliance considerations.

“Anticipated tax benefits need to translate into value that investors and lenders can underwrite,” said Mr. Sykes. “That requires tax considerations to inform commercial decisions early, rather than being addressed after the structure is set. Nandan and I have developed a close working relationship around that approach, and I am excited to bring it to Dechert’s clients as they evaluate new technologies and changing market conditions.”

Dechert’s corporate and securities practice advises clients across M&A, capital markets and finance, delivering integrated, commercially driven counsel throughout the entire transaction life cycle. The practice combines innovative thinking with leading-edge legal technology to provide efficient, practical solutions tailored to each client’s business objectives. Clients include public and private corporations, financial sponsors, asset managers and investment banking firms.

Dechert’s global tax practice, comprising lawyers in the United States and Europe, provides innovative tax solutions that meet the challenges and objectives of clients’ most sophisticated business dealings around the globe, from corporate transactions and restructurings to financial transactions and fund formation and investing.

text:
Ford is developing a new Universal Electric Vehicle platform to build profitable and affordable EVs.

Innovations from the new EV platform will be applied across Ford's gasoline and hybrid vehicles.

The first vehicle from this platform will be an electric pickup named Fathom, starting around $30,000.

Ford Motor Co. engineers in Dearborn are continuing to work on the new Universal Electric Vehicle platform to find additional innovations to improve both the future new electric vehicles off the Universal EV architecture, but also be applied across Ford's broader gasoline and hybrid powertrain vehicles.

Ford CFO Sherry House told investors at Barclay’s 17th Annual Global Automotive and Mobility Tech Conference webcast on Nov. 18 that Ford has started sharing learnings from its Universal EV development with the broader company. She added that Ford foresees its new EVs off the Universal EV platform as being profitable, which would be a marked change for Ford given it has lost about $5 billion a year on its EV sales for the past several years.

"When we designed this product, we were designing it against a product that we thought could be like a BYD (vehicle) built in Mexico," House said, referring to the Chinese automaker BYD. "What would that build material cost look like? We feel that we have done what we set out to do with respect to getting the right cost basis to set us up for profitability. So that was our starting point."

She said Ford next "co-located" its engineering, manufacturing and the supply chain so that the team would be together "to be able to problem solve and drive those efficiencies." Ford has been retooling its Louisville Assembly Plant to start building the vehicles there later next year. The first vehicle to come off the UEV platform will be the all-electric midsize pickup called Fathom starting at $29,945, including the destination fee.

Sam Fiorani, vice president of global vehicle forecasting at AutoForecast Solutions LLC, said Ford's new Universal EV platform, if developed properly, will improve the automaker's design process, its manufacturing processes, and allow Ford to be in new vehicle segments.

"Not only will the Fathom appeal to EV buyers who thought they couldn't afford a new electric vehicle, but also provide the basis for fully autonomous vehicles when that market establishes itself as a profit center," Fiorani told the Detroit Free Press.

Ford's new Fathom

Fathom is the first product designed by Ford's whiz-kids known as the "Skunk Works" team. That team works out of Ford's secretive Electric Vehicle Development Center (EVDC) in Long Beach, California.

Ford has said it has plans for several affordable EVs to follow Fathom — including a small SUV and possibly a sedan — off the UEV platform, which uses fewer parts and a streamlined production process to keep costs down. House said the platform will bring benefits to the entire company.

"As we move forward, we're going to take those (shared) learnings, not just into the future Universal EV platform, but also back into the larger Ford and we've been setting up these workshops where the Dearborn engineers are working with the Universal EV platform," House said. "They just recently were able to identify additional opportunities to improve the UV platform even further. Then the UEV platform is showcasing different technologies that can be integrated back into the core business, as well as, additional tools."

House did not provide specific examples of which learnings might be applied to other vehicles in Ford's lineup other than to say that "we're now going to be using the 3D CAD (computer assisted design) tools that we're using within the UEV platform now back in the larger organization."

Ford's sharing of innovations from the Universal EV platform across the company will provide Ford with significant savings across its infrastructure, House said.

"The plan is that this is going to become more profitable as you are layering on the top hats within the factory," House said. Top hats refers to the different body styles of EV such as a pickup or an SUV or a sedan.

What about the future?

When asked if the UEV can be the basis for an autonomous vehicle platform, House said the Universal EV platform has the most advanced electrical architecture and, " It does have a lot of the capacity that would enable an advanced data system."

Fiorani said it makes sense that Ford would design the platform for future innovations.

"Any new platform developed today needs to look five to 10 years into the future because a new architecture will require that kind of planning in order to return the investment," Fiorani said. "When engineers plan a decade in advance, they need to anticipate new technologies that might be just on the horizon, and autonomy is here today. If today's new vehicles are not expected to integrate semi- or full autonomy, they could be irrelevant in just a couple of years."

Fiorani said to compete with new manufacturers from China — which are fast to innovate and with government subsidies can sell high-tech cars at affordable prices — it will require a "complete overhaul of every costly part of making cars and trucks."

It is something that Ford appears to be doing because not only is the new Universal EV platform using fewer parts to create cost efficiency to price the vehicles at a more affordable starting point, but Ford will also switch up how it builds those EVs. Ford is moving from a traditional single assembly line to a parallel "assembly tree." That means it will make large aluminum unicastings and a structural battery pack then the casting assembled in three parts then brought together in the end for final assembly. The innovation is interesting, but not enough yet, Fiorani said.

"Gradually improving Henry Ford's century-old moving assembly line will not provide the quantum leap needed to play in this new and highly competitive arena," Fiorani said. "Shaking things up, breaking things, hurting feelings, and getting new perspectives is necessary, unless legacy manufacturers are ready to throw in the towel."

WASHINGTON, D.C. — The Trump administration appealed a court decision ordering it to end its freeze on funding for Solar for All, the congressionally mandated program that aims to boost clean energy and lower costs for homeowners, renters and communities across the nation.

Solar for All aims to invest $7 billion in federal funding into states from Alaska to West Virginia to build solar and lower costs for underserved communities. Before the Environmental Protection Agency halted the funding last year, 32 states plus other entities were awarded funding, and they got to work on programs to get nearly one million households connected to low-cost solar power.

Solar for All is aimed at households where energy bills pose the highest burden and, by law, its programs must cut household energy bills by at least 20%. Most projects would dramatically exceed that mandate.

The following is a comment from Adam Kent, senior director for green finance at NRDC (Natural Resources Defense Council):

“Skyrocketing utility bills are putting a squeeze on Americans from Anchorage to Orlando, but the Trump administration is ignoring their plight. Instead of getting out of the way of a program that will lower energy bills, the Trump administration is continuing its obstruction and delay.

“Solar for All is a rare government program that drew enthusiasm across the nation and across the partisan divide. Whether you care about grid resilience or energy security; climate change or job creation, Solar for All is for you.

“That, apparently, is not reason enough for this administration to let off its attacks. Everyone should be for more energy, more jobs and lower bills, but the Trump administration is continuing unabated in its endless attacks on the new energy sources we need now more than ever.”

text:
Solving the Winter Reliability Challenge

Written by Michael Reed & Brent Bennett

Download the full paper here.

Key Points

Because of the ERCOT grid’s heavy reliance on wind, solar, and energy storage to meet rapid demand growth, a 1-in-10-year winter storm in 2030 would result in over 40 hours of outages and excess energy costs of almost $11 billion.

Adding 12 GW of new natural gas generation over the next 4 years, with a corresponding reduction in new wind and solar would bring the ERCOT grid into compliance with its reliability standard while keeping costs relatively constant.

A more reliable generation mix would reduce the extent of outages during a major winter storm in 2030 by almost 90% and save $12 billion in energy costs and direct economic losses.

The upcoming triennial reliability assessment from ERCOT provides an opportunity for the PUC and stakeholders to evaluate market reforms that better value the long-duration dispatchable generation and demand response needed to prevent future outages.

Executive Summary

The improved performance of the Electric Reliability Council of Texas (ERCOT) grid during recent winter storms in Texas has given the impression that Texas has largely solved the winter reliability problems that led to the devastating outages during Winter Storm Uri in February 2021. However, as the first paper in this series documented (Reed & Bennett, 2026), the reliability improvements due to power plant weatherization, expanded ancillary services, and enhanced emergency practices are being outweighed by a resource mix that continues to lean more heavily into solar and energy storage. Over the past five years, 10 GW of wind, 36 GW of solar, and 22 GW of energy storage have been added to the ERCOT region, along with only 4 GW of new natural gas generation (ERCOT, n.d.-a). If this investment trend continues through 2030, a 1-in-10-year winter storm would result in over 40 hours of outages.

This paper applies the same 2030 modeling regime as the first paper in this series to examine the impact of removing post-2026 wind and solar additions and replacing them with enough new gas generation to maintain a constant reserve margin. Shifting the generation mix to include more gas and less wind and solar results in stable market prices under normal weather conditions while improving the performance of the ERCOT grid during 1-in-10-year winter and summer extreme weather scenarios. In the winter storm scenario, the shift in generation reduces the magnitude and duration of outages by nearly 90%, cutting power costs by $5.6 billion and saving $6.3 billion more in direct economic losses from the outages. The additional firm generation also provides a higher reserve margin during a modeled summer heat wave without increasing overall energy costs.

Ultimately, the analysis concludes that ERCOT’s single clearing-price market structure undervalues both dispatchable generation and longer-duration demand response, contributing to underinvestment in reliability. To prevent escalating outage risks, the region must adopt market reforms that appropriately value reliable, dispatchable power generation and long-duration solutions like demand flexibility. ERCOT’s forthcoming triennial reliability assessment (PUC, 2026c) offers an opportunity to assess these options, and policymakers should make that assessment as thorough as possible.

Introduction: The Challenges Facing the ERCOT Wholesale Market

In the five years since Winter Storm Uri in February 2021, the electric grid governed by the Electric Reliability Council of Texas (ERCOT) has undergone many policy and structural changes. Power plants are now subject to winter weatherization requirements, ancillary services have been added and modified, and market operations and emergency coordination practices have been improved. There have been multiple weather events since 2021 that have tested the ERCOT grid, including a heat wave in September 2023 and several winter storms, most recently Winter Storm Fern in January 2026. The grid avoided outages during these events, demonstrating the changes during the past five years have improved the reliability of the system.

However, what has not changed since Uri are the investment patterns that directed nearly $100 billion into wind and solar generation prior to 2021 (ACPA, n.d.)1 instead of into reliable generation. Since 2021, about $60 billion (ACPA, n.d.)2 has been invested in 36 GW of solar, 22 GW of energy storage, and 10 GW of wind in Texas (ERCOT, n.d.-a). Only 4 GW of new gas generation has been built during that time (ERCOT, n.d.-a). With solar and storage comprising over 80% of the projects that are nearing completion (ERCOT, n.d.-b) and rising demand from data centers (ERCOT, 2025a, p. 13), the improved performance of the grid will not be able to overcome the fundamental shortage of reliable capacity, particularly during long-duration winter storms.

The first paper in this series (Reed & Bennett, 2026) demonstrated that if current trends continue, a 1-in-10-year summer heat wave or winter storm in 2030 will lead to multiple days of outages and billions of dollars in increased cost to consumers. The research shows that even significant additions of wind and solar capacity do not improve the situation because those resources sometimes produce almost no electricity; for example, wind and solar produced less than 10% of their total combined capacity during the peak demand period of Winter Storm Fern (Woodfin, 2026, p. 6). Even the substantial amount of energy storage expected to be added over the next few years does not provide enough long-duration capacity to cover off these outages.

What’s needed are policy changes that redirect market revenue from variable to reliable resources, instead of paying all resources a single clearing price for energy, as is currently the case in ERCOT. While a dramatic shift toward more reliable resources significantly reduces the magnitude and duration of outages during these stress scenarios in 2030, it will likely take longer than just a few years to bring the grid into compliance with the Public Utility Commission of Texas’s (PUC) reliability standard (16 TAC §25.508). What is needed is both urgent action from policymakers to mitigate this problem before it gets worse and then steady patience while the wholesale market adjusts and the system builds the reliable generation needed over the next decade to dig out of the reliability deficit that has been created over the prior decade.

Footnotes

1 This number is taken from a version of this factsheet that was posted in 2021 but is no longer available online.

2 This number is derived by taking the total given in the current version of this factsheet and subtracting the amount from the version of the factsheet that was posted in 2021.

Model Assumptions: Adjusting the Forecast Generation Mix Toward Greater Reliability

As in the first paper in this series (Reed & Bennett, 2026), the models in this paper were created using the UPlan Network Power Model (UPlan-NPM) from LCG Consulting (LCG, n.d.). The initial generation mix for the models (hereafter called the “no firming” or “non-firm” case) was provided by LCG and modified based on data from ERCOT’s December 2025 capacity, demand and reserves (CDR) report (ERCOT, 2025b). This is the same generation mix used in our previous paper (Reed & Bennett, 2026, p. 10). The installed capacities for each generation resource used in the model are shown in Table 1.

Table 1

2030 Winter Installed Capacity by Fuel Source in MW, No Firming Forecast vs. Forecasts with Policies to Add Reliable Generation

To shift the generation mix in the model from the non-firm 2030 case to a scenario that assumes policies that shift the mix of new generation from wind and solar to natural gas (this new scenario will be termed the “firm” or “firming” case throughout this paper), we removed all new wind and solar that begins commercial operations after January 1, 2027 and added enough natural gas to keep the reserve margin—the difference between the amount of firm capacity in the system and the peak demand—almost constant. That process resulted in removing 19 GW of solar and 6.5 GW of wind while adding 12.5 GW of gas.

After these modifications, the base case model (with no extreme weather scenarios) was still showing some unserved load in August, likely due to transmission constraints caused by geographic mismatches between the wind and solar that we removed and the gas we added. Notably, these constraints appear to be occurring mostly at lower voltage levels and are only slightly improved by the presence of the proposed 765-kV lines, which are included in this model. To eliminate the unserved load, we added back 25% of the wind and solar that we originally removed to arrive at the installed capacities shown in the “Firming” column in Table 1.

To test whether additional gas generation beyond the firming scenario would completely eliminate outages in the winter stress scenario and provide other benefits to the system, we added another 5.8 GW of new gas generation (see the “Additional Gas” column in Table 1) resulting in 18.3 GW more gas generation than in the no firming case. As detailed below, this additional gas generation only produced marginal improvements over the firming case during the winter storm due to limitations with our model.

The Benefits of More Reliable Generation During a 2030 Winter Storm

The first step before we assess the impact of a 1-in-10-year winter storm is to rerun the base case model without any increased demand to ensure that the change in generation mix doesn’t produce any unexpected outcomes. As shown in Table 2, the base case is purposefully designed to produce no outages (i.e., no unserved energy), such that outages only occur during the stress scenarios. The winter and summer stress scenarios use the same demand curves as in our previous work, with a peak demand of about 125 GW in the summer and 110 GW in the winter (Reed & Bennett, 2026, p. 11). In the winter stress scenario, wind and solar output are reduced by 60% and 40% during the storm compared to their output in the base case, and outages of gas and coal power plants are set to about 15% of their total installed capacity, comparable to what was experienced during Winter Storm Fern (Woodfin, 2026, p. 12).

In the non-firm cases, the winter stress scenario results in outages lasting over 40 hours, with 210 GWh of unserved load and energy costs of over $11 billion. The firming scenario produces a significant improvement, with the unserved load declining by almost 90% to 32 GWh and energy costs falling from $10.8 billion to about $4 billion during the week of the storm. Figure 1 provides a visual representation of the improvement during the winter storm, with the area plot showing the generation plus the flexible load that is deployed, the black line the total demand, and the white space in between in between area plot and the black line shows the energy that is unserved.

Table 2

Summary Results for the Non-Firm Cases

Table 3

Summary Results for the Firming Cases

Figure 1

Forecast Generation and Demand During a Long-Duration Winter Storm in 2030, Firming Case

Note. The battery area on top of the generation curve indicates batteries discharging, and the battery area below the generation curve indicates batteries charging. The generation curve sits above the black demand curve during the periods when batteries are charging because the excess generation is being used to charge the batteries. This same convention is used in Figure 2.

In this case, the duration of the outages is still close to about 40 hours, which exceeds the parameters set forth in the PUC’s reliability standard (16 TAC §25.508), but the magnitude drops significantly, from 18 GW without firming to 8 GW with firming. During most of the hours in which outages occur, the amount of power short is less than 1 GW, indicating that the outages are isolated in one or two regions of ERCOT and that most customers across Texas will still have power at those times. The amount of energy curtailed by flexible load also dropped by about 80 GWh compared to the non-firm case, indicating that prices were not as high through the entirety of the storm thanks to the extra firm generation.

It is important to point out that not all of the available thermal generation in the model is being fully utilized during the winter storm, and if it was used optimally, the ERCOT system would be able to avoid outages entirely under the firming scenario. The problem is that transmission constraints and suboptimal geographic placement of generation and transmission in the model are preventing all of the generation from being used. In the real world, where market participants optimize the placement of new generation based on nodal prices, we expect these geographic issues would be less of a problem, and the benefits of firming would likely be better than what the model is able to show. But optimizing the UPlan model in this way is very difficult and outside the scope of this paper (see the sidebar for more explanation).

Sidebar: Modeling the Location of Generation and Transmission in ERCOT

One problem with the UPlan-NPM developed for this paper is the presence of transmission congestion in both the winter and summer stress scenarios, even though the model includes all of the 765-kV long-distance transmission lines in ERCOT’s latest regional transmission plan (ERCOT, 2025a, p. 14), which are designed to help alleviate this exact problem. In the winter storm with firming, natural gas generation never exceeds 68 GW despite almost 75 GW being available, and the summer, it never exceeds 69 GW despite 82 GW being available. A couple GW of coal is also consistently curtailed in the summer.

Also, the hourly ERCOT-wide average price only reaches the $5,000/MWh price cap for one hour in the winter storm with firming (see Figure 3) and never in the summer. This is evidence that the unserved load seen in Figure 1 is localized, with prices hitting the cap in regions that are short while the rest of the ERCOT region is seeing more normal price behavior. Under this scenario, ERCOT would probably initiate local load shedding, rather than systemwide rolling outages, and the outages would not be experienced by everyone in the ERCOT region. The mismatch of demand and supply across different regions also partially explains why flexible load is being deployed even at times when the thermal generation fleet is not being fully utilized.

While putting more transmission into the model would help alleviate this congestion, this problem is not definitive evidence that more transmission is needed in reality (recall that the model includes the 765-kV lines and a lot of new transmission compared to the system today). The congestion is mostly a product of sub-optimal placement of new generation in the model, which must be done manually with a fair amount of guesswork, relative to the existing transmission network, which was optimized for the model’s original generation mix and not our new mixes. In the real ERCOT grid, generators carefully consider demand, nodal market prices, and transmission congestion to optimize the location of each new power plant to a degree that is impossible to achieve in this model environment. In other words, most of the congestion in our model is likely a result of the model’s limitations and may not exist in the real world.

The model results also indicate that local upgrades at lower voltages (345-kV and below) are more critical to serving near-term demand than the 765-kV lines, which are more of a long-term play to resolve problems beyond 2030. However, as previous work from our team has shown (Bennett, 2026b), meeting the long-term reliability needs of the ERCOT region with more thermal generation, instead of more wind and solar as ERCOT’s base case models currently assume, would allow the 765-kV projects to be significantly reduced or avoided entirely. Our fundamental conclusion from all of this work is that market reform to get more thermal generation on the ERCOT grid would both improve grid reliability and reduce future transmission needs.

Although this work shows it is possible in theory to change the generation mix to meet the reliability standard by 2030, the time required for policy changes to take effect and for new generation to get built severely constrains the ability to make these rapid changes in practice. The only other option to meet the reliability standard by 2030 while adding more demand is to reduce system demand during the peak hours. As demonstrated in our previous series on winter reliability, a roughly 5 GW reduction in demand on top of the extra reliability provided by the firming of the generation fleet is enough to enable compliance with the reliability standard (Bennett, 2026).

However, while demand response can provide a reliability boost in the short run, over the long run, supply must eventually rise to meet whatever the expected peak demand is. Consistent use of demand response will cause prices to converge to whatever the expected peak demand is, with or without flexible demand. In other words, demand flexibility is a useful tool for providing reliability, but it is not by itself a panacea for a market design that misprices reliability, as the ERCOT market is doing right now. The only permanent cure to this problem is to properly price reliable generation to meet expected peak demand.

The Impact of More Reliable Generation on Summer Outage Risk

As in the winter stress scenario, the summer stress scenario uses the same demand curve as in Part 1 of this series (Reed & Bennett, 2026, p. 11), with a peak demand of about 125 GW. The generation mix is then adjusted in the same manner as in the winter scenario, except that the solar and wind generation curves and thermal power plant availability are not adjusted downward during the heat wave as they were during the winter storm.

Figure 2

Forecast Generation and Demand During a Summer Heat Wave in 2030, Firming Case

As described in Part 1 of this series (Reed & Bennett, 2026, p. 14), the deployment of flexible load was needed to prevent outages during the summer stress scenario. Flexible load is also used in this case, but the quantity used drops slightly, from 232 GWh to 199 GWh, because there is sufficient thermal generation to cover off the overnight hours. In fact, there is enough generation capacity to cover all hours in this scenario without using flexible load, but the uneven distribution of solar across Texas and transmission congestion between different parts of the ERCOT grid means that some regions are still short of power in the afternoons. Also, some of the flexible load has a lower strike price than some of the highest priced gas and storage, and as a result, it deploys before the generation resources.

One other point that Figures 1 and 2 make clear is that energy storage is more effective when used as a marginal, short-duration resource instead of a long-duration resource. All of the batteries in the 2030 model, over 38 GW of installed capacity, can only store about 75 GWh of energy, which is roughly equal the output of a 1 GW gas plant for the 3-day duration of the winter storm. The extra 12.5 GW of gas in the firming scenario produced about 500 GWh of energy during the modeled winter storm. Replacing that output with batteries, assuming the batteries come into the storm with full charge and perform optimally, would require $100 billion of batteries (assuming $200/kWh battery cost). However, when batteries have sufficient time to charge with excess generation, they can cover off many short-duration outages by using their capacity several times over. This is why batteries are more effective during summer stress scenarios, where they can charge during the early-morning hours when demand is lower and there is excess solar on the grid.

Effects of Adding More Gas Generation Than the Firming Scenario

Notably, the firming case has enough available thermal capacity, about 92 GW after accounting for outages, to meet the peak net load (demand minus wind and solar generation) for all but 13 hours during the modeled winter storm, with a maximum deficit of 9 GW. If this generation was being fully utilized, along with the existing energy storage and flexible load, the system should be able to avoid outages entirely. However, the maximum amount of thermal generation dispatched during the storm is only 84 GW. To test our theory this problem was being caused by misalignments between the location of the new demand and generation in the model, combined with transmission constraints, we added more gas generation beyond the 12.5 GW added in the firming scenario in an attempt to eliminate all unserved load during the winter storm.

Table 4

Summary Results for the Winter Stress Case for the No Firming, Firming, and Additional Gas Cases

We added up to 5.8 GW of new gas generation and still could not fully eliminate the unserved load, with about 17 GWh going unserved during the storm and many hours showing just a few hundred MW of outages. In fact, the maximum amount of thermal generation dispatched only rose by about 1.7 GW, so only a third of the new additions were actually being used. This proved our hypothesis that the suboptimal geographic matching of generation and demand in the model is causing the unserved load in the firming scenario, not an overall shortage of power. In the real world, more optimal placement of generation and transmission would result in better outcomes for the firming scenario because more of the firm power would actually be used.

The change in prices when moving from the non-firm generation mix to the firm mix is significant, with the average real-time price falling from $942/MWh to $388/MWh during the week of the winter storm. Adding more gas generation drops the average energy price during the week to only $289/MWh. By eliminating the extent of outages and reducing scarcity across many regions, the firm generation keeps the systemwide average price below the $5,000/MWh price cap, even when some regions are still short and experiencing outages. In the firming case, the systemwide average price is above $1,000/MWh for only 14 hours and only hits the price cap for one hour (see Figure 3), and with more gas generation beyond the firming case, the systemwide average price is above $1,000/MWh for only 9 hours.

Figure 3

Real-Time Energy Prices During the Winter Stress Scenario, for the No Firming, Partial Firming, and Full Firming Cases

Another important point that must be considered is not just the change in energy prices but the overall economic losses due to outages. Ignoring those losses heavily skews any analysis toward undervaluing reliability (Orr & Rolling, 2026). Because the amount of unserved load is reduced by almost 90% in the firming scenario and slightly more than that in the additional gas scenario, both scenarios significantly reduce the total economic costs of the storm. Taking the PUC’s value of lost load, which is currently set at $35,000/MWh (PUC, 2024), as a proxy for direct economic losses, the total value of the unserved energy would be $7.4 billion in the no firming case, $1.1 billion in the firming case, and, of course, zero in the case with additional gas generation that incurs no outages.

Conclusion

Over the past decade, the ERCOT region has been moving into a regime where peak demand begins to substantially outstrip firm supply, and with demand increasing rapidly over the next few years, the situation is quickly reaching a critical juncture where even minor winter storms could lead to significant outages. The main conclusion of this research is that the more intermittent resources are relied upon to meet demand during extreme weather situations, especially in the winter, the higher the risk of longer and deeper outages. In addition, energy storage is of limited usefulness during long duration storms when there is no opportunity to recharge and the storage capacity can only be used once.

This grim conclusion should not overshadow the fact that wind and solar can be useful marginal resources if the energy output is correctly priced in the wholesale market. The problem is that the single clearing price for energy, which is the premise on which the ERCOT wholesale market is designed, does not properly value the difference between dispatchable and intermittent resources. Whatever resources are producing at any given time are paid the same market price. To make matters worse, because the lowest marginal cost resources are dispatched first, wind and solar generators are able to bid almost all of their power into the market (subject to transmission constraints) while gas and coal generators are pushed to the side, unable to count on consistent market revenue and forced to endure costs from ramping up and down to balance wind and solar output.

The other problem that must be addressed—which this research makes even more clear than our prior work did—is that the single clearing price does not value the difference between long- and short-duration resources. A battery is paid the same price as a gas generator for the power it puts into the system even though the battery may not be able to discharge at that same rate during the next hour or at the same time the following day. A gas generator, on the other hand, can reliably be counted on to produce the same power across all hours.

Similarly, there is no price signal for long-duration demand reductions from large consumers, even though our research makes it clear that such responsiveness is likely necessary in the near-term to avoid outages and, if priced appropriately relative to reliable generation, can also help reduce volatility and improve reliability in the long-term. In this context, the large load demand management service (PUC, 2026a), which the Texas Legislature mandated last year (SB 6, 2025, pp. 9-11), the large load interconnection standards currently under consideration (PUC, 2026b), and planning guide revisions to help ERCOT incorporate a higher proportion of controllable loads (Sharma Frank, 2025) all present opportunities to create helpful tools for closing the reliability deficit if the programs are designed and sized appropriately.

The upcoming triennial reliability assessment from ERCOT (PUC, 2026c) is likely to show that the region will fall short of the PUC’s reliability standard in a few years, given that recent modeling work by ERCOT staff and consultants (Collins, 2025, p. 3) is largely in agreement with the assessment provided by this paper. By rule, if the reliability assessment determines that a deficit exists, ERCOT is required to present a menu of market reform options for closing that deficit, and the PUC is required to assess those options (16 TAC §25.508). This process will present a timely opportunity to pick up where previous market reform discussions have ended, and it must be taken seriously by the PUC, ERCOT, and market participants.

As part of these deliberations, the PUC should reopen its reliability requirement for new generation and, as we have recommended before (TPPF, 2025), set a strong enough penalty so that generators will be incentivized to buy new firm capacity. The 90th Texas Legislature should also take up again legislation (see SB 715, 2025 and HB 3356, 2025) that would apply this reliability requirement to existing wind and solar generators while providing better incentives for reliable generation. A strong reliability standard that requires variable wind and solar to participate in the market on equal footing with reliable generation would go a long way toward meeting the goals outlined in this paper. Future work in this series will assess the efficacy of this specific reform and other market reform options to reduce electricity costs for Texans and the likelihood of severe winter outages.

text:
Many climate scientists would agree that the choice to shutter a fossil fuel plant is simple. Of the U.S. power sector’s total CO2 output in 2021, coal was behind 60% of emissions.

Yet, nationwide, there are entire rural communities propped up by coal plants serving as the primary economic engine for their region — driving taxpayer funds for public schools, civic projects and more.

When the plants shut down, the towns — and sometimes entire tribal nations — are rocked. In 2019, when the Navajo Generating Station closed, the Navajo Nation lost an estimated 1,000 jobs and $40 million in annual revenue, per the Navajo Times.

The burden on rural and tribal communities is often quite high, especially in Arizona, where there are no guaranteed financial protections for transitioning communities whose plants close. But researchers at the Just Energy Transition Center, a unit within Arizona State University's Julie Ann Wrigley Global Futures Laboratory, are envisioning a different kind of future.

In their latest policy brief, the team put forth nine recommendations for state legislators based on 18 months of community-centered research. With a grant from the Resilient Energy Economies Initiative, the project began with inquiries launched by a PhD student into how other industries, such as military or timber, have historically handled similar challenges and transitions.

Armed with spending formulas from other sectors, the ASU team convened a statewide advisory committee made up of a former utility executive and utility regulator, a community advocate, a state senator, a school superintendent and other experts. Together, they produced a comprehensive set of policy recommendations that the center’s director, Amanda Ormond, hopes will benefit communities in Arizona coal country, whether their plants face closures, repowering or other disruptions.

Here, Ormond speaks with ASU News about the project.

Note: Answers have been edited for length and/or clarity.

Question: Many in the climate space think of closing fossil fuel plants as a wholesale good idea. What are they missing when they advocate solely for those closures?

Answer: Really, it's the human dimension that sometimes gets missed. There are profound implications when a very large fiscal asset like a power plant closes. Coal plants are typically in rural areas, they certainly are in Arizona. And so, whole communities build up around these large industrial complexes, and most of the community’s economic activity, or a lot of it, can be based around the coal plant. These coal plants are typically the largest taxpayer in a county. They also are the largest taxpayer for the school system.

It's not fair to take the water, the land, the air of rural communities, and then when the plants close, turn our backs. We need to support people.

Q: What can happen to a community when its power plant closes?

A: So you've got the fiscal impact of a plant closure, which is quite dramatic. The other impact is the social impact. If the plant closes, then a lot of times, the coal worker might have to move for another job, so you have split families. Because these are usually high-paying jobs — like $100,000 or more — one worker might support an entire family, with grandparents, children, grandchildren, and losing that income really weakens a family system.

Then, the utility that owns the coal plant typically does a lot of philanthropic funding in the communities; they might support the baseball team or help do the Fourth of July parade. So when you don't have as much money running around the community, then there's not as much opportunity to do some of the civic things. There's the economics, but I think what is not appreciated as much is some of the social impacts.

If plants close over time because they're old or becoming out of date, it's one thing. But what we're seeing is that their closures are sometimes not anticipated, which is really the case of the Navajo Generating Station. It closed extremely quickly. But even when there's a 10-year notice, what we find is that it's very hard for the communities to start working on transition in advance. Nobody wants to believe that the plant is actually going to close. But the flip side is that early acceptance of the plant closure gives more time to think about what can come next and what economic diversification or bringing in other businesses can mean.

Q: Why did you structure this project the way you did, around community input?

A: What's so good about this work (with JET) is that we are out in the impacted communities. We go out and we do visioning sessions. Sometimes we're the front line talking to the community about how their plant's going to close. And then we lead them through an exercise to help them think about what it is that they want to maintain, what they might want to grow. And then part of our role is as hands and capacity.

Maybe these communities want a study done of a gas plant, or maybe they want a study of a battery recycling facility. We have gotten federal monies to be able to do the studies and provide some of the work that they couldn't do themselves.

And so Gary Dirks, who I work for, likes to use the term “co-create,” and I really like that, because ASU does not know what's best for these communities. We would never go in presuming that. We need to go in and listen and hear and learn.

Q: What was the most surprising takeaway from working with the advisory committees?

A: We’ve learned that if you are going to close a coal plant — if you want to figure out a percentage of the value that might be replaced in the community — it's important to know what the coal plant has provided. The way that Arizona does taxing for these types of large assets, a county will get an amount of money for taxes, but it's not broken out by assets. So they might have money from a coal plant and they might have money from another industrial facility, but the county doesn't know how much money comes from which.

So part of the recommendations we have is to do specific studies of what's been lost. That in part is necessary because we can't get that information from the state because of the way that the state taxing laws are written. So that's a challenge. I mean, it would be nice if we knew, oh, OK, Apache County is losing $4.26 million over a 10-year period from this coal plant. We don't have that information.

I think the other thing that was gratifying is that we had a committee of school district folks, ex-utility people, a former commissioner, city town people, and it was unilateral, the support that this process had, that there has to be something for coal plant communities.

Q: How can we talk about the green energy transition in a more inclusive way that doesn't leave behind these communities?

A: There’s a concept that's taken hold called Community Benefit Agreements. The idea of a Community Benefit Agreement is that when something's being developed, there is a negotiated agreement on the front end to pay benefits during and after the asset closes to the community. So let's say, for example, you are putting in a renewable development, or a new gas plant or whatever it might be. That facility's going to use your town’s roads, it's going to impact water, it's going to impact sewer. For any type of development — this doesn't have to just be energy — these community benefit agreements can help the community make sure that development is beneficial and won't leave them in a hole when something is closed or changed.

And it's interesting too, because from my perspective, we require and expect so much more out of the solar and wind and battery industry than we've ever held the coal and gas industry to. So these Community Benefit Agreements are becoming more common for renewable development, but they should apply to all development. We've got new pipelines going into Apache County and through Navajo County right now. These pipelines should be paying community benefits as well as the clean, green stuff.

Q: Could the repowering of these coal plants as gas plants potentially provide employment opportunities for some of the coal workers?

A: (Coal workers) might not get anything from these repowering initiatives — I've heard that two-thirds of the jobs from the coal plants will be lost when they repower to gas. I don't know that there's any meaningful discussions from the utilities to support the communities in that transfer because they look at it as, well, we're keeping some jobs.

So I think it's still a really important issue because we've got closing coal plants, but we've also got coal plants and energy facilities of all kinds that are changing.

Q: And you can't necessarily slot a coal worker into a gas job just like that.

A: Correct. You need different skills and often different people. I was told that a number of the people employed to run the gas plants don't have to be local, they can manage the gas facility from remote places. And so even if a third of the jobs are retained, they're going to be different jobs. A lot of the jobs from a coal plant are actually physically moving the coal, bringing it in, making sure it goes into the hopper, having it burn. So all of those will be gone.

Q: How likely do you think it is that your team’s policy recommendations get adopted as you envisioned?

A: This research grew out of a lack of policy from the state government. Many other states that have had closing coal plants have a process or have gone through either rate cases or settlement agreements with the utilities where there's an agreement for when the plant closes: They will provide this much money to a community, or they will help them with identifying other businesses, or offer job training, or other forms of worker support. But we don’t have that in Arizona.

Our first recommendation is actually to designate a state agency that would be responsible for helping communities, because there is no such thing now. And so that's something that could be done by the governor without legislation, quite easily. We’re also asking for a study so you can tell what the fiscal and job impacts of closures are. There is a recommendation in there to form committees for each plant that's transitioning. A lot of these things can be done without mandates or legislation.

The end recommendations talk about funding communities, which will need more approvals. If you have a regulated utility and there's a recommendation to have, say, APS give money to the Cholla community, that has to be approved by the Arizona Corporation Commission. So when you get to the money, which is really the most important part, probably, that's going to take more leadership. But a lot of the earlier recommendations set up the process to support a community.

text:
Ford began battery-cell production in Marshall, Michigan, in October and has started shipping cells for prototypes, a step toward bringing lower-cost lithium iron phosphate batteries into future U.S. vehicles.

The shipments are headed to prototypes of the Fathom, Ford’s small electric pickup. The roughly 2 million-square-foot facility represents a $3 billion investment. Ford is in the early stages of certifying its manufacturing processes as it prepares to increase output.

The project is part of Ford’s effort to adopt lithium iron phosphate, or LFP, cells for U.S. vehicles. The battery chemistry originated in the United States but was commercialized largely in China. Ford licensed technology and manufacturing support from Chinese battery maker CATL to help establish LFP production more quickly.

Alan Clarke, Ford’s vice president of advanced development projects, said the company needs to move quickly to produce affordable electric vehicles in the United States. He described CATL as the best supplier to provide the technology and help Ford learn how to make LFP cells.

The Marshall plant is expected to be capable of producing 40 battery cells per minute, equivalent to 20 gigawatt-hours of annual capacity for electric vehicles and energy storage. That is below Ford’s earlier plan for as much as 40 gigawatt-hours a year, amid a pullback in electric-vehicle plans at Ford and across the industry. The facility is highly automated, and Ford says its planned production pace will help reduce battery costs. It also has room to add capacity if needed.

The project has drawn criticism from some lawmakers and U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy over Ford’s ties to CATL. In September, Duffy wrote to Ford CEO Jim Farley, expressing concern that the company’s ties to Chinese businesses could harm Ford and the U.S. auto industry. The White House praised Ford’s domestic jobs and manufacturing the following day.

Ford plans to ramp up cell production next year. The Fathom pickup is expected to launch in the fourth quarter of 2027.

— John Walsh, Founder and CEO of Endera

SAN JOSE, CA, UNITED STATES, November 18, 2026 /EINPresswire.com/ — Imagry, the global leader in autonomous public transport, and Endera, an American premium specialty bus manufacturer, today announced a partnership to deliver the first Buy America-compliant autonomous buses and shuttles for U.S. public transit. By pairing Imagry’s Level 4 autonomous driving system with Endera’s American-built vehicles, the partnership gives every transit operator in the country, from state-level transportation authorities to city and regional agencies, a self-driving option it can buy with federal transit funds. No Buy America waiver needed.

Imagry and Endera built the partnership around two goals, to give any U.S. operator that wants a self-driving bus or shuttle an American-made option, and to keep federal transit dollars at home, where they support American manufacturers, suppliers, and workers. The timing matters, as the Federal Transit Administration (FTA) weighs a proposed waiver (Docket FTA-2024-0018) that would let agencies spend federal dollars on imported minibuses, on the premise that no American manufacturer offers a suitable vehicle.

“The future of public transit is undoubtedly autonomous and electric,” said John Walsh, Founder and CEO of Endera. “By combining our vertically integrated EV manufacturing with the scale of our legacy business, this partnership will bring Buy America-compliant, FTA-eligible autonomous minibuses to market and dramatically drive down the cost of moving people from one place to another.”

Over time, self-driving buses and shuttles will change what public transit can offer riders. As autonomous fleets grow, agencies will be able to run service more often and later into the night, and reach the suburban and rural corridors, campuses, airports, and hospital centers that current service often leaves underserviced. Because each vehicle moves many passengers at once, autonomous transit can widen access for the people who rely on it most, including older adults, people with disabilities, and those without a car, while easing congestion on city streets. The partnership lets agencies begin building toward that future with the federal funding they already count on.

“For years, America’s self-driving conversation has focused on robotaxis, which add more cars to already crowded streets and serve only the riders who can afford them,” said Eran Ofir, CEO of Imagry. “Now we can finally turn that technology toward the sector that matters most: moving whole busloads of people, students, seniors, commuters, and workers who depend on public transit every day. Imagry’s partnership with Endera means every operator can buy that future with federal funds, made in America, with no waiver required.”

Imagry’s camera-centric AI-based technology drives without HD maps, LiDAR, or a cloud connection, and it needs no changes to existing road infrastructure. Frost & Sullivan, which recently awarded Imagry its 2026 Enabling Technology Leadership Recognition in the global autonomous bus industry, found that operating without HD maps spares operators both the upfront cost and the ongoing expense of keeping those maps current. As a result, agencies can bring autonomous service to new routes faster, with more flexibility and at lower cost.

About Imagry

Imagry, working since 2018 on an AI-based full autonomous driving software stack, has developed a reliable, HD-mapless autonomous left- and right-hand side driving software solution for public transportation (for M1, M2, and M3 category vehicles). Imagry’s solution has been field-proven since 2019 in autonomous vehicles on public roads in the U.S., Germany, Japan, and Israel. Imagry’s system has been selected by Transportation Operators, Transit Authorities, and OEMs to support L3 and L4 in heavy-duty electric buses. Imagry received “Best Practices” awards from Frost & Sullivan in 2023, 2025, and 2026. Visit https://www.imagry.co

Dive Brief:

The Virginia State Corporation Commission began its evidentiary hearings about the proposed merger of Dominion Energy and NextEra Energy on Tuesday, hearing opening statements from parties to the case. Several offered varying interpretations of the Virginia legal statute the SCC will rely on in deciding whether to approve the merger.

That statute — theUtility Transfers Act — states that the SCC “shall be satisfied that adequate service to the public at just and reasonable rates will not be impaired or jeopardized” by granting an acquisition, and the commission “shall make such order … as it may deem proper.”

Ashley Macko, deputy general counsel for the commission, testified on behalf of SCC staff that the standard “requires the commission to consider the consequences of the proposed merger ... including both short and long-term impacts to adequate service and just and reasonable rates ... To call it a simple ‘do no harm’ standard is not quite right.”

Dive Insight:

The proposed merger between Dominion and NextEra, announced in May, would create the largest regulated electric utility in the world, with a 130-GW large load pipeline. Clean energy groups, local Virginia officials and leaders of the state’s executive branch have raised concerns about the potential impact of the deal on rates and data center development.

McGuire Woods partner Joe Reid, representing the joint petitioners NextEra and Dominion, said the case “is simply not the one to litigate the cost of service, and nor is it the case to litigate who’s paying their fair share and ensuring everybody pays their fair share, including the data centers.”

Reid noted that the proposed acquisition is a “consequential combination, but its size does not change the requirements of the Transfers Act or the analysis required to determine whether the statute’s requirements have been met.”

SCC Chair Kelsey Bagot asked Reid if the commission “should not consider longer-term benefits in evaluating this proposed transaction,” and Reid replied that the commission “should consider all the evidence that is in front of it.”

Nate Benforado, a senior attorney with the Southern Environmental Law Center, argued that the Transfers Act is less narrow than the joint petitioners claimed.

“The analysis that the Utility Transfers Act requires is broad,” Benforado said. “Petitioners must prove that this transaction will not impair or jeopardize adequate service at just and reasonable rates … This is not simply a ‘do no harm standard’. This looks at virtually everything a utility does.”

Will Reisinger, representing the Piedmont Environmental Council, pointed out that the statute provides that “before approving this merger, the commission ‘shall be satisfied’ that adequate service to the public at just and reasonable rates will not be impaired or jeopardized.”

“That standard, satisfied, is subjective,” he said. “This is not a matter of calling a ball or a strike. This decision is 100% within your judgment, within your discretion.”

Will Cleveland, the attorney representing Google, said that the company plans to present testimony from energy economist Carolyn Berry, “who will testify that the minimum demand charge approved as part of Dominion’s 2025 biennial rate case discourages large loads like data centers from taking advantage of their statutory right to retail choice.” Dominion has said “they don’t think this testimony is relevant to the case,” Cleveland said, but Google disagrees.

Amazon’s attorney, Brian Greene, said that that company would want to see Dominion address two issues if the commission were to approve the transaction: “One is reforming the large load interconnection queue, and second is addressing the need for new capacity through bring-your-own options,” he said.

description:
