text:
This is partner content, brought to you by ev.energy. Nate Kinsey is the company’s director of policy.

Residential virtual power plants aren’t a new pitch. Utilities and regulators have heard for more than a decade that thermostats, home batteries, heat pumps, and EVs could be coordinated by the thousands to act like a power plant. What’s new is the urgency. Load is growing for the first time in two decades; bills are rising; and the poles, wires, and power plants needed to keep up take years to build.

This year, states started acting. Hawaii opened a VPP docket in April, Virginia approved a ratepayer-funded VPP pilot in August, and last week New Jersey regulators approved a two-year statewide VPP program, PowerUp NJ, set to launch by October 1, 2027. Virginia’s and New Jersey’s programs start where VPPs always have: cutting system peak demand. That’s the right first step, but it isn’t where the opportunity ends.

Distribution spending is now among the fastest-growing parts of utility budgets, and New Jersey’s own program envisions VPPs moving from peak-shaving to deferring or avoiding traditional infrastructure upgrades. Getting there means moving VPPs down the grid, from the system peak to the feeder and substation, and moving dispatch events from the peak to everyday grid operations.

That’s where utilities remain skeptical. At Latitude Media’s Flex Summit in October, Eversource’s director of distributed energy solutions put it plainly: “What happens if they’re not there in 10 years?” A substation takes a decade to build. There is no plan B.

The skepticism is fair. The honest answer is that the same devices won’t be there. The question for regulators is whether the capacity will be, and that depends on how we design the programs.

Today’s programs can deliver, but they can’t promise deferral

Across the country, single-DER VPPs are already relieving local grid constraints. In a randomized, controlled pilot with a U.S. utility, ev.energy layered feeder-level dispatch onto an existing managed charging program, and evening dispatch succeeded in every event tested, with no rebound. The technology isn’t the limit; the program design is.

Consider one household across the decade a planner is asked to bank on. In 2027, the household enrolls in the utility’s thermostat program and a leased EV in a managed charging program. In 2029, the lease ends and the new car is a brand the program doesn’t support. In 2031, the family adds a battery and enrolls it in a third program. In 2033, a heat pump and new thermostat replace the furnace. In 2035, a new family moves in with an EV of its own.

The household’s flexibility grew every year. The utility’s programs recorded it as churn, because they were designed around devices, not households, and the devices that remained enrolled were dispatched in silos, not as one VPP resource. As my colleague Nick Woolley has written, operators should plan for about 30% of devices turning over every year. A program built around a fixed roster of siloed devices can relieve this year’s feeder. It can’t promise the same kilowatts in 2035.

That’s the gap between relieving a constraint and deferring an upgrade, and it’s a gap that regulators and utilities can work to close in the coming years.

What tomorrow’s programs could deliver

Picture the same household in a program designed for change. Its thermostat, EV, battery, and heat pump join one portfolio, dispatched together so each covers for the others. When a device changes, the household stays in. When a new family arrives, its devices join the same portfolio.

The utility isn’t buying a power plant made of devices. It’s buying an outcome: a specific grid service provided at a specific part of the system and at a specific time. The VPP provider is accountable for delivering as the devices underneath come and go. A monoculture fails when its one crop does. A mixed garden keeps producing as individual plants change.

Xcel Energy’s Aggregator VPP in Colorado shows this can be written into a tariff today. It settles portfolios of any device mix on delivered kilowatts, pays a premium on constrained feeders, and penalizes aggregators that fall short. New Jersey’s program hasn’t launched, but it allows multiple device providers or one aggregator to work with a household. Hawaii’s VPP program design is still being designed, but draft tariffs filed by the local utility and DER advocates in August both propose performance-based compensation. Together, these programs seek to answer the distribution planner’s question with a contract instead of a forecast.

What regulators and utilities can do in 2027

At the National Association of Regulatory Utility Commissioners annual meeting in Puerto Rico, I heard commissioners and their staff say they’re optimistic that VPPs can help put downward pressure on rates. That optimism is well founded. But if residential VPPs are going to meet utilities’ distribution needs, the programs approved next year have to be designed differently.

The first change is to let participation follow the household, not the device, so the family that switched EVs in 2029 and added a battery in 2031 never leaves the program. The second change is to buy what the grid needs, not device enrollments. Define the grid need at the feeder, substation, or bulk system level, and procure it as an obligation the VPP provider is accountable for delivering, regardless of the devices underneath. The third change is to ensure every device is eligible to participate. That will require industry work on data standards and interoperability for the entire range of devices. But broad eligibility helps a portfolio scale and gives every type of household a way to take part.

None of this means starting from scratch. Today’s thermostat, battery, and managed charging programs have built the device base and customer trust needed to launch the new VPP successfully.

Utilities are right to ask whether a VPP will be there in ten years. The devices won’t be. A well-designed program will.

text:
EQT is pleased to announce that EQT Transition Infrastructure (“EQT”) has entered into a definitive agreement to acquire Flatiron Energy (“Flatiron” or the “Company”) from Hull Street Energy (“HSE”).

Founded in 2021, Flatiron develops, builds, owns, and operates utility-scale energy storage projects across New England, New York, and the Mid-Atlantic power markets. The Company develops projects in dense, capacity-constrained areas, where storage supports grid reliability at times of peak demand. Since HSE’s initial investment in 2022, Flatiron has expanded its portfolio by nearly ten-fold to 24 GWh of capacity, been awarded 6 GWh of long-term contracts, and is in construction on 2 GWh of batteries – including the largest urban energy storage project in the world.

In Flatiron’s markets, electricity demand is growing rapidly as older power plants retire and more renewable generation connects to the grid. This dynamic increases the need for battery projects, which store power when it is plentiful and deliver it when the grid needs it. As a result, energy storage capacity is expected to grow in these markets from 2 GWh operating in 2026 to 108 GWh in 2035.

EQT will support Flatiron’s management team as the Company delivers its contracted projects, helps communities meet their energy needs, and expands into new markets. EQT intends to invest in the Company’s team and capabilities, drawing on its deep experience of building energy storage platforms and significant expertise across energy and digital infrastructure. EQT has over $100 billion in digital and energy infrastructure assets, with over 260 GW across operating, under-construction, and pipeline energy assets, and a portfolio over 100 data centers, making EQT one of the largest data center developers globally.

The acquisition is made through EQT Transition Infrastructure, a strategy that applies EQT Infrastructure’s industrial experience and sector expertise to scale emerging but proven businesses supporting the transition to a decarbonized, more resource-efficient economy. It builds on EQT’s investments in battery storage, including Statera Energy in the UK and Ju:niz Energy in Germany.

Benjamin Bygott-Webb, Partner, EQT, said: “Battery storage has become essential to keeping the grid reliable and electricity affordable, as an ageing grid, a changing generation mix and rapidly growing power demand continue to put the system under strain. Flatiron has secured scarce, well-located sites and built a strong record in the communities where it operates. Building on EQT’s deep experience investing in critical infrastructure, our expertise in scaling energy platforms and the opportunities for collaboration across the EQT infrastructure portfolio, we look forward to supporting the Flatiron team as they deliver their projects and bring more firm capacity to the region.”

Rob Brink, Chief Executive Officer, Flatiron Energy, said: “We started Flatiron with the mission to bring reliable energy where it’s needed most, in the communities that rely on it every day. EQT is an exceptional firm with a strong track record of scaling platforms in the energy transition, and we couldn’t be more excited to partner with them on our next stage of growth. My co-founders and I are incredibly grateful to HSE, whose unwavering support and belief in our strategy brought us to this point.”

Sarah Wright, Founder and Managing Partner, HSE, said: “This transaction underscores HSE’s approach to identifying attractive opportunities and creating long-term value in a rapidly growing and decarbonizing power sector. HSE is highly selective about the management teams we back, and Flatiron is an excellent illustration of why this matters. Because the Flatiron team has a strong track record in the sector and a rigorous, fundamentals-driven approach to setting strategy, they have been able to deliver material growth and value accretion. HSE has appreciated the collaborative partnership with the team as they worked to build the project portfolio and establish Flatiron as an industry leader.”

The transaction is subject to customary conditions and approvals. It is expected to close in Q4 2026.

Simpson Thacher & Bartlett LLP acted as legal counsel and Santander acted as financial advisor to EQT.

Kirkland & Ellis LLP acted as legal counsel and Guggenheim Securities, LLC acted as financial advisor to the Company.

Faegre Drinker Biddle & Reath LLP acted as legal counsel to HSE.

title: Explainer-What to know about the energy permitting overhaul bill before US Congress
description:
• Speed environmental reviews.
The bill would impose deadlines on many federal reviews, require agencies to coordinate permitting decisions and create a federal permitting tracker.
• Make data centers pay.
Critics argue that loosening permitting requirements for all industries will only make data centers easier to build.
Supporters argue delays in permitting power plants, transmission lines and other infrastructure raise costs for consumers and businesses.
text:
By Nichola Groom

Nov 18 (Reuters) – The future of wind farms, data centers, oil pipelines and transmission lines could hinge on whether the US Congress approves a permitting overhaul that backers say would cut electricity costs, but critics warn would weaken environmental protections.

The 400-page Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, expected to receive a final vote in the Senate this week, would accelerate approvals for major energy and infrastructure projects ​by cutting timelines for environmental reviews and litigation.

WHAT PROBLEM IS THE BILL TRYING TO SOLVE?

Democrats and Republicans alike have argued for decades that the US ‌takes too long to build large infrastructure projects.

The issue has taken on urgency as AI’s rapid growth drives electricity demand, raising concerns about power prices, transmission bottlenecks and whether the grid can expand quickly to support new data centers.

SunZia, a 550-mile (885-km) transmission line to deliver wind power from New Mexico to Arizona and California, for example, took nearly two decades to move from proposal to completion.

WHAT WOULD THE BILL DO?

• Speed environmental reviews. The bill would impose deadlines on many federal reviews, require agencies to coordinate permitting decisions and create a federal permitting tracker. The bill ‌would set ​a two-year target for major federal environmental reviews, compared with an average of more than four years now, ⁠according to the White House Council of Economic ⁠Advisers.

• Make data centers pay. One of the bill’s most closely watched provisions would require large data centers to bear more of the transmission and infrastructure costs associated with their electricity demand.

• Expand transmission development. The legislation includes provisions intended to accelerate planning, siting and construction of transmission lines and upgrades to existing infrastructure.

• Increase permit certainty. The bill would limit circumstances under which permits can be revoked or challenged in court. It establishes a 150-day window ​for many legal challenges after permits or reviews, replacing a patchwork of deadlines that can allow litigation to emerge months, even years, after approvals.

• Supporters say permit certainty would give investors confidence to move forward. Critics argue it limits accountability and judicial review.

WHAT ABOUT TRUMP’S FREEZE ON WIND PROJECTS?

The provisions meant to prevent ⁠challenges and delays were included to prevent political swings resulting in project cancellations. Former Democratic President ⁠Joe Biden, for example, canceled the Keystone XL oil pipeline permit while President Donald Trump’s Republican administration has frozen and ​delayed wind projects.

Some Democratic lawmakers and environmental groups say they need further assurances that Trump would follow the law, after he said this month: “I will not approve wind turbines ​because wind turbines are a major loser.”

WHY HAS THE BILL BECOME TIED TO DATA CENTERS?

In response to widespread opposition to data ‌center development from communities nationwide, the bill would require large computing facilities to bear more of the costs they impose on the grid.

Critics argue that loosening permitting requirements for all industries will only make data centers easier to build.

HOW WOULD THE BILL LOWER ENERGY PRICES?

Supporters argue delays in permitting power plants, transmission lines and other infrastructure raise costs for consumers and businesses. The White House Council of Economic Advisers estimated the bill could increase annual economic output by $82 billion to $164 billion and reduce average household ⁠electric bills by roughly $178 to $251 per year.

Independent analyses generally conclude the bill would lower costs. Resources for the Future estimated it would significantly expand transmission capacity and generate $350 billion in savings through 2050, while Rhodium Group found it could lower climate-warming emissions.

WHY ARE ENVIRONMENTAL GROUPS AND TRIBES OPPOSED?

Environmental groups including the League of Conservation ⁠Voters, Sierra Club and Natural Resources Defense Council support the ‌bill’s transmission and clean-energy provisions but argue it would also accelerate fossil-fuel development and weaken protections for public lands, ⁠water, wildlife and communities.

Tribal organizations, including the National Congress of American Indians, say the bill prioritizes faster approvals over protections ​for sacred ‌sites and tribal consultation.

WHY ARE DEMOCRATS DIVIDED?

The biggest Democratic disagreement is about whether to pass the bipartisan bill now ​or pursue a ⁠stronger version next year, when the party takes control of the House of Representatives and Senate.

Democratic Senators Martin Heinrich of New Mexico and Sheldon Whitehouse of Rhode Island, who authored the bill with Republicans Shelley Moore Capito of West Virginia and Mike Lee of Utah, say voters want lower energy costs now and that Congress can strengthen environmental protections later.

WHAT HAPPENS NEXT?

The Senate has voted overwhelmingly to clear two procedural hurdles.

The bill still faces a final Senate vote, expected this week, and consideration by the House. Passage in the House this year remains uncertain due to the divide among Democrats and as Congress works to fund the government before federal funding expires on December 11.

(Reporting ​by Nichola Groom; Editing by Rod Nickel)

name: Congress
title: Midterms' 'blue tsunami' gives Congress and states an opportunity to take action on climate change
description:
These state trifectas create a chance to enact policies to advance clean energy and respond to voters’ concerns about energy affordability.
When he took office in January 2025, Trump refused to spend money that Congress had appropriated for clean energy.
It also cut other clean energy provisions of the Inflation Reduction Act, despite the law overwhelmingly benefiting Republican-held districts.
The administration has also intervened in permitting, holding up hundreds of wind and solar power projects.
They can use this authority to investigate the administration’s refusals both to enforce environmental regulations and to spend money allocated for clean energy.
text:
The 2026 U.S. midterm elections are sweeping Democratic majorities into Congress and state legislatures across the country. That’s creating an opportunity to shift the country back to responding to climate change.

But faced with a president who staunchly opposes policies that could help slow climate change, what will these leaders with newfound power actually be able to do?

Democrats in Congress will have a stronger hand to play in their negotiations with the White House come January, and they may have leverage in pursuing climate policies during negotiations over the federal budget. Yet for the next two years, their ability to enact comprehensive climate legislation will likely be limited by President Donald Trump’s promised veto.

Beyond the federal level, six states – Arizona, Michigan, Minnesota, Nevada, Pennsylvania and Wisconsin – will have new Democratic trifectas: Democratic governors and Democratic majorities in both chambers of the legislature. These state trifectas create a chance to enact policies to advance clean energy and respond to voters’ concerns about energy affordability.

We study the politics and policies around climate change. Here are some ways we see potential for real change.

What can Congress do to restore clean energy spending?

When he took office in January 2025, Trump refused to spend money that Congress had appropriated for clean energy. The courts ruled that the move was illegal.

A few months later, Trump’s federal budget bill eliminated tax credits for producing wind power, investing in solar power and purchasing electric vehicles. It also cut other clean energy provisions of the Inflation Reduction Act, despite the law overwhelmingly benefiting Republican-held districts.

The new Democratic Congress will have authority over taxing and spending, known as the “power of the purse.”

U.S. Rep. Chellie Pingree, a Democrat from Maine who serves on the House Appropriations Committee, plans to withhold funding for federal agencies if the administration does not spend funds allocated to clean energy. Further, advocates believe Democrats can leverage budget negotiations with the White House to restore wind and solar tax credits.

How can Congress respond to federal agencies’ anti-environmental stances?

In his second term, Trump has doubled down on his wide-ranging effort to eliminate environmental regulations. His administration has handed out exemptions from air pollution rules to many facilities, including 71 coal-fired power plants. The administration has also intervened in permitting, holding up hundreds of wind and solar power projects.

Congressional majorities have the power to exercise oversight of federal agencies, including the ability to subpoena documents. They can use this authority to investigate the administration’s refusals both to enforce environmental regulations and to spend money allocated for clean energy.

Since Congress has limited legal means to force the administration to comply with investigations, its oversight powers give it leverage largely through bad press and lower approval ratings for Trump.

Congress has seen some movement lately on legislation that could boost renewable energy. A proposed bipartisan permitting reform bill could speed up construction of electricity transmission lines and clean energy sources such as wind, solar and geothermal power.

However, many climate advocates oppose the bill for accelerating fossil fuel projects and weakening environmental laws. For instance, opponents warn that the bill removes checks on environmentally harmful projects. U.S. Rep. Jared Huffman, a Democrat from California, has called for the new Congress to renegotiate the legislation.

What can state governments do to slow climate change?

Former Washington Gov. Jay Inslee, a Democrat, contends that “almost every (climate) policy you can think of … can be done at a state level.”

In recent years, unified Democratic control has allowed Michigan and Minnesota to pass ambitious climate laws, such as policies requiring that 100% of electricity comes from clean energy sources by 2040. Both are back under Democratic control, and incoming governors Jocelyn Benson and Amy Klobuchar each campaigned on expanding renewable energy.

Those and other states with new trifectas can now enact legislation that has been stalled for years due to partisan opposition.

In Pennsylvania, for example, Democratic lawmakers have advanced proposals that would allow community solar power, regulate data centers – these are huge electricity users – and require utilities to store excess electricity. But those proposals stalled under Republican control of the state Senate. That could change with Democrats gaining a trifecta.

Democrats also broke Republican trifectas in Georgia, Iowa, New Hampshire, Ohio and Texas. Given Texas’ burgeoning wind industry and solar power potential, a shift in its energy policy could help to significantly reduce emissions. Texas’ renewable energy requirements once drove wind power expansion. But electric utilities successfully pushed for weakening the law’s targets for solar power, and the state’s Republican government repealed the policy in 2023.

While Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa in Texas has focused more on affordable energy than renewable energy, she supports wind and solar power as a means of lowering energy costs. Advocates believe her victory will prevent the enactment of two proposed bills that would impose administrative hurdles and fines on renewable energy generators.

Unlike his predecessor, Ken Paxton, incoming Attorney General Nathan Johnson has signaled that he will not bring Texas into litigation against progressive federal policies such as environmental regulations.

What do US voters want?

Climate policies are broadly popular with Americans, though less so among Republicans. They are more popular than most people and politicians think.

In recent ballot measures, such as Nevada’s 50% renewable energy target in 2020 and Washington state’s cap-and-trade repeal effort in 2024, voters have favored climate policy. However, many Americans currently rate other priorities, such as healthcare, the economy and lowering high prices, as more important.

Taken together, this polling data suggests that bold climate actions may be more likely to flop among voters if they are seen as worsening other issues that voters care about. For example, if voters worry that climate legislation will increase costs, they may be less likely to support the politicians behind it.

In contrast, if politicians can reassure voters that their climate policies are complementary to addressing other public concerns, such action may be less likely to backfire and could even boost politicians’ popularity – even potentially among Republican voters. U.S. Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse, a Democrat from Rhode Island, argues that Democrats should explain how renewable energy can lower electricity prices – a current priority for voters.

Looking back, looking ahead

text:
The solar energy landscape continues to grow from strength to strength courtesy of companies that are aiming to take advantage of the opportunities that they currently have and generate as much revenue as they can while they still can. The energy sector transforms at such a rapid pace nowadays, meaning companies are better served taking full advantage of certain moments and playing their role in shaping the future of the energy sector. One of the ongoing patterns in recent years is companies aiming to predict where the energy sector is headed and positioning themselves to benefit when that time comes. One of the most recognizable companies, Duke Energy, proposed 300 MW of Florida solar with $1 billion in projected customer savings.

The overall influence of Duke Energy in the modern solar landscape

One of the leading solar energy companies in the United States is Duke Energy, a Fortune 150 company headquartered in Charlotte, N.C. It is one of America’s largest energy holding companies, which is a tremendous achievement considering the abundant competition that exists in the United States, one of the leading solar energy-producing countries in the world.

According to reports, the company’s electric utilities serve 8.7 million customers in North Carolina, South Carolina, Florida, Indiana, Ohio, and Kentucky. This means it has contributed significantly to those places not just from an energy generation perspective but also from an economic perspective because projects create employment for the general population.

As such, there is a strong belief among industry experts that it will be among the select few companies leading the next generation of the solar sector.

Duke Energy owns 55,700 megawatts of energy capacity. The company is currently seeking to execute an energy modernization strategy, prioritizing customer value as it invests in electric grid upgrades. As such, there is a strong belief among industry experts that it will be among the select few companies leading the next generation of the solar sector.

Taking massive strides: Duke Energy proposes 300 MW of Florida solar with $1 billion

A press release from Duke Energy Florida revealed that the company has filed plans with the Florida Public Service Commission to build four new solar energy sites by mid-2028. Together, the sites are expected to add 300 megawatts (MW) of clean energy to the electric grid while delivering an estimated $1 billion in customer savings over their operational lifetimes.

A commendable aspect of the United States’ approach to the clean energy transition is how much different states are willing to work with private companies in order to ensure that the most beneficial projects are executed at a rapid pace. Duke Energy has created a brilliant reputation with the state of Florida, being at the center of many groundbreaking initiatives.

Breaking down Duke Energy’s influence on Florida’s solar sector

Duke Energy Florida is in a position where it can use the Inflation Reduction Act to transfer an estimated $75 million in production tax credits to customers per year, which reduces their monthly bill by at least $2.50 per 1,000 kilowatt-hours of electricity used.

That amount will only increase as more solar energy sites come online. From an environmental perspective, the emission-free energy produced at each solar energy site saves an estimated 1.1 million cubic feet of natural gas.

A general overview of Florida’s solar energy sector as of 2026

At the moment, Duke Energy Florida owns, operates, and maintains 25 solar energy sites that combine 1,850 MW to the grid. Each site can power about 15,000 homes, helping meet the rising demand for electricity across the third-fastest-growing state in the nation. This is why the company has developed a good reputation in the state as it hopes to elevate its position further.

name: Texas American Energy
title: Republicans could expedite bill to make big oil immune to lawsuits, warn experts
description:
Gas prices are skyrocketing, but why would we spend our time giving special treatment to big oil, who are also simultaneously enjoying record profits at our expense?
The immunity bill follows a pattern of powerful industries asking Congress to shield them from liability – although not all have succeeded.
That gun law may have inspired the push for a big oil immunity law.
“The fossil fuel industry explicitly invokes the liability waiver given to the gun industry in 2005 as its model for what it’s trying to achieve,” said Mulvey.
At the state level, fossil fuel company allies are engaged in a similar effort to shield them from liability.
text:
Climate groups fear lawmakers could pass a bill by the end of the year that would give fossil fuel companies immunity from lawsuits and legislation that aims to hold them accountable for the climate crisis.

After the blue wave election, Republican lawmakers are rushing to pass high-priority bills before newly elected Democrats are sworn in. Hundreds of elected leaders and climate groups sent a letter to Democratic leadership urging them to reject any proposal that would shield fossil fuel companies from liability for the climate crisis.

Iyla Shornstein, political director for the Center for Climate Integrity, said the election results showed voters don’t want this type of legislation. “Voters at the polls sent a clear message about how costs are impacting their everyday lives. Gas prices are skyrocketing, but why would we spend our time giving special treatment to big oil, who are also simultaneously enjoying record profits at our expense? … The elections sent a pretty clear message that our elected leaders need to be spending their time helping working families, not major corporations like big oil.”

In April, Republicans introduced the Stop Climate Shakedowns bill that would shield fossil fuel companies from various attempts to hold them accountable. Ted Cruz and Harriet Hageman, two Republican lawmakers, introduced companion Senate and House bills. “Radical environmental groups have waged a coordinated campaign to weaponize our judicial system against American energy producers, including many in Texas,” Cruz said in a statement announcing the Senate bill. “They’re using meritless lawsuits to bankrupt our energy industry, kill good paying jobs and drive up the cost of electricity and gasoline for hardworking families.”

Eleven states, two tribal governments and dozens of municipalities have filed lawsuits against big oil companies to hold them accountable for the climate emergency. The lawsuits are grounded in science that connects climate disasters to emissions from fossil fuel companies and increasing evidence that the companies deceived the public about their own internal science warning them about the dangers of fossil fuels.

Another accountability effort has come from states such as New York and Vermont that have passed climate superfund laws to recover costs by shifting the financial burden from climate disasters onto the fossil fuel companies that caused them. Both New York and Vermont’s superfund laws have faced opposition including challenges by the Department of Justice; a judge struck down the New York superfund law in September, the state’s governor, Kathy Hochul, is appealing.

The fossil fuel immunity bill has four key parts, said Shornstein: it would dismiss existing climate liability lawsuits against fossil fuel companies, prohibit new lawsuits, void climate superfund laws and assert that the federal government is the sole authority over the regulation of greenhouse gas emissions and climate crisis, which pre-empts states from acting on it.

Stopping climate lawsuits and superfund laws was a top priority for the American Petroleum Institute this year, but the bill stalled in September when the House judiciary committee failed to advance it.

Shornstein said Republican lawmakers could still rush through the bill or attach immunity language to other legislation before the end of the current Congress. “We’re at a critical moment, because Trump and the GOP and big oil’s allies want to bail out the fossil fuel industry while they still have power,” she said. “Immunity for big oil has been high on the list of priorities, so this is their last ditch effort.”

“We need to be extremely on our toes and vigilant and ready to mobilize to make sure that Congress rejects this sweeping giveaway to big oil,” said Kathy Mulvey, program director for fossil fuel accountability at the Union of Concerned Scientists. “I expect that they would see the lame duck session as a real opportunity to push through the Cruz-Hageman bill.”

The bill would block source attribution science, a growing field of science that connects climate disasters to the emissions of specific oil and gas companies. The bill says such scientific efforts “lack scientific credibility and are, therefore, arbitrary”.

“The fact that [they] are specifically going after this field of science and the scientists who are playing a leading role indicates really how much they’re threatened by being held accountable for the harms that they’re causing,” Mulvey said.

The immunity bill follows a pattern of powerful industries asking Congress to shield them from liability – although not all have succeeded. In the 1990s, when tobacco companies faced dozens of lawsuits seeking to recover costs from smoking-related illnesses, they unsuccessfully lobbied Congress to introduce legislation to shield them. And in 2005, in response to a wave of lawsuits attempting to hold gunmakers liable for violence, the National Rifle Association (NRA) achieved a lobbying victory when Congress passed a liability shield law, the Protection of Lawful Commerce in Arms Act.

That gun law may have inspired the push for a big oil immunity law. In a letter last yeat to Pam Bondi, the former US attorney general, Republican state attorneys general asked for a liability shield for big oil, which they directly compared with the shield law for gun manufacturers. “The fossil fuel industry explicitly invokes the liability waiver given to the gun industry in 2005 as its model for what it’s trying to achieve,” said Mulvey.

At the state level, fossil fuel company allies are engaged in a similar effort to shield them from liability. A ProPublica investigation reported that immunity bills introduced in a number of Republican-controlled state houses were part of a coordinated effort by a rightwing network that included activist Leonard Leo and the American Legislative Exchange Council.

In a statement to ProPublica, Leo did not dispute the findings. “For decades, the left had leveraged immense resources to capture the institutions that shape our society,” he wrote in a text. “That takeover resulted in a radically woke culture that does not reflect the will of the American people, or the pillars of limited constitutional government that made our country great. That is why our enterprise supports organizations that are committed to crushing liberal dominance and restoring balance in the institutions that shape society.”

“We’re also seeing this push at the state level too,” Shornstein said. “There were five states that enacted legislation this cycle that provides pretty expansive legal protections to the industry. So they’re taking a very holistic, if you will, approach to escaping accountability.”

name: Detroit American Energy
title: China and the U.S. are still the biggest polluters, but only China is doing better
description:
The rise of electric vehicles means China is also reducing its oil use.
But last year, U.S. emissions went in a different direction.
U.S. greenhouse gas emissions rose in 2025, as the country burned more coal for power and oil and gas for heating.
Two-thirds of passenger vehicle sales in China are now electric vehicles, according to recent data from the China Passenger Car Association.
China will be promoting trade of its clean tech technologies at the conference, says Li Shuo, director of the China Climate Hub at the Asia Society Policy Institute.
text:
As more than 200 countries meet in Turkey for the annual United Nations climate talks, COP31, the two largest emitters of greenhouse gases remain China and the United States. Now the countries' stories are diverging.

For years, China's climate pollution was growing, driven by increased coal use. But for the past two and a half years, China's emissions have been flat or falling.

"And that is a remarkable change," says Lauri Myllyvirta, lead analyst at the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air.

China is driving down emissions by increasing renewable energy and batteries, which is displacing coal. The rise of electric vehicles means China is also reducing its oil use.

"Those are bigger reductions than we expected," Myllyvirta says, "and I think anyone expected."

But last year, U.S. emissions went in a different direction. U.S. greenhouse gas emissions rose in 2025, as the country burned more coal for power and oil and gas for heating. A recent report from United Nations scientists notes that the U.S. sticks out as the only major economy where planet-warming pollution increased significantly last year.

This year, emissions in the U.S. are projected to fall slightly. The country will likely burn less coal than last year. But the U.S. could reduce its emissions more if it were deploying large-scale renewable energy and batteries like China, says Alex Wang, a professor at UCLA Law and an expert on Chinese climate policy.

The problem, Wang says, is the U.S. hasn't had long-term policy support for these climate technologies. The Biden administration increased funding for solar, wind, batteries and electric vehicles. The Trump administration reduced that funding and created regulatory hurdles for those industries.

" What we're suffering through these days is the policy whiplash that comes with the political divisions in the U.S.," Wang says.

Here are the four things you need to know about U.S. and Chinese emissions.

China had long-term planning

China started building the infrastructure that is allowing it to reduce emissions about twenty years ago. Back then, China was still known as a manufacturer of low-cost items. Air pollution in major Chinese cities was also reaching record levels.

Chinese leadership made policies to tackle both the country's economic identity and its air quality. Five-year plans from the central government helped provinces pivot into the clean energy sector.

"Because the policy direction was so consistent and clear," Wang says, "they used that to drive the development of all of these industries that really didn't exist before."

The government set up nationwide supply chains for technologies like solar panels, batteries, wind turbines and electric vehicle manufacturing. Today, China is the unparalleled global leader in producing, deploying and exporting these clean energy technologies.

"On the electrification front, they're going gangbusters," Wang says.

These technologies are helping China reduce its emissions, Myllyvirta says. His research group found that last quarter China's emissions dropped 3% – the largest decline since the COVID-19 pandemic.

In the power sector, emissions are falling as coal use decreases and solar, wind, and nuclear energy increase. China has built many new coal plants in recent years, but they often don't run at full capacity and instead are used for backup generation.

Industries like cement and steel manufacturing are also reducing climate pollution. In the transportation sector, electric vehicles are displacing demand for gasoline and diesel. Two-thirds of passenger vehicle sales in China are now electric vehicles, according to recent data from the China Passenger Car Association.

The U.S. has flip-flopped, experts say

While China has consistently invested in clean technologies, that hasn't been the case in the U.S. The U.S. has struggled to scale up climate tech industries that reduce emissions because of flip-flopping by the federal government, Wang says.

Under the Biden administration, Congress passed new financial incentives for renewable energy and electric vehicles, and policies that cut greenhouse gas emissions in sectors like the oil and gas industry. The Trump administration has reversed those policies, putting up roadblocks for solar and wind projects, canceling tax breaks for home solar and electric vehicles, and proposing to cut regulations on methane — a super planet-heating gas.

The Trump administration frequently cites its "energy dominance agenda," which prioritizes keeping coal plants running.

Asked about increased U.S. greenhouse gas emissions last year, White House spokesperson Taylor Rodgers wrote in an email to NPR, "The United States is in a position of strength thanks to the President's energy dominance agenda which has unleashed affordable, reliable, secure energy sources. America is the world's leading producer and exporter of oil and gas, and many nations rely on the United States for their energy supply."

This is a growing problem as the country builds more energy-hungry data centers, says Ben Haley at consulting firm Evolved Energy Research. Most of those data centers are now being powered by fossil fuels like natural gas and coal.

"The pace and scale at which they come online tends to increase emissions," Haley says. "You can't really match that with clean energy deployment at scale, currently."

A new study finds that carbon dioxide emissions from about 400 large U.S. data centers equal almost as much as an entire country like Denmark.

Chinese exports equal emissions reductions

Wang says it's great that China's emissions seem to be plateauing. But he says, "We shouldn't forget the fact that their emissions really are outsized compared to the rest of the world."

Still, the country is exporting clean technologies like solar, batteries and electric vehicles to countries including Pakistan, Nepal and the Philippines. That's helping these countries reduce their dependency on fossil fuels.

Chinese clean tech exports have only increased since the beginning of the U.S. war with Iran, says Kingsmill Bond, an analyst at the energy think tank Ember.

The ongoing U.N. climate talks in Turkey will have a large emphasis on getting countries to commit to increasing electrification. China will be promoting trade of its clean tech technologies at the conference, says Li Shuo, director of the China Climate Hub at the Asia Society Policy Institute.

As China gets a bigger share of the global clean tech trade, it will be harder for the U.S. to compete, he says.

"This dominating position will not go away, and if anything, it will be further consolidated in the coming years," Li Shuo says. "The U.S., I think, will struggle."

name: Clean Energy
title: Opinion: Care about affordability? Then you have to care about this. - The Salt Lake Tribune
description:
The status quo has left us completely unable to build the energy system we need.
The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act is the joint work of Sens.
A significant backlog of energy projects is waiting to be built or hooked into our overloaded, archaic energy grid.
At the end of 2025, more than 85% of the energy projects seeking to get plugged into the grid were renewable sources and storage.
The fossil fuel projects of the past are already built and connected; the green energy projects being built are not.
text:
When I say it this way, it sounds like such an easy call: The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026 is the largest reimagining of the federal permitting process in a generation. It would make it far easier to build new energy infrastructure of all kinds: wind and solar farms and interstate transmission lines and, yes, natural gas pipelines. It would make it easier to build much else, too: rail and transit infrastructure and affordable housing and broadband internet.

The bill represents Democrats and Republicans deciding that the fight over what gets built should play out in elections and markets rather than in the bowels of administrative agencies and courts. It should be driven by what people want, in public, rather than what they can block, often in private. I do not expect, in every case, that that would lead to outcomes I like. But leaving the system unchanged is a guarantee of calamity. The status quo has left us completely unable to build the energy system we need.

Still, I don’t want this column to read as more confident about this bill than I really am. It is more than 400 pages, with much of it dedicated to technical changes to other laws. I’ve been unnerved, while reporting this story, by Capitol Hill staff members telling me precisely opposite things about the same provisions. Legislation at this scale rarely plays out exactly as its architects expect. The laws that the act would revise, like the National Environmental Policy Act and the National Historic Preservation Act, work quite differently today than what was expected when they were signed into law in the 1960s and ’70s.

But at its core, the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act would do the same thing over and over again: It would make it faster and simpler to build energy infrastructure by rolling back the opportunities for delays, lawsuits and vetoes that have proliferated in recent decades. This is a bill that would remove procedural and legal obstacles to building. It would not decide what gets built. Whether the act is part of a Green New Deal or a natural gas resurgence would depend on what Democrats do next.

The single most important climate policy going forward is for Democrats to win elections so that they have the power to set climate policy in the future. The Democrats who won Senate seats, or look likely to win them, in Kansas, Mississippi, South Carolina, Texas and Alaska ran on an all-of-the-above energy strategy. Democrats everywhere ran on putting affordability first.

The bill is an early test of whether they meant it. A Democratic Party that was saying what voters wanted to hear, but has no intention of doing what voters asked them to do, will not hold power for long.

The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act is the joint work of Sens. Martin Heinrich, D-N.M.; Sheldon Whitehouse, D-R.I.; Mike Lee, R-Utah; and Shelley Moore Capito, R-W.Va. For Heinrich, the story of this bill goes back almost two decades, to when he first saw the way that delay and lawsuits could be weaponized even against clean, pro-labor projects.

“When I got elected to Congress in 2008,” Heinrich said, “there was an opportunity to build a clean energy project in New Mexico and connect it to the rest of the country with a 550-mile transmission project. Today it’s in service with roughly $20 billion of economic impact across a couple of different states and one of the largest project labor agreements in the history of the Southwest. But it took us roughly 18 years to permit and build — and the build part was like two years and the permit part was like 16 years. That, to me, is the nut that we’re trying to solve.”

The National Environmental Policy Act, for example, originally provided examples of environmental reports that were less than a dozen pages. Now those reports can stretch hundreds or thousands of pages, take years to complete, and invite interminable litigation. That can be deployed to stop bad projects, but it is an obstacle for good ones, too. NEPA, as it is known, does not impose an environmental benefit test on projects. The requirements are purely procedural. Agencies are trying to prevent grounds for a lawsuit or an administrative delay, not prove their project is green. That’s why NEPA, despite its name, can be wielded with equal ferocity against clean and dirty projects alike.

The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, or BAAJA, creates a more neutral and swift permitting system, and green energy advocates believe that system would be of particular benefit to their technologies. A significant backlog of energy projects is waiting to be built or hooked into our overloaded, archaic energy grid. That backlog is overwhelmingly tilted toward green energy. At the end of 2025, more than 85% of the energy projects seeking to get plugged into the grid were renewable sources and storage. The fossil fuel projects of the past are already built and connected; the green energy projects being built are not.

I talked to several Democrats who are skeptical of the act, and those conversations always began the same way — with President Donald Trump. Asked whether he would approve new wind turbines on federal land under the bill, he said, “No, I will not approve wind turbines.” When he was informed that approving those turbines was part of the deal, he doubled down: “I know, but I won’t approve it.”

It’s hard to argue with the Democrats who think it’s crazy to make a deal with a president who has made it clear that he has no intention of upholding his side of the deal, and has often acted lawlessly to boot. “I cannot support a bill that relies on a handshake promise from the same administration that’s spent the last two years waging a war on new clean energy projects to hold up its end of the bargain, and continues to do so even after negotiating the reform proposal,” Sen. Ron Wyden, D-Ore., said in a statement.

But capriciously blocking wind power is what Trump is doing now. The bill makes it harder for Trump to sit on wind projects in the future. “His departments have to give an answer, yes or no, and the answer has to be justified, and there’s a time frame by which they have to deliver it,” said Daniel Palken, an energy permitting expert at Arnold Ventures (and a former Senate staffer). The remedies here become severe, including one that says agency heads cannot travel more than 25 miles from their headquarters if a permit is more than 60 days delayed.

There are also fears that Trump will use the bill to pillage public lands. The concern here is somewhat complex. The bill does not remove any protections that public lands currently enjoy. The worry, rather, is that there could be an unintended consequence from something that the Democrats wanted.

Parts of the bill attempt to ensure something called “permit certainty,” wherein a future (or current) president can’t upend existing permits in a discriminatory manner. The genesis of those sections of the bill is that Trump has done exactly that to wind and solar projects, and Democrats want him to stop.

But that’s created a new fear: That Trump would issue all manner of illegal permits to drill on public lands that will then be protected by the bill’s provisions in the future. That is the question that has caused me the most concern while reporting this column. If that’s true, then yes, that’s a huge problem. But the bill’s architects don’t think it’s true. The bill was amended to make it clearer that illegal permits would not stand and were not protected by courts. But multiple environmental groups and Democratic offices still fear the possibility. Further amendments, like one that’s been offered by Sen. Cory Booker, D-N.J., stating this even more sharply would be welcome.

That said, if Trump were going to be president for another decade, I would be less eager to see this legislation pass. But it will be future presidential administrations that most benefit from the bill, as many of the new rules and new capacities the act envisions will take years to write and implement.

A conversation I had with Brian Deese, director of the National Economic Council under President Joe Biden, drove this home for me. When I asked him what difference the act would have made to the green energy infrastructure push under the Biden administration, he said that “almost everything would have been different.” But it would have depended on when the act would have passed. “If we had passed something like this bill alongside the Inflation Reduction Act, it would have been good,” he said, referring to the 2022 law that included significant incentives for clean-energy projects. “If we passed it two years before the IRA, it would have been game changing.”

That, to me, is the single best argument for the act. If you believe that Democrats will build on the blue tsunami and take the presidency in 2028, perhaps with even larger House and Senate majorities, then the case for this bill is extremely strong. It’s a force amplifier of anything they might do on clean energy. That’s why Janet Yellen and Jared Bernstein, who led Biden’s Treasury Department and his Council of Economic Advisers, both backed the bill.

Others fear that we are too far down a calamitous climate path to allow new natural gas to be built, and that the surge in artificial intelligence data center construction makes the legislation more dangerous than it might have been a few years ago. But I don’t see a scenario in which new demand for energy would not be met. The data center build-out might be stopped by communities organizing against their construction. But once they are approved and built, they are going to be powered.

The problem, right now, is that we cannot meet enough new demand — whether from data centers or electric vehicles or heat pumps or anything else — with renewables. What the act might make possible is the construction of an energy grid where there is enough renewable power to meet new demand. In the absence of that energy system, new demand would be met by fossil fuels. And the absence of that system describes our reality today.

“The gas build-out we’re seeing today is symptomatic of our inability to build enough electricity infrastructure,” said Jane Flegal, a senior fellow at the Searchlight Institute. “The reason there is so much gas build-out is there’s a sudden surge in demand for electricity and our system for siting and permitting renewables and building transmission lines is totally broken. This bill will go a very long way to fixing that.” (It’s also worth noting that the bill includes a provision forcing new data centers to swallow the transmission costs they impose on the grid, rather than making ratepayers foot part of the bill, as often happens now.)

The Senate vote to move forward on the bill was telling. Among Democrats from states that went for Kamala Harris by 10 points or more, the vote was 2-1 against it; among Democrats representing more purple or red states, it was 2-1 in favor. Something Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer said last week has been ringing in my ears: “If affordability doesn’t prevail, we’re in trouble,” he said. “We cannot impose on people what we think is important. We have to listen to what’s important to them and then deliver.” (Schumer voted to advance the bill.)

Some Democrats want to wait for the new Congress to be seated so they can renegotiate this bill to gain more leverage and extract better terms. That makes sense in theory, but most analysts I talk to think it would fail in practice. This bill was a bipartisan project from the start. Whitehouse, one of its architects, is perhaps the most relentless climate voice in the Democratic caucus. And it’s hard to imagine the conditions for dealmaking improving when Democrats begin investigating Trump and his administration and family in earnest and as Stephen Miller settles into his new role as White House chief of staff. We are entering an era of renewed partisan collision, not a renaissance of bipartisan dealmaking.

“ The folks that argue that there’s going to be some mythical negotiation in the future, I think that’s just absolute lunacy,” said Rep. Josh Harder, D-Calif., who chairs the Build America Caucus. To Harder, it’s a mistake to present this bill as a painful compromise: “ It’s so rare in Congress that you have an opportunity to strengthen the economy and accelerate growth, create jobs, reduce climate emissions and lower prices for consumers all at the same time. We’ve got to pass this.”

text:
The University of Liverpool has launched a new research centre bringing together expertise in clean energy, industrial decarbonisation and environmental sustainability to address major challenges, support UK energy priorities and drive clean growth across the Liverpool City Region.

The Centre for Energy and Environmental Technologies (CEET) will draw on expertise from across the University to create new opportunities for collaboration with industry and partners. It will connect research more closely with the needs of industry and society, helping to translate innovation into real-world applications.

The new Centre will also support UK energy priorities, including strengthening energy independence, reducing carbon emissions and accelerating the transition to net zero. It will also help drive clean growth across the Liverpool City Region.

CEET was announced at the University of Liverpool’s annual Vice-Chancellor’s Conference, Innovation for Growth, which explores how University research and innovation can act as an engine for local and national economic growth.

Interdisciplinary research and innovation

CEET will harness significant interdisciplinary expertise in renewable energy technologies, including batteries, energy storage and fuel cells; nuclear energy, including fission and fusion; sustainability, including sustainable feedstocks; and resilient energy systems, spanning energy policy and environmental impacts.

World-class facilities and expertise

It will bring together facilities and expertise from across the University, including the Stephenson Institute for Renewable Energy (SIRE) and the new Chadwick Institute for Nuclear Innovation, alongside specialist, industry-facing facilities such as the Materials Innovation Factory (MIF) and Digital Innovation Facility (DIF).

Together, these facilities and capabilities provide a platform for collaborative research and innovation spanning energy technologies, advanced materials, digital technologies, nuclear energy and environmental sustainability.

Skills and training

Skills development and training will also be an important part of CEET’s work. The University already provides and contributes to postgraduate training in areas including clean energy, radiation protection, nuclear safety and fusion energy. CEET will build on this expertise to help develop the highly skilled workforce needed to deliver the clean energy transition.

Professor Laura Harkness, Pro-Vice-Chancellor and Head of the Faculty of Science and Engineering, said: “This new Centre will bring together the University’s expertise in clean energy and environmental technologies, strengthening our ability to work with industry and partners to address some of the key challenges in delivering a sustainable, net-zero future.”

“The University’s expertise is far-reaching, and CEET will provide a strong interface between our research and innovation strengths and the clean energy sector. By bringing together researchers from across disciplines, we can help develop the technologies, skills and solutions needed to support a cleaner, more resilient energy future.”

Inaugural Jenkins Professorial Chair

CEET will be led by a new Director, who will also hold the Jenkins Professorial Chair, a role supported by a donation from businessman, philanthropist and University alumnus, Huw Jenkins.

Huw is Chair and CEO of Engelhart, where he focuses on energy transition and decarbonisation.

Huw Jenkins said: “Addressing some of the world’s most pressing environmental and energy challenges is a priority for the long-term future of society and the economy.

“Through the establishment of CEET and the new Jenkins Chair, I hope to support research and leadership in areas that matter for long-term energy and environmental outcomes. The University has extensive interdisciplinary research and innovation expertise in this area, and I am pleased to support its ambition to translate that expertise into real-world impact.”

Supporting clean growth across the Liverpool City Region

CEET aims to support Liverpool City Region’s growing clean energy ecosystem by connecting University expertise with industry and regional partners to drive innovation, skills development and the adoption of new technologies.

text:
CHARLOTTE, N.C., Nov. 18, 2026 — Phelan Green, through its clean fuels subsidiary Phelan eFuels, selected Honeywell Technologies (NASDAQ: HON) to provide Advanced Solvent Carbon Capture (ASCC) technology and modular engineering services to help accelerate electro-sustainable aviation fuel (eSAF) production for the first phase of its Saldanha Bay, South Africa facility. The announcement follows Phelan Green’s decision earlier this year to deploy Honeywell Technologies UOP Fischer-Tropsch (FT) Unicracking™ process technology at the facility.

Phelan Green recently announced it has reached final investment decision for the first phase of its eSAF project. Honeywell Technologies’ end-to-end solutions – including HyCOgen™ and FT-CANS™, jointly developed by bp – will help Phelan Green streamline execution, reduce integration risk and accelerate commercial eSAF production through a single provider. Once fully operational, the facility will produce up to 140,000 metric tons of eSAF annually, addressing growing demand for a reliable supply of jet fuel by adding new energy sources to the mix.

“Phelan Green is bringing together proven technologies across the eSAF value chain to help establish South Africa as a competitive producer and exporter of lower-carbon aviation fuel,” said Blair Phelan, Phelan Green Group Managing Director. “Honeywell Technologies’ integrated offering gives us a coordinated pathway from carbon capture through fuel synthesis and final upgrading, while the modular delivery model is designed to simplify execution.”

“Cost remains a key challenge to scaling SAF production and adoption, and developers need efficient technologies to build investor confidence and move large-scale projects forward,” said Rajesh Gattupalli, president of Honeywell Technologies UOP. “With process technologies that already support 30% of the world’s SAF production, Honeywell Technologies combines deep process expertise, digital and connected capabilities, and an integrated, end-to-end approach to help reduce execution risk and accelerate deployment. As global demand continues to rise for scalable, lower-carbon aviation fuels, our integrated and connected offerings enable producers to more quickly produce these fuels.”

The Saldanha Bay facility is part of the broader Phelan Green Hydrogen Project, a planned $2.5 billion, private investment that has been recognized by the South African government as a trailblazer in its nationally strategic Green Hydrogen program.

###

Phelan Green is a clean energy developer with more than 20 years of experience. Its sustainable fuels development platform is advancing large-scale green hydrogen, eFuels and industrial decarbonization projects. title: The outages America has suffered weren't an attack, but the next failure could be
description:
The recent outages are not the opening shots of war.
The recent string of outages is a statistical cluster that exposes real fragility, not coordinated sabotage — but it should still wake us up.
Officials, including Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, have stated they are highly confident these were unrelated technical issues, not a cyberattack.
Electricity would fail, water systems would stop, banking and payments would freeze, and cell networks would go dark — all at once, like a sudden thunderclap.
The recent outages are not the opening shots of war.
text:
The recent outages are not the opening shots of war.

The recent string of outages is a statistical cluster that exposes real fragility, not coordinated sabotage — but it should still wake us up.

Over the past week, Microsoft 365 services, including Outlook, went dark worldwide after a latent defect from a July network update surfaced under heavy load. Next, the FAA ordered a rare nationwide ground stop after routers at sites in Arkansas and Texas overwhelmed aging air traffic control systems. Then Chase and other banks saw transaction slowdowns from a software bug. United delayed departures because of an internal system failure. And finally, reports emerged of disruptions to the NSA’s classified internal network. Officials, including Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, have stated they are highly confident these were unrelated technical issues, not a cyberattack.

But we humans are wired to seek patterns. Events this close together feel ominous. In this case, the evidence points to a predictable downside of efficiency: concentrated cloud computing dependencies and incompletely tested updates that create single points of failure across email, aviation, finance and more.

That does not mean the threat is imaginary. If China or Russia decided to inflict serious damage, we would not experience scattered inconveniences. Electricity would fail, water systems would stop, banking and payments would freeze, and cell networks would go dark — all at once, like a sudden thunderclap. Such an attack would almost certainly accompany or immediately precede kinetic action, most obviously a Chinese move against Taiwan, intended to slow or deter a U.S. response.

Even Iran, North Korea or elements of the Mexican narcostate have some capacity to harm our critical infrastructure, with Iran being the prime suspect in water system attacks over the past few months.

Further, hostile nations do probe, looking for vulnerabilities. They may even conduct small-scale attacks to test response times. And, of course, there are gray-zone operations that offer significant asymmetric advantages and plausible deniability while imposing costs (economic, psychological and diversion of defensive resources) without crossing into open war. The recent attacks on industrial food freezers and blood banks in Europe and on U.S. military bases are examples of this, with the Russians as likely culprits.

China has already laid the groundwork. Volt Typhoon, assessed as linked to the People’s Liberation Army, has pre-positioned access inside U.S. critical infrastructure — energy, water, transportation and communications — with the goal of enabling disruption or destruction in a crisis. Salt Typhoon, tied to China’s Ministry of State Security, has focused on intelligence collection, penetrating telecommunications networks to intercept communications and metadata at scale. One prepares to break things; the other listens in on us. An example of the former was discovered during the first Trump administration when a kill switch was found in a high-voltage transformer imported from China.

Closer to home, the Mexican government under MORENA and President Claudia Sheinbaum increasingly frames relations with the United States in terms of a righteous struggle against “Norte Americanos.” U.S. efforts to arrest high-ranking narcotraffickers on Mexican soil or destroy drug production facilities are treated as grave threats to sovereignty that require an answer. Mexico’s military (SEMAR and SEDENA) has acquired roughly 2,400 short-range intelligence, surveillance, reconnaissance and attack drones while building domestic manufacturing capacity, according to Ammon Blair, senior fellow at the Texas Public Policy Foundation. Officials have signaled interest in longer-range systems as a deterrent, putting U.S. infrastructure such as the electric grid and refineries at risk — precisely the lesson of drone warfare in Ukraine.

The United States — federal and state governments, as well as private industry — is beginning to address these critical vulnerabilities.

The Department of War is finally starting to learn to use our counter-drone technology along our 1,954-mile border with Mexico. State governments are taking stock of their vulnerabilities in the event of a conflict across the Pacific. And industry is stepping up to the challenge of reshoring critical manufacturing capacity.

One such vital component is the high-voltage transformers that make our electric grid possible. Essential to move electricity from power plants to homes, factories and data centers, these massive transformers are mostly imported (often from China) with lead times of two to four years. Roughly 70% of America’s existing units are more than 25 years old.

Demand is exploding from data centers, electric vehicles and industrial growth. Startups such as Resolute Grid in Austin, Texas, are responding with domestic production. Many of its engineers are Tesla and SpaceX veterans who could have retired after those companies’ successes; now they are applying the same urgency to building large transformers that can be delivered in months rather than years. The firm’s CEO, Marcus Owenby, noted, “Resilience isn’t just keeping the lights on. It’s how fast you can replace what breaks.” Because without power, water, fuel, communications and finance all fail.

Domestic manufacturing, strategic stockpiles, faster permitting and a clear preference for American production over adversarial supply chains are practical steps, not abstractions.

The recent outages are not the opening shots of war. They are a reminder that complex, efficient systems fail and that determined adversaries have both the intent and the access to make failures far worse.

Preparation, not panic, is the rational response.

KITCHENER, ON, Nov. 18, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Canadian Solar Inc. (the "Company" or "Canadian Solar") (NASDAQ: CSIQ) announced today at RE+ 2026, one of North America's largest clean energy events, that e-STORAGE, its energy storage solutions business, has signed agreements with X-ELIO, a global renewable energy developer, to supply five battery energy storage projects totaling 590 MW / 1.43 GWh DC. In both markets, the systems will shift midday solar output into the evening peak—addressing Texas's tightest supply hours after sunset and supporting coal retirement goals in New South Wales. text:
RALEIGH, NC (WWAY) — A new report from the Sierra Club warns that growing electricity demand from artificial intelligence data centers could reverse 15 years of progress in reducing carbon emissions while driving up energy costs for customers.

The report, titled “Artificial Intelligence, Real Pollution,” was released Tuesday and examines how the rapid expansion of data centers could increase pollution as utility companies turn to natural gas and other fossil fuels to meet rising energy demands.

According to the report, carbon dioxide emissions from the U.S. electric sector could reach 2.3 billion tons annually by 2030, returning to levels last seen around 2011.

The environmental organization says nearly 250 gigawatts of new natural gas power plants are planned or under construction nationwide, with data center demand contributing to that expansion.

In North Carolina, the report raises concerns about Duke Energy’s changing emissions projections.

According to data from the nonprofit RMI cited in the report, Duke Energy Carolinas and Duke Energy Progress projected in 2023 that their carbon emissions would decrease by 50% between 2025 and 2035.

However, updated projections in 2026 instead showed emissions increasing by 16% over that period.

The Sierra Club said those projections were based on earlier utility energy plans and do not account for the new Carbon Plan approved by the North Carolina Utilities Commission on Monday.

“Clean energy and affordability are a package deal, and Duke is failing its customers as utility executives prioritize expensive new gas-burning plants and delay coal plant closures to serve data centers,” said Mikaela Curry, the Sierra Club’s Beyond Coal campaign manager in North Carolina.

The report also warns that increased reliance on natural gas could expose customers to higher electricity bills while contributing to air pollution in communities near power plants.

To address those concerns, the Sierra Club is calling for stronger regulations and greater transparency for data center developers and utility companies.

The organization recommends expanding renewable energy production, including tripling solar and doubling wind generation on the nation’s electric grid.

According to the report, those investments could reduce carbon emissions by 25% compared to 2025 levels and lower average annual electricity costs by more than $5 billion nationwide compared with a business-as-usual scenario, even with moderate data center growth.

The Sierra Club also argues that voluntary efforts by data center companies to reduce their environmental impacts have been limited and that additional oversight is needed.

“For over a decade, communities, advocates, and changemakers have stepped up to protect our air and water from toxic pollution and taken swift action to protect our planet from climate change,” said Holly Bender, the Sierra Club’s chief program officer.

“But now, these artificial intelligence data centers and their power demand threatens to undo all of the work we’ve accomplished.”

The findings come as North Carolina utilities plan for growing electricity demand while working toward the state’s goal of achieving net-zero carbon emissions by 2050.

The Sierra Club is urging state lawmakers, regulators and utility companies to adopt stronger policies to limit pollution and protect customers from potential increases in energy costs.

The report’s projections represent potential outcomes based on future energy development, rather than emissions increases that have already occurred.
