What the Tesla Hertz Uber Antitrust Lawsuit Alleges

Based on the available reporting, the complaint makes three linked claims. First, it says Tesla used government EV subsidies to let Hertz purchase Model 3 vehicles at prices below average variable cost. Second, it says that pricing limited rival EV manufacturers’ access to rental platforms. Third, it says the same arrangement limited rivals’ access to ride-hailing platforms, which is where Uber enters the case.

Notice what the complaint does not need to prove for a headline to work. It does not need a court to agree yet. It needs only to survive a motion to dismiss, and the bar for that stage is plausibility, not proof. Many antitrust suits die at that gate, and many survive it and then spend years in discovery.

The defendants are three very different businesses. Tesla builds and sells the vehicles. Hertz rents them to travelers and, in some markets, to drivers. Uber connects drivers and riders through an app. The plaintiff’s theory treats them as a chain: a manufacturer with market power, a fleet buyer that moves volume, and a platform that decides which cars reach drivers. Whether the law sees a conspiracy, a series of ordinary commercial deals, or neither is the question the court will eventually face.

The available reporting does not confirm the plaintiff’s name, the case number, the filing date, the damages sought or any ruling. Those gaps matter. Readers should treat any article that fills them in with confident detail as suspect, including this one if it ever did so. We report only what the record establishes and label the rest as unconfirmed.

The $4.2B Hertz Order: What Was Announced in October 2021

Hertz announced in October 2021 that it planned to buy 100,000 electric vehicles from Tesla. Media reports put the deal at approximately $4.2 billion.

A simple division of the two reported figures gives about $42,000 per car. Treat that as arithmetic, not as a price list. The available material does not establish an official per-vehicle purchase price, a verified discount, or how any incentive entered the math. A blended figure across a large order can hide options, trims, delivery terms and timing differences.

That caveat is not pedantry. The lawsuit’s central claim is that the effective price fell below a cost benchmark. Proving or disproving that needs invoices, incentive paperwork and Tesla’s internal cost accounting. A headline order value cannot answer it.

The announcement also arrived with messy details. Musk commented publicly on the deal’s status soon after Hertz went public. One claim in the available material says there was no specific deal between the companies, but it is not independently verified here. The court will have to sort the paper record from the press cycle.

Musk’s Full-Price Response and the Core Factual Dispute

Musk has said the Model 3 vehicles Hertz bought went at full price. If true, the below-cost theory weakens sharply, because a car sold at the list price is hard to describe as a predatory sale. His 2021 comments, reported by the BBC, drew the same line. In his words, as reported by the BBC: “To be clear, cars sold to Hertz have no discount. Same price as to consumers.”

Musk added a supply argument in the same period. He said, per the BBC’s reporting: “Tesla has far more demand than production, therefore we will only sell cars to Hertz for the same margin as to consumers.” The logic is straightforward. A seller that cannot build enough cars has little reason to cut prices for a bulk buyer.

Those statements date to 2021, and they are not evidence about what the invoices later showed. The plaintiff’s counter is built into the complaint. It argues that subsidies changed the effective price Hertz paid even if the sticker price matched what consumers saw. That theory treats tax credits as part of the price calculation for a fleet buyer, not as a separate consumer perk.

So the factual dispute has two layers. Layer one asks what Hertz paid per car, in dollars, after every adjustment. Layer two asks how subsidies fit into that number and whether they count toward an antitrust cost test. Both layers need documents. Public statements from either side, however confident, settle neither.

What Below “Average Variable Cost” Means in Antitrust Law

The phrase comes from predatory-pricing doctrine. Courts generally use average variable cost, the per-unit cost that rises and falls with output, as a proxy for whether a price is low enough to hurt rivals instead of competing on merit. Selling above that line is usually treated as legal even if it hurts competitors. Selling below it draws scrutiny.

The two-part test courts apply

In the 1993 Brooke Group decision, the US Supreme Court set out a two-part test for predatory pricing claims. A plaintiff must show the prices were below an appropriate measure of cost. A plaintiff must also show a dangerous probability that the seller will later recoup its losses through higher prices once rivals fade. Courts have treated that second element as hard to prove, which is why successful claims are rare.

The Tesla suit has to climb both steps. Showing a below-cost sale is only half the job. The plaintiff must also persuade a court that Tesla could recoup in a market that now includes many EV sellers from several countries. That is a real obstacle, and defendants will lean on it.

Why fleet deals complicate the analysis

Fleet orders carry features that muddy cost comparisons. Large buyers often get delivery scheduling, bundled services or volume terms that individual buyers never see. A court must decide which of those belong in the price and which belong in the cost. Subsidies add another wrinkle, since government incentives can attach to the buyer, the vehicle or the seller depending on the program.

Variable cost for a car is also not a single number. Battery cells, motors, labor and logistics all move at different rates, and manufacturers account for them differently. Expect expert economists on both sides, each with a model, each with a different answer.

EV Tax Credits in the Complaint: What Is and Is Not Established

Law360’s headline links the suit to EV tax credits and the $4.2 billion fleet deal. The search results on the case identify allegations involving EV tax credits, but they do not establish which credits the complaint cites, how large they were, which vehicles they covered, or whether anyone obtained a credit improperly. We flag that plainly because the headline can read as a fraud claim when the reporting supports a pricing-and-competition claim.

The distinction carries weight. An antitrust claim asks whether conduct harmed competition. A tax-credit misuse claim asks whether someone broke the rules of a government program. The complaint, as described, uses subsidies as a tool inside the antitrust theory. It does not, on the available record, accuse the companies of tax fraud.

Incentive rules for EVs have changed repeatedly in the years since the 2021 order, and they differ for consumers, businesses and leased vehicles. Anyone reading the case should check which program and which year a filing refers to before drawing conclusions. A credit that existed in 2021 may not apply the same way today.

Credits also show up in the used-car channel, which sometimes confuses coverage. Notebookcheck reported on Hertz listing a used 2021 Model 3 at 50% off with a tax credit. That is a resale story about older cars, not evidence about what Hertz paid Tesla. We cite it to show how easily the words “Hertz,” “Model 3” and “tax credit” blur together.

The Fact Ledger: Confirmed, Alleged and Unconfirmed

The table below sorts every major detail by how well the available record supports it. Use it as a filter when you read other coverage of the case.

Nine rows, and only one of them, the 2021 announcement, rests on a confirmed event. Everything else is either a claim, a reported figure or a gap. That ratio is typical for the first days of a big civil case, and it explains why seasoned litigators tell clients to wait for the first substantive ruling before reading too much into the filing.

How Rival EV Makers and Rental Platforms Fit In

The complaint casts rival EV manufacturers as the injured parties. It says the alleged below-cost sales limited their access to rental and ride-hailing platforms. In plain terms, if Hertz filled its lots with Model 3 sedans, a competing EV maker had fewer chances to put its cars in front of renters who might later buy one.

Rental fleets do work as showrooms. Many drivers try a model on a business trip before they consider owning one. Ride-hailing works the same way for riders, with an added twist: drivers choose their vehicles, so platform policies and incentives can steer which cars show up in the app. The plaintiff’s theory depends on that channel effect being large enough to matter to a manufacturer’s sales.

Defendants will answer on market definition. They can argue the relevant market includes every vehicle, not just EVs, and that rental fleets are a thin slice of total demand. They can also point to the many other sellers that compete for fleet business. If the court accepts a broad market, the monopoly claim gets harder. If it accepts a narrow EV market, the plaintiff’s case gains weight.

The available reporting does not identify which rival makers, if any, are plaintiffs or witnesses. We will not guess. Watch the docket for amicus filings, subpoenas to other manufacturers and any rental company that signals it is willing to testify about Tesla’s offers.

Hertz’s Own EV Fleet Reversal: Context, Not Evidence

Hertz’s later EV experience will color how many readers see the lawsuit. Teslarati reported that Hertz announced a strategic decision to slash its EV fleet. Fleet shrinkage by itself says nothing about whether the 2021 purchase prices were lawful. A rental company can overbuy, change its mind and still have paid a fair price.

Stephen Scherr, a former Hertz CEO, spoke about the economics in terms of resale values. He said, in comments published by The Cool Down: “The MSRP [manufacturer suggested retail price] declines in EVs over the course of 2023, driven primarily by Tesla, have driven the fair market value of our EVs lower as compared to last year, such that a salvage creates a larger loss and, therefore, greater burden.”

Read that carefully. Scherr describes Tesla’s price cuts as hurting Hertz’s resale values. That is the opposite of a story in which Tesla subsidized Hertz at a loss to crowd out rivals, though it does not decide the legal question either. The two narratives, a supplier cutting prices to win a fleet and a supplier cutting prices later and hurting the fleet, can both be true at different times.

Tesla’s own legal history provides a broader backdrop. Our coverage of the SEC’s move to close a $41.5 million fair fund involving Musk and Tesla shows the company has faced regulators before and that those matters can run for years. Past disputes do not make the new claims true, and a court should weigh this complaint on its own record.

Uber’s Role: Ride-Hailing as a Second Channel

Uber’s inclusion is the least explained part of the available reporting. The summary says the complaint alleges Tesla’s relationship with Hertz and Uber restricted rival EV makers’ access to rental and ride-hailing platforms. It does not describe a specific Uber contract, program or price. A suit against a platform usually rests on how it treats vehicle suppliers, drivers or incentives, and none of those details is confirmed here.

That uncertainty cuts both ways. Uber can say it is a marketplace, not a car buyer, and that any vehicle partnerships it signs are ordinary commercial arrangements. The plaintiff can say a platform with enough drivers can function as a gatekeeper. Which framing wins depends on facts nobody has shown publicly.

Do not confuse this case with Uber’s other headline this month. Our report on the breach that hit 149,346 drivers through Fireworks AI is a security story with no reported connection to the antitrust complaint. Searchers often lump “Uber lawsuit” stories together, so the separation is worth stating.

For drivers who rent EVs through ride-hailing programs, the practical effect today is nil. No court has ordered any change to rental rates, vehicle availability or incentives. The suit may eventually reshape those terms if the plaintiff wins, but that outcome sits well beyond the current stage.

Historical Context: Why Pricing Fights Take Years

Monopolization cases against dominant technology firms tend to run long. Our explainer on how Microsoft’s 1998 case still shapes three big tech suits shows how arguments about market power, bundling and exclusion recur across decades. The Tesla complaint borrows from the same playbook, with a hardware twist: the alleged exclusion runs through vehicles and fleet channels instead of software bundles.

Predatory-pricing claims have a particularly rough record. Since the Brooke Group decision in 1993, plaintiffs have struggled to meet the recoupment requirement, and many cases end at summary judgment. Defense lawyers know that history and will cite it early.

The industry context is also different from past pricing fights. EV demand has swung, price cuts have rippled across the market, and many manufacturers have launched or expanded their EV lines since 2021. A court asked to find a dangerous probability of recoupment must reckon with that crowded field. Rivals’ growth is not proof of competition in every channel, but it complicates a monopoly narrative.

Government subsidies add a modern complication. Earlier predatory-pricing cases rarely involved public incentives that follow the buyer, the lessor or the manufacturer depending on the rules of the year. The court may need to decide whether a subsidy that lowers a buyer’s net cost counts as the seller’s price cut. No settled answer exists, and an early ruling on that point could matter well beyond this case.

Market Impact: What Investors and Fleet Buyers Should Watch

The available reporting contains no damages figure, so any claim about financial exposure would be guesswork. What investors can do is read the disclosure documents. Tesla’s annual and quarterly filings describe legal proceedings and risk factors, and a new antitrust claim would normally show up there if the company views it as material.

For fleet buyers, the question is contract risk. Large buyers may now ask suppliers to document pricing terms more carefully, including how incentives are allocated. A procurement team that signs a 100,000-vehicle order in the next few years will want a paper trail that survives an antitrust audit. That is a cost, but a manageable one.

Rival EV makers face a different calculation. If the case advances, they may gain leverage in negotiations with rental companies and platforms, since those partners would want to avoid looking like they favor a single supplier. If the case collapses early, that leverage disappears and the status quo holds.

Short-term market moves around a single filing are usually small and fade quickly unless a ruling changes the economics. Our hardware coverage hub tracks the larger forces, such as battery supply, vehicle pricing and charging, that will shape EV fleet decisions regardless of how this lawsuit turns out.

Competitive Comparison: Three Legal Theories Side by Side

The complaint rests mainly on predatory pricing. A plaintiff in a case like this could also have chosen other theories. The table compares the three most common approaches, which helps explain why the pleaded theory is both ambitious and fragile.

The table shows a pattern. Each theory has a clean fit with part of the story and a clear weak spot. Plaintiffs often plead several theories at once for that reason, and the court’s first ruling will reveal which ones the judge thinks can carry weight.

The Hardware Angle: Vehicles as Fleet Assets

A fleet vehicle is a depreciating asset with a cost of capital, a maintenance profile and a resale value. When a manufacturer changes prices, every one of those numbers moves for the buyer. Scherr’s comments on salvage losses make that point from Hertz’s side, and the lawsuit makes it from the competition side.

Tesla is now moving toward new hardware for commercial use. Our report on the Cybercab order page at $29,990 with a $1,000 deposit shows a company pitching vehicles built for fleet and autonomous service. Any court finding about fleet pricing in 2021 will carry weight when regulators look at how Tesla sells to fleets in the future.

Manufacturing scale also feeds the pricing debate. Our look at Tesla’s $3.3 billion Cybercab expansion plan at Giga Berlin shows how much capital goes into capacity. Higher volume lowers per-unit cost, which in antitrust terms moves the line that separates a lawful low price from an unlawful one. A seller that builds more cars can cut prices without crossing the cost floor.

That dynamic works in Tesla’s favor if it can show costs fell with scale. It works against Tesla if the plaintiff can show the 2021 sales happened before those savings arrived. The timing of cost curves relative to the Hertz deliveries may turn into the most contested technical issue in the case.

What to Watch: Procedural Milestones

Civil antitrust cases follow a familiar sequence. The table lists the stages in order, what each one decides and what a reader should look for. We give no dates because none are confirmed.

Most of these stages take months. A single discovery fight can take longer than the first motion. Readers following the case should plan for a long timeline and treat any early headline as a waypoint.

Five Predictions for the Case

These are our analytical judgments, not reported facts. Each one rests on how similar cases have moved and on the gaps in the current record.

Defendants will move to dismiss. Expect Tesla to attack recoupment and market definition, Hertz to say it was a buyer with no motive to exclude anyone, and Uber to argue it never set vehicle prices.

The tax-credit angle will narrow. Courts need a clear rule for counting subsidies as price. Absent one, the judge may confine the case to ordinary pricing evidence.

Discovery will center on Hertz’s invoices. The full-price statement from Musk will be tested against paperwork, and whichever side controls that record will shape the case.

Rival makers will watch but not pile on soon. Copycat suits are unlikely before a ruling shows the theory has legs, since predatory-pricing claims carry a poor track record.

Fleet contracts will get more detailed. Even if the suit fails, procurement teams will document pricing and incentive terms more carefully for future orders.

The takeaway: this antitrust lawsuit is a slow case with a fast headline. The 100,000-vehicle, $4.2 billion order is real and the lawsuit is real, but the claim that Tesla sold below cost remains an allegation that Musk has publicly denied. Until documents surface, neither side has proved much.

FAQ: Tesla, Hertz and Uber Antitrust Lawsuit

Who is being sued, and in what court?

The suit names Tesla, Inc., Hertz Global Holdings, Inc. and Uber Technologies, Inc. It was filed in federal court in California, according to Law360. The case number, the plaintiff’s identity and the filing date are not clearly confirmed in the available reporting.

Has any court found Tesla, Hertz or Uber liable?

No. The claims are allegations in a complaint. No ruling on the merits has been reported, and the defendants have the right to contest every point.

Did Hertz buy Tesla cars at a discount?

The complaint says the pricing fell below average variable cost. Elon Musk has said Hertz paid full price for the Model 3 vehicles. The available material does not establish an official per-vehicle price or a verified discount, so the question is unresolved.

How big was the Hertz order?

Hertz announced a plan in October 2021 to buy 100,000 electric vehicles from Tesla, in a deal reported at approximately $4.2 billion. A rough average of $42,000 per car comes from dividing those two reported numbers and is not an official price.

What does “average variable cost” mean?

It is the per-unit cost that changes with production volume, and courts often use it to judge whether a price is predatory. Sales above that measure are usually treated as lawful competition, while sales below it can support a pricing claim if other elements are also met.

Does the lawsuit change anything for Tesla buyers or renters today?

No. No court has ordered changes to Tesla pricing, rental terms or ride-hailing programs. Consumers and renters see no direct effect unless the case produces a ruling or settlement later.

The geothermal startup Quaise Energy has landed a major first customer for its novel, superhot project in central Oregon.
Quaise will deploy advanced drilling techniques and unique rock-melting technology to access significantly hotter geothermal resources than traditional plants can.
Google said it plans to use the energy to help run its existing data center operations in northwest Oregon as early as 2030.
The deal is valued at more than $500 million, Quaise confirmed.
(Another startup, Mazama Energy, recently nabbed $135 million to accelerate its own superhot geothermal project near the Newberry Volcano.)
text:
The geothermal startup Quaise Energy has landed a major first customer for its novel, superhot project in central Oregon.

On Tuesday, the Houston-based firm announced that Google has agreed to buy 50 megawatts of carbon-free power from Quaise’s first commercial project, called Project Obsidian, near the Newberry Volcano. Quaise will deploy advanced drilling techniques and unique rock-melting technology to access significantly hotter geothermal resources than traditional plants can.

Google said it plans to use the energy to help run its existing data center operations in northwest Oregon as early as 2030.

The deal is valued at more than $500 million, Quaise confirmed. The startup is working to find offtakers for an additional 200 MW in future capacity at the Oregon site.

“We started Quaise to make the Earth’s most abundant energy source universally accessible — and this agreement marks a critical next step, not just for Quaise but for the entire clean energy sector,” Carlos Araque, Quaise’s CEO and president, said in a Tuesday statement.

Quaise is one of at least four U.S. geothermal companies to land agreements with tech giants to pursue next-generation plants. Fervo Energy, the startup that’s furthest along in project development, recently inked a landmark deal to supply Google with nearly 400 MW of clean electricity from the Cape Station facility in southwest Utah. Sage Geosystems and XGS Energy are both partnering with Meta to develop facilities in Nevada and New Mexico, respectively.

Tech firms are seeking to secure sources of clean, around-the-clock power for their vast buildout of data centers. For geothermal startups, winning customer contracts like these is an essential step toward raising the financing they need to build first-of-a-kind facilities. Their technologies, while promising, have yet to be deployed widely at commercial scales — and questions remain about how effectively they’ll be able to operate over long periods of time.

Google is investing in other nascent technologies, too, including long-duration energy storage and advanced nuclear power. ​“The scale of power that we’re looking for and also the scale of impact we’re trying to have on the grid requires us to foster that ecosystem,” Lucia Tian, who leads Google’s advanced energy technologies team, told the Wall Street Journal.

Quaise said its Oregon project will cost about $350 million to build. The company raised $180 million in equity financing in August, which included investment from the oil-and-gas drilling firm Nabors Industries. (Another startup, Mazama Energy, recently nabbed $135 million to accelerate its own superhot geothermal project near the Newberry Volcano.)

At the Project Obsidian site, Quaise will initially use oil-and-gas drilling technologies to develop an enhanced geothermal system. The emerging approach involves fracturing rocks and pumping them full of water to create artificial reservoirs. Surrounding rocks heat the water, which is used to drive turbines on the surface to produce power.

Fervo is deploying this method at Cape Station, which began selling power from an initial 33-MW unit in September — becoming the first utility-scale, next-gen geothermal facility to hit such a milestone worldwide.

Quaise’s goal is to go deeper and hotter. After using conventional tools to drill down some 2.5 miles, the company plans to switch to its millimeter-wave drilling techniques, which involve deploying high-frequency beams that melt and vaporize rocks. Quaise aims to tap into superhot rock, with temperatures above 572 degrees Fahrenheit, to derive more energy from a relatively smaller number of wells.

The startup is still testing the unique technology it plans to deploy for the Google-backed power plant. Quaise said it drilled through more than 330 feet of granite at its field site in central Texas last year, and is now working to reach down over 3,200 feet, or about 0.6 mile, at the same site.

title: HYBRID DEMAND REVS UP | USA TODAY US Edition - PressReader
description:
The aver­age days’ sup­ply of new hybrid vehicles in stock at deal­er­ships in the United States on March 1 was about 60 days, Roberts said.
An example of one would be the Toyota RAV4 hybrid or the Ford Mav­er­ick hybrid.
For example, the Toyota High­lander hybrid ver­sion accounts for 65.7% of the vehicle’s sales, the Toyota Grand High­lander hybrid accounts for 61.5%, and the Ford Mav­er­ick hybrid at 59.9%.
Mean­while, Toyota offers the largest hybrid lineup in the United States, includ­ing mod­els where hybrid is the stand­ard or primary offer­ing, such as the Toyota Camry Hybrid, Toyota RAV4 Hybrid, Toyota Corolla Hybrid, Toyota Crown and Toyota Grand High­lander Hybrid.
Hyundai sells the Hyundai Elantra Hybrid, Hyundai Son­ata Hybrid, and Hyundai Tuc­son Hybrid.
text:
DETROIT – Vehicles with a hybrid power­train are hav­ing a moment and Asian auto­makers are bene­fit­ing.

Accord­ing to the Car­Gurus Third-Quarter Intel­li­gence Report, hybrids are the only main­stream power­train see­ing new vehicle sales growth this year, to the point that demand for them is out­pa­cing sup­ply and when the vehicles are avail­able, they are com­mand­ing a premium that could range from $1,300 to $2,400 – a price many car buy­ers are will­ing to pay, the report said.

It’s all because of the price for reg­u­lar gas­ol­ine, which reached $4.48 per gal­lon in late Septem­ber, the highest national aver­age ever recor­ded for this time of year, accord­ing to AAA.

“Hybrids already had seen really good growth in 2025, and it con­tin­ued into 2026,” Car­Gurus’ Dir­ector of Eco­nomic and Mar­ket Intel­li­gence Kevin Roberts told the Detroit Free Press, part of the USA TODAY Net­work. “I think that would have con­tin­ued without gas prices. Gas prices were just an accel­er­at­ing factor towards addi­tional demand out there because, as gas prices go up, con­sumer interest in the more fuel effi­cient vehicles fol­lows.”

The res­ult is demand out­pa­cing sup­ply. The aver­age days’ sup­ply of new hybrid vehicles in stock at deal­er­ships in the United States on March 1 was about 60 days, Roberts said. At the end of Septem­ber, the aver­age day sup­ply of new hybrids dropped to 38 days, he said.

The aver­age day sup­ply of new cars in elec­tric and gas­ol­ine power­trains is also lower at the end of Septem­ber com­pared with March 1, but not as dra­mat­ic­ally. The aver­age day sup­ply of new EVs on March 1 was 135.8 and sup­ply of new gas vehicles was 87.7 days. On Sept. 30, the aver­age day sup­ply of new EVs was 68.9 days and gas­ol­ine cars was 80.7 days.

Win for Asian auto­makers

A tra­di­tional hybrid vehicle com­bines a gas­ol­ine engine with an elec­tric motor and self-char­ging bat­tery pack to move the car.

“Most auto­makers went pretty much on the EV path. Toyota and Honda, and now Hyundai, are kind of more on the dif­fer­ent path of hav­ing more hybrid options out there. So they’re obvi­ously bene­fit­ing right now on that front.”

Kevin Roberts

Car­Gurus’ Dir­ector of Eco­nomic and Mar­ket Intel­li­gence

So unlike plug-in hybrids or EVs, a tra­di­tional hybrid never needs to be plugged into a power out­let. It recharges its bat­tery using energy from the gas­ol­ine engine and regen­er­at­ive brak­ing. These are the hybrids, Roberts said, that are in the most demand. An example of one would be the Toyota RAV4 hybrid or the Ford Mav­er­ick hybrid.

A typ­ical hybrid can get 40 to 60 miles per gal­lon of fuel eco­nomy. Most mod­ern gas­ol­ine powered vehicles get 25 to 30 miles per gal­lon, accord­ing to Mer­cury Insur­ance.

With that in mind and con­sid­er­ing the rising gas prices, Car­Gurus’ report shows that sales of new cars with hybrid power­trains are up 24% through the end of the quarter com­pared to the same period a year earlier. Even the sales of used cars with hybrid power­trains are up nearly 33%.

Mean­while, sales of gas­ol­ine-powered cars are down 2% and sales of allelec­tric vehicles are down 48%. Roberts said Car­Gurus con­sidered the fact that some big sellers, such as Toyota’s RAV4, are only offered in a hybrid power­train, so he con­duc­ted the study to focus on mod­els where there is a higher demand rate for hybrid power­trains over the gas­ol­ine power­train option.

Roberts wrote in the report that across sev­eral vehicle mod­els, sales of new hybrids now out­sell their gas coun­ter­parts. For example, the Toyota High­lander hybrid ver­sion accounts for 65.7% of the vehicle’s sales, the Toyota Grand High­lander hybrid accounts for 61.5%, and the Ford Mav­er­ick hybrid at 59.9%. The trend is a win for the Asian auto­makers, which dom­in­ate the mar­ket in hybrid offer­ings, whereas Detroit­based auto­makers chose to focus on gas­ol­ine and elec­tric vehicles, with few hybrid power­trains to offer.

“Most auto­makers went pretty much on the EV path,” Roberts said, not­ing that Detroit car­makers formed their busi­ness plans sev­eral years ago when gov­ern­ment policy was point­ing towards EVs as the future. “Toyota and Honda, and now Hyundai, are kind of more on the dif­fer­ent path of hav­ing more hybrid options out there. So they’re obvi­ously bene­fit­ing right now on that front.”

Hybrid offer­ings in North Amer­ica

In North Amer­ica, Stel­lantis sells the 2026 Jeep Cher­o­kee as a tra­di­tional hybrid; Ford Motor sells the Mav­er­ick mid­size pickup and F-150 full-size pickup in tra­di­tional hybrid offer­ings, and Gen­eral Motors sells the Chev­ro­let Cor­vette ERay, a tra­di­tional hybrid.

Mean­while, Toyota offers the largest hybrid lineup in the United States, includ­ing mod­els where hybrid is the stand­ard or primary offer­ing, such as the Toyota Camry Hybrid, Toyota RAV4 Hybrid, Toyota Corolla Hybrid, Toyota Crown and Toyota Grand High­lander Hybrid. Honda offers the Honda Accord Hybrid and Honda CR-V Hybrid. Hyundai sells the Hyundai Elantra Hybrid, Hyundai Son­ata Hybrid, and Hyundai Tuc­son Hybrid. Kia offers Kia Niro Hybrid and Kia Sorento Hybrid. Mazda has the CX-50 Hybrid.

Hybrids still ‘rel­at­ively’ afford­able

Roberts said Car­Gurus data showed that, on its web­site, con­sumer views of new cars with hybrid power­trains are up by 23% as of Sept. 30 com­pared with March 1. Con­sumer views of EVs is up 21%. But con­sumer views of gas­ol­ine powered cars is down 4%.

The rising demand for hybrids and the dwind­ling sup­ply of them means for top-selling 2026 mod­els, which are offered in gas­ol­ine and hybrid power­trains with sim­ilar trims, the aver­age hybrid premium is $1,300 – $2,400 above the price, Roberts said.

Still, the shift in interest to hybrids, is more than people just want­ing bet­ter fuel effi­ciency. “The top-selling new hybrids also sit in a rel­at­ively access­ible range: the Ford Mav­er­ick aver­ages $34,200, the Toyota Camry $35,900, the Honda CR-V Hybrid $40,800, and the Toyota RAV4 $41,300,” Roberts wrote in the Car­Gurus report. “Toyota accounts for 47.2% of new hybrid sales and holds four of the top five spots among the top-selling new hybrids. Its most pop­u­lar mod­els barely touch the lot: the RAV4 turns in 15.6 days, the Grand High­lander Hybrid in 16 days, the Sienna in 17.3 days, and the Camry in 21.7 days.”

Still, Roberts said when look­ing at over­all sales of new hybrid vehicles as a per­cent­age of total new vehicle sales, hybrids remain “a minor­ity num­ber” with gas­ol­ine being the dom­in­ate power­train option in the United States. But hybrid power­train options give auto­makers an oppor­tun­ity for new vehicle sales growth, he said.

“Par­tic­u­larly as more hybrid options come out in pop­u­lar vehicles that are already (gas­ol­ine) options, if the premium is not sig­ni­fic­ant, I think there’s def­in­itely oppor­tun­ity for those auto­makers to increase their hybrid share when they come to mar­ket,” Roberts said.

text:
Appalachian Power is investing $17 billion in new natural gas-fired electricity generation, in addition to a separate $7.5 billion commitment to upgrade existing coal-fired power plants, West Virginia Governor Patrick Morrisey announced.

Appalachian Power’s $17 billion investment will add 3 GW of natural gas-fired generation, with all new capacity expected to be operational by 2031. The investment is expected to create approximately 2,050 construction jobs and 100 permanent jobs. The announcement surpasses the approximately 2.9-GW John Amos Power Plant announcement from the early 1970s as the largest single power generation announcement by capacity in West Virginia history, Governor Morrisey’s office noted. Appalachian Power also committed $7.5 billion toward upgrading its existing coal-fired power plants through 2050.

“West Virginia has some of the greatest energy resources in the country, and our people should benefit from them,” said Governor Morrisey. “Families are struggling with rising costs, and too many are seeing more of their paychecks consumed by electric bills. We’re tackling that problem from both directions, helping families reduce their energy use while increasing the supply of affordable, reliable electricity.”

The expansion will move forward under Governor Morrisey’s ratepayer protection pledge, which is meant to ensure that infrastructure costs associated with these new developments are not shifted onto existing residential and business customers.

The new generation brings the total announced since the Governor launched his 50 by 50 initiative in September 2025 to 11.67 GW, representing more than 34% of the additional capacity needed to reach 50 GW by 2050. With the $17 billion generation investment, West Virginia has now announced $113.6 billion in private-sector investment and 21,030 projected jobs since October 2025.

“While other states are restricting energy production and retiring reliable power plants, West Virginia is increasing its energy supply,” said Governor Morrisey. “By protecting our existing generation and building the capacity we’ll need for decades to come, we will strengthen reliability, create good-paying jobs, and work toward more affordable electricity for West Virginia families and businesses.”

The Governor also highlighted Google’s $10 million Energy Impact Program, including an initial $1 million investment through the West Virginia Office of Energy to help families in Putnam, Kanawha, Cabell, Mason, Jackson, and Lincoln counties make home repairs necessary to qualify for energy rebates, while supporting efficiency improvements for local governments and nonprofits.

text:
Just 403 hyperscale datacenters consumed an estimated 1.8 percent of US electricity in 2024-25, and their carbon dioxide emissions were roughly two to three times an earlier forecast for 2018.

Research led by the Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health and the Harvard Data Science Initiative looked specifically at hyperscale facilities, the largest class of server farms that typically support cloud computing and AI processing.

The published study, "Assessing the carbon emissions and energy consumption of US hyperscale data centres," estimates their combined electricity use approached that of a single state such as Indiana, Michigan, or Tennessee under the highest-load scenario.

The researchers identified 403 hyperscale facilities by using a larger datacenter dataset, satellite imagery, and building footprints on OpenStreetMap.

Rather than reading electricity meters, the researchers worked out consumption from each site's electrical capacity, the hours in a year, and assumptions about how heavily the facility was running.

Across four operating scenarios, ranging from low-intensity use to AI-heavy workloads, electricity draw was believed to total 68-99 terawatt-hours (TWh). Each of those states consumed approximately 100 TWh during the study period.

The researchers also calculated carbon dioxide (CO2) emissions using eGRID2023 plant-level generation and emissions data from the US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA). Emissions ranged from 21 million to 31 million metric tons of CO2 across the scenarios, with a central estimate of 25.7 million. That compares with 10.5 million for 2018.

The study covered May 2024 to April 2025, so electricity demand and carbon emissions are likely to be even higher now, the researchers say.

"What we're seeing is already striking, but it's only a snapshot of a rapidly expanding industry," said Gianluca Guidi, lead author on the paper and postdoctoral fellow in the Department of Biostatistics at Harvard.

"The datacenter boom hasn't slowed down since our study period ended in April 2025. New facilities have been built, existing campuses have expanded, and demand for AI computing continues to grow. That means the electricity use and carbon footprint we're reporting could already be substantially larger now in 2026."

Harvard's report also considers the mix of fuels being used to generate the electricity that powers all those hyperscale data houses. The mix varies considerably between regional grids, so where a hyperscale facility is built makes a substantial difference to its attributed emissions.

Across the sites studied, roughly 54 percent of the electricity attributed to their consumption came from fossil fuels, mainly natural gas and coal. The electricity attributed to these facilities nevertheless had a lower average carbon intensity than the US grid overall.

The researchers acknowledge limitations, including that there wasn't enough available data to study all hyperscale sites in the US, and that the data did not allow them to differentiate between power used for general-purpose compute versus AI-specialized operations at individual campuses. ®

text:
conservationalliance

18h

A bill is moving through Congress that could threaten our public lands. The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA) is being labeled by proponents as a “clean energy bill,” and while it does address important issues related to energy development, as it is currently written, it could lead to several concerning outcomes:

❌ Key landscapes like Thompson Divide, the Boundary Waters, and Chaco Canyon could face near-inevitable development - even after being protected by prior administrations.

❌ Bedrock environmental laws like the National Historic Preservation Act (NHPA), the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA), the Endangered Species Act (ESA), and the Clean Water Act (CWA), could be weakened.

❌ Stakeholder consultation could be made optional, limiting the ability of Tribal nations, states, and other groups to steward and protect sacred landscapes and sites.

Legislators are pushing to pass BAAJA before the end of the year - but we’re urging our nation’s leaders to amend the bill before it advances in the Senate and on to the House. The Conservation Alliance and our over 200 business members hope to see a clean energy future that supports our outdoor economy, recreation, access, and gateway communities across the U.S.

description:

text:
U.S. Senate Republicans are pushing a plan to redirect about $2 billion, budgeted for building electric vehicle charging infrastructure, to other transport projects. Concerns are growing that state projects that have already begun building chargers could face disruptions.

Cleantechnica reported on Nov. 17 that Senate Republicans proposed using about $1.97 billion allocated to the National Electric Vehicle Infrastructure (NEVI) program for general road and rail projects in a draft 2027 transport appropriations bill.

Republicans earlier redirected about $500 million in NEVI funds for other uses in the 2026 fiscal year budget. If the latest proposal is also implemented, additional burdens are expected for projects under way across the United States to expand fast-charging networks.

NEVI is a program that supports states in building fast-charging stations under the bipartisan infrastructure law enacted in 2021. All 50 states, Washington, D.C., and Puerto Rico have had their plans to use the funds approved, and more than half of the available budget has already been allocated to individual projects.

A representative case is Texas. The Texas Department of Transportation last month announced a plan to use $226 million in federal support to build 321 additional charging sites. Ohio, where charging stations are already widely in operation, could also have difficulty securing remaining project funding.

Environmental group Sierra Club criticised the move, saying it would hinder EV adoption and the expansion of access to charging. Katherine Garcia (캐서린 가르시아), director of the Sierra Club's Clean Transportation for All, pointed out that "it is unacceptable that, following delays caused by the Trump administration's freeze of NEVI funds, an additional diversion of the budget is now being pursued."

The Trump administration had frozen the execution of NEVI funds shortly after taking office, but the freeze was lifted after lawsuits by Sierra Club and state governments. After that, support for charging projects worth hundreds of millions of dollars resumed in each state.

The budget diversion, however, is a legislative proposal that has not yet been confirmed. The impact on projects could vary depending on whether it is reflected in the final appropriations bill. Uncertainty over federal financial support for EV charging infrastructure is expected to continue for the time being.

text:
The Trump administration is reassessing a permit for a wind farm planned off the New Jersey coast as the Senate nears a vote on legislation to overhaul the federal process for approving large energy projects.

The US Army Corps of Engineers said Tuesday it is reevaluating an approval for EDF Renewables North America’s Atlantic Shores South, which has proposed constructing as many as 200 wind turbines about 9 miles off the coast of Atlantic City.

A spokesperson for France-based parent company Electricite de France SA did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The move comes as wind projects have become a flash point as the Senate considers a broad energy bill. The legislation would expedite the federal approval process for a range of projects including oil pipelines, electric plants and power lines as artificial intelligence drives surging electricity demand.

The Army Corps’ reconsideration of the wind farm also comes after the Trump administration invalidated a key Environmental Protection Agency air pollution permit for the project in March weeks after president said he wished it was “dead and gone.” Another key approval was remanded to a federal court for reconsideration by the Interior Department in August.

The Trump administration has begun lifting a blockade that had stalled several onshore wind farms on national security grounds in what has been cast as a show of good faith — and a partial fulfillment of an administration promise to advance some wind projects needed to garner Democratic support for the permitting reform bill.

Still, opponents of the bill have seized on President Donald Trump’s remarks last week as the Senate began reviewing the legislation that he didn’t plan to approve wind projects in the future.

“The bill hasn’t been fully negotiated,” Trump said in response questions about the reforms, which the president said he supported. “I will not approve wind turbines because wind turbines are a major loser.”

A White House official said at the time the president stands behind the permitting bill and has been working in good faith with Senate Democrats for a month to get the bill passed to unleash more American energy and lower costs.

text:
A Novi battery maker that once set its sights on powering electric vehicles is now headed for Wall Street instead. Our Next Energy and Wen Acquisition Corp. announced Monday a definitive business combination agreement that would take the Michigan company public, valuing the combined business at roughly $1 billion in pro forma equity.

The deal, first detailed in a release distributed via GlobeNewswire, is expected to close in the first half of 2027, pending shareholder approvals and other customary closing conditions. Once the transaction wraps up, the combined company is expected to trade on Nasdaq under the ticker symbol ONEE. As Crain's Detroit reported, the move caps a dramatic turn for a company that began with ambitions to electrify the automotive industry.

From EV Dreams to Rail and Defense Contracts

Our Next Energy, headquartered in Novi, Michigan, originally built its business around electric-vehicle battery technology. That changed in January, when the company announced it had suspended its automotive electrification efforts entirely, redirecting its focus toward rail, defense and utility-scale energy storage. The announcement at the time stated plainly that the company had moved away from the EV market it once hoped to serve.

The shift wasn't just strategic messaging — it reshaped the company's Novi footprint. The same January announcement said the facility had been retooled for three rail-industry products while retaining the ability to manufacture grid-scale energy storage system modules. Today, the company builds battery energy storage systems used in hybrid locomotives, mobile microgrids and large-scale grid storage, using its own packs and electronics at its Novi headquarters.

Revenue Claims and a Contested Funding Detail

Per the announcement circulated on GlobeNewswire, Our Next Energy's Novi facility still houses a battery-pack production line with a stated annual capacity of 3 gigawatt-hours. The company says it has built $40 million in cumulative revenue and has more than $200 million in binding multiyear contracts.

The financing picture tied to the deal carries some ambiguity. The GlobeNewswire release states that $30 million of a $100 million private investment in public equity, or PIPE, was committed at the time of the announcement. But an account from TipRanks describes that same $30 million differently, characterizing it as identified to date through $20 million funded in October and a separate $10 million non-binding letter of intent. The two accounts don't fully align on how firm that funding commitment is.

A Grid-Storage Market on the Rise

Our Next Energy's pivot toward grid-scale storage lands amid rapid growth in that sector nationally. According to the U.S. Energy Information Administration, operators added 8.3 gigawatts of battery storage capacity during the first half of 2026, pushing total nameplate battery storage capacity to nearly 52 gigawatts nationwide. That broader buildout offers some context for why a company once focused on EV batteries might see opportunity in grid infrastructure instead.

For now, the deal remains unfinished business — contingent on shareholder votes and other conditions before any shares change hands on Nasdaq. Whether the public markets embrace a company that abandoned its original EV mission in favor of rail, defense and grid contracts will likely become clearer as the 2027 timeline for closing approaches.

title: If BAAJA passes, then what? - by Bill McKibben
description:
Sometime late tonight or tomorrow, it seems highly likely that the Senate will pass the “permitting reform” legislation doing business under the name “BAAJA” for Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act.
So I’d guess it’s going to become law, which means it’s worth thinking about the context, and the room for maneuver going forward.
BAAJA isn’t quite like that.
The American Petroleum Institute and other oil lobbyists clearly think that BAAJA is going to help, not hurt, them.
“Looks like it’s powered by ten hairdryers,” said Paul Lucas, a British travel influencer, on his X account.
text:
Sometime late tonight or tomorrow, it seems highly likely that the Senate will pass the “permitting reform” legislation doing business under the name “BAAJA” for Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act. (Vote Tracker website here, courtesy of the people at No Dirty Data Center Deal). I’ve been urging its defeat, and I’ll keep at it—in case you’re still trying to persuade your Senator or Congressperson, here’s some segments from Ed Markey’s 30-minute speech opposing the bill, here’s Naomi Klein making an impassioned argument about how out-of-step all this is with the recent election, here’s the forever eloquent Ayana Johnson laying out ten easy-to-understand reasons why it should be beaten, here’s old hand Colin Rees making the argument from COP in Turkey, and here’s the Center for Western Priorities explaining the damage that’s likely to come for iconic American landscapes. Oh, and here’s some guy named Al Gore, also at the global climate talks in Turkey and speaking out with particular passion:

“The fact that President Trump endorsed it enthusiastically is a clue, the fact that the American Petroleum Institute is giving out free tacos in Washington to support it is also a clue. I hope they reconsider because I think it would be a very, very serious mistake.”

“Trump will implement any legislation given to him in a way that continues to redeem his unethical pledge to the fossil fuel industry during his campaign,” Gore said, referencing Trump’s promise to provide help to oil and gas executives in return for donations prior to the 2024 election.

Keep passing the messages on to the decision-makers—DC is a strange place and who knows exactly how it will end up. (Kate Waxman in Inside Climate News reports some chance the House may slow the process). But there’s no filibuster in the House, the GOP still has a majority until January, and Big Oil is big behind this bill. (And Stephen Miller has listed it as one of his top priorities!). So I’d guess it’s going to become law, which means it’s worth thinking about the context, and the room for maneuver going forward.

The laws that will be rendered much less powerful—things like the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA) and the Clean Water Act were products of the 1960s environmental upheaval, which began with Silent Spring and reached its zenith with the first Earth Day in April of 1970, and the elections that fall when ecology campaigners knocked off a bunch of the congressmen it had identified as a “dirty dozen.” It was, that is, the product of a broad societal consensus that had emerged that we needed to do something to stem pollution.

BAAJA isn’t quite like that. As Emily Atkin points out there’s been essentially no media coverage (Substack, not the tv networks or metro newspapers, is where most of the fight has taken place). This far-reaching reset of the nation’s environmental laws is being rushed through a lame-duck Congress without hearings, and opposed by a fairly wide swath of civil society—environmental groups, racial justice groups, and the like. Its chief champion in the Senate is Sheldon Whitehouse, but he hasn’t been able to bring along any of the other Democrats on the Environment and Public Works committee where he’s the ranking member—indeed, many of the other members of the upper chamber historically most committed to environmental action are actively opposing it, including Jeff Merkley who will soon take over the committee. It’s also opposed by a number of tribal groups—Emily Pontecorvo has a good explainer on those issues, and if you’re still on Twitter Julian Brave Noisecat has been keeping up a steady commentary.

The momentum to pass the bill is coming largely on the back of one book, Abundance by Ezra Klein and Derek Thompson, and the YIMBY movement that helped empower. (As a book-writer myself, I confess to always being pleased when a volume exerts real political power, even if I disagree with the outcome). Klein offered a straightforward and non-hyperbolic defense of the idea in the Times last week that comes with a reasonable dose of humility

I don’t want this column to read as more confident about this bill than I really am. It is more than 400 pages, with much of it dedicated to technical changes to other laws. I’ve been unnerved, while reporting this story, by Capitol Hill staff members telling me precisely opposite things about the same provisions. Legislation at this scale rarely plays out exactly as its architects expect.

The question here is less whether Klein is right or wrong to back the bill (Abigail Dillen of Earth Justice offers a spirited point by point response here) than it is to say nobody really knows—it is a black box of a bill. And unlike paving the way for more housing or train tracks or other items on the YIMBY agenda, there’s a real danger here: if, as many expect, it lets us lock in lots of natural gas pipelines in the next couple of years, the longer-term clean energy gains may be overwhelmed by the flow of methane and carbon into the atmosphere.

But there’s no question that Klein’s argument—which again is a real argument, drawing on longstanding frustrations with our ability to get stuff built in this country—has persuaded the class of people who sit, say, on the boards of big nonprofits. That these are rarely people who have to rely on existing laws to protect people and communities they care about is notable; there’s a certain hubris that goes with deciding your sense of the common good outweighs the ability of people to defend their places. Just randomly this morning I got an email from some farmers in North Carolina trying to stop a Duke gas pipeline from going through their land.

“With new gas infrastructure proposed on this tract, we are asking for an updated ecological survey and public scrutiny of how this history is being considered. What remains deserves a thorough assessment before further disturbance.”

Here’s some coverage that explains things a little more, and a recent poster from their fight:

I fear this kind of project is going to be very hard to fight post-BAAJA, and I think it’s going to be very strange for Americans to find that they essentially have no real way to make a case against the rich and powerful. It’s possible, again, that the common good may trump all these individual cases, which I think is part of the Abundance argument—but it’s definitely going to be very different. In fact, I’m willing to predict it’s going to piss a lot of people off, who will want to know why they’ve been disempowered.

So, assuming it passes, there should be pressure on Democrats in Congress—and on presidential primary candidates—to figure out how they’re going to rebalance things here, to give Americans new ways to stand up to concentrated power. Things like “polluter pays” bills that target the fossil fuel industry are going to be more important than ever; advocacy at public utility commissions and state agencies will be ever more crucial. The American Petroleum Institute and other oil lobbyists clearly think that BAAJA is going to help, not hurt, them. (Here’s a picture of the truck they hired to cruise Capitol Hill, handing out free tacos)

We’re going to need some tools to stand up to that power, and hopefully there will be some chastened Senators to provide them.

The clean-tech industry has been squarely behind the BAJAA laws—but of course that’s because it will help their businesses even if it doesn’t do much for the planet. (A solar business can prosper even as fracked gas does the same). Still, it is something of a consolation to be at the big RE+ renewable energy trade show in Las Vegas today, with 34,000 attendees gathered to sign deals, network, and show off their astonishing mountains of gear.

There are vast chambers filled with—pile driving machines, robots that can install solar panels, robots that can clean solar panels, robots that act as artificial sheep trimming grass (I prefer sheep sheep—there are a bunch of those out in the parking lot, munching on hay around a solar panel), and all the other stuff you need to run a renewable economy. The rooms go on forever—this is clearly an industry that’s reached some early stage of maturity, no longer “alternative energy” but now a clear competitor for providing this most important of commodities.

The one thing that’s lacking (except for the sheep) is any sense of romance. This technology, and this technology alone, runs some chance of preserving a livable, beautiful planet. This technology stands some chance of giving us a peaceful world where we don’t fight endlessly for oil. This technology is inherently liberating, a way to produce a planet where each community has some control over its own destiny. This technology will let people have free electricity, as they already for three hours a day in Australia. And yet you’d never know that from wandering these vast sheds of equipment, all sold on the premise that its makers have connected six gigawatts or delivered 80,000 continuous hours of power.

The best argument I’ve heard for permitting reform came from Jigar Shah, longtime clean energy advocate, who said at the Vegas convention this afternoon that the permitting reform set up a “fair foot race” between clean energy and dirty, adding, as he pointed to the businesspeople around him, “I believe in you guys.” I fear, of course, that he’s not correct, and that in fact BAJAA ties a heavy rock to the ankle of solar and wind. But if he’s right, or close to it, then victory still depends on the clean energy industry telling its story in ways that connect with people—in building the information apparatus to compete with the absurd but effective myths of the fossil fuel guys.

We’re in a new world, we’ve got to figure out the rules, and we’ve got to fight like hell. As if everything depends on it, because it does.

In other energy and climate news:

+The Guardian has a sobering roundup of the year’s bad weather

After the world’s hottest summer since records began in 1850, the death toll from extreme weather in 2026 is already in the high tens of thousands. That is a conservative estimate and is certain to rise much higher.

As Cop31 continues and scientists warn that climate breakdown may be accelerating, the Guardian looks back at a year of droughts, fires and floods as a reminder that, unless the world takes urgent action to cut emissions, this disastrous year will be one of the best of the rest of our lives.

+Who’d a thunk it? New evidence, reports Rebecca John, shows more depth on the evidence that Shell knew all about the damage ahead from climate change

Evidence uncovered by DeSmog in collaboration with Rolling Stone reveals explosive new details of Shell’s decades of climate research that warned the company burning fossil fuels could lead to worsening storms — including studies conducted at the Climatic Research Unit (CRU), the UK’s first specialist climate research center established by Shell on the campus of a university in eastern England in 1972.

Some of these documents might have been lost forever, had a sharp-eyed faculty member not rescued them from a dumpster where they’d been thrown out after the retirement of the CRU’s first director, the UK’s leading climatologist, Hubert Lamb. Now preserved inside the temperature-controlled archives at the University of East Anglia, a few miles outside the medieval city of Norwich, these and other files contain handwritten notes, official correspondence, and reports that hold secrets of Shell’s early climate research, detailing a program that would give the company advance warning of the numerous threats climate change posed to its business — if not to the people, like Arnold and his island neighbors, liable to suffer the most harm.

Documents from the late 1960s show Shell playing a pivotal role in establishing the center before paying the CRU to carry out an in-depth “North Sea Storms Study” beginning in the mid-1970s. The findings warned Shell that storms in Europe’s North Sea — home to the company’s burgeoning offshore drilling business — were increasing. Rising atmospheric carbon dioxide (CO2) levels due to the burning of fossil fuels might be the most likely explanation, the Shell-funded study concluded.

+Absurdly, the UK is banning climate author Andreas Malm from entering for a speech. As Matthew Weaver explains,

Malm, a respected Swedish climate academic and author of How to Blow Up a Pipeline, was prevented from travelling to the UK. Officials told him that his presence was “not considered to be conducive to the public good”, but no further reasons were given.

Title aside, Malm is a serious writer and his voice deserves to be heard.

+The Times reports on a study showing that the carbon emissions of America’s big data centers are collectively larger than a large nation like Kenya. I mean, that’s silly. Here’s Harry Stevens:

Across all 403 facilities, 54 percent of the electricity came from burning fossil fuels, mostly natural gas and coal.

Much of the analysis in the study amounted to detective work, underscoring the secrecy under which A.I. companies have been allowed to operate. Without a public list of data centers to work with, the researchers began by consulting a commercial dataset whose licensing rules prevented them — and The New York Times — from publishing facilities’ addresses, names and owners.

The researchers spent hours studying building footprints and satellite imagery to confirm the location and size of data centers, estimated how much electricity they could use and then calculated their emissions based on the mix of power plants supplying each regional electricity grid.

“The fact that we had to go through such an extensive reconstruction process just to understand where the infrastructure is and how large it is tells you something about the lack of transparency itself in the industry,” said Gianluca Guidi, the Harvard scientist who led the research team.

+New York State got a new slate of climate champions out of the election, Collin Kinniburgh reports

The newly expanded Democratic supermajorities in the state Assembly and Senate include some 50 newcomers to the legislature, among them a slew of climate-minded progressives.

In the Hudson Valley, county legislator Lisa Kaul, who’s said she “entered electoral politics because I really wanted to do something about climate change,” flipped a Republican-held Senate seat.

In the Buffalo area, democratic socialist Adam Bojak — a housing rights lawyer who wants to build green public housing and expand transit — won an Assembly seat.

And across the state, candidates rode a tide of anger over energy-hungry data centers and high utility bills to oust incumbents.

Altogether, at least 15 incoming Senate and Assembly members campaigned explicitly on climate issues, according to a New York Focus tally. About a dozen championed greater public control of the energy system — through building more publicly owned wind and solar, taking over local utilities, or both.

+Farai Mutsaka, with an update on the rapid spread of e-bikes and tricycles across Africa

Across parts of Africa, motorcycles and three-wheelers are emerging as a route to electric mobility, particularly in rural communities long overlooked by conventional mobility businesses. While electric cars gain ground in wealthier markets, these smaller vehicles can operate with less extensive and expensive charging infrastructure, offering a potentially cheaper leapfrog to electrification for the continent of 1.5 billion people.

The shift also has potential public health benefits. Electric motorcycles and three-wheelers produce no exhaust fumes, offering an opportunity to reduce roadside pollution. In Kenya’s capital, Nairobi, where motorcycles are part of public transport culture, road transport alone is responsible for 40% of fine particle air pollution, according to the Clean Air Fund.

A 2025 study published in the World Electric Vehicle Journal also found that electrifying Nairobi’s motorcycle fleet would eliminate tailpipe particulate emissions from those vehicles, while cutting daily automotive carbon dioxide emissions by about 85%.

Meanwhile, in Bangladesh, a huge switch away from natural gas in the wake of the Iran war, in one of the world’s fast-growing nations

A cramped market in the heart of Dhaka has become an unlikely ground zero for Bangladesh’s energy transition. Down narrow aisles crowded with shoppers and delivery workers, tiny storefronts are overflowing with rows of solar panels and batteries.

Monju Hossain, a sales representative for Dongjin Group Bangladesh, said the retailer is struggling to keep up with demand, with sales jumping 50% in recent months from a year earlier. The country’s worsening energy crisis, triggered by the war in the Middle East, is pushing households and businesses to seek alternatives to an increasingly unreliable grid.

Oh, and check out the airplane that took to the skies in China last week. They’re calling it the “hairdryer plane” because of the rows of small engines along the wing

The 10-tonne CE-25A completed a 38-mile circuit lasting 17 minutes. There were two pilots and an engineer on board the aircraft, which is designed for 19 passengers plus crew.

Painted revolutionary red, the aircraft’s most striking feature is its array of 10 electric-ducted fans, with five mounted on top of each wing.

“Looks like it’s powered by ten hairdryers,” said Paul Lucas, a British travel influencer, on his X account.

Comac’s video of the test flight immediately went viral on social media, with many posts speculating whether China might dominate the electric aircraft market in the same way it now does for electric vehicles.

Congress is weighing a transportation proposal that would add a recurring expense for drivers whose cars do not use gasoline.

Here's what to know

Electric vehicle owners would pay a federal fee of $130 a year, and plug-in hybrid owners would pay an annual charge of $35. For electric vehicle owners, the fee could climb by $5 each year until reaching a $150 ceiling, according to a CNN report published by WAFB.

The charges are part of a surface transportation bill and have not taken effect. Congress would need to approve the legislation before drivers would have to pay.

Buying gasoline generates tax revenue that covers a portion of the cost of road projects.

Supporters describe the proposed fee as a way to collect contributions toward road costs from electric vehicle drivers. Those drivers do not pay gasoline taxes because fully electric cars require no gasoline, according to CNN.

What's being done?

With the existing surface transportation funding authorization set to expire in December, Congress is considering legislation that includes the proposed charges. December is the earliest drivers could be charged the federal vehicle fees, and that start would depend on Congress approving the legislation.

text:
The “blue wave” could lead to stronger protective climate policies in Los Angeles, though it remains contested at the federal level, legal experts said at a UCLA School of Law panel Nov. 9.

UCLA’s Laboratory for Environmental Narrative Strategies hosted the event as part of its 10-year anniversary series to unpack how the results of the 2026 midterm elections will affect climate policy in the United States.

Democrats won control over both chambers of Congress in the midterms, flipping eight Senate seats and more than 40 House of Representatives seats in what has been named the “blue wave.” The 55-seat Senate majority would be the second-largest for either party since 1994, according to CNN.

Earlier on the same day of the panel, the U.S. Senate voted to advance the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026, which aims to expedite federal environmental reviews and permits for building infrastructure and energy projects.

While some panelists said the bill was rushed and could weaken certain environmental protections from the Biden administration, others said it could help by increasing long-distance power lines.

“The fact that the Democrats, after a generational victory last week, were willing to make a deal with Republicans on a bill that is pretty bad for the environment,” said Alejandro Camacho, a professor of law, “it’s quite remarkable.”

Environmental policymaking in Congress will remain highly contested despite a Democratic majority because polarization in the executive branch will likely continue to complicate the process of reaching agreements, Camacho said.

He added that although the blue wave could lead to a stronger push for affordable clean energy, environmental justice and the regulation of data centers, he is still skeptical of decision-making in Congress.

“Concerns I have are about whether the leaders of the Democratic Party are willing to be sufficiently bold, to take the actions that are in front of us, to actually deal with the major stakes that climate change raises,” Camacho said. “Only time will tell. They have the social capital to do it, whether they actually decide to do it or whether they decide to favor special interests or not.”

California State Assembly Speaker Emeritus Anthony Rendon said at the panel that he believes the effectiveness of policymaking in Congress depends on whether leaders are willing to listen to the voices of younger constituents.

He cited the passage of Senate Bill 32 – which requires the California Air Resources Board to reduce greenhouse gas emissions to 40% below 1990 levels by 2030 – as an example of Democrats and Republicans finding common ground.

“In California, when we did SB 32, we got five Republican votes, which allowed for the two-thirds – we wouldn’t have gotten two-thirds without it, (SB 32) wouldn’t have passed without it,” Rendon said.

Marta Segura, founding chief heat officer for the city of Los Angeles, said she is hopeful for the future of climate change policies in California – especially in LA – because of the progressive visions of the state’s newly elected leaders.

Mayor-elect Nithya Raman, who defeated incumbent Karen Bass in the midterms, plans to expand eco-friendly projects and use various funding streams to fund projects to plant street trees and add cooling centers across the city, Segura said.

The SoCalGas franchise fee, which the Southern California Gas Company pays to operate its gas distribution system in LA, will go to the Climate Equity Account to support climate mitigation, adaptation and decarbonization, according to a 2026 LA County Board of Supervisors letter.

Measure PRK, which passed in the midterm elections, aims to double the current minimum budget allocated to the Department of Parks and Recreation over 10 years, according to voting information hub California Choices.

“I’ve never been more hopeful for the city of Los Angeles,” Segura said.

Elias Jabbe, a climate communication strategist who attended the event, said he is concerned about extreme heat, poor air quality and worsening pollution. He added that he hopes to see newly elected officials regulate artificial intelligence to mitigate their negative impacts on the environment.

“I’ve been writing about climate change for a long time, and I’ve been observing, as a volunteer for nonprofits, extreme heat. … I believe it’s an issue that pertains to us now,” Jabbe said.

People should continue to think critically about the issues around them to make positive change on the environment, whether it be through pushing for or voting on essential policies, Segura said.

“I just want people to follow their dreams, follow their passion, but always be civically engaged,” Segura said. “Do things that reward your soul, because I think that’s what makes life meaningful and purposeful. … Those dreams can become reality.”
