title: States No Longer Must Write Carbon Plans for Fossil Steam Plants as EPA Repeal Kicks In
description:
The Environmental Protection Agency's repeal of most of the 2024 Carbon Pollution Standards for fossil fuel-fired power plants takes effect today, Nov. 16, 2026.
The change matters because power plants are a large source of U.S. climate pollution.
Coal, gas and oil-fired plants produce about one-quarter of the nation's greenhouse gas emissions, second only to transportation, according to the Associated Press.
So are the 2015 New Source Performance Standards, including a partial carbon capture requirement for new coal plants.
States no longer have to write plans for greenhouse gas emissions from existing fossil fuel steam plants.
text:
Update Note: This article reports new information involving EPA's repeal of the 2024 power plant carbon standards following Nature World News' earlier coverage of the September announcement. The final rule takes effect Nov. 16, 2026. Sources checked include EPA's rule page, the Federal Register publication of Sept. 17, 2026, and court filings reported through Oct. 1, 2026.

The Environmental Protection Agency's repeal of most of the 2024 Carbon Pollution Standards for fossil fuel-fired power plants takes effect today, Nov. 16, 2026. As of now, states no longer have to write plans to control greenhouse gas emissions from existing coal-, oil-, and gas-fired steam power plants, and the carbon capture requirements that were set to begin in the 2030s are gone.

The change matters because power plants are a large source of U.S. climate pollution. Coal, gas and oil-fired plants produce about one-quarter of the nation's greenhouse gas emissions, second only to transportation, according to the Associated Press.

For households, nothing changes on this month's electric bill — the practical effects show up in utility planning, state regulatory work and court dockets, and in a second EPA proposal that would remove the remaining standards entirely.

The Requirements That End Today

Nature World News previously reported on EPA's September decision to repeal most of the standards. That rule, signed by Administrator Lee Zeldin on Sept. 14 and published Sept. 17, has now reached its effective date.

The repeal removes, in their entirety, the 2024 emission guidelines for existing coal-fired steam units and for existing natural gas- and oil-fired steam units. Those guidelines were what required states to submit compliance plans. For long-term coal units, EPA reversed its finding that 90 percent carbon capture was the best system of emission reduction, saying it had not been adequately demonstrated.

Also repealed are the requirement that coal plants retiring between 2032 and 2039 co-fire 40 percent natural gas, the carbon capture standard for coal units making large modifications, and the Phase II carbon capture standards for new base load gas turbines, according to an analysis by the law firm Davis Polk. EPA adopted no replacement standards.

What Still Applies, for Now

Some federal greenhouse gas rules for power plants remain. Phase I efficiency standards for new and reconstructed combustion turbines, which do not require carbon capture, are still in place. So are the 2015 New Source Performance Standards, including a partial carbon capture requirement for new coal plants.

Those may not last — in a supplemental proposal, EPA would rescind its greenhouse gas findings for fossil fuel power plants and repeal every remaining Section 111 greenhouse gas standard for the sector, as summarized by Harvard's Environmental and Energy Law Program. Public comments closed Nov. 2, and the AP reported the agency expects to finalize it next year.

The proposal would not affect standards for conventional air pollutants or hazardous air pollutants such as mercury, which are governed by other rules.

Cost Savings Versus Health Costs

EPA says the final repeal will save Americans and the power sector up to $310 billion, and that the supplemental proposal would save an additional $370 million in direct compliance costs. The agency argues the 2024 rule relied on technology that was not ready, and that its approach conflicted with the Supreme Court's 2022 ruling in West Virginia v. EPA. "The administration has come in to protect American energy and to make sure you can afford to keep the lights on," Zeldin said when the repeal was announced.

Coal industry groups, including America's Power, have said the repeal will protect grid reliability and shield customers from higher costs. In its supplemental proposal, EPA also argues that eliminating all U.S. fossil power plant carbon dioxide would have at most a minimal effect on modeled global temperature.

Critics point to EPA's own earlier numbers. In 2024, the agency estimated the standards would deliver $370 billion in net climate and health benefits through 2047 and prevent about 1,200 premature deaths in 2035 alone by reducing soot and smog-forming pollution. The Environmental Defense Fund's preliminary analysis puts the cost of repeal at more than 80,000 additional premature deaths through 2047, a figure from an advocacy group that EPA has not adopted. Harvard's tracker notes the repeal is projected to increase nitrogen oxides, sulfur dioxide and fine particles.

The two sides are measuring different things over different time frames, which is why their totals are hard to compare directly.

Lawsuits Already Filed

Legal challenges were filed quickly. Environmental and public health groups filed American Lung Association v. EPA in the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit on Sept. 17. A New York-led coalition of states and municipalities filed New York v. EPA on Oct. 1.

Those cases are expected to take significant time, and it is unclear whether challengers will ask the court to pause the repeal while the case proceeds. The supplemental proposal would likely face separate lawsuits if finalized, and the outcome of litigation over EPA's February 2026 rescission of the 2009 endangerment finding could shape both.

What Utility Customers and States Should Watch

For utility customers, any cost effect will come slowly through state rate cases and long-term resource plans rather than overnight. Utilities that had begun planning for carbon capture or gas co-firing can now drop those compliance paths, though state laws, market prices, and existing retirement plans also shape what gets built.

States lose the federal deadline to submit plans, but many have their own clean energy or emissions laws that still apply. Residents near coal plants, who live closest to soot and smog-forming emissions, have the most direct stake in how those state decisions play out.

The bottom line: as of Nov. 16, the core 2024 power plant carbon requirements are gone, a narrower set of standards remains, and EPA is moving to repeal the rest. The next developments to watch are the D.C. Circuit cases and EPA's final decision on its broader proposal.

What Readers Want to Know

What changed on Nov. 16, 2026? EPA's repeal of most of the 2024 power plant carbon standards took effect. States no longer have to write plans for greenhouse gas emissions from existing fossil fuel steam plants.

Which requirements were removed? The emission guidelines for existing coal, oil, and gas steam units, the 90 percent carbon capture standard, the 40 percent gas co-firing requirement, and carbon capture standards for new base-load gas turbines and modified coal units.

What standards remain? Phase I efficiency standards for new combustion turbines and the 2015 standards for new power plants remain, though EPA has proposed repealing them.

How much of U.S. emissions come from power plants? About one-quarter of the nation's greenhouse gas emissions, second only to transportation.

Will my electric bill change? Not immediately. Any effects would come over time through utility planning and state rate decisions.

text:
COLUMBIA, S.C. (WIS) - Protesters rallied in Columbia before the last of three November public hearings on the proposed merger of Dominion Energy and Florida-based NextEra Energy.

The hearing was held at the South Carolina Department of Archives and History.

Protesters chanted, “No big merger, no rate hike.”

Public hearing

The rally took place ahead of a South Carolina Public Service Commission meeting on the proposed $67 billion merger, if approved. The meeting has drawn more attention over the past month.

Dominion serves more than 800,000 customers in South Carolina. Some of those customers spoke at the public hearing.

“This is a huge decision and the whole process has to slow down,” public witness Deborah Billings said.

“At a certain point, we have to talk about this for what it is. Billionaires and government in cahoots to accumulate wealth and power at the expense of the people,” public witness Samantha Rainwater said.

What the merger would do

The merger would create the nation’s largest regulated electric utility, with around 10 million customers.

Dominion and NextEra officials said South Carolina customers would get a $10 monthly bill credit for two years as a benefit.

Opposition

Opponents of the merger think the decision is moving too fast. They also said South Carolina is not getting the best package compared with other states, such as North Carolina and Virginia.

“We need people in South Carolina making decisions for us, not in Florida,” said Annie Mahaffey, organizer of Stop NextEra SC.

Dominion response

Dominion Energy South Carolina President Keller Kissam said there will not be a change in how Dominion operates in South Carolina.

“We went through a merger before we were South Carolina Electric and Gas, then we were Dominion, and now Dominion to potentially NextEra,” Kissam said. “I’ve been at this company for 30-plus years, the logos might change, but the people don’t. We know how important it is, the product we deliver. We know it has to be affordable. We understand that electricity drives our economy and it drives people’s individual lives. Keep it safe, reliable and affordable, and increasingly clean — that’s our mission.”

Next steps

Regulators are expected to use testimony from the three November public hearings. The commission is expected to take up the case in December before issuing a final order by the end of January.

text:
A coal-fired power plant in east Orlando that was supposed to start shutting down earlier this year poses significant risks to public health and the environment, according to health experts and local leaders.

“In my office, I can prescribe an inhaler, and I can help the parents have an asthma action plan,” said Dr. Michelle Kirwan Bythwood, a Miami-based pediatrician. “But the decisions made about what goes into the air that a child breathes are made far beyond my exam room.”

Kirwan Bythwood was part of a small group raising concerns about coal at a press conference Tuesday in Avalon Park, less than three miles away from two coal-fired units at the Stanton Energy Center. The Orlando Utilities Commission has planned to either retire or switch both coal units over to cleaner-burning natural gas, according to OUC’s 10-year site plan published last year.

In 2021, the city-owned utility’s board voted to retire Stanton Unit 1. That retirement process would begin with a required “extended cold shutdown” period, which was supposed to start by the end of May 2026.

But Unit 1 is still operational. A federal emergency order, initially issued in early June and later extended, demands that OUC keep the coal plant online. Stanton Unit 1 is one of seven facilities nationwide, including six coal-powered facilities, affected by similar orders from the Department of Energy.

RELATED: Energy secretary orders OUC to keep a coal-fired power plant running

“We had a plan in place: to close down this power plant, to move away from coal,” said former State Rep. Anna Eskamani, a Democrat currently running for Orlando mayor. “And the Trump administration has inserted itself in preventing us from doing that.”

The federal emergency order mentions data centers, stating that Florida’s long-term energy projections “lag behind what is needed to support new data centers and other large loads.”

The current order affecting Stanton Unit 1 will expire after Nov. 30, unless it’s extended again.

Scientists overwhelmingly agree that burning fossil fuels like coal is a leading cause of climate change, which is driving up global temperatures and intensifying weather events like hurricanes and heat waves.

Burning fossil fuels also releases particles into the air, which can be inhaled and cause damage to human health. The most dangerous are fine particles or PM2.5, which generally measure 2.5 micrometers or less in diameter, according to the Environmental Protection Agency.

If stories like this deepen your connection to our community, take the next step—support the independent journalism that makes them possible.

Donate

Research indicates PM2.5 from coal-fired power plants is particularly dangerous. One study conducted over more than 20 years found coal PM2.5 exposure is associated with a mortality risk more than double that of exposure to PM2.5 from other sources. That study, published in late 2023, found 460,000 deaths attributable to coal PM2.5.

When inhaled, fine particles can make their way deep into human lungs and trigger asthma attacks — a risk that can be especially high for children, Kirwan Bythwood said. “Children spend more time outdoors, typically, than adults do, and they breathe more air. They breathe faster, so they're bringing in more pollutants per body mass than an adult.”

Air pollution can be detrimental even before a baby takes their first breath, Kirwan Bythwood said. It has been linked to premature births, higher heart attack and stroke risk, and other health concerns.

“Families and our healthcare systems bear these costs. You'll never see them on an electric bill,” Kirwan Bythwood said.

Orlando District 1 Commissioner Tom Keen called it “frustrating” that a federal mandate is interfering with OUC’s efforts to “manage costs, pursue cleaner energy alternatives and provide savings to its customers.” Keen pointed to the utility’s recent proposal to lower rates by about $5 a month.

Meanwhile, Valencia College student Jason Thornton called out OUC for not sufficiently prioritizing the retirement of Stanton Unit 1. Thornton is the lead organizer for Valencia’s chapter of genCLEO Action Fund, a youth-led climate justice organization affiliated with the Miami-based CLEO Institute.

“Young people have been let down by the Trump administration, but also from Mayor (Buddy) Dyer and the OUC board,” Thornton said, arguing the DOE’s emergency order would’ve been moot had OUC moved more quickly to retire Stanton Unit 1.

“We are in such a vital time right now to make the switch to renewable energy,” Thornton said.

The OUC board is slated to meet on Dec. 15, when it will vote on an updated version of its Electric Integrated Resource Plan, or EIRP. The current EIRP was adopted in late 2020.

An analysis by the Environmental Defense Fund estimates the monthly cost of operating Stanton Unit 1 at $6.2 million. An OUC spokesperson refuted that estimate, writing by email that such claims “do not reflect the comprehensive analysis OUC regularly undergoes to balance reliability, affordability, and sustainability.”

The OUC spokesperson had been asked how much the facility does cost to operate per month. He did not provide that information.

text:
Earlier this month, Michigan voters handed Democrats a trifecta of state government control after campaigning on promises like cracking down on both utilities and data centers. Now, Gov.-elect Jocelyn Benson is tasked with turning those promises into actual relief for customers once she takes office in January.

Early next year, Latitude Media has learned, state-level clean energy and ratepayer groups expect lawmakers to release a package of bills aimed at tying utility profits to more reliable and affordable service, as well as scaling up distributed energy resources like community solar and home batteries. Some have been introduced before, while others are new.

Meanwhile, given Benson’s campaign promises, they also anticipate the governor-elect will issue a moratorium on new data center construction until the state puts in place guardrails around costs, land and water use, and public disclosures. This would mirror what Gov. Greg Abbott did earlier this year in Texas with executive authority alone, though in Michigan siting is largely decided locally and a construction pause may require the legislature’s buy-in.

Michigan in 2027 will be among nearly two dozen states where Democrats control all three branches of government. But Benson’s agenda specifically will be a key test of whether the party’s energy affordability platform can actually deliver. Michigan is simultaneously trying to achieve 100% clean energy by 2040, upgrade an aging grid, and absorb a wave of new data center demand from hyperscalers including Oracle, Google, and Microsoft — all while limiting rate hikes for customers.

Benson was one of the most aggressive gubernatorial candidates in the country on issues like taking on utilities and data centers, according to Bob Allison, deputy director of the Michigan League of Conservation Voters. “We think she’ll follow through on that and more, especially with the backing of a legislature that ran on these issues,” he told Latitude Media.

A spokeswoman for Benson’s transition team didn’t return requests for comment about how the incoming administration plans to implement its agenda.

Plummeting utility approval

Benson pledged to increase bill credits for residents who experience power outages, fund a home energy efficiency program to help lower utility bills, institute performance-based utility profit standards, and ensure residential ratepayers don’t subsidize data centers.

Most of those actions will likely require legislation, said Laura Sherman, president of the Michigan Energy Innovation Business Council. The Michigan Public Service Commission does have an open docket on potential incentives and penalties for utilities aimed at reducing outages and integrating virtual power plants, among other flexible grid resources. However, state law currently limits what the commission can do on its own.

“The PSC has also required a number of things related to data centers to ensure costs aren’t passed on to other customers,” Sherman said. “But in terms of clean energy requirements, we haven’t seen the commission require that of utilities. That is something we’re working on legislatively.”

Beson’s platform hit at public furor over monopoly utilities that had been building for years in Michigan. Residents pay the highest electricity rates in the Midwest but consistently experience some of the longest power outages nationwide, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration. In 2025, Michigan’s average restoration time was more than seven hours, or roughly triple the U.S. average of 2.4 hours. Combined, the investor-owned utilities DTE Energy and Consumers Energy serve about 80% of state residents.

“There are just a lot of minutes every year that people are without power,” Douglas Jester, managing partner at 5 Lakes Energy, a consultant firm that does policy analysis for clean energy and ratepayer advocacy groups. “I sometimes characterize it this way: Every year, Michigan has the worst reliability in the country of any state that didn’t have hurricanes.” (That’s other than West Virginia, he caveated, “which is always worse than Michigan.”)

Jester said reliability has improved somewhat since 5 Lakes Energy more than a decade ago began conducting research for the Citizens Utility Board of Michigan, which publishes a comparative utility performance report each year. But progress is slow.

Meanwhile, both DTE and Consumers have regularly requested rate increases over the past seven years. Their CEOs earn millions of dollars in annual compensation, and they’ve donated millions to state elected officials.

That political spending became a focal point of the midterms. Michigan LCV launched a “No Utility Money Challenge,” which Benson signed along with more than 100 candidates on the November ballot, including Attorney General-elect Eli Savit and the incoming leaders of both the House and Senate. That challenge called on politicians to refuse campaign donations from DTE and Consumers.

LCV also helped build support for Prop 2, a ballot measure that bans regulated utilities from directly donating to state politicians and their PACs. The measure passed with 81% support.

Hannah Buscemi, a DTE spokeswoman, said in an email that DTE’s residential bills remain below regional and national averages, and bill growth since 2021 has been among the lowest in the country. That is true, in part because Michigan households use less electricity than those in other states. But the actual average unit price is higher than the U.S. average.)

“We want to keep working with lawmakers to find ways to keep bills down while delivering the reliable power our customers expect,” Buscemi said.

In February, the Michigan Public Service Commission is expected to rule on DTE’s $474-million rate-hike request. The utility last April said it intends to freeze rates for two years, as long as its first data center project comes online as planned by the end of 2027. That project is being built for Oracle.

Consumers Energy did not reply to a request for comment by the time of publication.

Flexible grid reform

Beyond greater scrutiny of utilities and data centers, clean energy advocates want state lawmakers to pass legislation that mandates greater grid innovation and flexibility to help drive down costs. That includes virtual power plants, community solar, and other emerging technologies to bolster existing poles and wires.

“There are potentially thousands of customers who have a device that could participate in a virtual power plant, such as smart thermostats, electric vehicles, or solar and storage,” said Samarth Medakkar, who leads Advanced Energy United’s work in Illinois and Michigan. “We want to unlock the flexibility of those devices and provide upfront incentives to enroll in a program.”

Medakkar added that it’s critical that independent companies — not just utilities — can develop VPPs and other flexible grid solutions to spur competition and potentially drive down costs.

text:
Quaise Energy, a developer of utility-scale superhot geothermal energy, on Nov. 17 announced that Google has signed a power purchase agreement for 50 megawatts of superhot geothermal power from Project Obsidian, Quaise's flagship project in Central Oregon.

"The agreement will help catalyze the commercial development of superhot geothermal energy, providing benefits for ratepayers and helping protect the environment," Quaise said.

Beginning as early as 2030, Google will purchase 50 MW of power from Project Obsidian. The initial phase of development will use conventional drilling technology to access superhot geothermal conditions at commercial scale.

"Superhot geothermal is a virtually limitless energy source that uses the Earth’s natural heat to generate up to 10x more clean power per well than traditional geothermal systems," Quaise said.

The second phase of development at Project Obsidian is expected to be the first in the world to use millimeter wave drilling, a technology designed to uniquely access superhot geothermal conditions worldwide.

Unlike traditional geothermal energy, which is limited to regions with naturally occurring hot water reservoirs rarely exceeding 600°F, Quaise develops Enhanced Geothermal Systems (EGS) at superhot conditions, which are expected to enable utility-scale projects to compete with today’s most efficient power plants.

Quaise is simultaneously advancing the development of millimeter wave drilling, a technology that can plug into existing drilling rigs to economically reach superhot geothermal conditions, it said.

The agreement builds on Google’s clean energy portfolio and support of geothermal energy, Quaise said.

From 2010 to 2025, Google signed more than 240 agreements to purchase nearly 35 GW of new clean energy, including more than 29 GW in North America across 148 projects.

Google pays for 100% of the power its data centers use, and as the company builds data centers, Google covers the infrastructure needs directly driven by its growth, Quaise said.

In Oregon, the company’s three data center campuses have already achieved 83% carbon-free energy, with residents of Northern Wasco County People’s Utility District’s service territory having the third-lowest energy rates in the state.

The Quaise partnership "further extends Google's clean energy and geothermal leadership, while accelerating the development of superhot geothermal as a cost-effective, clean energy resource for Oregon residents and businesses."

"This new investment extends Google’s track record as a leader powering economic growth in Oregon. Google has proudly called Oregon home since 2006, when it built its first owned-and-operated data center in The Dalles," Quaise said.

In the last 20 years, Google has invested more than $7 billion in the state, ranks as the largest taxpayer in Wasco County in recent years, and in 2025, the company helped provide $9.3 billion of economic activity for tens of thousands of Oregon businesses, nonprofits, publishers, creators, and developers.

authors: Anton L. Delgado And Suzan Fraser, Associated Press

text:
ANTALYA – In the global power game of U.N. climate talks, tiny islands form a small, but vocal bloc of nations demanding the world act on the climate crisis that threatens their existence.

This year's climate conference is in its second and final week in Turkey's resort town of Antalya. These talks follow months of climate-induced disasters, geopolitical shocks and an intensifying El Niño that is making life in the world's smallest countries even more precarious.

“We don’t need more studies. We don’t need more negotiations. We just need more action,” Tonga Prime Minister Fatafehi Fakafānua said in an interview with The Associated Press.

As one of the world's “big ocean states,” Tonga has maritime territory that dwarfs its land mass. Like many islands, Tonga's existence is threatened by climate change. Record-breaking ocean temperatures jeopardize the marine life Tongans depend on, and melting glaciers cause sea level rise that can increase erosion or flooding.

Tonga and other small island developing states, or SIDS, often play the role of a conscience to a warming planet, pleading with larger and more polluting nations to curb emissions before it’s too late. The islands are demanding that richer, more polluting countries pay for them to adapt to changing climates, mitigate their negative impacts and recover from climate-induced disasters.

“On our own, individual SIDS are small economies. We have little leverage, but when you put us together and we speak with one voice, we can speak pretty loudly and pretty strongly,” said Ilana Seid, chair of the Alliance of Small Island States and U.N. ambassador from Palau.

Many of the agreements made at these talks are voluntary and nonbinding. The world has yet to agree on how to transition away from the fossil fuels that cause climate change. This is driving growing criticism of the Conference of the Parties, or COP, process.

Leaders, negotiators and activists alike said this year's COP31 talks need to restore hope that these conferences really make a difference on climate action.

“I feel that my future and the future of generations after me are on the line,” said Atiterentaai Rinimarawa, a 24-year-old youth representative from the island nation of Kiribati. “We are not asking for sympathy, but we are calling for climate justice, stronger commitment and real action.”

Island nations unite in Turkey

Turkey and Australia are co-hosting COP31. Leaders from the Pacific islands said they have had a more prominent role through Australia this year, especially with Fiji hosting a pre-COP meeting in October.

“I absolutely think that our voice has been elevated,” Fakafānua said. “It just speaks to how far we have come, and it’s taken this long, up to COP31, for us to be really center stage.”

There are 39 small island states in the alliance, which Seid described as a “powerful bloc.”

“Our vulnerabilities are so consistent, regardless of if you’re from the Pacific, or the Caribbean, or the African region,” Seid said. “The spotlight on the small island developing states is a little brighter this year.”

Small islands spell out demands

Global climate goals are dangerously off track, with the U.N. announcing that the world is unlikely to reach its ambition of capping global warming at 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit) above preindustrial levels.

Island nations are demanding that this goal is kept alive.

“It’s really not a temperature threshold for us, it’s a survival threshold,” said Adelle Thomas, senior director of the Natural Resources Defense Council, who is from the Bahamas. “The real question is going to be whether political ambition is catching up with the lived reality that people are facing.”

While the world may overshoot its 1.5-degree goal, climate talks have kept global warming from hitting even higher temperatures. This proves COP works, but just not at the same pace as climate change, said Thomas, who is also vice chair of an Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change working group.

“It is a long-term game, which unfortunately doesn’t align with the level of impacts that we’re seeing, but I don’t think that we should give up on COP,” she said.

For the second year in a row, the government of the world’s largest economy and a major emitter, the United States, is absent from the talks.

The process is undoubtedly frustrating, Fakafānua said, but “we’ve definitely made progress and we’re better with COP than without.”

The island alliance also wants to walk out of COP31 with $500 million in funding for climate resiliency programs and $200 million for natural disaster early-warning systems.

“It’s only fair that those who are suffering from the effects of climate change are assisted by those who were at fault,” Fakafānua said.

Climate talks must ‘renew faith’

This year has been especially rough for island nations.

The world's oceans hit their hottest temperatures on record in August and this year's record-breaking El Niño is still intensifying. Geopolitical shocks, like the Iran war, have also sent energy prices soaring.

“Average citizens around the world are experiencing climate impacts in their homes and in their communities and that directly links to what’s going on in these international negotiations,” Thomas said. “It’s absolutely up to individual citizens and communities to make sure that their leaders are tackling the climate change crisis.”

COP31 is competing for international attention, as other global summits in China and the Philippines begin.

“These climate talks need to renew faith,” said Qiyun Woo, a youth environmentalist from the city-state of Singapore in Southeast Asia. “Faith young people should have in these processes and in world leaders helping to secure a more livable future for generations to come.”

___

Delgado reported from Bangkok.

text:
What should we measure to understand whether communities are becoming more resilient to climate change? Resilience metrics can help safeguard people, infrastructure, cultural assets, public budgets, and the environment—but there is no single measure that works everywhere. Unlike greenhouse gas emissions, resilience depends on local hazards, priorities, assets at risk, and the decisions communities need to make. This webinar will explore how communities can identify useful measures, who those measures should serve, and how they can support public engagement, investment, accountability, and learning over time.

Speakers

Benjamin DeAngelo has years of experience bridging science and policy on climate change issues both in domestic and international settings. DeAngelo departed the U.S. federal government in 2025 after serving for over 27 years through senior positions held at the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), and at the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy in President Obama’s Administration. His last federal position was as the inaugural Director of EPA’s Office of Climate Adaptation and Sustainability. His federal career highlights include co-authoring EPA’s 2009 greenhouse gas endangerment finding under the Clean Air Act, helping to lead the 4th National Climate Assessment, serving as Chair of the Arctic Monitoring and Assessment Program under the Arctic Council, and creating a partnership between NOAA and the American Society of Civil Engineers. After leaving federal service, DeAngelo started Operation Future, LLC focused on climate adaptation and resilience for both subnational governments and private organizations. DeAngelo is also an Adjunct Professor at Howard University and a Fellow of the Environmental Protection Network. Mr. DeAngelo received his bachelor’s in geography at Pennsylvania State University, his master’s in geography at the University of Toronto, and was a Fulbright Scholar in Germany.

Maurie Kelly is the Director of Informatics at Penn State’s Institute of Energy and the Environment, where she manages multiple data projects and programs. She is the director of Pennsylvania Spatial Data Access (PASDA), and her team also manages the PA Flood Risk Assessment Tool, the PA Mine Map Atlas, PennPilot, and other geospatial data projects. Her research includes big data and crisis/resilience, with a particular interest in community response to flood disasters.

text:
A group of nine environmental organizations has asked Gov. Jared Polis to request the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency reclassify the Northern Front Range as being in “extreme” noncompliance with federal ozone standards, which would trigger greater restrictions on emission producers ranging from oil-and-gas rigs to drivers of individual vehicles.

Business groups, including Denver South and the Colorado Chamber of Commerce, are pushing back on the request and asking the Democratic governor to look at other, more pragmatic options than seeking a voluntary reclassification. At stake is the level of regulations that energy and industrial firms, as well as many commuters, could face until the stubbornly high ozone levels come down in an area stretching from Douglas County north to the Wyoming border.

The Northern Front Range has been in violation since 2008 of standards that first limited ozone levels to 75 parts per billion and then, in 2015, lowered them further to 70 parts per billion. State leaders have passed many regulations to try to bring levels down — on oil-and-gas producers, manufacturers, commercial buildings and more — and while sectors like utilities and manufacturing have cut emissions greatly, ozone levels remain elevated.

This spring and summer, during what is known as peak ozone season, the area recorded 66 days of ozone over 70 parts per billion and 42 days over the 75 parts-per-billion mark — days that exacerbate asthma and other respiratory conditions for residents. Some observers have pushed back by noting the poor air quality is often coming from wildfire smoke — Regional Air Quality Council Executive Director Mike Silverstein attributed at least 12 of the bad air days to smoke during a September meeting — and have argued that severe restrictions will hurt the economy without cleaning the air.

Why the groups want the new ozone designation

Still, on Oct. 14, environmental groups including the Center for Biological Diversity, Colorado Sierra Club and 350 Colorado asked Polis to seek a voluntary noncompliance upgrade to “extreme,” the highest level on the EPA’s scale.

Under the Clean Air Act, they noted, the EPA must approve any such reclassification requests from governors, as it did two years ago when Polis requested a voluntary upgrade from “moderate” to “serious” for the portion of the Front Range in violation of the 2015 standards. Much of the area, however, is now classified as being in severe violation of the 2008 standard because of the length of time of noncompliance.

Such an upgrade would trigger several key steps, noted Jeremy Nichols, senior advocate for Center for Biological Diversity, in the letter and in a follow-up email to The Sum & Substance in response to a request for more information. Those could include:

Lowering the permitting threshold for major stationary sources of pollution from 25 tons of volatile organic compounds and nitrous oxide annually to 10 tons, which would pull more businesses under the stricter permitting regime for Title V emitters;

Give the state more authority to limit traffic and motor-vehicle emissions, which it discussed but has not done yet; and,

Trigger required emissions offsets, allowing the state to demand that producers cut 1.5 tons of emissions for every ton that the state allows new facilities to produce — a step that Nichols called “critical” as officials continue to permit new wells and industrial facilities.

Groups suspect EPA won’t act on its own

Colorado now faces an August compliance deadline with the ozone standards, but EPA won’t be required to act until February 2028, the letter from the coalition stated — and even then, it isn’t likely to act unless it’s sued, it speculated. Polis requesting the voluntary reclassification would send a message that Colorado is willing to take big steps to bring its air quality to an acceptable place, it said.

“While we sincerely hope the region experiences the lowest amount of ozone pollution possible in coming years, it seems unrealistic to believe the region will achieve the exceptionally low ozone levels needed to comply,” the letter states. “Although some emission measures have been adopted, the state has yet to utilize the fullest suite of tools available to confront pollution under the Clean Air Act.”

Business leaders, in letters sent to Polis on Oct. 30, argued that this reclassification not only could do major harm to the state’s already slowing economy but wouldn’t actually lead to cleaner air. And they asked Polis instead to require an evidence-based assessment of how much benefit additional controls could bring to the state and to prioritize feasible, cost-effective improvements instead.

Reclassification could mean at least 55 new facilities qualify as major emissions sources and must go through extensive permitting at a time when the permitting backlog for such projects already has stretched over two years, the Colorado Chamber letter noted. While that would slow commerce and discourage facilities from investing in upgrades, it wouldn’t mandate any emissions reductions, as major-source permitting requires new monitoring and reporting obligations but not a lowering of emissions limits, it added.

Higher restrictions unlikely to clean air, business leaders say

In fact, a study of nonattainment areas across the Rocky Mountain West shows that emissions reductions brought about by compliance-seeking restrictions have failed to produce commensurate ambient ozone reductions, the letter stated. And with the topography and meteorology of the Northern Front Range trapping ozone precursors like VOCs and NOx that constant sunlight transforms into ozone, an increase in restrictions and fines likely still won’t bring this area into compliance, it states.

Instead of seeking reclassification to “extreme” noncompliance, the state should look at more practical pathways that give it a greater range of ways to try to reduce ozone, said Colorado Chamber regulatory affairs adviser Dave Kulmann, writing for two of the organization’s policy councils. Those include seeking a Section 179B exemption from EPA reclassification due to exceptional events and international emissions as Arizona and Utah has done, which would give the state more options of air-cleaning steps to take.

“Colorado should not confuse additional regulatory obligations through reclassification to Extreme nonattainment with progress toward attainment,” Kulmann wrote. “The state can take its ozone challenge seriously while insisting that regulatory decisions be supported by evidence, that legally available relief be evaluated and that the consequences for business, government and households be considered before additional burdens are imposed.”

Ozone could become part of legislative debate

Quinn Schulz, director of policy and legislative affairs for economic-development group Denver South, added in a separate letter to Polis that an extreme reclassification risks speeding through regulations that haven’t been assessed thoroughly. Schulz pointed specifically to proposal put forth recently in the RAQC Blueprint, including regulation of indirect sources of emissions that attract a lot of vehicles, including entertainment and sports venues, warehouses and airports.

RAQC leaders, while pushing for study of the ideas before imposition of emissions limits on those areas, have said that such ideas are necessary because other regulations imposed over the past decade have failed so far to bring the state into federal compliance. The debate over whether steps such as those are necessary could find its way into legislative discussions in 2027.

Neither the environmental organizations nor the business groups that have penned letters to Polis on this matter made similar requests yet to Gov.-elect Phil Weiser, who is set to succeed the term-limited Polis on Jan. 12, leaders of those coalitions said. If Polis does not take any of the actions requested by either side, however, it’s likely that the debate will continue and possibly ramp up with the new administration.

text:
ALEX WANG: China’s emissions are starting to come down because of policies that began 20 years ago.

JULIA SIMON: This is Alex Wang. He’s a professor at UCLA Law and an expert on Chinese climate policy. Wang says back 20 years ago, China was still known as a manufacturer of low-cost items. Air pollution was terrible. So China’s leaders decided to pivot to build new industries with more advanced manufacturing that would also reduce air pollution. The government decided to build supply chains in solar, wind, batteries, electric vehicles.

WANG: The policy direction was so consistent and clear they used that to drive the development of all of these industries that really didn’t exist before.

SIMON: Now, Wang says, they are global leaders.

WANG: On the electrification front, they’re going gangbusters.

SIMON: All of this is having an impact on China’s greenhouse gas emissions. Lauri Myllyvirta is an analyst at the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air. His analysis found that in the third quarter of this year, Chinese emissions fell 3% – the largest drop since the COVID-19 pandemic. It’s part of a bigger trend.

LAURI MYLLYVIRTA: China’s emissions have been flat or falling for 2 1/2 years, and that is a remarkable change.

SIMON: Myllyvirta says three big things are going on. First, in many Chinese provinces, coal use is declining, and solar and wind use is increasing across the country. Second, China is reducing emissions in its industries, like cement and steel production. And third, electric vehicles. Now about two-thirds of Chinese passenger car sales are electric [Julia Simon, “China’s Emissions Have Plateaued—and May Even Be Falling,” NPR: Morning Edition, 2026.11.16].

John Red Cloud wiped his hand across a large plastic panel held within a worn wooden frame that sits conspicuously just outside the door to the office of Red Cloud Renewable Energy Center, a solar education facility located on the Pine Ridge Indian Reservation.

For a moment on a sunny day in September, Red Cloud became a bit sentimental as he described the contraption and its unique place in the history of the nonprofit training center that prepares Native American adults for jobs in the sustainable energy workforce.

“This is where it all started, with just some tinkering by my father,” Red Cloud said. “This was the solar hot air furnace that kicked off my father’s vision.”

The somewhat makeshift yet inexpensive device contains a solar panel that generates hot air that is then circulated by a small fan. Red Cloud’s father, Chief Henry Red Cloud, began to mass produce the furnaces in the early 2000s, ultimately bringing low-cost heat to about 1,200 homes on the reservation known for its frigid winters and high poverty rate.

After seeing the benefits of the furnace, and realizing the sustainable power of the sun, Henry Red Cloud launched Lakota Solar Enterprises, among the nation’s first Native-owned renewable energy companies.

When word of his energy prowess spread, and as other individuals and tribal nations sought to replicate his success, Henry Red Cloud would eventually develop the Red Cloud Renewable Energy Center that has since taught solar functioning and installation to more than 1,100 people, mostly young Native Americans seeking a path out of poverty and into prosperity.

“There’s a lot of doom and gloom on our reservation, but there’s a few pockets of hope that are happening,” said John Red Cloud, who serves as vice president of the training center that launched in the 2000s. “There’s a few good things that are coming out of here because of the people responding to the call, and I believe we are part of that new hope.”

…Roughly 1,100 students — more than 95% of them Native Americans — have completed the programming at Red Cloud Renewable and about 80% of graduates are working in the solar industry, Red Cloud said.

The graduates are referred to as “solar warriors” who can work in the field but also help bring other interested students to the center to obtain job training, said Red Cloud, who is a sixth-generation descendant of the famed Chief Red Cloud who was an influential Native leader in Nebraska and South Dakota in the 1880s and early 1900s [Bart Pfankuch, “Pine Ridge Solar Nonprofit Trains Workers for High-Paying Jobs,” South Dakota News Watch, 2026.10.23].

The order comes in response to a bipartisan state law requiring monopoly utility Duke Energy to reduce its carbon pollution to net zero by 2050.
The plan filed by Duke Energy does not put North Carolina on a sustainable or affordable path to comply with North Carolina law.
These groups also highlighted missed opportunities by Duke in recent years to deploy those clean resources that were included in prior commission-approved carbon plans, which would have saved customers billions of dollars.
The clean energy advocates’ reactions are below.
text:
CHAPEL HILL, N.C.— The North Carolina Utilities Commission issued a Carbon Plan today that puts North Carolinians at risk of increasing energy bills for polluting methane gas plants while underinvesting in the clean energy resources that are needed to meet state law requirements. The Southern Environmental Law Center intervened in the Carbon Plan proceeding on behalf of the Southern Alliance for Clean Energy, the Sierra Club, and Vote Solar.

The order comes in response to a bipartisan state law requiring monopoly utility Duke Energy to reduce its carbon pollution to net zero by 2050. The plan filed by Duke Energy does not put North Carolina on a sustainable or affordable path to comply with North Carolina law.

Largely approving Duke’s proposal, the plan opens the door to building several risky, expensive gas plants while putting less reliance on the diverse array of clean energy resources that would have saved customers billions of dollars in lost federal tax credits and other cost savings. Endorsing Duke’s massive buildout of new gas plants also puts too much faith in the utility’s load growth projections, which includes data centers premised on an uncertain AI future and speculative projects that may never get built.

“It’s disappointing to see Duke continue to miss opportunities to push for deployment of a more balanced portfolio, including wind, pumped hydroelectric storage, and distributed resources like rooftop solar paired with batteries, leaving households on the hook for escalating fuel costs,” said David Neal, a senior attorney at the Southern Environmental Law Center. “While we appreciate the commission’s approval of the utility scale solar and battery storage in Duke’s near-term plan, we cannot afford to keep delaying the development of a broader array of renewable resources that would lead to significant cost savings and enhanced reliability for customers.”

Earlier this year, the commission issued an order that paused solar and battery procurement and the delay effectively canceled the procurement, making it impossible for 2026. Canceling solar for this year threatens the utility’s progress towards North Carolina’s 2050 carbon pollution reduction requirement goal and risks increased fuel bills for communities already burdened by rate increases.

Throughout the proceedings, the clean energy groups advocated for Duke to take full advantage of energy efficiency, load flexibility, renewables, and storage, which remain the most affordable and fastest suite of options for meeting rising energy demand. These groups also highlighted missed opportunities by Duke in recent years to deploy those clean resources that were included in prior commission-approved carbon plans, which would have saved customers billions of dollars.

The clean energy advocates’ reactions are below.

“It’s unsettling that the commission is not checking Duke’s dirty plans, including delaying the retirement of expensive, aging coal infrastructure, and not directing Duke to take near-term actions to better ensure compliance with the bipartisan law that requires the utility to reach net zero emissions by 2050,” said Mikaela Curry, Beyond Coal Campaign Manager for the Sierra Club. “Duke continues to fail families and small businesses by delaying affordable, clean, and reliable resources that reduce pollution and keep our communities healthier and safer. The NCUC must do a better job of holding Duke accountable.”

“Duke proposed a resource plan that favors new gas plants, prioritizing their own profits over the long-term interests of North Carolinians,” said Maggie Shober, research director for the Southern Alliance for Clean Energy. “Families are already experiencing costly energy bills. If Duke had focused on more affordable renewable resources, families would have some relief from higher bills.”

“Time and time again, Duke Energy develops plans that fail North Carolinians in a multitude of ways, and the commission largely approves them,” said Jake Duncan, southeast senior regulatory director at Vote Solar. “This was a missed opportunity to develop a plan that recognizes the benefits of solar and other proven clean energy resources that have helped families and businesses across the state relieve the weight of rising energy costs.”

text:
Arlington Mayor Jim Ross and city officials discussed environmental issues and goals with residents Tuesday, presenting details on how the city wants to move forward with community requests on oil and gas operations and an increased electric vehicle presence.

Tuesday evening’s town hall meeting at the Texas Rangers Golf Club marked the third installment in a series of public meetings hosted by Ross called Arlington Unfiltered: Straight Talk with the Mayor.

He led the discussion on the city’s oil and gas wells, the prospect of data center development and Arlington’s goal to increasingly invest in EVs. The session allowed residents to ask questions and voice their concerns.

Ross explained the meetings are designed to allow more direct conversation between himself, residents and other city officials on sensitive community issues.

“All too often, when we have to do stuff at city council and people are coming to voice their opinion for one side or the other of a particular issue, it’s done in such a fashion that doesn’t allow direct engagement,” Ross said. “This type of format here lets you be very active.”

The mayor prefaced the discussion on gas wells by saying he understands the sentiment the community has historically expressed on oil and gas drilling.

“We’re going to talk about what we can and what we can’t do,” Ross said.

The city receives most of the complaints related to gas drilling at the beginning and end of a well’s operational life, Ross said. When met with public health concerns, city staffers have limited authority over gas drilling, he added.

As in previous council meetings, Ross told residents Tuesday that Texas House Bill 40, passed in 2015, gives the state full authority over oil and gas operations while extending local governments only a limited ability to regulate above-ground activity.

As a result, Arlington has since established city codes to define minimum and maximum setbacks between gas well sites and nearby properties. The codes include requiring public hearings on new permits and adding daycares as a protected use in order to enforce setback requirements.

The city cannot increase existing setbacks without violating state law, Ross explained.

Lon Burnam, a former state representative and longtime environmental activist, argued that cities lobby at the Capitol during legislative sessions, questioning what Arlington’s priorities will look like in regard to regulating oil and gas.

“What is the city of Arlington committed to do in the next upcoming legislative session to lobby to change the many repressive, anti-local government pieces of legislation they’ve passed over the last decade, including HB40?” Burnam asked.

In response, Ross said city officials and TotalEnergies — the French energy conglomerate that owns and operates the majority of Arlington’s gas pads — are exploring an agreement that would determine a date when the company would cease applying for additional gas well permits.

Ross clarified that TotalEnergies has not applied to operate additional gas well sites, but the agreement would specify a date to implement a cap on expanding or operating new wells in the company’s existing sites.

“We can do anything that the state tells us to do,” Ross said in response to a question about the possibility of increased setback requirements if applicable law changes are made in the upcoming legislative session.

“If the state says municipalities cannot do something, they’re superior to us. They get to control those things,” Ross said. “We don’t know what’s going to happen.”

Ranjana Bhandari, founder and executive director of advocacy group Liveable Arlington, voiced her concern about a lack of awareness around new wells in drilling zones.

Under city ordinance, operators are required to notify all homes within 1,320 feet from a zone of operations involving drilling and fracking.

Asked about the prospect of publishing those notices on the city’s website, Ross responded by asking city officials to explore the move.

“I think that’s a very reasonable request. Let’s see if we make that happen,” he said.

What does Arlington’s future look like for EVs?

Arlington wants to expand its fleet and use of EVs.

The city has 14 all-electric vehicles and operates 38 chargers for its municipal fleet. It is working on bringing 12 publicly accessible EV charging stations to three parks.

“We’re not where we need to be yet, but we’re making progress to go greener and healthier,” Ross said.

Arlington resident Russ Gamber asked if the city would consider deploying more EVs across city services, including the city’s On-Demand transit system through Via and garbage collection services.

While staffers couldn’t immediately respond to the potential for EV garbage trucks, transportation director Alicia Winkelblech said a lack of adequately-sized EVs has presented the city challenges in migrating away from gas-powered cars for its On-Demand service.

“There’s just not a ton of options out there, but we talk to (Via) constantly about this. So as soon as we can get our hands on a vehicle, we’ll be moving in that direction,” Winkelblech said.

Land development assistant director Ken Bloom added that staffers are looking into ordinances that would require more EV charging stations in developments to better reach the city’s goal of housing more green infrastructure.

“Here’s the reality: EVs are growing in popularity and people are going greener with this type of stuff,” Ross said. “We want to make sure that all of our new places can stay with that trend.”

Large data centers unlikely

Ross also echoed presentations about proposed data center regulations made by city staff in September and October. In those meetings, staffers said the city has a low chance of large data center development due to a lack of developable land.

Those proposed regulations were brought forth at the mayor’s request, Ross said.

“I’m going to be real candid and honest with y’all. I didn’t know what the hell a data center really was until a few months ago when these things started becoming really, really public,” he said. “They are new to the vast majority of us who don’t fully understand what they are.”

Some residents questioned officials about why their presentations to council members on data centers did not detail impacts on water use and water quality.

Bloom explained the recommended ordinances presented to council members would call for “zero-water” data centers. He previously told council members the proposals were not set in stone and are subject to change.

text:
WINSTON-SALEM, N.C. —

A new law in North Carolina will ban throwing away lithium-ion batteries in household trash or in municipal landfills, beginning on December 1, 2026.

LITHIUM-ION BATTERY BAN FROM DISCARDING IN TRASH, LANDFILLS

Lithium batteries are found in everyday items like cellphones, laptops, toys, electric shavers, power tools, and rechargeable electronics. Lithium-ion batteries pose a serious fire risk.

The batteries can explode, causing intense and fast-spreading fires that burn hotter and are more toxic than gasoline fires, according to the North Carolina Department of Environmental Quality.

Get the latest news stories of interest by clicking here

LITHIUM-ION BATTERY FIRE RISK

Lithium batteries also pose a fire risk to garbage trucks, waste collection facilities, recycling centers, and the people who work there. Battery fires can spread quickly and cause significant damage. That’s also why it’s so important to properly dispose of the batteries.

>>>Find out more about the new law here.

Watch video below as a dog sets a house on fire after getting hold of a lithium battery.

DESIGNATED BATTERY COLLECTION SITES

Residents will need to dispose of lithium batteries at county designated battery collection locations.

Find a list of drop-off locations in North Carolina below.

LITHIUM-ION BATTERY HANDLING TIPS

Never put lithium-ion batteries in your household trash or recycling bin.

Take used batteries to an authorized battery recycling program or household hazardous waste collection facility.

Before drop-off, tape the battery terminals and place each battery in a separate bag.

Check with your local county for designated battery collection locations.

text:
The 400 largest data centers in the United States put more heat-trapping gas in the air in one year than the entire nation of Denmark did, and that was before the artificial intelligence boom really got going, according to a Harvard University study published Monday.

READ MORE: Opposition to AI data centers in the midterms foreshadows tougher regulations ahead

Meanwhile, negotiators at the United Nations COP31 climate talks in Antalya, Turkey, launched a voluntary pledge Monday for companies and countries to power the world's data centers with clean energy and be more open about their power and water consumption and emissions.

"We cannot ask people to accept higher bills, more planet heating pollution and deeper inequality today in exchange for promises of a better tomorrow," United Nations climate chief Simon Stiell said Monday during the launch of the pledge. "Claims about future emissions savings cannot excuse rising pollution now, making climate disasters even worse."

The pledge also calls for focusing the power of artificial intelligence on solving the so-far intractable problem of climate change and reflects burgeoning concerns about AI's ever-expanding environmental footprint. The political backlash has played out in U.S. elections and major local objections for new sites.

The explosion of new and planned data centers also has prompted a push for new sources of power generation that has the biggest tech companies failing to reach their climate goals, with their electricity consumption rising 240% between 2022 and 2025, according to a new report by the advocacy group Climate Action Against Disinformation.

Study quantifies how much big data centers pollute

Harvard researchers looked at 403 of the largest U.S. data centers between May 2024 and April 2025 using available data and modeling to analyze their electricity use and emissions. They estimated electricity use by the centers produced around 28.3 million tons (25.7 million metric tons) of carbon dioxide, according to a study in Monday's Nature Sustainability.

More than half their 82 terawatt hours of electricity use — enough to power nearly 7 million homes for a year — came from fossil fuels, which are the primary cause of global warming, the researchers found.

The emissions estimate is two to three times what previous studies had shown, said study senior author Francesca Dominici, a Harvard biostatistics professor.

"It is the equivalent to the CO2 emission of an entire state like Michigan or a small European country," Dominici said, adding that plans for 2,000 more data centers make that quantity more worrisome for the future. "We are going backwards toward the goal of controlling CO2 emissions."

Several outside experts in climate, energy and artificial intelligence said Monday's study made sense and reached realistic conclusions, finding the use of modeling reasonable because companies aren't open about power consumption and pollution.

"We cannot manage environmental impacts effectively without reliable measurements and disclosure," said Fengqi You, a Cornell University energy systems scientist who wasn't part of the study. "Ultimately, the environmental footprint of AI is not fixed. It depends on where we build data centers, how efficiently they operate, and how we supply their electricity."

A voluntary pledge proposed at climate talks

The "Antalya Artificial Intelligence Pledge," launched by U.N. climate talks host Turkey and the International Telecommunication Union, says data centers should use clean power and efficient energy and water systems.

The pledge also calls for AI systems to be designed and managed responsibly, using environmental standards and reusing or recycling infrastructure and hardware. It says the environmental impacts of data centers should be assessed and shared and signatories should support using artificial intelligence as a climate solution.

COP31 President Murat Kurum has said world leaders at the talks must openly discuss AI's growing energy consumption and start setting the terms.

AI produces pollution but also offers hope

One of the biggest climate fighters, former U.S. Vice President Al Gore, said while it is essential that data centers are powered by carbon-free energy, he is less concerned about the emissions from AI than others. And he is hopeful that its computing power can find novel ways of fighting climate change.

READ MORE: To make AI morally good, tech companies are turning to religion. But some experts say it isn't that simple

In an Associated Press interview, Gore quoted a study by prominent British economist and climate advocate Nicholas Stern who predicted by 2030 "we will see 6 to 9% reduction in emissions of greenhouse gases because of the use of advanced AI in finding new ways to be far more efficient in the use of materials and energy."

Caleb Max, president of the National Artificial Intelligence Association said, "AI will solve not only the energy usage issues that data centers face, but unlock numerous currently unknown advances in science and technology that will address climate change and make lives better for humanity. I respect the concerns about energy and water consumption from data centers, but the fears may be overblown."

But Climate Action Against Disinformation spokesman Philip Newell was skeptical.

"We have hope in one hand and then harms in the other," Newell said. "They're selling us hope while hiding the harms from us."

Capturing heat from data centers

The computing equipment in data centers generates a lot of waste heat that is vented into the atmosphere. One approach to reducing data centers' environmental impact is to capture heat that can be used for nearby homes and businesses.

The Danish engineering and manufacturing company Danfoss said waste heat is "the world's largest untapped energy source," and reusing it can replace natural gas as a heat source. It identified data centers as a significant source of constant heat, particularly as their power consumption grows.

The International Energy Agency estimates data centers could provide enough heat for around 10% of European homes by 2030, if that heat was fully integrated into district systems that supply heat and hot water to residents.

In remarks broadcast during COP31, European Commissioner for Energy and Housing Dan Jørgensen said Europe must replace imported fossil fuels by capturing heat that is going to waste and tapping into geothermal.

In another example of this approach, industrial development firm BaRupOn is building an advanced manufacturing campus in Texas that plans to use recaptured heat to generate additional electricity on site, CEO Balaji Tammabattula said. In North Dakota, the company is planning a data center that could feed heat to the community.

University of Colorado Boulder Professor Gregor Henze said it's a perfect marriage because modern data centers that rely on liquid rather than air cooling are a fairly constant source of heat at the right temperature for thermal energy networks.

text:
The Senate just took another step towards passing the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA), which fulfills Big Oil’s Project 2025 wishlist by gutting our foundational environmental protections to accelerate the buildout of polluting, climate-wrecking fossil fuel projects and AI data centers.

text:
Flatiron Energy develops, builds, owns, and operates utility-scale battery storage across the Eastern U.S., with a 24 GWh portfolio, following significant expansion under Hull Street Energy

Rising electricity demand, retiring power plants, and state-backed storage programs are driving demand for firm capacity that supports grid reliability and ratepayer affordability

EQT will support Flatiron's management team in delivering its contracted projects and scaling its presence, drawing on EQT's deep expertise across energy and digital infrastructure

STOCKHOLM, Nov. 17, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- EQT is pleased to announce that EQT Transition Infrastructure ("EQT") has entered into a definitive agreement to acquire Flatiron Energy ("Flatiron" or the "Company") from Hull Street Energy ("HSE").

Founded in 2021, Flatiron develops, builds, owns, and operates utility-scale energy storage projects across New England, New York, and the Mid-Atlantic power markets. The Company develops projects in dense, capacity-constrained areas, where storage supports grid reliability at times of peak demand. Since HSE's initial investment in 2022, Flatiron has expanded its portfolio by nearly ten-fold to 24 GWh of capacity, been awarded 6 GWh of long-term contracts, and is in construction on 2 GWh of batteries - including the largest urban energy storage project in the world.

In Flatiron's markets, electricity demand is growing rapidly as older power plants retire and more renewable generation connects to the grid. This dynamic increases the need for battery projects, which store power when it is plentiful and deliver it when the grid needs it. As a result, energy storage capacity is expected to grow in these markets from 2 GWh operating in 2026 to 108 GWh in 2035.

EQT will support Flatiron's management team as the Company delivers its contracted projects, helps communities meet their energy needs, and expands into new markets. EQT intends to invest in the Company's team and capabilities, drawing on its deep experience of building energy storage platforms and significant expertise across energy and digital infrastructure. EQT has over $100 billion in digital and energy infrastructure assets, with over 260 GW across operating, under-construction, and pipeline energy assets, and a portfolio over 100 data centers, making EQT one of the largest data center developers globally.

The acquisition is made through EQT Transition Infrastructure, a strategy that applies EQT Infrastructure's industrial experience and sector expertise to scale emerging but proven businesses supporting the transition to a decarbonized, more resource-efficient economy. It builds on EQT's investments in battery storage, including Statera Energy in the UK and Ju:niz Energy in Germany.

Benjamin Bygott-Webb, Partner, EQT, said: "Battery storage has become essential to keeping the grid reliable and electricity affordable, as an ageing grid, a changing generation mix and rapidly growing power demand continue to put the system under strain. Flatiron has secured scarce, well-located sites and built a strong record in the communities where it operates. Building on EQT's deep experience investing in critical infrastructure, our expertise in scaling energy platforms and the opportunities for collaboration across the EQT infrastructure portfolio, we look forward to supporting the Flatiron team as they deliver their projects and bring more firm capacity to the region."

Rob Brink, Chief Executive Officer, Flatiron Energy, said: "We started Flatiron with the mission to bring reliable energy where it's needed most, in the communities that rely on it every day. EQT is an exceptional firm with a strong track record of scaling platforms in the energy transition, and we couldn't be more excited to partner with them on our next stage of growth. My co-founders and I are incredibly grateful to HSE, whose unwavering support and belief in our strategy brought us to this point."

Sarah Wright, Founder and Managing Partner, HSE, said: "This transaction underscores HSE's approach to identifying attractive opportunities and creating long-term value in a rapidly growing and decarbonizing power sector. HSE is highly selective about the management teams we back, and Flatiron is an excellent illustration of why this matters. text:
If you thought having 40 days left to complete Christmas shopping was stressful, imagine being a member of Congress with just over two weeks to finish the nation’s business.

That’s what’s left of the legislative calendar after a midterm election which produced a shift of power from Republicans to Democrats when the 120th session of Congress convenes on Jan. 3. The remaining working days of November and December, known as the “lame duck” session, will be packed with attempts to pass bills that have lingered through what Pew Research anticipates will be the second-least-productive session of Congress in four decades.

Several of those bills have big implications for the Rocky Mountain West, touching on forest management, wildfire preparedness, energy development and wilderness designation.

“Every lame duck presents an opportunity for deal-making, and we expect members of Congress to try and solidify their legacies with end-of-year dealmaking,” James Campbell, director of federal affairs for the policy advocacy group Megafire Action told Mountain Journal on Nov. 12. “The real question is whether precious legislative floor time can be secured to debate and vote on this legislation with many other competing issues.”

Campbell said his organization saw bipartisan support for major legislation such as the Fix Our Forests Act which has passed the House and cleared the Senate Agriculture Committee. The bill affects a wide range of public land management topics, including changes to federal wildfire policies on prescribed burns, response times and preparedness. On Nov. 16, Megafire Action announced a nationwide publicity campaign pushing for the bill’s passage. Montana Republican Sen. Tim Sheehy is a co-sponsor of the bill. Sheehy did not respond to requests for comment on Fix Our Forests or other legislation he’s focused on in the lame duck session.

In the legacy department, Montana Republican Rep. Ryan Zinke has yet to receive a committee hearing for his A River Runs Through It Act, which would designate new wilderness, recreation and timber areas around the Bob Marshall Wilderness Complex. Fellow Montana Rep. Troy Downing has signed on as a co-sponsor.

During a September visit to Missoula announcing the bill, Zinke told Mountain Journal he hoped it could be considered in the lame duck session before he leaves Congress at the end of his second term in December. The bill copies much of an effort by former Democratic Sen. Jon Tester, who repeatedly tried to pass similar legislation starting in 2009.

“We’re excited to get together … and send a message all the way to Washington: It’s time to pass this bill,” Barb Cestero, Montana state director for The Wilderness Society told Mountain Journal in advance of a Nov. 16 rally for the bill in Helena. “Montanans have spent more than 25 years finding common ground on the future of the Blackfoot. Now it’s Congress’ turn to get the job done.”

The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act cleared a Senate procedural vote on Nov. 9, but still has an uncertain lame-duck future. Critics say even new amendments don’t resolve their concerns that the bill strips public participation in project decisions, undermines the Endangered Species Act and Clean Water Act and ignores Tribal sovereignty claims. And President Donald Trump has pledged support for it while saying provisions aiding wind energy are unacceptable, leaving it unclear if he will veto the final product.

“The number of significant questions and concerns from so many different interest groups makes clear that this bill is not ripe for consideration, especially by a lame duck Congress,” Emily Denny, senior communications manager for The Wilderness Society, said in an email.

Sen. Steve Daines is also leaving the Senate at the end of his second term. His America the Beautiful Act has cleared committee but not yet received a full Senate vote. The bill would reauthorize $2 billion in funding for national parks and public lands, which Trump initially passed in 2020. Daines did not respond to a request for comment on his lame-duck legislation.

The 119th Congress has squeaked past the 118th to avoid becoming the least productive session of the past four decades, according to Pew Research. Since it convened in January 2025, this session has passed 121 laws, beating the 118th’s 106 by this point in the two-year term. By comparison, the 100th and 110th sessions each passed 440 laws in 1989 and 2009, respectively.

However, Pew’s analysis found that lame duck sessions have become the workhorse of a divided government. In the congressional terms between 1987 and 2025, more than 60 percent of public laws were passed in the two months between Election Day and the end of the year.

The House shows 16 working days left in the session on its official calendar, although that could change. The Senate potentially has 20 days, given breaks around the Thanksgiving and Christmas holidays.

Congress members have proposed several ambitious projects for those days, including a major tax package, reauthorization of the FISA surveillance law, and $30 billion in new funding for air traffic control. They also hope to pass a National Defense Authorization Act, which has cleared every one of the past 65 sessions.

The NDAA often becomes the last train out of Washington for smaller bills. For example, Megafire Action’s Campbell said some congress members have pushed to insert Fix Our Forests into it. And a continuing resolution to carry federal spending into 2027 must be passed to avoid a government shutdown. Republicans in both chambers may push for a party-line reconciliation bill that would lock in their budget priorities over Democratic objections, including $350 billion in Iran war spending.

Meanwhile, new matters are lining up for attention in next year’s congressional business. A strategic plan released by the Interior Department this week will likely face legislative battles next year. In its goal to improve collaboration with states and tribes, the plan states it will “work to decrease the size of the federal estate by offering to states, localities and Tribes the opportunity to purchase federal lands.” It pledges to return some of the profits back to the buyers so they can improve access to those lands “while at the same time decreasing the federal taxpayer’s financial responsibility to manage federal lands.”
