text:
This blogpost was co-authored with Sital Sathia

As anticipated early in the year, 2026 broke all sorts of temperature records. A rapidly intensifying super El Niño, now the strongest on record combined with a perfect storm of killer heat brought on by the climate crisis, drove energy prices so high it sparked an affordability crisis, putting people at higher risk. With the hottest average temperatures on record this summer, the US also notched the highest need for cooling in 48 states. That combination of extreme heat and rising energy prices affected those who could least afford it during the 2026 Danger Season, the months between May and October when North America experiences some of the worst extreme weather due to fossil fuel-caused climate change. And, very likely, the worst is yet to come in 2027, when the Super El Niño is expected to bring warmer global temperatures, which could fuel more intense heatwaves in the US.

Most of us were hit with extreme heat in 2026

In the US, 94.6% of the total population in the lower 48 states experienced major or extreme heat risk at least once during the 2026 Danger Season. These two heat risk categories are the most dangerous especially for anyone without cooling or hydration, according to the National Weather Service. The figure below, assembled from archived data provided by the National Weather Service’s Heat Risk Tool, shows that during the 2026 Danger Season, there were seven multiday heat episodes where between 30% and 63% of the area of the lower 48 states was under at least moderate heat risk (represented by the orange, red, and purple bars)—an area equivalent roughly to 3-7 times the size of Texas. While moderate risk is not as severe as the major or extreme categories, it can still threaten those who are sensitive to heat.

Cooling needs rose in places where AC is less affordable

As heat becomes more intense and persistent, staying safe increasingly depends on access to reliable cooling. But having air conditioning alone is not enough: households also have to be able to afford the energy it takes to power it. Census data show that about 9.2 million US households lacked an AC unit in 2023, while millions more reported experiencing uncomfortably hot indoor temperatures even when cooling equipment was present.

In 2026, that need for cooling was especially pronounced. The 2026 Danger Season had the highest average number of cooling degree days across the lower 48 states. Cooling degree days (or CDD) measure how much temperatures exceed 65°F and are used to estimate cooling needs. The higher the CDD, the greater the need for air conditioning and potentially the higher the energy demand. CDD do not measure actual household electricity use or bills, but they help show how sustained cooling demand was this summer.

The map below shows how 2026 Danger Season’s CDD compared with the average for Danger Seasons past. Almost everywhere in the lower 48 states there were many more CDD during the 2026 Danger Season than during the 1991-2020 Danger Seasons. This shows clearly that cooling demand rose this year due to more heat. In fact, in 97% (or 233 out of 241) of major US cities analyzed by Climate Central, cooling degree days were on average 37% higher than in the 1970s.

And some of that need showed up in electricity use. Residential electricity consumption was 6% higher in the third quarter of 2026 than during the same period in 2025, according to US Energy Information Administration (EIA) estimates, in part because hotter weather increased cooling needs.

While these estimates reflect total summer electricity spending, not the cost of air conditioning alone, they underscore the growing financial pressure households face as staying cool becomes increasingly essential. And of course, rising electricity costs do not affect every household equally.

That’s where energy burden, one measure of energy affordability, becomes important. Energy burden is the share of household income spent on home energy, and 6% or greater is considered high energy burden.

Using 2022 data prepared by the Energy Equity Project (EEP) from the Department of Energy’s Low-Income Energy Affordability Data tool (DOE LEAD), we found a substantial divide by income. That inequity was evident whether income differences among households were assessed based on the federal poverty level (FPL) or the Area Median Income (AMI). The table below clearly shows that average energy burdens are much greater for lower-income households than for households with higher incomes.

These burden estimates help show which households were already facing energy affordability challenges before the extreme heat of 2026 and point to an important inequity: households with the fewest financial resources are devoting substantially more of their income to meeting basic home energy needs. When dangerous heat persists for weeks and keeping homes at safe temperatures can mean using more electricity, working families are faced with impossible choices, having far less room in those household budgets to absorb another expense.

Having AC doesn’t mean you can afford to run it

But the energy burden only tells part of the story. It tells us how much households spend relative to their income, but it does not necessarily tell us whether they are able to access all the energy they need. Some households cope with unaffordable energy costs by using less energy than they need, turning up the thermostat, cooling only part of the home, or going without air conditioning altogether.

And there are differences in how households with different income levels deal with cooling needs. For example, the difference in the temperature at which lower and higher-income households turn up the AC is defined as the energy equity gap. In Arizona, it was estimated that low-income households wait longer to turn up the AC, typically waiting for outside temperatures that are 4.7°–7.5°F (2.6°–4.2°C) hotter than higher-income households. Researchers argue that these kinds of energy-limiting behaviors can remain hidden in conventional measures of energy affordability. A relatively low bill may reflect affordability, but it may also mean that a household is going without the energy it needs to remain comfortable and safe.

That distinction matters during extreme heat. While energy burden measures how much of a household’s income goes toward energy bills, energy insecurity reflects the broader struggle to meet basic energy needs, whether because of high costs, unreliable service, or inadequate heating and cooling.

Recent federal data underscore that millions of households experienced some form of energy insecurity in 2024, including unhealthy indoor temperatures and an inability to use AC. And as energy justice scholar Dr. Tony Reames has emphasized, the underlying premise of addressing energy insecurity is that “energy is a basic human right.” During dangerous heat, that principle becomes especially tangible: electricity can be essential to keeping a home at a safe temperature. Yet whether households can use enough of it to protect their health still depends, in part, on whether they can afford the bill.

So where did the repeated dangerous heat of 2026 overlap with places where households were already facing greater energy-affordability challenges?

Rising cooling demand in energy-burdened communities

Above we showed how much higher cooling demand was in the 2026 Danger Season compared to recent decades. But how did that heat overlap with energy burdens? In the map below, we combined the Cooling Degree Days anomaly map with fine-scale energy burden data to assess the overlap of dangerous heat and energy burdens in 2026, and we found that it was substantial. The most frequent dangerous heat in 2026 coincided in communities with already-high electricity burdens, adding another layer of vulnerability to staying safely cool.

The dark pink and purple areas clustered in the Southern Great Plains and parts of the Southwest contain about 24 million households that experienced the largest increases in cooling demand during 2026, (between 401-900 more than during 1991-2020). Most of these have energy burdens of 0-5%, but there are scattered areas in the central and western parts of the country in dark blue with the largest increase in CDD and also the highest energy burden (6-10%).

For households already devoting a meaningful share of their income to home energy, repeated periods of dangerous heat can leave even less room to absorb the additional electricity cost needed to stay safely cool. Taken together, the map shows that the risks intersect in different ways across the country: some communities faced repeated dangerous heat, others greater energy affordability pressures, and millions of households faced both. What does it look like in states with large fractions of households in the highest combinations of cooling demand and energy burden? Below we sliced the top 15 states by percentage of households in the top-right quadrant of the combinations on the previous map. These are the combinations of the highest CDD anomalies and medium energy burden (purple), the highest energy burden and medium CDD anomalies (steel blue), and the highest values on both (dark blue). They represent about 12.2 million households across the country. In four states (Oklahoma, Arkansas, Mississippi, Kansas, and Nevada), households in the 3%-5% energy burden bin and the highest CDD anomaly (401-900) represent at least half of all households in each state.

Compounding events increase heat risk

While there were chronic exposures to heat this Danger Season, acute extreme weather events also piled heat-related risks on vulnerable and marginalized communities. Perhaps the most illustrative case of 2026 is the derecho (a widespread, long-lived storm with powerful winds that moves in a straight line) that knocked out power in mid-August for many in Indiana. But it was the people of Gary, a predominantly Black community in the state, who were left without power for 2-3 weeks after the storm. Many in the town faced indoor temperatures of about 85°F—without AC.

The country’s crumbling electrical transmission infrastructure that is not hardened to withstand extreme weather combines with the egregious callousness of systemic racism that neglects not just emergency repairs during blackouts, but also electricity infrastructure investments in Black and Brown communities. Recent UCS research has shown that a rigorously-planned, reliable, and climate-resilient grid can help reduce energy burden disparities.

What can households expect to face in 2027?

A record strength Super El Niño is unfolding on top of the long-term warming caused by fossil fuel-driven climate change, and climate scientists expect global temperatures to remain high in 2027, increasing the likelihood of extreme heat events that are longer, deadlier, and that in some cases hover around places for days, creating repeated dangerous heat conditions.

At the same time, households are also heading into 2027 weighed down by several years of rising electricity prices. In a 2026 PowerLines/Ipsos survey, 61% of utility billpayers said their energy bills were adding to their financial stress, and 77% are concerned their bills will rise again this year. Among households earning less than $50,000 a year, nearly half reported difficulty budgeting for their monthly gas and electricity bills.

EIA now forecasts the national average residential electricity price will rise by another 2.6% in 2027 from 2026, bringing projected 2027 prices to nearly 8% above 2025. That increase will not translate into the same bill change for every household. But when dangerous heat increases the electricity needed for cooling, rising prices can further squeeze households that are already having difficulty making their energy costs fit within their budgets.

The exact heat levels we will face in 2027 are uncertain. What is clear is that millions of households are entering another year of increasing climate risk while already struggling with energy affordability and no relief on the way.

How to address these threats

Future Danger Seasons will arrive in a climate that is fundamentally changed, with households and communities carrying very different levels of vulnerability into it. We may not be able to predict every detail of what comes next, but we already know a good deal about what helps people stay safer through extreme heat—and what makes the risks worse.

The recent mid-term elections clearly demonstrated that the US electorate connected the dots between the energy and affordability crises and rejected the politicians and policies that are worsening unaffordability of all aspects of life in the country by supporting fossil fuel interests.

And we already know many of the things that can help. There are programs and policies designed to make energy more affordable, homes safer, and communities more resilient, for example:

We can protect and strengthen programs such as the Weatherization Assistance Program (WAP), which helps lower-income households reduce energy use and costs through home efficiency improvements.

We can expand and improve the Low Income Home Energy Assistance Program (LIHEAP), which help households manage home energy costs and can provide assistance during times of need.

We can expand access to safe and affordable cooling and to clean energy options such as community solar. Pairing renewable energy with storage can help homes, community facilities, and microgrids keep essential power available when the larger grid goes down.

We can strengthen protections against utility disconnections when losing electricity can itself become a health and safety risk, while investing in a grid that is more reliable and resilient under increasingly extreme conditions.

Across all these efforts, communities, particularly those that have historically borne greater energy burdens, received fewer clean infrastructure investments while also being overburdened with polluting fossil-fueled infrastructure, should have a meaningful role in deciding what gets built, where investments go, and what resilience looks like for them.

We can plan for extreme heat as something we know will continue to happen every year, rather than waiting until people are already in danger to respond. And we can continue working to reduce the climate pollution that is driving more dangerous heat in the first place.

While we cannot prevent every extreme heat event or every disruption, we can shape what happens when they arrive: whether homes can stay safely cool, whether an unexpected bill becomes a crisis, whether the power stays on, and whether communities have the resources they need to recover.

And that is where the possibility of a different outcome begins.

Preparing equitably means investing most where the risks are greatest, while strengthening the systems we all rely on. When homes are safer, energy is affordable, communities have a voice, and the grid is more resilient, we are all better prepared for what comes next.

We may not be able to predict exactly what the next Danger Season will bring, but science can help us prepare for what is ahead. With equity as our guiding principle, we can make choices to reduce the risk of climate change while ensuring that everyone is able to stay safe.

text:
This audio is auto-generated. Please let us know if you have feedback.

Most major U.S. grid operators have now submitted their highly anticipated proposals for interconnecting data centers and other large loads to the grid in response to directives issued by the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission.

FERC in June issued “show cause” orders saying that it appeared that regional transmission organizations and others lacked adequate rules for adding large loads to the grid. FERC asked them to propose reforms to address the agency’s concerns or to explain why their existing rules were just and reasonable.

FERC detailed five issues it wanted the grid operators to address in their large load interconnection rules: efficient transmission service application and study processes, including the consideration of alternative transmission technologies; prevention of cost shifts and transparency into transmission costs; co-location and behind-the-meter generation; new transmission services for flexible large loads; and a study process for generating facilities that serve “electrically proximate” large loads and co-located loads.

The move by FERC comes amid a surge in data center development in many U.S. regions and a corresponding pushback on that development, which includes concerns that existing utility customers will pay for some of the data center-related electric infrastructure.

Below is a summary of the proposals at FERC, which were filed on Monday, except for ISO New England’s. The Southwest Power Pool is slated to file its proposal by Friday.

PJM Interconnection

The centerpiece of PJM’s plan is a Fast Energization Process, under which the grid operator would revamp its interconnection study process by studying large load and generation interconnection requests in a single, one-year process — about twice as fast as the current process, according to PJM.

In its filing on Monday, PJM said its proposed Fast Energization Process is designed to address “insufficiently fast interconnection processes for load and generation, parallel and duplicative study processes, speculative requests, limited visibility into the drivers of transmission upgrades, and an ongoing resource adequacy shortfall.”

Keep up with the story. Subscribe to the Utility Dive free daily newsletter

The proposed process marks “the next evolution of PJM’s interconnection process and further enhancement to the currently effective Cycle process,” Donald Bielak, director of interconnection planning at PJM, told FERC in a separate filing.

PJM’s overall proposal also addresses co-location and behind-the-meter generation rules that were at issue in a separate show cause proceeding, according to the grid operator. PJM filed a separate proposal that requires large computational loads to be able to ride through grid disturbances.

PJM’s transmission owners filed their own proposed tariffs that establish rates, cost allocation, cost recovery mechanisms, financial protections, revenue-crediting requirements and transparency measures for transmission service they provide to co-located loads and large loads.

California Independent System Operator

“The proposed reforms strengthen accountability and protect existing customers,” CAISO told FERC. “They improve transparency, operational visibility, technical standards, cost responsibility, and protection against speculative development.”

The CAISO and transmission owner tariff revisions create streamlined paths for large loads to connect to the electric system, according to the grid operator. “Standardized application information, deposits, milestones, study coordination, and service agreements will make the process more transparent and predictable,” CAISO said.

As part of its proposal, CAISO plans to offer new service options for flexible large loads that can cut their electric use when transmission capability is unavailable.

Read More in Generation

ISO New England

In its filing on Friday, ISO-NE and the region’s transmission owners said they fully addressed FERC’s show cause order. In response to the agency’s transparency concerns, ISO-NE proposed that it maintain on its website a list of the network upgrades identified for each large load, categorized by upgrade type, and the cost estimates for those upgrades.

To address FERC’s concerns about resource adequacy in New England, ISO-NE said it plans to require that large loads bring their own new capacity and that certain large loads will be excluded from ISO-NE’s capacity market’s installed capacity requirement. The grid operator plans to work with stakeholders to craft the details of its proposed framework, with a goal of filing a proposal at FERC later this year.

Midcontinent Independent System Operator

MISO said its proposal builds on its other reform plans recently filed at FERC: the Zero Injection Generator Interconnection Agreement, Interconnection Reliability Requirements for Large Loads and Large Load Addition Resource Study.

The just-filed proposal includes a Large Load Project Review process, new transmission service options and tariff revisions and pro forma cost recovery agreements designed to prevent cost shifting onto existing utility customers, MISO said. In a separate filing Monday, MISO proposed Grid Responsive Integration Transmission Service for large loads that can limit their electric use under certain price and reliability conditions.

MISO’s proposals at FERC represent “an important milestone, not an endpoint,” the grid operator said. “MISO remains committed to further enhancing its planning, operational, and market frameworks as experience is gained and system needs grow.”

Read More in Generation

New York Independent System Operator

Among other things, NYISO’s proposal provides new types of transmission services — Firm Withdrawal Service and Non-Firm Withdrawal Service — that reflect the unique characteristics of NYISO’s transmission model and of co-located large loads, large load with behind-the-meter generation, and flexible large loads, the grid operator said.

The proposal includes a compromise approach to resource adequacy requirements, called the State Exempt Load Project exception, which aims to reconcile the NYISO’s reliability responsibilities with the New York Public Service Commission resource adequacy authority, the grid operator said.

text:
About 70 units of the electric midsize SUV roll off the assembly line every day.

BMW expects to manufacture 60,000 electric vehicles there in 2027.

To minimize its risk, BMW currently uses Chinese battery cells and a modular assembly line that can make both combustion-powered and electric models simultaneously.

The upcoming 2027 BMW iX5 has now entered production at the company’s Spartanburg, South Carolina assembly plant, with about 70 units coming off the assembly line every day.

About five months after having been revealed, the new generation of the BMW X5 and its electric counterpart, the iX5, have entered production in the United States.

While the X5 has been manufactured in South Carolina since the launch of the first generation in 1999, the iX5 is the first electric BMW model to be made in the United States.

According to the automaker, it won’t be the last, as BMW still says it will make six new electric vehicles in the United States by 2030.

The targeted sales volumes for EVs have been reduced, however, now standing at 60,000 for the 2027 calendar year, down from 100,000.

The automaker has reportedly told its local suppliers to be ready for the production of about 175,000 electric vehicles in Spartanburg in 2028 and 2029, but this could be adjusted up or down depending on the state of the market.

Even with the reduced numbers, electric vehicles will make up a significant portion of the factory’s total production, as the plant usually makes about 400,000 vehicles per year.

To support this expected EV volume, BMW invested $1.7 billion over the last few years in South Carolina.

In addition to a 1 million square foot addition to the assembly plant itself, this investment included a new battery plant in nearby Woodruff, South Carolina, which opened last week.

This facility will assemble the battery packs used in the iX5 and future electric models built in Spartanburg.

Despite a shaky EV market that led many automakers to downsize or abandon their electrification efforts over the last two years or so, losing significant sums in the process, BMW is optimistic in this regard.

Indeed, the German automaker seems to have taken a number of precautions that should protect it against a downturn in EV sales while also making it able to compete should EVs increase in popularity over the coming months.

For a start, the automaker’s South Carolina assembly plant uses a modular assembly line that can manufacture gasoline, plug-in hybrid, and electric vehicles simultaneously.

This means that BMW can adjust production volumes of the X5 and iX5 on the fly depending on market demand, but also that it won’t be stuck with unusable production capacity if either electric or gasoline-powered models become significantly less popular over the coming years.

Additionally, BMW’s Spartanburg assembly plant relies heavily on exports, with about half of its annual production being sent to other markets, including Europe. This actually makes BMW the largest automotive exporter in the United States in terms of value.

This means that if the EV market continues to stagnate in the U.S., BMW can still benefit from rising global EV sales by exporting a larger proportion of iX5s.

Finally, unlike many of its competitors, BMW is not making its entire battery packs internally.

Indeed, the company’s new American battery plant uses cells from supplier AESC, which are made in China.

This approach would likely be less profitable in the long term than making the cells in-house, but it significantly reduces the up-front costs required to set up an EV production line and therefore minimizes the damage a collapse of EV demand could cause.

While AESC had announced a South Carolina-based battery plant specifically to supply BMW EVs, this project has been cancelled, and the automaker will instead transition to LG Energy Solutions as its cell supplier toward the end of the decade, when the South Korean company will be able to supply cells produced in Arizona.

A battery cell plant in South Carolina could still happen someday even without BMW’s support, as the state is also home to Mercedes-Benz and Volvo assembly plants that both produce electric vehicles.

text:
Hyundai is expanding its presence in the United States with a $26 billion investment and 58 new or refreshed North American models scheduled through 2030. One of them is the new Elantra, which comes to revive the affordable sedan segment. The roadmap also includes 22 models from its luxury sister brand, Genesis.

As a matter of fact, several major model reveals and arrivals on the market are confirmed for the immediate future: the 2027 Hyundai Elantra and the 2028 Elantra Hybrid are part of the plan. The next-generation compact sedan makes its U.S. debut at AutoMobility LA on Thursday, November 19, 2026.

The model features sharper styling, as we have seen on the model sold in South Korea as the Avante, a more spacious cabin, and Hyundai's new Android-based Pleos Connect infotainment system with the Gleo AI assistant. The gas version arrives as a 2027 model, followed by the 2028 Hyundai Elantra Hybrid.

The automaker has yet to announce official U.S. pricing for the redesigned 2027 Elantra or 2028 Elantra Hybrid, but it is expected to arrive at under $30,000 in an attempt to steal market share from the Toyota Corolla and Corolla Hybrid or Honda Civic and Civic Hybrid.

The Toyota Corolla, which starts at $24,620 ($26,470 for the Corolla Hybrid) is America's best-selling sedan with 217,905 units sold from January through October 2026. Honda Civic is keeping up with its, with 213,095 units moved this year to date.

The Civic starts at $26,290 for the base LX, while the Civic Hybrid is a $30,990 deal. That is where the all-new Elantra and Elantra Hybrid have to fall in order to stay competitive in an market that these models won't let die. Hyundai sold 140,614 Elantras from January to October in the United States.

Hyundai Ioniq 6 N is on its way to the U.S.

Hyundai has also confirmed to Cars.com that the Hyundai Ioniq 6 N will arrive in America in the spring of 2027 in limited numbers. Hyundai doesn't say how many but says the model will have "extremely limited availability" at select dealerships. Pricing details will be disclosed closer to market launch date. The high-performance Ioniq 6 N the sole version of the Ioniq 6 offered in the U.S. for 2027, but customers have no reason to complain.

The high-performance sedan with zero tailpipe emissions is powered by a dual-motor setup, operating in an all-wheel-drive layout. The system produces 641 horsepower (650 metric horsepower) along with 568 pound-feet (568 Newton meters) of torque with the N Grin mode on. That is enough to make the sedan run from 0 to 60 mph (0 to 97 kph) in 3.2 seconds with N Launch Control and all the way to 159 mph (257 kph).

A lithium-ion battery pack with a capacity of 84.0 kWh (about 80.0 kWh usable) stores enough energy to make the Ioniq 6 N drive as far as 245 miles (394 kilometers) before it needs to be plugged in again, as rated by the EPA. Chassis reinforcements, larger brakes, upgraded cooling hardware, and the battery pack push the sedan's curb weight to roughly 4,775 pounds (2,166 kilograms).

The 2027 Hyundai Tucson and Tucson Hybrid are already listed on the official Hyundai USA site for an early 2027 arrival. The redesigned SUV introduces a next-generation powertrain, integrating either the 1.6-liter turbocharged inline-four with zero electric assistance or the same engine assisted by a dual-motor setup and a 1.49-kWh lithium-ion battery.

Expectedly, the hybrid variant will sit at the top of the lineup with 233 horsepower and 280 pound-feet (380 Newton meters) of torque, put down through either the front wheels or all four corners with the help of the HTRAC AWD system. The all-new Tucson also gets the new Pleos Connect and a rugged XRT PRO trim.

Starting in 2027, Hyundai plans to introduce its first extended-range electric vehicles, including an upcoming Santa Fe EREV, estimated to be capable of over 600 miles (966 kilometers) of total range.

Massive investment in U.S. production

As part of its 2030 roadmap, Hyundai has also confirmed plans to enter new North American segments with a midsize body-on-frame pickup truck, which would give the Ford Ranger and the Toyota Tacoma a run for their money, along with a large commercial van.

To support its North American lineup and avoid tariffs imposed on imported goods, Hyundai is investing $26 billion in the United States. The move is expected to create 25,000 direct jobs and add 500,000 units of production capacity at the brand’s plants in Montgomery, Alabama, Ellabell, Georgia, and Donaldsonville, Louisiana.

While Hyundai is expanding the Metaplant in Georgia to produce hybrids and EVs, alongside a $12.6 billion battery joint venture, nearly $500 million is invested in Montgomery to build engines for the next-gen Tucson and Santa Fe, as well as Hyundai’s first extended-range EVs.

Hyundai will also build a $5.8 billion low-carbon steel mill in Louisiana to supply its auto plants in the United States.

title: US power plant carbon rollback takes effect, removing key driver for carbon capture
description:
The US Environmental Protection Agency has repealed most of the 2024 power sector carbon standards, including requirements based on carbon capture for new baseload gas turbines.
A separate proposal would revoke the remaining federal greenhouse gas standards for fossil-fired power plants.
The repeal weakens the regulatory case for some US power sector carbon capture projects.
The Trump administration’s partial repeal of US power plant greenhouse gas standards took effect on Monday, removing federal rules that would have pushed some coal and gas generators towards carbon capture and storage (CCS).
A separate EPA proposal would remove the remaining greenhouse gas standards in the source category, a further step that would require its own final rule.
text:
The US Environmental Protection Agency has repealed most of the 2024 power sector carbon standards, including requirements based on carbon capture for new baseload gas turbines.

Efficiency standards for new turbines remain in place for now. A separate proposal would revoke the remaining federal greenhouse gas standards for fossil-fired power plants.

The repeal weakens the regulatory case for some US power sector carbon capture projects. The federal tax credit for carbon sequestration remains available to qualifying projects.

The Trump administration’s partial repeal of US power plant greenhouse gas standards took effect on Monday, removing federal rules that would have pushed some coal and gas generators towards carbon capture and storage (CCS).

The measure was finalised in September and is being challenged in the US Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit by a coalition led by New York Attorney General Letitia James.

The rule rescinds the 2024 emissions guidelines for existing fossil-fuelled steam generating units, which include much of the coal fleet. It also removes standards based on 90% CCS for coal units undergoing major modifications and for new baseload stationary combustion turbines.

Efficiency-based standards for new turbines survive this round. A separate EPA proposal would remove the remaining greenhouse gas standards in the source category, a further step that would require its own final rule.

The EPA argues that CCS was insufficiently demonstrated for the applications covered by the 2024 rule and that the requirements would have put pressure on plants to close. Its regulatory analysis estimates the present value of avoided compliance costs at $280 billion over 2026-47 using a 3% discount rate, or $180 billion at 7%.

Those figures are modelled industry costs. They cannot be read directly as expected savings on electricity bills, which depend on how utilities invest, dispatch their plants and recover costs.

James’s coalition argues that the agency failed to properly consider alternatives or the costs of allowing more greenhouse gas pollution. “Future generations are going to pay the price for our federal government’s callous disregard for Americans’ health and the environment,” James said when announcing the challenge on 1 October. The coalition also gave notice of a separate intended action over the EPA’s treatment of existing gas plants.

A different CCS investment test

For a US generator weighing a retrofit or a new gas plant, a federal emissions standard could have made capture part of the cost of staying open or building a plant designed to run frequently. Its removal gives utilities more scope to defer that spending.

Projects can still qualify for the federal Section 45Q tax credit, although they still need to make the economics of capture, transport and storage work. Utilities can also face state-level requirements and commercial pressures that vary by market.

The UK is trying to make gas with CCS investable through project-level contracts that pay for availability and account for some of the extra costs of running a capture-equipped plant. That makes British projects a potential source of orders for suppliers if US power sector demand weakens.

Fewer US projects could also slow the accumulation of operating experience that helps lenders and developers price risk elsewhere. UK procurement will depend on how quickly projects secure contracts and access to carbon transport and storage.

title: Catawba College Aces a Clean Energy Curriculum
description:
They’re all part of Catawba College’s clean energy story, and you can find them all on campus.
Whether it’s a solar-powered Christmas tree, carbon-free cookout, or an electrified rideshare service, there’s never a shortage of exciting clean energy progress at Catawba.
Join the Clean Energy Generation Catawba College is one example of folks across the Southeast taking action to prioritize clean, affordable energy and make it accessible to everyone, no matter your age, income, zip code, or abilities.
Like Catawba, we all can play a role in the clean energy transition.
Join the Clean Energy Generation movement, and we’ll share ideas and tools for you to make a difference in your community.
text:
What do an electric rideshare service, repurposed coal smokestack, solar-powered racecar, and energy-efficient dormitory have in common? They’re all part of Catawba College’s clean energy story, and you can find them all on campus.

Catawba became the first Southeastern college to reach carbon neutrality in 2023 — an achievement borne from always asking what’s next, then doing it. Whether it’s a solar-powered Christmas tree, carbon-free cookout, or an electrified rideshare service, there’s never a shortage of exciting clean energy progress at Catawba. You can even check it out on their

Check out four recent additions to Catawba’s renewable energy record below.

Electric Rideshare Goals: CatawbaGO

In August 2025, I talked to Noah Upchurch, one of Catawba College’s Sustainability Program Directors, on the launch day of CatawbaGO, a free, on-demand electric van rideshare service operated by Slidr for Catawba students, staff, and faculty.

The fleet currently consists of two Volkswagen ID Buzz vans, having replaced its previous Ford E-Transit van. And it has exceeded expectations: over 17,000 rides have been completed as of November 2026, most with a five-star rating. Last school year alone, CatawbaGO moved the equivalent of the school’s entire student body, about 1,350 students, ten times over.

Michael Dorin, a third-year online student who has been a driver of one of CatawbaGO’s two electric vans since the program began, shares that enthusiasm. “I have enjoyed every second of driving an EV,” he says. “I love that we are giving students who can’t afford a car a way to get around town. The first-time riders are always excited…a lot of oohs and aahs are common.”

The college is happy, too. It costs as low as $7 to fully charge each EV, which is equal to less than $1 per gallon of gas. And it wasn’t rocket science: CatawbaGO is proof that a micro-transit program doesn’t have to be expensive and complicated. “This isn’t a million-dollar program,” Noah says. “The economics speak for themselves, and more entities should be doing this.”

CatawbaGO’s routes are influenced by what students, faculty, and staff need most. Riders can propose new routes during a two-week window at the start of each semester. Riders who live off-campus aren’t left out: this summer, Catawba computer science students evaluated the advantages of having a commuter-only route and van in the future and found it could save money, cut more emissions, and reduce wait times.

Riders can also reserve rides in advance, which is especially helpful for working students and athletes.

Even the community’s small businesses benefit from CatawbaGO, offering a reliable route to downtown Salisbury where riders can do their shopping, instead of at big-box stores off-route and farther away.

So, what’s next? Catawba recently signed an addendum extending CatawbaGO for up to three more years and is looking at expanding beyond its current two vehicles.

Centennial Hall: the First Passive Residence Hall in NC

This year, Catawba College’s Centennial Hall became the first residence hall in North Carolina built to Passive House standards. Passive House is a building certification from Passive House Institute United States (PHIUS) that emphasizes safety, resilience, comfort, and energy efficiency.

Centennial Hall is designed to be up to 70% more efficient than similar buildings, but before it can earn PHIUS certification, it must perform as modeled. The 130 students living in the hall during its inaugural fall 2026 semester will play a major part in testing that performance.

On screens throughout the hall, “tips of the day” promote energy-saving choices and connect residents to clean energy efforts across campus. Residents are learning how to work together to keep clustered HVAC usage low and how the campus-wide geothermal system helps power Centennial Hall’s heat pumps.

Students can also learn about the energy efficiency tests the college regularly conducts, such as blower door airtightness testing. Catawba partners with a company that conducts the tests, then shares and discusses the results with students. This turns the hall into a living-learning laboratory where students can dive deeper into energy efficiency and explore potential career pathways in the industry.

But Noah, the Sustainability Program Director, stresses that the building’s performance doesn’t all fall entirely on residents. Centennial Hall is airtight, which means it has quieter spaces to live and study and cleaner air to breathe.

“We want our students to not have to think super hard about how they are living, but just know that they are living in a responsible way because of the structure we set up for them,” Noah says. “They may not know or really care about all of the nuances, but that’s okay. Having a really nice experience and associating that with sustainability is the goal.”

E-Vroom! Catawba College’s Solar Racing Team

This summer, Catawba College participated in its first American Solar Challenge (ASC), a cross-country road rally for collegiate teams who design, build, and race solar-powered vehicles. Catawba’s team was one of the smallest and one of only three non-engineering schools among the 39 competing.

It started with flyers posted around campus asking, “Can you build a solar race car?” Students from Catawba and nearby community colleges answered the call, coming from many majors and backgrounds, united by an interest in cars.

“Since none of us are engineers, we get to learn and solve problems in non-traditional ways,” says Phoebe Dell’Arena, the team’s media lead and a sophomore Environment and Sustainability student at Catawba. Phoebe joined to learn basic car repair skills. “I remember my first time learning how to change a tire — it was on the solar car, which felt so cool,” she says.

After basic training from Appalachian State University’s team Sunergy, the team revived an old solar race car acquired from App State. Ten students traveled to the competition in Brainerd, Minnesota, along with two advisers: Noah, and Dr. Lee F. Ball Jr., Catawba’s Vice President of Sustainability and Executive Director of its Center for the Environment. Ball advised App State’s team for years. For two weeks, teams camped and competed at the track, an atmosphere Phoebe says felt like “another planet.”

“I’ve never been around people so competitive and passionate,” Phoebe says. “That’s what keeps me thinking about this trip: we did something we’d never experienced before, and we endured it with such resilience.”

After five days of grueling safety inspections, late-night work sessions, and even a windstorm that ripped the roof off their car, a defective battery module kept the team out of the race.

The team found other ways to stay engaged, from donating their hands-free radio system to the Georgia Institute of Technology’s team to lending a truck and trailer to a team from Montreal. In the end, Catawba won the Dr. James Hill Sportsmanship Award.

“It still felt like we won the whole race, based on how much we all got from the experience,” Phoebe says. “Just looking at the pictures that I took from the beginning to the end – our progress was crazy.”

Since returning to campus, team members have hosted open workshops on practical mechanical skills they learned from building the car, which can help students repair their bicycles or, for some, open career pathways for a school located in the heart of race country.

The team is already preparing for next year’s ASC track race: Phoebe just finished designing the team’s logo and branding, and they recently unboxed their next car. “We’re ready to go even bigger,” she says. “We really are starting this up. It’s so important and just feels special that I get to be here.”

The Smokestack: Once a Coal Plant, Not Always a Coal Plant

The tallest building on Catawba’s campus is its retired coal-fired power plant. It stands proud and bears the school name, though it hasn’t billowed black smoke since the 1990s.

This summer, Catawba College began the process of reclaiming the dormant building as a net-zero, carbon-neutral commons where students can spend time and study in one of the most visible symbols of Catawba’s decarbonization efforts. After all, the finished Smokestack will be LEED Platinum and Living Building Challenge certified, the highest green building certifications a building can reach.

There’s good reason why Catawba gave up burning coal – it’s dangerous, toxic, and outdated, to name a few – but they didn’t want to give up on the iconic building. Historic preservation of the college’s neo-Gothic architecture reminds the community of the school’s legacy, and reclaiming old buildings with a focus on the environment ensures that legacy will be an upstanding one.

The Smokestack will also be resilient: a battery fed by a 60 kW solar array will help keep power on in the event of extreme storms made worse by climate change, like the historic Winter Storm Gianna that hit Salisbury in February.

The old coal plant sits in the middle of campus – so the new Smokestack will be the heart of campus, Noah says. Right behind the student center, it will offer the best view of all Catawba has to offer: the school’s beach volleyball solar array, the lot where CatawbaGO vehicles park, and Centennial Hall right next door.

Join the Clean Energy Generation

Catawba College is one example of folks across the Southeast taking action to prioritize clean, affordable energy and make it accessible to everyone, no matter your age, income, zip code, or abilities. Like Catawba, we all can play a role in the clean energy transition. Join the Clean Energy Generation movement, and we’ll share ideas and tools for you to make a difference in your community.

text:
RALEIGH, NC (WWAY) — The North Carolina Utilities Commission has issued a new carbon plan for Duke Energy, drawing criticism from environmental advocates who say the plan relies too heavily on natural gas and could lead to higher electricity bills for customers.

The plan largely approves Duke Energy’s proposal to expand natural gas infrastructure while also allowing for additional solar energy and battery storage projects.

The decision comes as Duke Energy works toward meeting a state law requiring the utility to achieve net-zero carbon emissions by 2050.

The Southern Environmental Law Center, which represented the Southern Alliance for Clean Energy, Sierra Club and Vote Solar during the proceedings, argues the plan does not do enough to prioritize affordable renewable energy resources.

Environmental advocates say the commission’s decision could leave customers paying more for natural gas plants while delaying investments in solar, wind and other clean energy alternatives.

They also raised concerns about Duke Energy’s projected increases in electricity demand, including anticipated growth from data centers and artificial intelligence operations.

“It’s unsettling that the Commission is not checking Duke’s dirty plans, including delaying the retirement of expensive, aging coal infrastructure, and not directing Duke to take near-term actions to better ensure compliance with the bipartisan law that requires the utility to reach net zero emissions by 2050,” said Mikaela Curry, Beyond Coal campaign manager for the Sierra Club.

Earlier this year, the commission issued an order pausing solar and battery procurement, effectively preventing the projects from moving forward in 2026, according to environmental groups.

Advocates argue those delays could make it more difficult for Duke Energy to meet the state’s long-term emissions goals while potentially increasing costs for customers.

However, the groups acknowledged that the newly issued plan includes approval for utility-scale solar and battery storage projects in the near term.

“While we appreciate the Commission’s approval of the utility scale solar and battery storage in Duke’s near-term plan, we cannot afford to keep delaying the development of a broader array of renewable resources that would lead to significant cost savings and enhanced reliability for customers,” said David Neal, senior attorney at the Southern Environmental Law Center.

Maggie Shober, research director for the Southern Alliance for Clean Energy, also criticized Duke Energy’s approach.

“Families are already experiencing costly energy bills. If Duke had focused on more affordable renewable resources, families would have some relief from higher bills,” Shober said.

Environmental advocates are calling for greater investment in renewable energy, energy efficiency and battery storage as North Carolina works toward its 2050 carbon emissions target.

The commission’s decision establishes a framework for Duke Energy’s future energy planning, although individual projects may still require additional regulatory approvals.

title: The BAAJA media blackout - by Emily Atkin - HEATED
description:
If you haven’t heard about BAAJA, you’re not alone; a Data for Progress poll shows 65 percent of likely voters haven’t heard anything about it.
The voices opposing BAAJA—tribal nations, environmental groups, justice groups and more—have gone entirely unrepresented.
Support independent climate media BAAJA coverage worth your time Let’s be real: cable news isn’t really great for keeping yourself informed about big-picture policy issues anyway, especially when it comes to issues affecting the climate.
Lisa Martine Jenkins has the full breakdown of why environmental groups are so opposed to the bill.
Andrew R. Chow looked at both sides of the argument for and against BAAJA from a data center/artificial intelligence perspective.
text:
Here’s a little secret: I watch cable news.

Well, “watch” is probably too strong a word. I sometimes turn on cable news while I’m cooking or doing the crossword or disassociating on my couch. It feels semi-productive to periodically look at the television and assess what millions of Americans watch on a daily basis; after all, 63 percent of us still get our news from TV at least sometimes. With cable news on, I feel like I’m getting a window into what corporate media thinks is worth paying attention to, and what many Americans hear about—and don’t hear about—as a result.

I’m telling you this because, late last week while I was roasting a squash, it occurred to me that I hadn’t heard anything on cable news about BAAJA since it was introduced back in September.

If you haven’t heard about BAAJA, you’re not alone; a Data for Progress poll shows 65 percent of likely voters haven’t heard anything about it. It stands for the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, and it’s a massive permitting reform bill that the Senate just voted to stop debate on last night, and move to a full floor vote later this week. 21 Democrats joined in the vote.

It’s hard to overstate how big a deal this bill is. The League of Conservation Voters calls it “potentially generational legislation,” because it would weaken some of the nation’s oldest environmental and tribal laws in the name of making it easier to build both fossil fuel and renewable energy. Oh, and also data centers.

And though the bill was co-written by Democratic Sens. Martin Heinrich of New Mexico and Sheldon Whitehouse of Rhode Island—two of clean energy’s loudest supporters in Congress—it has caused huge rift in the climate community. Techno-optimist climate wonks like billionaire Tom Steyer; Volts host Dave Roberts, and “abundance” advocates like Ezra Klein say the bill is important for climate progress because it will fast-track interstate power lines, therefore getting more wind and solar onto the grid. But environmentalists like Al Gore, Bill McKibben and groups like Earthjustice say the trade-off will be an explosion of fossil fuel infrastructure, data data centers, and ICE detention centers, as well as and the weakening of laws that allow communities and tribes to halt these developments. And that trade-off is unacceptable. (FWIW, Big Oil and the Trump administration both love the bill).

Anyway, it’s all a huge mess, and it’s all moving so quickly, and all it’s so consequential—and yet, it felt to me (and others) like corporate media was entirely ignoring the whole thing.

But feelings aren’t fact. So last week I asked Media Matters to run an analysis of cable news coverage since BAAJA was introduced, to see if major news networks have at least been trying to tell people about what the Union of Concerned Scientists has called “the most significant legislative reversal in environmental and community protections in decades.”

Folks—they have not.

Here’s what the Media Matters analysis for HEATED found. From the day BAAJA was introduced in the Senate until Friday, November 13, the big three cable networks have run a combined 26 minutes of coverage about it. Fox News aired the most, with a combined 13 minutes; MS Now aired a total of 9 minutes; And CNN ran 4 minutes.

How did these networks frame BAAJA when they did cover it? Fox News ran five segments, each framing the bill as a positive way to get energy projects built faster and criticizing environmental groups for holding it up. On CNN, there were no actual segments; just passing 20-30 second mentions with little substance, according Media Matters.

MS Now ran two segments, each on Money, Power, Politics with Stephanie Ruhle. One praised the bill for its bipartisan support and its promise to make data centers pay for power and grid upgrades. The second segment was a 5-minute interview with John Arnold, a billionaire who made his name as a gas trader for Enron, making his case for the bill.

In other words, cable news has barely covered BAAJA. When they have covered it, the only people given a microphone were the ones supporting the bill. The voices opposing BAAJA—tribal nations, environmental groups, justice groups and more—have gone entirely unrepresented.

Of course, cable news is not entirely to blame for the majority of people not knowing about this bill. The Senate has made it very hard for people to follow BAAJA. There have been no committee hearings, markups or legislative reports on the bill. Its sponsors put out a 494-page rewrite on a Saturday, and by Monday senators were already casting their first procedural vote. As the National Congress of American Indians pointed out, that gave Tribal Nations all of one weekend to figure out what the rewrite would mean for them.

I can’t insulate myself from this critique, either. Until yesterday, I haven’t been involved in the coverage of this bill aside from infrequent Bluesky posts. My weak excuse is that I’m one person and there was an election and this bill has literally moved so fast that I’ve not had time to both read the entire thing and talk to enough people to feel confident opining on it before it reached a cloture vote.

And yet, that’s the whole point, isn’t it? A lame-duck Congress is rushing through a bill that Defenders of Wildlife’s Chris Westfall says poses “one of the most sweeping attacks on the Endangered Species Act in the law’s more than 50-year history,” that the Center for Biological Diversity calls “a climate kill shot,” and that a coalition of “Abundance” groups says would be “the most significant modernization of the federal permitting system in a generation.”

It doesn’t matter where you fall on BAAJA: Pushing something that consequential through Congress in six weeks feels pretty undemocratic, particularly when voters just elected a new Congress that could give the bill a full public hearing in January.

At the very least, a bill this meaningful ought to be the kind of thing you hear about on the news while you’re roasting a squash. Preferably while there’s still time to call your senator.

Support independent climate media

BAAJA coverage worth your time

Let’s be real: cable news isn’t really great for keeping yourself informed about big-picture policy issues anyway, especially when it comes to issues affecting the climate.

If you want to be more informed about BAAJA, here are some outlets that have been doing a great job covering it from different perspectives:

Heatmap News. Robinson Meyer and Jael Holzman went through the 494-page rewrite and explained what changed for power lines, data centers, and the federal permits that future presidents might want to undo. Holzman has also covered the case House moderates are making for the bill.

Latitude Media. Lisa Martine Jenkins has the full breakdown of why environmental groups are so opposed to the bill.

Boise State Public Radio. Daniel Spaulding spoke with the Northern Arapaho Tribe’s historic preservation director about how the bill could affect the tribe’s ability to protect sacred sites.

NPR. Rachel Treisman dove into how the bill would affect the National Historic Preservation Act, calling it “the most serious threat in its 60-year history.”

TIME. Andrew R. Chow looked at both sides of the argument for and against BAAJA from a data center/artificial intelligence perspective.

Reuters. Valerie Volcovici reported on the fight among Democrats over whether to take the deal now, try to change it in the House, or wait until the new Congress takes office.

The Guardian. Oliver Milman spoke with Al Gore and Sheldon Whitehouse at COP31 about what each expects Trump to do with the bill if it passes.

text:
By: Matt Rascon, Natasha Qamar

| Published 11/17/2026

Energy leaders gather at event in The Woodlands to help displaced workers

THE WOODLANDS, TX — As layoffs and hiring challenges collide across the energy industry, Global Energy Transition (GET), a Houston nonprofit working to fill the gap, held its Fourth Annual Awards of Excellence on Friday, Nov. 13, at Entergy Texas Headquarters. More than 120 people attended the ceremony, bringing together corporate executives, industry leaders, elected officials and community supporters around the themes of community, resilience and upskilling amid significant workforce shifts. The U.S. energy economy shed a net 86,000 jobs in 2025, including about 28,400 in the fuels sector, according to the Department of Energy's 2026 U.S. Energy & Employment Report. Among employers that hired, roughly two-thirds to three-quarters reported difficulty finding workers. Locally, the Greater Houston Partnership's 2025 Houston Region Economic Outlook forecast a loss of about 3,200 oil and gas extraction jobs in 2026, even as the region was projected to add 30,900 jobs overall. Since its founding, GET says it has helped more than 600 displaced energy workers, professionals, and entrepreneurs through education, scholarships, coaching, networking, and employer partnerships. GET's focus is helping workers transition between jobs, most often within the energy industry itself, although GET Chairwoman Sonia Clayton says securing new positions in oil and gas has become increasingly difficult. “The GET Awards of Excellence celebrate leaders who understand that the energy transition is ultimately about people,” said Clayton, who is also the president and CEO of VIP-Global. “Our mission has always been to ensure that workers, families, and communities are not left behind as industries evolve.” One example is Victoria Gerber, who was laid off from an oil and gas company in 2022 and spent nearly two years looking for work. With a GET scholarship, she completed a sustainability certificate program at Stanford University and now holds a leadership role at Parkhill, one of the organizations recognized at Friday's ceremony. GET's 2026 honorees included EDP Renewables North America, Parkhill, Entergy, SLB, Holland Parker, OGCS Global, CoVolt Power, SolomonEdwards and KHOU 11. “As industries transform and new opportunities emerge, it is essential that we equip workers with the skills, knowledge, and support needed to succeed,” Jeff Williams, chief strategy officer at Parkhill and former mayor of Arlington, Texas, said before the event. “GET is building bridges between talent and opportunity, and I am proud to support an organization that is helping individuals transition into rewarding careers while strengthening the workforce that drives our nation’s economic future.” Jim “Mattress Mack” McIngvale, founder and CEO of Gallery Furniture, shared his story of resilience and entrepreneurship, encouraging attendees to persevere through challenges. “When you invest in people, you strengthen entire communities. Every good job creates opportunity, dignity, and hope for families. That’s why I support GET’s work,” McIngvale said before the event. “Personally, I believe there is no greater investment than helping people find meaningful, long-term employment and achieve their full potential.” Montgomery County Judge Mark Keough presented an official proclamation recognizing GET and spoke about the importance of community, leadership and investing in people. KHOU 11 news anchor Jacob Rascon served as master of ceremonies. “Behind every placement is a person. Behind every person is a family. And behind every successful career transition is a renewed sense of purpose, dignity, and hope,” Clayton said following the event. About Global Energy Transition Global Energy Transition (GET) is a Houston-based 501(c)(3) nonprofit that supports displaced workers, professionals, and entrepreneurs through education, workforce development, coaching, networking, scholarships, and employer partnerships. GET helps people navigate career transitions across traditional energy and adjacent industries, including power, technology, infrastructure, and advanced manufacturing. Learn more at www.getenergyjobs.org.

title: As U.S. Boycotts U.N. Climate Talks, California Leads State/City Efforts to Combat Climate Crisis
description:
AMY GOODMAN: This is Democracy Now!, democracynow.org, The War and Peace Report.
I’m Amy Goodman.
As negotiations continue here at the summit, one notable absence is the United States.
If you separate California from the rest of the United States, fourth biggest.
AMY GOODMAN: Well, maybe with other presidential candidates announcing, they will follow Gavin Newsom’s lead, whether or not he runs himself.
text:
AMY GOODMAN: This is Democracy Now!, democracynow.org, The War and Peace Report. I’m Amy Goodman. We’re broadcasting from the U.N. climate summit in Antalya, Turkey. It’s the COP31. That means 31 years of the conference of the parties.

As negotiations continue here at the summit, one notable absence is the United States. For the second year in a row, the Trump administration has not sent an official delegation. Shortly after returning to the White House, President Trump withdrew the U.S. from the landmark 2015 Paris Climate Agreement.

But while the Trump administration is staying away, American state and local officials are making their presence here felt at COP in Turkey. More than 120 U.S. state and local leaders have been here, including at least three governors: Tim Walz of Minnesota, Michelle Lujan Grisham of New Mexico and Gavin Newsom of California. This is part of what Governor Newsom had to say last week.

GOV. GAVIN NEWSOM: In the context of the United States, our country continues to thrive despite headwinds on environmental policy in Washington, D.C. And I’m here — final words — to remind you that California is a stable partner in these endeavors. And that’s why I’m honored to be back here at COP, despite the fact that my federal government is once again a footnote in these conversations. But I assure you, in two years, change will come. Thank you.

AMY GOODMAN: We’re joined right now by Mark Hertsgaard, executive director of Covering Climate Now and the environment correspondent for The Nation magazine, author of several books, including Hot: Living Through the Next Fifty Years on Earth. He’s covered the U.N. climate summits since the 1992 Earth Summit. His new piece for The Guardian is headlined “California governor Gavin Newsom endorses global fossil fuel phaseout.”

Welcome back to Democracy Now!, Mark. It’s great to have you with us. Why don’t you start off by talking about the significance of what Governor Newsom has to say, and also the mayors and governors of the United States trying to fill the gap, the total absence of the United States here?

MARK HERTSGAARD: I’ll be happy to, but first I want to start off by really congratulating and applauding Democracy Now! You and I have been at these summits — I think at least I remember you at Copenhagen in 2009. And I will just say, as the head of Covering Climate Now, which is a global network of news organizations, if every news organization showed the commitment to telling the climate story that Democracy Now! does and that The Guardian does and that The Nation does, these conferences would be a different experience, and our world would be a different place. So, good on you guys for doing that.

As far as Gavin Newsom, he said to me for this interview on Friday that, yes, he, as the head of the fourth-biggest economy in the world, was one —

AMY GOODMAN: And then, I just want to be clear on this: not the fourth-biggest economy in the United States, the fourth-biggest economy in the world.

MARK HERTSGAARD: In the world. If you separate California from the rest of the United States, fourth biggest. U.S. is the biggest, then China, then Germany, and California just barely behind. So, real economic power. And Newsom said that he is, quote, “100% behind” the Santa Marta effort of these other major economies to push a global phaseout of fossil fuels. At Santa Marta, which I covered, as well —

AMY GOODMAN: In Colombia last year.

MARK HERTSGAARD: In Colombia. That is really giving us a new way to look at these summits, because, essentially, what happened there began a year ago at COP30, where 87 countries supported a global phaseout of fossil fuels, but a handful of petrostates, led by Saudi Arabia and Russia, blocked that by using the presumption that all decisions at COPs have to be made by consensus. That actually turns out to be false. It is not true. It is widely believed at these summits. It has become the convention, the norm, the culture, if you will. But the very — you mentioned the very first COP was held in 1995. And countries debated there: Do we make decisions by consensus or majority? You’ll never guess who was behind the effort to say, “Oh, we can’t do it by majority.” Of course, it was the United States. And so, it was left unresolved. But over time, it has become consensus. And consensus allows a small group of states to block what everyone else wants.

The Santa Marta coalition responded to that in COP30 in saying, “You know what? We’re no longer going to put up with that.” If you know the Samuel Beckett play Waiting for Godot, they basically said, “We’re not waiting for Godot any longer, because Godot ain’t coming. And you know what? We don’t have to wait for Godot. We are some of the biggest economies in the world.” If you put those 87 countries together, you put their GNPs together, they are the biggest superpower, economic superpower, on Earth, bigger than the U.S. If you add in California, they’re as big as the U.S. and China together.

And essentially, what they are betting, the Santa Marta coalition, is that their example and their economic power, by — if they phase out fossil fuels, that they can push and lead and encourage the rest of the world in the same direction, because if that much buying power gets withdrawn from the petro economy, from the fossil fuel economy, it’s going to send a message to financial markets and investors around the world: If you stay invested in fossil fuels, you’re going to be left with a lot of nearly worthless stranded assets. So, that’s what we’re seeing. This is now playing out here in COP31. And one of the stories I’m following here is: Will that Santa Marta coalition push an initiative here?

AMY GOODMAN: The Fossil Fuel Treaty Initiative.

MARK HERTSGAARD: Well, that’s — those are two separate but related things. The Santa Marta meeting last year, there was a push there for treaties, but not all those 57 countries are in favor of that treaty, certainly haven’t signed on to it yet. But they are signed on to what they call roadmaps, roadmaps to phase out fossil fuels. And Germany has done one. France has done one. We hear that the U.K. may announce one here this week. And so, it’s more of an economic play.

And so, it’s — as I say, it’s given us a new way to evaluate the success of international climate action: less who is going to sign a diplomatic treaty, and more what have the economic — who has the economic power to drive the world in a different direction. Because, as I say, the petrostates have made it abundantly clear, under the current rules of consensus, they are never, ever going to allow COPs to succeed. They’re just not going to sign that agreement. So, essentially, the Santa Marta coalition is making an end run around that, using economic power rather than playing ridiculous diplomatic games.

AMY GOODMAN: You mention in your piece for The Guardian, “California’s economy has run on 100% clean electricity nine out of every 10 days during much of [this year], with batteries emerging as 'a game changer', as Newsom described it. As the costs of clean energy continue to fall, [he] expects more [counties] to follow California’s example because 'the markets are moving in our direction,'” he said.

It’s interesting Trump is going to be meeting with Chinese President Xi in just a few days, on Thursday, in China. When we’re talking about renewable energy, talk about China and the example it has for the United States, and why the U.S. is falling behind, with President Trump’s enormous emphasis on oil and gas and coal.

MARK HERTSGAARD: President Trump wants to go back to the 19th century, while China is winning the 21st century. Now, you remember that the third superpower that’s going to be there is Russia. And Russia is — we just learned today, new research reported in The Guardian, that Russia is the biggest — over time, has exported the most carbon destruction around the world. So, it’s not surprising that Russia last year joined Saudi Arabia.

The other interesting thing about Gavin Newsom saying this is that, look, he’s going to run for president, it’s pretty clear, in 2028. If he were to win — I’m not endorsing or not, but if he were to win, that opens the possibility that the United States, as a nation-state, would also join the Santa Marta push to phase out fossil fuels.

And the other, the second-biggest economy in the United States, Texas, now has a new governor-elect in Gina Hinojosa, who is a real climate champion. This has not really been picked up yet by the national media. She’s a total climate champion. If you had those two states, the two biggest oil-producing states in the United States, saying, “You know, we’re going to turn our back on our past, and we’re going to go in the new green direction,” that would be game-changing. And Hinojosa has already, as one of her first acts — she’s not even sworn into office yet — she’s saying, “We’re not going to sell Elon Musk 500 acres of Texas-owned public land so he can expand his data centers to wreck the climate.” So, watch what Gina Hinojosa is going to be doing as governor of Texas on the climate front.

AMY GOODMAN: Well, maybe with other presidential candidates announcing, they will follow Gavin Newsom’s lead, whether or not he runs himself.

MARK HERTSGAARD: Exactly.

AMY GOODMAN: Well, I want to thank you for being with us, and we’re going to continue to talk to you about these issues, Mark Hertsgaard, executive director of Covering Climate Now and the environment correspondent for The Nation. We’ll link to your new piece in The Guardian, “California governor Gavin Newsom endorses global fossil fuel phaseout.”

Coming up, we look at one of the most climate-destroyed countries, one of the poorest countries in the world, Bangladesh. Stay with us.

[break]

text:
Why It Matters

Carvana lobbying now includes a new firm. Carvana LLC hired Venture Government Strategies LLC, according to a new client registration signed Nov. 13. It lists the automotive industry issue area and "Issues impacting U.S. automotive e-commerce." ​

Carvana's earlier reports came through Ogilvy Government Relations (OGR), most recently in the third-quarter report signed Oct. 17. The registration lists one lobbyist, Ben Quayle.

By the Numbers

OGR's third-quarter report lists $50,000, as do its second-quarter report and first-quarter report. The new registration carries a $0 filing amount and names no bills. Quayle does not appear among the lobbyists on those three OGR reports.

Broader Context

The Internal Revenue Service (IRS) says in guidance updated Sept. 24 that clean-vehicle credits are unavailable for vehicles acquired after Sept. 30, 2025, and that the same cutoff applies to the previously owned clean-vehicle credit.

Congress.gov says H.R. 1777, the SECURE Notarization Act of 2025, introduced March 3, 2025, would authorize state-commissioned notaries to perform remote notarizations. Carvana's earlier reports listed the bill alongside electronic signatures on federal odometer disclosures. H.R. 2981, the USA CAR Act was introduced April 21, 2025, and referred to the House Ways and Means Committee. Carvana's report for the third quarter of 2025 listed it.

Plugin America reported on June 27, 2025, that Carvana and other auto-sector participants urged Congress to keep federal electric vehicle tax credits, asking for a gradual sunset rather than abrupt repeal.

Advertisement

Between The Lines

On July 23, Sen. John Neely Kennedy (R-LA) told the Senate Banking Committee at a business meeting on nominations that Carvana reports nearly 100% credit approval for its customers, which he called implausible. He asked for a commitment to investigate the company.

Competitive Landscape

Venture Government Strategies signed two other new client registrations the same day: Hawthorn Aero Inc. and Voyager Technologies Inc., both on aerospace and defense. Separately, TKO Group Holdings Inc. registered on its own behalf on Oct. 29 and also lists the automotive industry.

The Bottom Line

The registration puts Carvana on record with Venture Government Strategies for automotive e-commerce, a topic its earlier OGR reports did not list. Its issue area is the automotive industry, the same one its OGR reports carried.

text:
Dear Reader,

It never dawned on Dot to add solar panels to my wedding registry, alongside the gravy boat and the stainless steel pots and pans. But now I wish I had, like the smart brides and grooms in Nigeria who are taking the powering of their homes into their own hands, according to this story from Bloomberg News.

“The grid serving Africa’s most populous nation is so weak that in order to keep the lights on and appliances running, most Nigerians produce power at home. Domestic generators powered by petrol and diesel have for many years been the go-to option. But increasingly, solar equipment is gaining ground,” Bloomberg tells us. Consequently, “Solar panels, batteries that store their energy, and inverters that make the power usable, are turning up on wedding registries, alongside more traditional gifts such as bed linen and microwaves.”

Nigeria is simply getting on board the solar train that is already chugging along.

According to the BBC, “The world’s solar power is crossing a threshold. A decade ago, it barely registered on a global scale, providing just 1% of the world’s power. In 2026, it will almost certainly increase to 10% of power, and overtake nuclear, a mainstay of electricity since the late 1970s.” The article refers to solar as “offensively cheap.”
