title: GM's Solar Supplier Is Pulling Back to Michigan Projects | Environment+Energy Leader
description:
GM announced that it is the main customer for two NorthStar solar farms in Michigan under a virtual power purchase agreement (VPPA).
GM's Farms Stay With NorthStar Neither farm is for sale.
Branch Solar, a 200 MW project in Branch County, began commercial operation in June, and the 100 MW Lake Iris project in St. Clair County followed in August.
Both belong to the roughly 1,442 MW of Michigan gas and solar generation NorthStar plans to hold, and each took on a tax equity partner this year.
The Contract Terms GM Kept Private GM is pitching the deal as a way to steady a big expense.
text:
General Motors (GM) calls it the largest clean-energy project in its history. In July, CMS Energy's board decided to sell more than 630 MW of NorthStar Clean Energy projects, most of them outside Michigan, and to stop developing renewables beyond its regulated utility, the company disclosed in its third-quarter filing. GM announced that it is the main customer for two NorthStar solar farms in Michigan under a virtual power purchase agreement (VPPA).

GM's Farms Stay With NorthStar

Neither farm is for sale. Branch Solar, a 200 MW project in Branch County, began commercial operation in June, and the 100 MW Lake Iris project in St. Clair County followed in August. Both belong to the roughly 1,442 MW of Michigan gas and solar generation NorthStar plans to hold, and each took on a tax equity partner this year.

CMS took a $456 million earnings hit in the third quarter from impairment, disposal and exit costs tied to the plan. A few sales have closed or are under contract, and the company is still in talks with buyers for the other projects.

The Contract Terms GM Kept Private

GM is pitching the deal as a way to steady a big expense. Chief sustainability officer Cassandra Garber wrote that long-term renewable supply makes a significant operating cost more predictable as AI and electrification change how companies think about power. Factories are already competing with data centers for megawatts. The automaker expects the farms to produce about 539,000 MWh a year, close to what Factory ZERO, Flint Assembly and Lansing Delta Township Assembly use together, and puts their combined investment near $550 million.

How much protection GM gets depends on numbers it has not released. In a virtual agreement, the farms sell their power into the wholesale market and the two sides settle up against a fixed price, while GM's plants keep buying electricity from their utilities. GM did not say what that price is or how long the contract runs, the terms that decide how these deals pay off for a buyer. The renewable energy credits will count toward emissions from the electricity GM buys for manufacturing.

A Fight Over a Power Line

Branch hit its own grid trouble along the way. In October 2024, its lawyers told the Michigan Public Service Commission that a transmission line proposed by Michigan Electric Transmission Company would run straight through the project, which they called three years and hundreds of millions of dollars in the making. They asked to join the case and argue for a different route. Delays of that kind have left some corporate buyers short of the power they contracted for.

Bethel Township, home to Branch, used the project to win a $1 million Renewables Ready Communities Award, money now going toward a township hall expansion and road work. GM says the two farms employed more than 550 construction workers.

title: California Rewrote Who Loses Gas First in a Shortage - Environment+Energy Leader
description:
Earlier this month, Pacific Gas and Electric (PG&E) announced a new rulebook for deciding who loses gas service first when its system runs short.
Cuts to power plants protect factory gas for a time, while tightening the electricity supply the same factories depend on.
What the New Order Spells Out California regulators set the sequence in Decision 25-10-042, and PG&E's compliance filing, Advice Letter 5161-G, spells it out.
Power plants that are not scheduled to run lose gas first, followed by the partial cut to dispatched plants.
The review's recommendations centered on more gas infrastructure and better communication between the gas and power industries.
text:
Earlier this month, Pacific Gas and Electric (PG&E) announced a new rulebook for deciding who loses gas service first when its system runs short. The updated curtailment procedures bring the utility in line with California's other gas utilities, and they put power plants ahead of factories in the line for cuts. From November through March, PG&E can reduce gas to running power plants by up to 60% before it reaches industrial customers, who can then be cut by up to 100% on a shared, pro rata basis.

Manufacturers that burn gas for process heat and buy electricity from a grid that runs heavily on gas sit on both sides of that order. Cuts to power plants protect factory gas for a time, while tightening the electricity supply the same factories depend on. The new sequence at least tells a plant manager where the site stands before a cold snap, and that gives procurement and operations teams something concrete to plan around this winter.

What the New Order Spells Out

California regulators set the sequence in Decision 25-10-042, and PG&E's compliance filing, Advice Letter 5161-G, spells it out. Power plants that are not scheduled to run lose gas first, followed by the partial cut to dispatched plants. Large industrial users and cogeneration come next, with refineries keeping a preset minimum, and households sit last. Southern California Gas Co. already works from the same winter sequence, including the 60% step for power plants, so large users in both of the state's major gas territories now face one set of priorities.

Large customers get a maximum allowed usage when a curtailment is called, and PG&E says it "shall attempt to give the Customer, or its Authorized Agent, 24-hour notice of an impending service restriction." Gas used above the limit costs $50 per dekatherm plus the daily citygate index price. Emergency flow orders carry no minimum notice period at all, so the people who receive PG&E's postings on its Pipe Ranger site need to be the people who can actually throttle a line.

PG&E's own winter guidance puts much of that work on gas suppliers and their customers. It asks suppliers to agree on a plan with each large end user for a local curtailment and to set a protocol in advance for operational and emergency flow orders. It also encourages end users to sign up for Pipe Ranger E-XPRESS, which sends early warnings of cold weather events.

State Forecasters Expect a Quiet Season

The odds of reaching factories this winter look low. In an Oct. 22 staff report, the California Energy Commission (CEC) found the chance of curtailment low for both residential and large customers if supplies and demand hold near forecast. SoCalGas can meet an extremely cold day without curtailing large users, the report says, thanks to its pipeline supply and storage withdrawal capacity.

PG&E is tighter. On a 1-in-10 cold day, the commission projects demand of 4,305 million cubic feet per day on PG&E's system, with power plants accounting for 1,138 million of it, and the utility would need gas from independently owned storage to cover the gap. "The risk would first fall on lower-priority or more flexible resources," the report says, pointing first to independent storage withdrawals and interruptible service before any curtailment of large customers.

Last Winter Showed What Preparation Buys

A joint review by the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) and the North American Electric Reliability Corporation (NERC), released Sept. 10, found no significant disruptions in either the gas or electric systems during Winter Storms Fern and Gianna in January. Gas production declined only moderately, with "limited, short-duration force majeure events," and the review credited generators that committed capacity before the cold arrived.

"This winter showed that the steps industry has taken are making a difference," said Jim Robb, NERC's president and chief executive. He was just as direct about the margin involved. "We cannot let this be the new norm of operating the grid." The review's recommendations centered on more gas infrastructure and better communication between the gas and power industries.

One Plan for Two Contracts

Factories are drawing on that gas system more than ever. Industrial customers used a record 23.6 billion cubic feet per day in 2025, and the Energy Information Administration (EIA) expects new records in 2026 and 2027, led by chemical makers. Many plants still manage that exposure in two separate files, with a gas contract that sometimes carries minimum purchase obligations and a power contract owned by a different team.

California's order gives those teams a reason to sit down together before January. The gas side of the review covers the plant's curtailment zone, the lowest usage it could run on for a day and whether any process can switch fuels. On the electric side, buyers are checking how their supply contract treats a sudden production cut and whether its pass-through and delivery provisions would add charges during a cold snap. Comfortable storage levels have eased 2027 energy budgets, which leaves room to fund that work now.

Utilities outside California set their own curtailment priorities in tariffs, and the order of cuts varies. Large gas users in other states can find their place in line in the same tariff section, usually under curtailment or capacity allocation, and ask their utility for the notice procedures that apply this winter.

text:
Manufacturing electric vehicle components and batteries in Brazil, along with charging infrastructure, could generate a positive impact of $14.2 billion a year on the country’s economy through income and job creation. The estimate comes from a study by the International Council on Clean Transportation (ICCT), a nonprofit organization. To achieve that potential, Brazil’s automotive industry would need to manufacture locally the most expensive and complex component of electric and hybrid vehicles: the rechargeable battery that powers the motor. Of the estimated annual economic impact, $4.9 billion, or 34.5% of the total, would come from domestic battery production under a scenario of full localization of the manufacturing process.

“Battery production is a global challenge, not just a Brazilian one. Established markets such as the United States and Europe face enormous difficulties in building battery plants that can compete with China’s dominance in terms of cost, quality, and technology,” says Márcio Roberto Codogno, vice president of the National Association of Manufacturers and Sellers of Auto Parts for the Replacement Market (Anfape).

According to ICCT Brazil’s estimates, even in a scenario in which only the assembly of CKD (completely knocked-down) kits—vehicles shipped in fully disassembled form—takes place in the country, with no local production of batteries or other components, the resulting value added would reach $4.8 billion a year. In this case, the figure would mainly include transportation and vehicle sales services, as well as the actual assembly of the kits. The projections are based on a scenario of moderate electrification of Brazil’s vehicle fleet by 2030.

In September, Brazil’s fleet of electrified light vehicles—both electric and hybrid—reached 1 million units, based on cumulative registrations since January 2012, when the Brazilian Electric Vehicle Association (ABVE) began its historical data series. From January through August 2026, nearly 328,500 electrified light vehicles were registered, up 160.5% from the same period last year, according to the association.

The rapid expansion in sales, however, contrasts with a production base still largely reliant on the assembly of CKD and SKD (semi-knocked-down) kits. “Assembly using CKD and SKD kits requires significantly fewer workers and does not immediately foster the development of Brazil’s domestic auto parts industry,” Codogno of Anfape acknowledges. “On the other hand, this model has the advantage of bringing new automakers into the country, along with new production facilities. The federal government’s role is to encourage and guide the gradual transition from CKD/SKD kit assembly to the effective development of domestic suppliers, expanding the capacity and technological capabilities of local factories.”

In the ICCT’s view, to move up the electric vehicle value chain, Brazil should use existing incentives to align the domestic content of locally produced vehicles with the country’s industrial capabilities in the short term. Another recommendation is to adjust current policies supporting electric vehicle adoption to establish feasible, progressively higher local-content requirements for cars.

“The concrete opportunity we have today is that Brazil already has an automotive industry, including a strong auto parts supply chain, but it is heavily geared toward combustion-engine vehicles, with relatively low levels of technology in terms of the components and systems involved,” says economist Ricardo Bastos, president of ABVE. “The battery is perhaps the most complex component and represents a major share of the value. But there are also cameras and sensors, for example. Autonomous vehicles are coming. So we will also need a range of electronic equipment,” he adds.

Regardless of the transition to electric mobility, the trend in Brazil’s automotive industry is toward a declining share of domestic content. The proportion of imported intermediate inputs rose from 9.8% in 2010 to 16.1% in 2022, according to the ICCT. In terms of value added, the share attributable to foreign-made inputs nearly doubled over the same period, climbing from 14.7% to 27.8%.

Among the possible causes identified by the nonprofit are the growing technological content of vehicles and the impact of the Non-Produced Auto Parts Regime, an industrial policy that allows auto parts with no equivalent domestic production to be imported duty-free.

Fully assembled imported electric and hybrid vehicles currently face a 35% import tariff. The same rate applies to semi-knocked-down kits, although these products still benefit from temporary duty-free import quotas through the end of December.

Vehicles imported as completely knocked-down kits currently face a 14% import tariff and can also qualify for temporary zero-tariff quotas through the end of December 2026. As of January 1, 2027, the tariff on CKD vehicles will rise to 35%, while the temporary import quota benefits will also expire.

“As for the import duty exemptions or reductions for CKD and SKD kits, I think they were important as a starting point. And Brazil has got started. We have already seen reports of a manufacturer that has assembled more than 100,000 electric vehicles in the country,” says ICCT senior researcher André Cieplinski, author of the study on opportunities to localize electric vehicle production in Brazil.

Ricardo Bastos of ABVE sees the beginning of a new phase, following an initial period of straightforward imports of fully assembled electrified vehicles and a second stage in which cars are assembled locally from kits manufactured abroad. “We are about to enter the third phase. The second phase involves [the automaker] bringing vehicles to be manufactured in Brazil, still using imported components and parts, particularly high-tech components,” he says. Bastos also serves as director of institutional and government relations at Chinese automaker GWM’s Brazilian subsidiary.

text:
In a new study, researchers evaluated how information about emissions estimates for five kinds of electric vehicles (EV) influenced people’s views of the cars. They found that potential consumers understood complex information that could affect their purchasing decisions, and that political identity and charging feasibility were the main drivers of preference.

Researchers at Carnegie Mellon University completed the study, which appears in Transportation Research Part D.

“The elimination of federal subsidies complicates further growth in the market for EVs. This increases the value of information to potential EV adopters, including performance, range, and access to charging infrastructure,” explains Nicholas Z. Muller, Professor of Economics, Engineering, and Public Policy at Carnegie Mellon’s Tepper School of Business, who coauthored the study. “While many consumers who bought EVs early were driven by concerns about the environment, the broader market remains hesitant due to gaps in their knowledge about the benefits of EVs.”

Transportation remains the largest source of greenhouse gas emissions in the United States, accounting for about 28 percent of the national total. Over the last several years, U.S. vehicle electrification policy has shifted from a period of strong federal support to one of greater policy uncertainty. These changes reinforce the importance of understanding how consumers view different vehicle types without the price and social signals sent by incentives and regulations. As those incentives and regulatory frameworks change over time, sustained transportation decarbonization will increasingly depend on consumers making informed choices among competing vehicle technologies.

In this study, researchers evaluated how communication of state-specific emission estimates of five vehicle types (internal combustion engine, hybrid electric, plug-in hybrid electric, battery electric, and fuel cell electric) made by three major automakers in the U.S. market (Ford, Toyota, and Tesla) affected the perceptions of more than 900 licensed adults in four states (California, Florida, Pennsylvania, and Texas). Participants were recruited by Prolific, which connects researchers, AI developers, and product teams with people to take part in studies online.

Conducted from late 2023 to early 2024, the study examined whether the information provided influenced consumers’ preferences for vehicle types, manufacturer fleet composition, and brand images, as well as whether socio-demographic characteristics continued to shape these preferences even after consumers received it. The study found that:

While emissions information shifted individuals’ rankings of the vehicles, participants’ political identity and the availability of charging facilities were the primary determinants of top preferences. Younger, less educated, and politically conservative participants, as well as those who thought charging infrastructure was less reliable, were more likely than older, more educated, and politically liberal participants to prefer non-EVs over alternative technologies.

Complex, state-specific life-cycle emissions information was communicated in a way that was understandable, comparable, and relevant to decision-making for a broad and demographically diverse audience of mainstream consumers.

Consumers’ evaluations responded not only to vehicle technology itself but also to information regarding direct and indirect emissions.

Participants preferred that manufacturers offer a diverse mix of vehicle technologies rather than a single one, and emissions information reduced the share of high-emission vehicles they wanted in those fleets.

In a changing policy and market environment, transparent, evidence-based communication can offer a lower-cost, policy-neutral way to sustain consumer engagement with EVs.

“Our work suggests that potential consumers can understand emission estimates, are sensitive to their implications, and can express their preferences in terms relevant to manufacturers and policymakers,” notes Yujin Seo, a PhD student in the Department of Engineering and Public Policy at Carnegie Mellon, who led the study. “We hope clear communication will help people make more confident and appropriate decisions about vehicle purchases, in turn increasing trust in an industry with a potentially vital role in decarbonization.”

The study was funded by Toyota Research Institute.

OSLO, Norway--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Nov 17, 2026--

Myths and misconceptions about electric cars, from battery lifespan and fire risk to grid collapse, are the biggest barrier to EV adoption, according to respondents to the annual Global EV Driver Survey . The 2026 survey draws on responses from more than 29,500 EV drivers across 34 countries.

This press release features multimedia. View the full release here: https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20261117539716/en/



MYTHS. Battery lifespan (72%), fire risk (58%) and grid collapse (45%) top the list of EV myths reported by respondents to the 2026 Global EV Driver Survey, which gathered responses from more than 29,500 EV drivers across 34 countries.

“The EV transition is not just an infrastructure or affordability challenge. It is also an information challenge. Outdated information and misconceptions continue to influence decisions long after the technology has moved on,” says Ellen Hiep, from the Steering Committee of the Global EV Alliance (GEVA).

Myths the greatest barrier

Asked to identify the greatest barrier to EV adoption in their country, 74% of respondents cited myths about EVs, ahead of purchase price (49%) and charging access in apartment buildings (47%).

The most reported myths are that EV batteries do not last (72%), that EVs catch fire more easily (58%), and that the EV transition will eventually cause the electricity grid to collapse (45%).

EV batteries will outlast the car

“It is understandable that people compare EV batteries with phone batteries that need replacing after two or three years. But most EV drivers have a very different experience with their car batteries,” says Ellen Hiep.

In the survey, 65% of respondents disagree or strongly disagree with the statement “I am concerned about the lifespan of my battery”, while only 18% agree or strongly agree.

“Most EV drivers know from experience that modern EVs come with long battery warranties of eight years, and that most batteries will outlast the car,” says Ellen Hiep.

About the annual Global EV Driver Survey

The annual Global EV Driver Survey gathers insights into EV ownership, charging and barriers to adoption from 2024 and onwards. The 2026 edition draws on responses from more than 29,500 EV drivers in 34 countries and is presented by the Global EV Alliance (GEVA), a non-profit network of 71 EV associations across 41 countries. text:
The U.S. Senate plans to vote this week on a bill aimed at easing America’s affordability crisis and fighting climate change that hunting and fishing groups worry will also erode many of the nation’s bedrock conservation laws.

The complex and winding 400-page Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act focuses on lowering energy costs, something both Republicans and Democrats have championed and and that helped drive Democratic gains in the midterm elections. BAAJA also, however, ties jobs and household bills with curtailing public-lands protections. And in a twist that’s perplexing many conservation groups, the bill is co-sponsored by Sens. Martin Heinrich (D-N.M.) and Mike Lee (R-Utah), two lawmakers known for being on nearly opposite ends of the public-lands spectrum.

BAAJA is largely focused on permitting reform, something the country hasn’t tackled in decades, according to the Bipartisan Policy Center. In practice, the legislation would raise the standard for whether projects approved by one administration can be revoked by a future administration.

That means an industrial solar project permitted by one president, for example, could not be stymied by a future president intent on preventing renewables. It also speeds up permitting processes and cuts red tape for everything from energy projects to landscape-scale changes like prescribed fire.

But sportsmen and conservationists say the bill would not just expedite climate or environmentally friendly projects. BAAJA would also make it much harder — or potentially impossible — for an administration to overturn leases or approvals for projects as controversial as hyperscale data centers on public lands or mines in the same watersheds as sensitive wilderness areas. It’s a bill that prioritizes development, many observers say, at the cost of the very “red tape” that has been responsible for conserving many of the country’s most priceless fish, wildlife, and wild places.

“I understand this is a big, bipartisan bill — it has some things in it I would rather it not have. But I negotiated the deal based on what was actually possible to get signed into law,” Heinrich wrote in an email to Outdoor Life. “Because when I say climate change is an existential threat, I mean it. And I will not let an opportunity to do something about it pass by.”

Conservationists like Ingrid Lyons, executive director of Save the Boundary Waters, understand the need for stability around permitting development. The whiplash between issuing and revoking permits for public land development projects every time an administration changes has likely hurt the U.S.’s ability to move forward with important energy projects, including in renewables like wind and solar.

But she fears this bill could instead cement the creation of controversial projects like a copper-sulfide mine at the headwaters of the Boundary Waters Canoe Area Wilderness or a copper-molybdenum-gold mine in the salmon-rich waters of Alaska’s Bristol Bay. Permits for projects like these have been denied, among other issues, because of environmental risk. If permits are reissued in similar scenarios, legislation like BAAJA could prevent future administrations from stopping development in places that truly need protection.

“What about landscape certainty?” Lyons says. “We’re overlooking in some ways the impact to communities that are relying on protection and not just projects.”

Fears of Data Centers and Unchecked Development

The conservation community has become increasingly vocal in its opposition to the bill since Heinrich and Lee partnered with Sens. Sheldon Whitehouse (D-R.I.), and Shelley Moore Capito ( .), to introduce the legislation in late September. Lee has a clear track record of supporting public land sales and undermining existing public-lands conservation, including 2025’s attempt to include federal land sales in the One Big Beautiful Bill.

A lengthy version of BAAJA is before the Senate as of Tuesday. The current bill includes a variety of red flags for hunters, anglers, tribes, endangered-species advocates, and other conservationists.

Some of the main points include:

Preventing federal agencies from revoking, rescinding, withdrawing, suspending or otherwise altering any permit after Nov. 6, 2026, except in the case of six narrow exemptions including fraud, a court order, material breach of the permit, or urgent or substantial harm to life, property or human health.

Making the government (i.e., taxpayers) liable for a developer’s legal fees if a project is canceled or suspended and the developer sues and proves the government acted in bad faith.

Limiting the scope of the Clean Water Act by stating unless a project poses “imminent and substantial danger” to human health or the environment, a court could only remand a project permit back to an agency to fix it within 180 days. Meanwhile work on the project could continue.

Reducing the amount of tribal input into projects by drafting a project assessment before seeking tribal consultation and then only considering tribal feedback provided within 30 days.

The Theodore Roosevelt Conservation Partnership acknowledged the need for permit reform but said in a statement that “progress should not come at the expense of the conservation safeguards and public review that give hunters and anglers a voice in how our lands and waters are managed.”

For Lyons, it comes down to the potential unintended consequences of sweeping legislation like BAAJA.

“We need to be exceptionally aware of the implications of this bill, which could be that a lot of these really beloved places could have projects many communities have worked really hard to oppose cemented into place.”

A Push for Affordability

Many in the conservation community were surprised by the bill’s sponsors, given Heinrich’s history as a sportsman and conservationist who regularly defends public lands and sensitive places, and Lee’s general position as a proponent of development and public-lands sell-off.

But in Heinrich’s statement to Outdoor Life, he emphasizes the impact of climate change on our planet, including the places where people hunt, hike, bike and camp. Independent modeling, he said, predicts the bill will lead to a 20 percent reduction in power sector emissions, or the “equivalent to taking 39 coal plants offline for 10 years.”

“You cannot protect a trout stream without paying attention to the warming temperatures and declining flows that threaten it,” he wrote. “You cannot protect wildlife habitat while ignoring the impacts of increasingly severe drought and wildfire. We need to reduce emissions, and that means getting more clean energy onto the grid.”

In an Oct. 30 op-ed in the Albuquerque Journal, Heinrich explained how New Mexico’s SunZia Wind and Transmission project took 17 years to permit and build.

He also pushed back on what he called misinformation about the bill, stating he doesn’t believe data centers should be on public land. The bill also requires large scale data center operators to pay the full cost of electricity consumed by the facility.

The Izaak Walton League’s conservation director, Kate Miller, thinks each of the bill’s sponsors are acting in good faith and trying to do what is right for their constituents. Many projects, including those aimed at restoring forests and wildlife habitat, have been held up by litigation. Something like BAAJA could move those forward.

But Miller would have liked to see these issues tackled individually instead of in a massive bill. And while she hopes that, if the bill passes, the administration will respect existing laws, the past two years has brought an onslaught of changes to most of the nation’s bedrock environmental laws including the Clean Water Act, the Endangered Species Act, and the National Environmental Policy Act.

“We want to make sure what comes out is not something that sacrifices those core protections that allow us to have healthy waters and habitats,” Miller says. “That we don’t sacrifice one for the other.”

Read Next: Alaska Considers ‘Unprecedented’ Closure of Public Land to Hunting, Trapping Along Controversial Ambler Road

While the Senate is fast tracking the bill before the next Congress begins in January, it must move through the Senate and the House, and any changes be agreed upon by both chambers before the bill would land on President Trump’s desk. Meanwhile, both industry and conservation groups say they’re working to lobby lawmakers for changes and amendments. As a result, several conservation organizations declined to comment for this story.

OSLO, Norway--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Nov 17, 2026--

Myths and misconceptions about electric cars, from battery lifespan and fire risk to grid collapse, are the biggest barrier to EV adoption, according to respondents to the annual Global EV Driver Survey . The 2026 survey draws on responses from more than 29,500 EV drivers across 34 countries.

This press release features multimedia. View the full release here: https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20261117539716/en/



MYTHS. Battery lifespan (72%), fire risk (58%) and grid collapse (45%) top the list of EV myths reported by respondents to the 2026 Global EV Driver Survey, which gathered responses from more than 29,500 EV drivers across 34 countries.

“The EV transition is not just an infrastructure or affordability challenge. It is also an information challenge. Outdated information and misconceptions continue to influence decisions long after the technology has moved on,” says Ellen Hiep, from the Steering Committee of the Global EV Alliance (GEVA).

Myths the greatest barrier

Asked to identify the greatest barrier to EV adoption in their country, 74% of respondents cited myths about EVs, ahead of purchase price (49%) and charging access in apartment buildings (47%).

The most reported myths are that EV batteries do not last (72%), that EVs catch fire more easily (58%), and that the EV transition will eventually cause the electricity grid to collapse (45%).

EV batteries will outlast the car

“It is understandable that people compare EV batteries with phone batteries that need replacing after two or three years. But most EV drivers have a very different experience with their car batteries,” says Ellen Hiep.

In the survey, 65% of respondents disagree or strongly disagree with the statement “I am concerned about the lifespan of my battery”, while only 18% agree or strongly agree.

“Most EV drivers know from experience that modern EVs come with long battery warranties of eight years, and that most batteries will outlast the car,” says Ellen Hiep.

About the annual Global EV Driver Survey

The annual Global EV Driver Survey gathers insights into EV ownership, charging and barriers to adoption from 2024 and onwards. The 2026 edition draws on responses from more than 29,500 EV drivers in 34 countries and is presented by the Global EV Alliance (GEVA), a non-profit network of 71 EV associations across 41 countries. text:
by Sarah Leach

Nov. 15, 2026

PORT SHELDON TWP. — The U.S. Department of Energy has issued a seventh consecutive 90-day emergency order keeping the coal-fired J.H. Campbell plant in Port Sheldon Township available to operate through mid-February — despite a recent federal appeals court ruling striking down the original directive.

The new order, issued late Friday, Nov. 13, took effect Sunday, Nov. 15, and runs through Feb. 12, 2027. It instructs the Midcontinent Independent System Operator, or MISO, and Consumers Energy to maintain the 1,420-megawatt facility’s operational readiness for emergency grid needs while using economic dispatch to limit ratepayer costs.

Operating along the Lake Michigan shoreline since 1962, the 64-year-old plant had been slated to burn its final ton of coal on May 31, 2025 — roughly 15 years ahead of the end of its scheduled design life — under a 2022 state-approved clean energy transition plan expected to save ratepayers roughly $600 million by 2040.

Instead, just eight days before decommissioning, federal officials intervened with the first of several 90-day mandates. Keeping the aging facility running past its planned closure has added roughly $640,000 to $1 million per day in unbudgeted coal deliveries, maintenance and compliance costs, accumulating between $259 million and $295 million in extra expenses as of September 2026, according to federal court filings and estimates from state officials.

Read More: Cost of the Campbell: How a West Michigan coal plant became the epicenter for a U.S. energy war

U.S. Energy Secretary Chris Wright said in the latest order that keeping dispatchable coal generation active remains necessary to prevent winter blackouts across the region.

“President Trump and the Energy Department remain committed to doing everything in our power to stop power outages for American families and businesses,” Wright said. “Ensuring coal plants such as the Campbell Plant are available to operate has prevented blackouts and likely saved lives. Americans deserve access to affordable, reliable, and secure electricity regardless of whether the wind is blowing or the sun is shining.”

According to the DOE, ongoing reliability strains mirror events observed earlier this year. Officials pointed to a joint report from the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission and the North American Electric Reliability Corporation analyzing the Winter 2026 Arctic Cold Period — including Winter Storm Fern, during which MISO declared energy emergency alerts and Campbell generated more than 201,000 megawatt-hours of electricity.

Local political backdrop, community protests

Before federal officials intervened in May 2025, the debate over the plant’s future played out inside the Ottawa County Board of Commissioners’ boardroom, exposing local political divides over grid reliability and environmental impacts.

As reported by the Ottawa News Network, far-right Ottawa Impact commissioners pushed in early 2025 for the county to sue Consumers Energy to halt the shutdown — and some community members floated having the county take over the facility as a public utility.

While the full board rejected a lawsuit 7-4, commissioners voted 9-1 in February 2025 to approve a nonbinding resolution authored by then-Vice Chair Josh Brugger urging state regulators and the utility to pause the closure and review grid conditions.

“There was a concern by some constituents that the plant was going to close and they wanted it to stay open. There were also concerns by other members of the community who were concerned that it might stay open, and they wanted it to be closed for environmental issues among other things, so that came to the fore very quickly in 2025,” Brugger, who is now the board’s chair, told ONN earlier this year.

Reflecting on the board’s decision to weigh in on state and federal energy policy, Brugger added: “We felt, in the end, that we were kind of closest to the area of concern and so perhaps we had a different perspective. In hindsight, I’m not sure that we did, but that’s what we felt, and we felt we had an obligation to do that.”

Once the federal mandates took effect, frustration across Ottawa County spilled out of meeting rooms and into the streets through a series of rallies and demonstrations.

Ahead of the first 90-day order’s expiration, environmental advocates, medical professionals and local residents — organized by the Michigan League of Conservation Voters and the Sierra Club Michigan Chapter — gathered outside the gates of the Port Sheldon Township facility on Aug. 12, 2025, alongside state Rep. Stephen Wooden, D-Grand Rapids, and former Ottawa County Commissioner Chris Kleinjans.

Read More: Activists, officials call for closure of Campbell coal plant as utility looks to recover costs

Read More: Protestors rally in Holland, call for Campbell coal plant to close

Speakers warned about respiratory health risks from sulfur dioxide and particulate emissions, with Grand Haven-area resident Jeffrey Miller telling local media that keeping the plant open made no sense “financially, politically, economically, environmentally.”

Three days later, on Aug. 15, 2025, roughly 100 residents and youth activists assembled at Memorial Park and Window on the Waterfront in downtown Holland, marching to U.S. Rep. Bill Huizenga’s district office to demand an end to the federal coal mandate and criticize rising utility costs.

On May 21, 2026 — marking one year since Wright issued the initial emergency order — Michigan Attorney General Dana Nessel held a press conference directly outside the Campbell plant to condemn the continued extensions and highlight mounting costs passed on to ratepayers.

Legal challenges, environmental concerns

The latest federal directive arrives two months after a unanimous panel of the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit ruled on Sept. 11 that the DOE overstepped its statutory authority under Section 202(c) of the Federal Power Act when it blocked the plant’s May 2025 retirement.

Writing for the court, Circuit Judge Cornelia Pillard held that Section 202(c) emergency powers apply only when the agency identifies “a risk of substantial harm from inadequate electricity supply that calls for immediate action by DOE in particular,” rather than long-term resource adequacy concerns managed through state and regional planning.

“Permitting DOE to compel generation in a situation that can be resolved through the ordinary resource adequacy planning mechanisms … would render meaningless the constraints on federal power that Congress imposed throughout the Act,” the court wrote, warning that the department’s interpretation “would empower it to pick its preferred power sources in Michigan — or, presumably, any other state — and order them to operate” and “invites frequent federal interventions that are unsupported by the statute and threaten the stability of the energy market.”

In its Nov. 13 order, the Energy Department noted it has petitioned the D.C. Circuit for a full-court rehearing and continues to invoke its emergency authority.

Michigan officials, health professionals and environmental advocates have sharply criticized the repeated extensions, arguing the orders unlawfully override state regulatory planning while driving up electricity bills and prolonging air and water pollution along the Lake Michigan shoreline. Continued coal combustion emits sulfur dioxide, nitrous oxides and air particulates while adding to coal ash ponds and wastewater discharges that local residents worry threaten groundwater and Lake Michigan.

Nessel, who led the multistate legal challenge alongside environmental groups including the Environmental Law & Policy Center and the Natural Resources Defense Council, said in September that keeping the aging facility open had already cost $295 million.

“By forcing its continued operation, DOE tried a never-before-used tactic to illegally prop up the aging J.H. Campbell coal plant that nobody asked to keep, sticking ratepayers with a bill for a facility that should have been retired more than a year ago,” Nessel said in a statement challenging the federal orders.

Following September’s appellate victory, Environmental Law & Policy Center leaders emphasized that state regulators and utilities had already planned for reliable replacement power.

“No community should be forced to keep dirty, uneconomic coal power plants open when affordable clean energy solutions are readily available,” the group stated, adding that Michigan had already committed to a clean energy transition and that federal agencies should not interfere with state-approved resource plans.

Utility response, ratepayer impact

Consumers Energy — which did not request the emergency orders and has added 1,200 megawatts of generating capacity elsewhere in West Michigan to offset the planned retirement — confirmed it will continue complying with the federal mandate while seeking regional cost recovery so Michigan customers do not shoulder the entire expense alone.

Because the plant operates under a federal mandate rather than standard market economics, net operating losses — which Consumers Energy reported exceeded $135 million in net excess operational costs earlier this year out of nearly $260 million to $295 million in total gross operating and compliance expenses — are passed on to ratepayers across MISO’s 15-state regional grid footprint.

“Consumers Energy will continue to follow the law and operate our Campbell plant in West Michigan, complying with the seventh 90-day emergency order from the U.S. Department of Energy,” the utility said in a statement to WZZM-13 on Saturday, Nov. 14. “Consistent with these emergency orders, we will work to ensure that everyone who benefits from power from the Campbell plant across the Midwest pays their fair share.”

Once federal mandates expire and decommissioning formally begins, Consumers Energy expects the remediation and restoration process at the Port Sheldon Township site to take roughly five years.

title: What the First Democratic Attorney General In a Generation Could Mean For Texas
description:
For nearly three decades, the Texas Attorney General’s office served as one of the conservative legal movement’s most powerful institutions.
A little over a quarter-century ago, the Texas Attorney General’s office was a relatively quiet state agency.
That began to change under John Cornyn, who in 1998 became the first Republican elected attorney general in Texas since Reconstruction.
The election of Johnson as the state’s next attorney general is going to change all of this in a hurry.
During the administrations of Cornyn, Abbott, and Paxton, Texas saw what an ambitious attorney general can accomplish.
text:
For nearly three decades, the Texas Attorney General’s office served as one of the conservative legal movement’s most powerful institutions. It challenged Democratic presidents in court, developed legal theories that reshaped national debates, and cultivated a generation of conservative lawyers who would go on to occupy influential positions in the federal judiciary and Congress.

Now, for the first time since 1998, a Democrat is preparing to take office. The incoming administration of Nathan Johnson, a former state lawmaker, will have the opportunity to put these resources to a different use: defending workers, students, and reproductive freedom rather than challenging the protections they rely on, and using the state’s legal power to protect Texans from abuses by government and private interests alike.

A little over a quarter-century ago, the Texas Attorney General’s office was a relatively quiet state agency. Its work largely consisted of collecting child support and defending the state in court. That began to change under John Cornyn, who in 1998 became the first Republican elected attorney general in Texas since Reconstruction. During his tenure, Cornyn established the office of the Texas Solicitor General, a specialized team of appellate lawyers responsible for representing Texas in state and federal courts, including before the U.S. Supreme Court.

Cornyn was elected to the U.S. Senate in 2002, but his decisions created the infrastructure that Greg Abbott would use to transform the office into a vehicle to advance conservative causes. Abbott, who served for 12 years before being elected governor in 2014, gave the Texas Solicitor General, now-Senator Ted Cruz, a straightforward mission: “Look across the country. If there are conservative principles we can fight and defend, if we can make a difference defending the Constitution and the Bill of Rights, go do it,” Cruz recalled in 2019.

When President Barack Obama entered the White House in 2009, Texas became a central antagonist in efforts to block his administration’s agenda. Under Abbott, the state filed more than 30 lawsuits against the Obama administration in six years, challenging the Affordable Care Act, federal environmental regulations, and immigration protections for undocumented young people.

Abbott’s successor, Ken Paxton, took this strategy even further. In 2020, Paxton asked the U.S. Supreme Court to overturn election results in four states that Donald Trump had lost. The Court rejected that request, but in the years that followed, Paxton’s office filed dozens of challenges to President Joe Biden’s policies on immigration, the environment, and healthcare. Paxton also continued to fight to invalidate the Affordable Care Act and to restrict protections for LGBTQ people.

Under the leadership of Cornyn, Abbott, and Paxton, the Texas Attorney General’s office became especially adept at manipulating the federal court system to ensure that its lawsuits landed before sympathetic judges. For example, the Northern District of Texas does not randomize case assignments, and instead uses smaller divisions run by a single judge. Therefore, litigants can file in these single-judge divisions and be almost guaranteed they will get a conservative judge of their choice.

Then, after some Northern District judge inevitably rules in its favor, the Texas Attorney General’s office gets to defend those decisions at the Fifth Circuit Court of Appeals, the most conservative federal appeals court in the country. From there, appeals go before the conservative supermajority on the Supreme Court. This pipeline has helped fast-track some of the most consequential challenges to federal law and policy, turning cases that begin in Texas into national precedent.

But the office’s influence extends beyond the lawsuits it brings. It has also served as a pipeline for conservative lawyers looking to join the ranks of the federal judiciary. According to a Texas Tribune investigation, nine federal judges appointed by Trump between 2018 and 2020 had previously worked in the Texas Attorney General’s office, including Fifth Circuit Judges James Ho, Andrew Oldham, and Kyle Duncan.

The election of Johnson as the state’s next attorney general is going to change all of this in a hurry. As a native Texan, I believe the new attorney general should use the office’s authority to change how the state exercises power and whom it protects. That means looking beyond the cases the office can bring or defend, and recognizing its influence over the conduct of state agencies and the relationship between government and the people it serves. This is a substantially different conception of the attorney general’s role: using the office’s considerable resources to hold government officials accountable, confront abuses of corporate power, and defend the rights of Texans.

That responsibility begins with the office’s own use of state power. First, Johnson should abandon Paxton’s efforts to pursue out-of-state physicians who provide abortion medication to Texans. He should also withdraw the office from its agreement with Immigration and Customs Enforcement that authorizes state employees to perform certain federal immigration-enforcement actions—like assisting in investigations, apprehension, and detention—under ICE supervision. And where Paxton challenged federal protections for LGBTQ students, Johnson should take advantage of the state’s legal resources to defend students against discrimination, not to perpetuate it.

Furthermore, Johnson should take a different approach to economic and environmental protections. Under Paxton, the office sued to block expanded federal protections that would have made more than four million additional workers eligible for overtime pay. Paxton also challenged federal methane regulations requiring oil and gas companies to monitor leaks and reduce emissions—rules the EPA estimated would prevent approximately 58 million tons of methane emissions from entering the atmosphere between 2024 and 2038.

Johnson should stop using the office’s resources to undermine worker protections and reasonable environmental standards. Instead, the office should focus on ensuring labor compliance in emerging industries, protecting immigrant workers, and fighting misclassification of workers as independent contractors—deceptive practices that affect Texans in blue-collar or service-sector jobs. And in a state where oil and gas production touches nearly every corner of the economy, the office should take seriously its responsibility to protect communities from unlawful pollution, contamination, and other practices that put their health and property at risk.

During the administrations of Cornyn, Abbott, and Paxton, Texas saw what an ambitious attorney general can accomplish. But the measure of this new administration should not be how many of Paxton’s cases it abandons or how dramatically it departs from his politics. It should be whether Texans can feel the difference in how their government treats them. Whether workers can count on the state to pursue employers who steal their wages. Whether communities can hold polluters accountable. Whether civil rights mean something when government agencies violate them. And whether the state’s lawyers work for those who have too often been left to fend for themselves.

Texas does not need a less ambitious attorney general. It needs one willing to be ambitious about the right things—and most importantly, for the people.

text:
“We need to get permitting reform done to get things built in this country and to make life more affordable for American families.”

Click here to watch the video.

WASHINGTON — U.S. Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) today delivered the following remarks on the Senate floor:

Thune’s remarks below (as delivered):

“Mr. President, one of our priorities this Congress has been finding ways to make life easier for hardworking Americans.

“And one of the ways we’ve gone about that is by eliminating some of the red tape that drives up prices and causes headaches for consumers, businessowners, and builders.

“We’ve rescinded costly regulations through the Congressional Review Act that would have driven up prices for a host of items.

“In fact, we have voted [on] 25 different CRA – Congressional Review Act – resolutions of disapproval to undo burdensome Biden-era … regulations.

“Twenty-five times here, the Senate has voted on those, Mr. President, in an attempt to try and lessen the cost and the red tape of doing business and creating jobs in this country, and ultimately of driving up costs for consumers, which is what all that red tape, in the end, does.

“We passed the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act, which cuts some of the red tape that has driven up the price of housing by making it difficult to build new homes.

“And we’re continuing those efforts this week with the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act – a major permitting reform bill to help America build again.

“Mr. President, the federal permitting process is broken.

“Too often, projects are bogged down in bureaucratic delays for months, and often years, at a time.

“Delays cause project budgets to balloon, which then leads to higher costs for American consumers.

“And it’s not just the dollars-and-cents cost, Mr. President.

“Project delays have serious opportunity costs as well:

“Jobs put on hold because a new factory won’t open on time.

“Communities without internet access because broadband infrastructure is delayed.

“And Americans driving on bad roads and rickety bridges while plans for improvements are stuck in an office in Washington.

“Mr. President, it’s not that construction projects shouldn’t undergo a thorough review of their impacts on communities and the environment.

“Input from the local community, from state and local governments, and from other stakeholders is a critical part of determining whether and how to execute a project.

“But the federal permitting process has unfortunately gone far beyond these reasonable expectations.

“And that’s due in large part to senseless delays caused by cascading litigation from environmental groups and by agencies determined to study a project to death.

“We’ve seen those delays happen to everything from water projects to broadband deployment to affordable energy and improving roads and bridges.

“Mr. President, last week I mentioned the Potomac Interceptor, which burst earlier this year and sent nearly 250 million gallons of raw sewage spewing into the Potomac River.

“The local water company identified vulnerabilities in this 60-year-old sewer pipe a full seven years before it burst.

“But proposed repairs languished in the federal permitting process year after year after year.

“And the project was still undergoing an environmental review when the pipe burst and caused an environmental disaster.

“And that was just to replace something that had been there for decades.

“Mr. President, for Americans wondering why important projects aren’t making progress, the answer is too often federal permitting delays.

“It takes four and a half years on average for federal agencies to approve an environmental impact statement.

“Add another 15 months to that for a new bridge.

“And if a NEPA lawsuit is filed over a proposed project, it takes almost two years to resolve it.

“Mr. President, if we want better roads and bridges, if we want to strengthen American manufacturing, if we want to be energy independent, we need permitting reform.

“And I’m grateful to Chairs Shelley Moore Capito and Mike Lee for working with their Democrat counterparts to put forward a bipartisan permitting reform bill that I hope we will complete this week.

“This bill would streamline the review process, putting federal bureaucrats on the clock to give a yes or no answer to a project.

“This would make a huge difference on energy projects.

“As I said, projects are often stuck in limbo for years as they work their way through government approvals.

“That adds costs to the project, delays construction, and ultimately leaves American families paying higher utility bills.

“But by streamlining those processes, the Council of Economic Advisers estimates that provisions in this bill could save a typical household hundreds of dollars on energy bills and other expenses every single year.

“Importantly, this bill also provides much-needed certainty and clarity to a variety of stakeholders, including farmers and ranchers.

“For one, it extends Clean Water Act permits from five to 10 years, giving farmers more time to complete projects before having to renew their permits.

“It shortens reviews under the Endangered Species Act, allowing grazing-related projects – like a new fence on a ranch – to move along faster.

“And it ensures that local governments and landowners will continue to have a say in projects that affect them.

“Mr. President, for a lot of Americans, the type of project that most concerns them these days is a data center coming to their community.

“And I’m pleased to report that the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act would enact new protections for local communities when it comes to data centers.

“That starts with requiring – requiring – data centers to shoulder their own energy costs – whether that’s their operating and construction costs or the cost of grid improvements needed to accommodate them.

“This legislation ensures those costs don’t show up on household utility bills.

“It would also provide assistance to communities to help them understand and explore the impact a proposed data center would have on their locality – everything from the economic impact to the energy costs and infrastructure requirements that would be associated with the project.

“Mr. President, well-intentioned rules and regulations can quickly turn into death by a thousand cuts.

“Or, as is too often the case, death by delay.

“The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act restores the balanced approach to permitting that’s needed.

“It ensures local stakeholders have a say in projects in their community.

“And it provides accountability to ensure that bureaucrats in Washington don’t prevent needed projects from moving forward.

“A closed bridge.

“A burst sewer pipe.

“A factory built overseas.

“Bureaucratic delays, Mr. President, have real consequences.

“We need to get permitting reform done to get things built in this country and to make life more affordable for American families.”

title: Sodium batteries: Europe's chance to power its own future - Eunews
authors: Redazione, Redazione eunewsit, www.facebook.com, valeria.amendola
description:
Beyond lithium: what makes sodium batteries different?
Sodium-ion batteries offer an emerging alternative: they use sodium instead of lithium, reducing reliance on certain critical raw materials.
Sodium batteries: an opportunity for Europe Sodium is abundant in Europe.
The EESC highlights the possibility of producing sodium batteries entirely from European raw materials.
From innovation to industrial production The immediate challenge is industrial scale-up.
text:
By Hervé Jeannin, co-rapporteur for the EESC opinion on the potential of the sodium battery manufacturing sector

Europe’s energy transition requires an industrial base capable of delivering it. Batteries power electric mobility, facilitate the integration of renewable electricity and help households and businesses manage their energy consumption. Our ability to manufacture them will shape Europe’s competitiveness and energy security. Yet intense international competition and dependencies on materials, components and equipment are weakening this essential industry.

As co-rapporteur for the European Economic and Social Committee’s opinion on sodium battery manufacturing, I am convinced that sodium technologies offer a tangible opportunity to strengthen Europe’s capabilities while making better use of its own resources.

Beyond lithium: what makes sodium batteries different?

Today, lithium-ion batteries dominate the global market, powering everything from smartphones to electric vehicles and energy storage systems. Their production is heavily concentrated in Asia, particularly China, which leads in battery manufacturing and the processing of key materials. Sodium-ion batteries offer an emerging alternative: they use sodium instead of lithium, reducing reliance on certain critical raw materials.

Although they generally store less energy for the same weight, they could be cheaper to produce and are particularly promising for stationary energy storage and more affordable electric vehicles. China is already investing heavily in this technology, making it essential for Europe to develop its own manufacturing capacity before another strategic dependency takes hold.

Sodium batteries: an opportunity for Europe

Sodium is abundant in Europe. Suitable battery chemistries can reduce dependence on lithium, cobalt and nickel, while the hard carbon used for anodes can be derived from wood or agricultural waste. The EESC highlights the possibility of producing sodium batteries entirely from European raw materials. Turning this potential into strategic autonomy requires European capabilities across the entire value chain, from processing to recycling, and, above all, strong political commitment to driving the development of European solutions encompassing both raw materials and manufacturers.

Sodium should complement lithium-ion technologies. Each application calls for a different balance between energy density, cost, safety and durability. Sodium-ion batteries generally have slightly lower energy density, but weight and size matter less for stationary storage than for electric vehicles. Storing renewable electricity for households, businesses and grids therefore represents a particularly relevant market opportunity.

Public support must reflect technological maturity. Sodium-ion batteries offer prospects for deployment in the nearer term; sodium–saltwater systems require further research, particularly into solid electrolytes, to explore their potential for marine applications and longer-term storage. Our opinion also identifies the possibility of using sodium recovered from desalination by-products, linking water resilience to energy storage, subject to technical and environmental assessment.

From innovation to industrial production

The immediate challenge is industrial scale-up. A laboratory breakthrough alone does not create a competitive factory. Companies must demonstrate the reliability of their solutions, secure customers and finance production equipment. Small businesses often struggle to shoulder these risks. The EESC therefore calls for an updated industrial roadmap for lithium and sodium batteries, coordinated by the European Battery Alliance, with targeted investment support and cooperation with research and technology organisations.

Investing in Europe’s battery industry

The EESC’s opinion on the Battery Booster strategy makes a specific request: broaden funding to cover chemistries beyond lithium and explicitly include sodium. Support should reach SMEs, suppliers and recyclers alongside cell manufacturers, and should not be limited to electric vehicles. Critical chemicals, electrolytes and European-made machinery also deserve investment. Dependence on imported inputs and equipment leaves vulnerabilities that building more cell factories alone cannot resolve.

Affordable energy, predictable permitting procedures and timely funding are essential. The EESC calls for stronger and better-targeted funding for the Battery Booster strategy in the next EU Budget. Our opinion on sodium advocates an overall budget of at least EUR 220 billion for FP10.

International cooperation must help build lasting European expertise. Both opinions call for technology transfer; the Battery Booster opinion recommends making state aid, public procurement and subsidies conditional on technology transfer and local content. Investment must strengthen European research (80% of current projects are not launched for lack of funding in Europe), skills and suppliers, while ensuring that requirements for products entering the EU market are applied fairly.

Sustainability, jobs and regional development

Circularity must be built in from the outset. Ecodesign should facilitate disassembly and materials recovery, while production should minimise energy consumption and the use of hazardous substances. Recycling requires economically viable facilities, harmonised collection and the efficient transport of used batteries to authorised facilities within the single market. Materials recovery capacity must grow in step with production.

Industrial ambition must also benefit workers and regions. The Battery Booster opinion makes job quality and compliance with EU standards conditions for public support. Adequate staffing, training, investment in prevention and effective inspections are essential. Workers must be involved in identifying risks arising from new processes.

Keeping Europe on the global battery map

These priorities will guide discussions at the event Keeping Europe on the Global Battery Map – The Case for Innovation, jointly organised by the EESC’s Consultative Commission on Industrial Change and the Batteries European Partnership Association and to be held on 30 November in Brussels. The event will bring together Europe’s technological prospects and the public support and funding mechanisms needed to turn them into reality.

Europe has the scientific expertise and industrial talent needed to shape the next generation of batteries. Sodium offers an opportunity to harness these strengths. Sustained investment in production, infrastructure and skills can turn European innovation into European industrial capacity.

text:
Following a historic election in which voters delivered a decisive mandate against utility price-gouging and unchecked corporate giveaways, advocates are calling on the new pro-environment trifecta in Harrisburg to deliver immediate relief for working families.

The 100-day agenda focuses on two immediate tracks: establishing strict guardrails on power-hungry A.I. data centers to prevent massive utility rate spikes and rapidly expanding union-built clean energy projects to drive down electricity costs.

“Pennsylvania voters went to the polls and delivered an unmistakable mandate: They are fed up with skyrocketing electric bills and policies that further enrich Big Tech billionaires at their expense,” said Molly Parzen, Executive Director of Conservation Voters of Pennsylvania.

“For too long, working families have been forced to choose between keeping the lights on and paying for their groceries while corporate utilities rake in record profits. Our 'Unleashing Pennsylvania Power' agenda is a direct response to the voters. We are ready to hit the ground running on day one to hold Big Tech accountable, unleash local solar and battery storage and build an economy that works for everyday Pennsylvanians.”

“The challenges we face are all connected - from data centers to clean energy to climate to affordability. Pennsylvania must act quickly to enact strong data center regulations, invest in clean power, and stand up to corporate interests that are polluting our environment and making it harder for the rest of us to make ends meet," said Patrick McDonnell, President and CEO of PennFuture. “The affordability crisis is real. Severe storms and dangerous flooding from climate change are increasing. Our electric grid is straining to meet new demand. The time to act is now.”

To fulfill this mandate, the "Unleashing Pennsylvania Power" blueprint advances affordability through two main strategies:

Reining In Big Tech A.I. Data Centers

Hyperscale data centers require immense amounts of electricity and water, threatening to push grid capacity to its limits and shift hundreds of millions of dollars in substantial transmission upgrade costs onto local families.

The 100-day agenda establishes strict guardrails to protect working families and maintain the quality of life in local communities, including:

-- The “Developer-Pays” Standard: Tech developers must pay for 100% of their own grid interconnects, substations and transmission line upgrades. Corporate utilities will be prohibited from shifting these infrastructure costs onto the monthly electric bills of everyday families and local businesses.

-- Ending Corporate Secrecy & Protecting Local Control: The agenda bans non-disclosure agreements (NDAs) between tech developers and government officials. It also establishes a 180-day local planning pause to allow municipalities time to update zoning ordinances and safeguard residents’ quality of life.

-- Strict Clean Power Rules: Data centers must bring new, in-state clean power and battery storage online to meet their energy demand. The agenda strictly prohibits the use of dirty diesel and natural gas backup generators that pollute communities.

--PUC Enforcement with Teeth: The Public Utility Commission (PUC) will be granted expanded authority to enforce ratepayer protections and collect developer fees to shield local communities from negative impacts.

Lowering Electric Prices With Clean Energy

Expanding access to locally produced, union-made clean energy is the fastest way to stabilize the grid and permanently lower electricity prices. We know clean energy is the cheapest form of energy and can be brought online more quickly to meet surging demand.

The 100-day agenda prioritizes:

-- Unlocking Solar-Ready Warehouses: Requiring new logistics facilities and warehouses to be constructed solar-ready, turning industrial rooftops into clean power generators. This initiative has the potential to generate enough union-made electricity to power 1 million homes while preserving open space and farmland.

-- Grid-Scale Battery Storage Targets: Establishing state targets for utility-scale battery storage to capture cheap solar energy during the day and inject it back into the grid during peak evening hours. Pennsylvania will join 13 other states-- including Maryland, New Jersey and New York-- that have already adopted battery storage targets to prevent blackouts and blunt price spikes.

-- Community Solar: Passing long-overdue legislation allowing renters, multi-family housing residents and small businesses to subscribe to local solar projects, cutting monthly electric bills by up to 20%.

-- Virtual Power Plants (VPPs): Enabling smart-grid networks that link residential batteries, smart thermostats and electric vehicles to supply power back to the grid during extreme heat waves or winter storms.

-- Clean Energy Manufacturing Tax Credits: Establishing a 30% tax credit on eligible production costs for businesses manufacturing clean energy products here in Pennsylvania, driving economic growth and union job creation while positioning Pennsylvania as a national leader in the growing green economy.

-- Holding Corporate Utilities Accountable: Over the last five years, Pennsylvania’s working families have seen an average 60% increase in their utility bills-- with much of that going to pad the bottom lines of corporate utilities.

We need to rein in excessive profits from monopoly utility companies and institute critical consumer protections to curb unnecessary rate hikes and expand assistance to low-income and working families who are deciding each month between paying for groceries and paying their electric bills.

“Pennsylvania has long been an energy leader, yet we rank 47th in the country for renewable energy — unleashing Pennsylvania power has to mean the build-out of solar, wind, and battery storage to stay competitive, meet demand, and get costs under control,” said Rep. Elizabeth Fiedler (D-Phila.), chair of the House Energy Committee. “I’m hopeful about the first 100 days because so many of these measures passed the House already with bipartisan support. We have to get energy affordability policy over the line while we have the chance.”

“It’s a new day in Pennsylvania. For far too long, the Republican majority focused our energy policies single-mindedly on fossil fuels,” said Senate Environment Committee Chair Carolyn Comitta (D-Chester). “Now, for the first time in decades, we have an opportunity to explore, pursue, and enact sustainable alternatives to make our environment cleaner, our communities healthier and our energy bills more affordable.

“The voters delivered a mandate for change, and we have a responsibility to make it happen. I’m excited to work with our environmental organizations, stakeholders, legislative colleagues, and the governor to cut emissions, reduce costs and boost renewables in the Commonwealth.”

“For too long, the status quo has worked very well for utilities and energy generators while burdening families and small businesses with rising electric bills and the impacts of energy infrastructure,” said Rep. Danielle Friel Otten (D-Chester). “Rate increases get approved while households are forced to choose between keeping the lights on and buying groceries. My public interest legislation changes that by requiring the PUC to weigh factors like affordability, fairness, sustainability, and public safety before ruling in a ratemaking case or other substantive utility proceeding. I am grateful to PennFuture and Conservation Voters for making utility accountability a top legislative priority for the 2027-28 session. The families and small businesses I hear from every day are counting on us to get it done.”

“Everyday Pennsylvanians are feeling the squeeze of rising electric bills, and they deserve practical, modern solutions that put money back in their pockets,” said Rep. Nathan Davidson (D-Dauphin). “Virtual Power Plants empower everyday households to take control of their energy costs. This will modernize our system so consumers are not stuck paying for expensive, outdated infrastructure when smarter, cost-saving alternatives are already at our fingertips.”

Taken together, the full "Unleashing Pennsylvania Power" policy blueprint charts an historic course that will put Pennsylvania at the forefront of tackling the affordability crisis, creating union jobs and protecting the quality of life of communities under threat.

By delivering on voters’ demands for affordability, Harrisburg can demonstrate that state government can deliver tangible results, strengthen the middle class, lower costs and create union jobs.

text:
This audio is auto-generated. Please let us know if you have feedback.

Dive Brief:

Relatively few states are doing enough to support public and community-centered power systems or virtual power plants, according to a pair of “scorecards” from the Institute for Local Self-Reliance.

For its “community power” scorecard, the Washington, D.C.-based nonprofit assigned points based on the presence or absence of more than a dozen policies it sees as supportive of local control of — or, at least, influence over — energy systems. It subtracted points for policies it sees as counterproductive, including state laws that preempt local governments from banning new natural gas hookups, and “right of first refusal” rules that allow utilities to avoid competitive bidding for new transmission projects.

Most states earned a failing grade on the community power scorecard and only a handful — including California, New York, Maryland and Colorado — scored higher than a C on the VPP scorecard.

Dive Insight:

The scorecards were released shortly before the midterm elections, which saw mixed results for community power advocates and proposals.

In Georgia, Democrats now hold a majority on the Public Service Commission and are widely expected to push back on Southern Company’s plans to add some 10 GW of new generation, mostly natural gas, to meet rising data center demand.

Meanwhile, in Ann Arbor, Michigan, voters rejected a bid to separate from investor-owned DTE Energy and create a public power utility.

On the community power scorecard, the seven highest-scoring states were California, Colorado, Connecticut, Maryland, Massachusetts, New Jersey and Oregon.

The scorecard values policies that aim to make it easier to deploy and monetize distributed resources, including state community solar programs, customer-friendly net metering and interconnection frameworks, streamlined solar permitting, and virtual power plants.

Other criteria relate to what ILSR calls “utility accountability,” such as transmission right-of-first refusal, restructured energy markets, laws or regulations curtailing customer disconnections, and restrictions on utilities charging customers for new infrastructure during construction.

Though state lawmakers or regulators have significant influence over most of ILSR’s metrics, some also have a national nexus.

For example, a Federal Energy Regulatory Commission order in 2011 opened transmission-construction bidding to third parties, eroding vertically integrated utilities’ access to potentially lucrative infrastructure projects.

In April, Entergy, Xcel Energy and seven other utilities asked FERC to halt competitive bidding for transmission projects in the Midcontinent Independent System Operator and Southwest Power Pool regions, which cover parts of more than 20 states. They said the move would accelerate transmission development; competitive bidding advocates countered that it would raise project costs that ratepayers would ultimately bear.

If passed, the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, or BAAJA, could shift those rules.

Among BAAJA’s sweeping reforms to energy project permitting and regulation are a wholesale elimination of incumbent utilities’ federal right of first refusal and stricter regional transmission planning requirements.

Even states with relatively high marks on community power have room for improvement, ILSR said.

California, for example, earned B’s for solar permitting and and virtual power plants, but a D on community solar and F grades on disconnection prevention and market structure.

Texas, with an overall F grade on community power, scored a C on net metering and A grades on third-party DER ownership, right of first refusal and municipal franchise authority, which allows cities to negotiate better contracts with electric and gas utilities.

ILSR’s virtual power plant scorecard showed a similar dynamic.

No state met all of the group’s benchmarks for a perfect score, whose requirements include variable compensation based on demand and other factors; third-party aggregator participation; increased access or benefits for low- and moderate-income customers; multiple technology types; and multiple customer classes.

Six states earned a ‘B’ grade for their VPP policies: California, Colorado, Connecticut, Hawai’i, Maryland and New York.

New York and California’s VPP programs are the country’s best, according to ILSR. New York’s only deficiency was not prohibiting “participant clawbacks and fees,” such as early exit fees or penalties for failing to meet minimum performance standards.
