title: To Keep Its Second Place in the Global Battery Race, Seoul Needs More Teammates
description:
United States Korea should continue work on battery tech in the United States with a specific focus on active materials—the mixture of critical minerals that are essential to the battery’s function.
In addition, the United States has innovative battery material producers that might benefit from joint ventures with Korean metals giants.
Seoul faces tough decisions now over whether and how much more integration into the U.S. battery ecosystem is worthwhile or politically palatable.
The most obvious benefit to Koreans expanding their role in the Indian battery ecosystem is market access.
Korea’s second-place role in the global battery market is essential for balancing industrial power in this critical technology.
text:
Korea punches above its weight when it comes to producing lithium-ion batteries. Its three major battery firms are among the top ten global manufacturers and second only to China in terms of global market share. Its battery sector has benefited from close coordination between government and companies, particularly in targeted innovation and investment initiatives. Another core asset is the power of large conglomerates, or chaebol, that work closely with or acquire subject-matter experts and startups to expand competitiveness within Korea and internationally.

But Korea’s silver-medal spot on the battery innovation podium is at risk. As we write in a recent report on battery ecosystems, Korea’s successful approach has also “entrenched structural vulnerabilities,” including the need to import key raw materials and exposure to regulatory and geopolitical shocks. Our analysis finds that Chinese producers have access to unrivaled economies of scale, industrial ecosystems, and coordinated industrial strategy—all of which will make the global battery market more challenging for Korean producers.

Fortunately, Seoul is responding with its own policies, too. The Korean government announced a U.S. $289 million investment in September to accelerate sodium-ion and all-solid-state battery technology as a strategy to protect its industry from both Chinese competition and the slowdown in electric vehicle (EV) sales in some key markets. But to succeed in this diversification strategy, Korea needs not only innovation policies, but also core partners to help scale different parts of the battery value chain and deploy these new technologies. This is a strategy that Korean chaebols have successfully begun in the United States—but this external dimension should be accelerated and expanded, including to Europe and India.

United States

Korea should continue work on battery tech in the United States with a specific focus on active materials—the mixture of critical minerals that are essential to the battery’s function. It also should partner with next-generation startups to cultivate a key place in a cutting-edge and resilient battery ecosystem.

As Seoul has become concerned about U.S. security commitments, it has pivoted toward a broad strategy to leverage industrial capacity and competitiveness to help manage its alliance with Washington. Batteries have been a key part of this move. While initially feeling slighted by the Inflation Reduction Act, Koreans regrouped and expanded investments to spearhead the development of America’s Battery Belt.

Korean producers won out over Japan’s last battery manufacturing giant and myriad American startups to become the dominant player in the U.S. battery ecosystem, which is expected to become second only to China in battery manufacturing. Many of these Korean investments were joint ventures with major U.S. automobile makers, but after the administration of President Donald Trump eliminated EV subsidies, demand dropped. The Korean players have made a sound bet on retrofitting their assembly lines to also produce lithium-iron-phosphate (LFP) batteries to serve America’s booming market for large-scale battery storage on the power grid. This ensures Korean know-how in new chemistries while providing the United States a domestic alternative to Chinese LFP batteries.

Going forward, Korean firms should deepen their U.S. ties by working on active materials and next-generation tech—both are policy priorities of the Trump administration as well as the incoming Democratic-controlled Congress. One key finding of the Carnegie analysis is that the United States leads the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development in startups piloting emerging chemistries, but scaling up requires capital and know-how that startups lack. One option to explore is whether Korean firms’ U.S. factories, especially those facing weak demand, might offer assembly lines to U.S. startups (or to jointly scale new facilities, as already underway). In addition, the United States has innovative battery material producers that might benefit from joint ventures with Korean metals giants. Doing so advances Washington’s onshoring goals and Korean market share.

This said, Korean producers will need to navigate challenging years ahead, not just in market dynamics but also political pressure from Washington. Seoul faces tough decisions now over whether and how much more integration into the U.S. battery ecosystem is worthwhile or politically palatable. Washington may be expanding its expectations for Korean investment in U.S. energy development past what Seoul can commit.

Europe

Korea should view Europe’s battery conundrum as an emerging opportunity to strengthen industrial ties, science diplomacy, and overall cooperation with the European Union and member states to ensure Korean firms have access to state aid under the proposed Industrial Accelerator Act.

To brace for potential challenges in the American market, Korea should turn to other partners to continue to build out its battery edge. After the United States, European countries are a worthwhile target for Korea’s battery foreign policy—not only for market demand, but also for vital partnerships to promote innovation and supply chain resilience. The European EV and battery storage system markets are expected to continue growing as countries seek greater electrification in their own struggles for energy security, especially amid heightened fuel costs. However, Korean firms will need to navigate a more protectionist and less economically liberal Europe.

The Industrial Accelerator Act, Europe’s clean tech policy that prioritizes products made on the continent, has been pending since March. If or when passed, it will define European battery policy by creating incentives for local and allied battery supply chains to help fend off Chinese imports. Right now, member states are debating what exactly this looks like, and Korea should emphasize the importance of its products as a valuable strategic diversification play for Europe. To do so, the EU must agree that South Korea is included in its definition of “Made in Europe”—a key political question. In the meantime, continuing to partner and invest in European supply chains will buy goodwill in Brussels and other capitals and illustrate the importance of EU-Korea partnerships.

The chaebols might also consider deepening partnerships with European battery firms. Over the past decade, Europe’s battery ecosystem—which has excelled at basic R&D and regulation—has struggled to produce commercial scale. But it has important actors across battery materials and some novel chemistries. The most fruitful partnerships could center around Europe’s next-generation technology such as silicon anode, which is promising but cannot scale without Korean manufacturing expertise, capacity, and perhaps offtake (a commitment of purchase). Europeans need Koreans for manufacturing, while Koreans need Europeans for market access.

Lastly, Korea should use its partnership with the EU’s Horizon Europe R&D initiative to focus on breakthrough battery technology for the long term, particularly game-changing chemistries such as lithium-air—especially as Chinese rivals have revealed that they also are working on this technology. Although Europe has struggled to scale its own battery champions, it still holds an important presence in battery innovation and related patents. Focusing EU-Korea science diplomacy on battery technology is a sound win-win to ensure that Korea can pool research capacity and stay on the frontier.

India

Delhi presents the biggest challenge and biggest opportunity to Korea’s battery foreign partnerships.

India is at a fundamentally different starting point than the EU or United States, and it needs help scaling up and indigenizing an industrial base for battery production. Ultimately, India’s industrial policy has not succeeded in building a domestic battery sector, but its political ambition is very high. In some aspects, its industrial potential is also high, such as in graphite-based anodes, the part of the battery cell where the energy is stored. Starting in the early 2020s, India put forth subsidies in its Production Linked Incentive program, but much like Europe, it did not have the domestic industries to scale. Today, the government needs to step up its investment and coordination efforts to reduce dependence on licensed foreign technology. Indian firms face challenges in accessing crucial factory machinery from Chinese companies—a risk and an area where Korean firms can support.

The most obvious benefit to Koreans expanding their role in the Indian battery ecosystem is market access. While India’s battery demand is negligible today, it will grow thanks to a rapidly electrifying road transport fleet and a massive solar boom in need of batteries on the electrical grid. Koreans should view Indian partnerships as investments that could be costly and logistically tough in the near-term but will provide access to ecosystems beyond the United States and EU. This will require the two sides working through regulatory issues, such as localization requirements, potentially allowing joint projects between Indian and Korean conglomerates. It could extend beyond just battery cell production and come with specific carve-outs for Korean machinery, the exact technology to which China has blocked Indian access.

Historically, India’s industrial foreign policy and cooperation have been strongest with Japan, centering largely on more resilient supply chains. More recently, Delhi and Tokyo have decided to focus diplomatic and industrial attention on semiconductors, critical minerals, pharmaceuticals, clean energy, and information and communications technology. Korea might look to how Japanese businesses were able to enter the Indian market and create space for Japanese production as an example.

Korean companies are already making strides in that direction. Korean car manufacturers have built research partnerships with Indian universities and battery-makers. Over the past several years, the Indian and Korean governments have pledged to deepen and expand collaboration in tech industrial domains, especially in semiconductors and sustainable energy. The question for South Korea is how the chaebols can build effective joint ventures with Indian conglomerates that work best for both parties and gain access to Indian subsidies.

Building a Global Battery Network

The battery industry will only grow in the coming years, as access to energy becomes increasingly securitized and expensive and battery applications extend to new sectors. To meet the increasing demand for electricity, countries will look for more reliable and nimble solutions. Korea’s second-place role in the global battery market is essential for balancing industrial power in this critical technology. To capitalize on this position—and maintain it—Korean policymakers should focus on partnerships in the United States, EU, and India, with different strategies toward each.

Korea has core competencies that allow it to provide quality batteries at competitive prices and efficient timelines. But to realize the full potential of its industrial might in the global battery economy, Seoul needs to simultaneously build targeted and strategic partnerships in regions where it can improve both innovation and manufacturing. This offers gains for both Korea and the global energy ecosystem: It keeps battery geopolitics diversified and competitive by preventing Chinese battery dominance from eclipsing alternatives. For partner countries, it would help them build their own durable ecosystems.

text:
On the Dash:

New EV sales reached an estimated 83,262 units, up 3% year over year but down 3.9% from September. It was the first annual increase of 2026.

Used EV sales climbed 73.2% year over year and 4.7% month over month to an estimated 48,678 units.

New and used EV days’ supply increased from September, narrowing the gap with ICE+ vehicles, while new EV transaction prices rose and used EV listing prices declined.

According to Cox Automotive’s October EV Market Monitor, new electric vehicle (EV) sales reached an estimated 83,262 units in October, a 3% increase from October 2025 and a 3.9% decrease from September, marking the first year-over-year comparison against a month without the federal EV tax credit.

While EVs accounted for 6.2% of new-vehicle sales, down from 6.3% a year earlier and 6.5% in September, Tesla led the market with 47,850 units, followed by Rivian, Cadillac and Chevrolet. Tesla’s share of EV sales rose to 57.5%, and the Model Y remained the best-selling EV at 36,366 units, up 9.4% from September and accounting for nearly 44% of new EV sales. Meanwhile, used EV sales reached an estimated 48,678 units, up 73.2% from a year earlier and 4.7% from September. Used EVs accounted for 3.3% of used-vehicle sales, up from 2% a year earlier.

Sign up for CBT News’ daily newsletter and get the latest industry stories delivered straight to your inbox.

Tesla remained the leading used EV brand, followed by Chevrolet, Ford, Hyundai and BMW, although sales trends varied by model. The Tesla Model 3, Model Y and Ford Mustang Mach-E declined, while the Chevrolet Equinox EV, Blazer EV, Kia EV6, Nissan Leaf and Volkswagen ID.4 posted notable gains.

Days’ supply and sales pace

New EV days’ supply rose to 85 days, up 21% from September and down 40.4% from a year earlier, while gasoline-powered and hybrid (ICE+) vehicles had an 89-day supply, narrowing the gap between the two categories to about four days from 12 days in September. Slower sales drove the rise, as estimated daily sales fell 15.2% while inventory increased 2.7%. Honda had the leanest new EV supply at 38 days, Volkswagen had the highest, Hyundai posted the largest monthly increase, and Nissan’s supply fell 24 days to 76 days.

Used EV days’ supply rose 3% from September to 38 days, but was down 18.8% year over year. Used ICE+ vehicles averaged 47 days, narrowing the gap to nine days from roughly 12 days in September. Tesla had the leanest used EV supply at 32 days. Mercedes-Benz supply fell 16 days to 47, while Audi supply rose six days to 47.

However, the ATP for a new EV rose to $56,220, up 1% from September and down 2.7% from a year earlier, while the price premium over ICE+ vehicles narrowed slightly to $5,306. Higher-priced vehicles drove the increase, particularly the Tesla Model Y, whose price rose 0.8% to $53,492 as sales grew, offsetting declines in the Model 3’s price and sales. Average EV incentives rose to $6,375 per vehicle, or 11.3% of the transaction price, up from $5,949 or 10.3% a year earlier.

Meanwhile, the average listing price for used EVs fell to $36,582, down 0.5% from September and 1.9% from a year earlier, while the premium over ICE+ vehicles widened slightly to $2,236, or 6.5%. Lower prices for several high-volume models, including the Ford Mustang Mach-E, Nissan Ariya, Chevrolet Equinox EV and Volkswagen ID.4, drove the decline.

What shaped October demand

October offered an early look at demand after the federal tax credit expired, and EV share held roughly steady as inventory increased. According to Cox Automotive, inflation, fuel prices and consumer confidence may influence demand as the year closes, and the availability of lower-priced EVs and incentives will remain crucial.

The EU recently passed the ReFuel Aviation Law, requiring fuel suppliers at European airports to progressively raise the share of SAF blended into conventional jet fuel.

California-based Infinium Energy accomplished the first US commercial passenger flight using eSAF, according to CEO Robert Schuetzle. Its Project Roadrunner facility in Reeves County, Texas, is backed by Brookfield Asset Management and Breakthrough Energy Catalyst, and is expected to come online in 2027 with capacity of 23,000 tonnes per year, primarily producing SAF. Infinium has a long-term agreement with American Airlines and has sold into European markets, with clients including International Airlines Group. Chicago/Singapore-based Aether Fuels converts waste biomass, industrial waste gas or captured CO2 into SAF; CEO Conor Madigan said the company cut the syngas generation section of its plant in half through catalyst and reactor innovation.

Toulouse-based Beyond Aero is developing a hydrogen-propelled electric business aircraft targeting 800 nautical miles of range, which it says would cover 80% of business aviation flights in Europe. It plans to start with gaseous hydrogen, and Lead Hydrogen Airport Operations Manager Irwin Kerboriou stressed the need for airport operator support and a technical, operational, economic and regulatory framework for refueling at European airports. Stuttgart-based H2Fly has demonstrated liquid-hydrogen fuel cell systems, most recently on a 900 km test flight, according to CEO Ralph Müller, who said many of the hardest challenges stem from electrification rather than the fuel cells themselves. H2Fly also intends to begin with regional flights.

Hybrid Air Vehicles' lighter-than-air Airlander can cut emissions by 75% even on traditional fuels and aims for zero in the coming years, according to CEO Tom Grundy. The company has developed a 4-year program to build capacity for up to 24 aircraft a year at a site in northern England. The series concludes that decarbonizing aviation will require SAF, electric aircraft and lighter-than-air technologies working side by side.

text:
TeslaTSLA is making a huge bet on autonomous mobility, with Europe now becoming an important part of that strategy. The electric vehicle (EV) and tech giant plans to invest €3 billion (roughly $3.3 billion) to expand its Gigafactory in Grünheide, Germany, with a new facility designed to produce up to 1 million Cybercabs annually. Construction is expected to begin in the first half of 2027, with production starting in 2029.

The investment aligns with Tesla's priorities. CEO Elon Musk has pinned autonomous vehicles (AVs) and artificial intelligence as Tesla’s next growth chapters. He wants AVs to become a much bigger part of the company's business. However, building the manufacturing capacity is only one part of the challenge. Tesla must still prove that its driverless technology can support a commercially viable transportation service.

Giga Berlin Gets a Bigger Role in Tesla's Future

The planned expansion would give Cybercab a manufacturing base outside the United States. Tesla's German factory currently produces Model Y vehicles, and the new facility is expected to operate alongside existing vehicle production.

The expansion also comes as Tesla moves closer to bringing battery manufacturing in-house at Grünheide. The company manufactures battery electrodes at the site, but ships them to Texas for cell assembly before bringing them back. Per Teslarati, Tesla now aims to manufacture complete 4680 battery cells locally using its dry-electrode process, with annual capacity targeted at 18 GWh by mid-2027.

Together, the two projects could make Giga Berlin a more self-sufficient manufacturing hub, covering both battery and vehicle production. Tesla also expects local sourcing to raise European content in its Model Y vehicles to nearly 90%.

Reducing dependence on overseas suppliers could improve supply-chain resilience and strengthen Tesla's position in Europe. But the larger strategic significance lies in preparing the factory for a future in which AVs account for a substantial share of production.

Cybercab's Commercial Potential Still Unproven

Tesla is making additional room for Cybercab in the United States as well. To that end, it plans to wind down Cybertruck production in fall 2027 at Gigafactory Texas to free up space for Cybercab manufacturing. The two-seat vehicle, designed without a steering wheel or pedals, is central to Musk's transportation-as-a-service vision.

This could create recurring revenue opportunities and potentially improve the economics of Tesla's vehicle business. However, the model carries considerable execution risks. Tesla needs to demonstrate reliable driverless performance, secure regulatory approvals across different markets and build sufficient customer demand. High production capacity alone will not guarantee attractive returns if vehicles cannot be deployed profitably.

Competitive Landscape: Alphabet & Amazon

Tesla is expanding its robotaxi ambitions, but it is a competitive market. Alphabet's GOOGL Waymo is already a frontrunner in this domain. Tesla is gradually making progress. It recently moved narrowly ahead of Waymo in Texas' registered robotaxi fleet, with 1,302 vehicles compared with Waymo's 1,297 as of Nov. 10. However, fleet registrations should not be confused with vehicles actively providing commercial rides.

AmazonAMZN is another competitor through its Zoox subsidiary. Like Cybercab, Zoox's purpose-built robotaxi does not have a steering wheel or pedals. It has started offering paid rides in Las Vegas and is working toward expanding commercial operations to San Francisco and Austin.

Tesla's manufacturing ambitions could eventually give it an advantage in scaling autonomous fleets. But Waymo has an operating head start, while Zoox is developing a vehicle and service model directly comparable to Cybercab. For Tesla, the real test will be turning its manufacturing scale and autonomous technology into a profitable mobility business.

title: Susan Bodine on Climate Governance and Policy Frameworks | Vanderbilt Law School
description:
The conversation explored the legal and political challenges of addressing climate change, the limits of federal regulation, and the role of economic incentives, technological innovation, and public education in developing durable climate policy.
The discussion focused on how policymakers can make meaningful progress on climate change in an increasingly polarized political environment.
The Challenge of Climate Communication Bodine began by distinguishing between acknowledging climate change and characterizing it as an existential threat.
She accepted that climate change is occurring and human activity contributes substantially to it, but she cautioned against overstating its anticipated consequences.
The conversation then turned to the frameworks available to address climate change.
text:
Vanderbilt Law School’s Environmental, Energy, and Land Use Program welcomed Susan Bodine, a partner at Earth & Water Law and former senior Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) official, for its annual Distinguished Lecture on climate governance and policy frameworks. The conversation explored the legal and political challenges of addressing climate change, the limits of federal regulation, and the role of economic incentives, technological innovation, and public education in developing durable climate policy.

Bodine has served in the legislative and executive branches of government, including as chief counsel to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee, Assistant Administrator of the EPA’s Office of Solid Waste and Emergency Response during the George W. Bush administration, and Assistant Administrator of the EPA’s Office of Enforcement and Compliance Assurance during the first Trump Administration.

The discussion focused on how policymakers can make meaningful progress on climate change in an increasingly polarized political environment. Rather than relying exclusively on regulatory mandates, Bodine emphasized the importance of practical solutions that can attract bipartisan support and harness private-sector investment.

The Challenge of Climate Communication

Bodine began by distinguishing between acknowledging climate change and characterizing it as an existential threat. She accepted that climate change is occurring and human activity contributes substantially to it, but she cautioned against overstating its anticipated consequences.

In her view, predictions focused exclusively on the most extreme outcomes can undermine public confidence when those outcomes do not materialize within the predicted timeframes. “You’re eroding people’s trust in what they’re being told, and that’s just a mistake,” she explained. Bodine argued that policymakers and scientists should provide the public with accurate information rather than tell people what conclusions to reach. The objective, she suggested, should be to give people the information necessary to form their own judgments.

The conversation then turned to the frameworks available to address climate change. Bodine identified three principal approaches: regulatory mandates, economic incentives, and education. Regulatory measures include international treaties, congressional legislation, litigation, and agency rulemaking. Although she acknowledged the importance of regulation, she devoted much of her discussion to the political and legal obstacles that have limited its effectiveness.

The Limits of Federal Climate Regulation

Bodine traced the history of federal climate policy, beginning with the 1997 Kyoto Protocol, which was signed by the Clinton Administration in 1998 but never submitted to the Senate for ratification. A 1997 Senate resolution, sponsored by Senators Robert Byrd and Chuck Hagel, had passed unanimously, expressing opposition to any climate treaty that imposed emissions restrictions on developed countries without comparable commitments from developing countries such as China and India.

Bodine then discussed the Supreme Court’s 2007 decision in Massachusetts v. EPA, which established that greenhouse gases qualified as air pollutants under the Clean Air Act and that the EPA could regulate them upon making an endangerment finding.

The Obama Administration subsequently used that authority to regulate greenhouse gas emissions from vehicles and power plants. One of its most significant efforts was the Clean Power Plan, which sought to reduce emissions from existing power plants by allowing states to shift electricity generation away from coal toward cleaner energy sources. The plan faced substantial legal challenges, particularly over whether the EPA could use Section 111(d) of the Clean Air Act to require generation shifting.

Bodine also discussed the Trump Administration’s replacement of the Clean Power Plan with the Affordable Clean Energy Rule, which took a narrower approach by focusing on improvements within individual power plants rather than shifting electricity generation across states.

The debate ultimately reached the Supreme Court in West Virginia v. EPA (2022). The Court held that the EPA lacked clear congressional authorization to implement the Clean Power Plan’s generation-shifting approach, invoking the major questions doctrine. For Bodine, the case illustrated the limitations of relying on broad interpretations of existing statutory authority to accomplish sweeping climate policy objectives.

Economic Incentives and Technological Innovation

Rather than relying primarily on regulatory mandates, Bodine argued that economic incentives offer a more practical and politically sustainable path toward emissions reductions. She pointed to the bipartisan Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act of 2021, which allocated significant funding to traditional infrastructure, clean water projects, and energy infrastructure, including electricity transmission.

She contrasted that legislation with the Inflation Reduction Act of 2022, which included approximately $369 billion in climate-related investments but received no Republican votes in either chamber of Congress. In Bodine’s view, the difference demonstrated that spending-based approaches can attract broader political support than regulatory programs.

However, she also questioned whether federal climate investments were translating into completed projects. Citing funding data through the end of 2025, she noted that substantial portions of the money allocated through the 2021 and 2022 infrastructure bills had not yet been distributed or spent. Even among funded projects, many faced delays. Bodine pointed to permitting barriers as a significant obstacle and highlighted bipartisan efforts in Congress to reform the permitting process.

She also emphasized that market forces were already driving substantial changes in the energy sector. Coal-fired electricity generation has declined, while natural gas and renewable energy sources have expanded. Bodine highlighted the growth of solar power, battery storage, and other technologies as evidence that emissions reductions can occur through economic incentives and private investment, even without sweeping federal regulations.

She noted that Wyoming, a traditionally conservative state, has become a major producer of wind energy because of the economic opportunities it creates. The example illustrated her broader argument that climate solutions need not be framed exclusively as environmental regulation; they can also be understood as opportunities for economic growth and technological development.

Adaptation, Education, and the Role of the Private Sector

Beyond reducing emissions, Bodine stressed the importance of preparing communities for the effects of climate change that are already occurring. She discussed resilient rebuilding, pre-disaster mitigation, and the need to reconsider federal incentives that encourage development in vulnerable coastal areas.

She also pointed to the role of private companies in addressing climate concerns. Corporate reputation and public expectations can motivate businesses to adopt more sustainable practices voluntarily. Although she cautioned that companies undermine their credibility when they announce commitments they fail to meet, she maintained that private-sector participation remains an important part of the solution.

Education was another central theme. “People need to know the implications of their own actions, they need to know what the climate scientists are saying,” she noted, “but they also need to know the tremendous improvements that have already happened, and the reductions we’ve already achieved, and then the opportunity for more reductions.” She highlighted battery technology and small modular nuclear reactors as promising developments that could expand energy production while reducing pressure on existing electricity grids.

She also emphasized the importance of scientific literacy in legal education. When asked for recommendations on courses to introduce at law schools, Bodine suggested a course combining science and law. With courts increasingly responsible for evaluating complex scientific issues, particularly following the Supreme Court’s decision in Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo, she argued that lawyers and judicial clerks need a stronger understanding of scientific concepts and terminology.

A Bipartisan Path Forward

During the question-and-answer session, the discussion turned to whether conservative approaches to climate policy could attract broader political support. Bodine acknowledged that climate change had become increasingly polarized, making traditional regulatory approaches politically difficult in many conservative states. She identified economic incentives, technological breakthroughs, and recognition of companies that adopt effective environmental practices as potential alternatives.

She also discussed the importance of expanding electricity transmission infrastructure to move lower-cost energy across regions. Using a privately funded transmission project in Maine as an example, she described how litigation and permitting delays had held up a project designed to transport hydropower to Massachusetts for several years. Although the project ultimately became operational, she argued that the experience illustrated how existing regulatory processes can impede energy infrastructure development.

The conversation concluded with a question about how the current political system can protect future generations from climate-related risks, given the relatively short terms of elected officials. Bodine cautioned against making climate policy entirely dependent on constitutional litigation or an expansive regulatory system. Instead, she advocated allowing economic forces and technological developments to drive continued progress while investing in adaptation to address future risks.

“Change in the United States is slower than some people want, but it does happen, and it is happening on the climate issue, and certainly on greenhouse gas emissions issues,” she said. “It’s just happening more because of economic forces than regulatory forces, and I think we need to have the patience to let that play out.”

title: Data Center Boom Raises New Pollution Concerns - Biz New Orleans
description:
The findings are particularly relevant as Louisiana attracts more than $81 billion in announced data center investments, including Meta’s Hyperion development in Richland Parish, which is projected to become the world’s largest.
Entergy Louisiana is seeking approval for $12.9 billion in additional natural gas generation to power the development.
Including proposed on-site generation, nearly 250 gigawatts of new gas capacity could be associated with data center growth, according to the Sierra Club.
Data centers supplied through the electric grid alone could add 170 million short tons of carbon dioxide emissions annually by 2030, the report projects.
Local Concerns Over Data Center Development The Sierra Club’s concerns about Louisiana’s data center expansion predate its latest national report.
text:
NEW ORLEANS — A new Sierra Club report warns that growing electricity demand from data centers could reverse 15 years of progress in reducing U.S. power sector emissions, raising questions about the environmental and health implications of Louisiana’s rapidly expanding data center industry.

“For over a decade, communities, advocates, and changemakers have stepped up to protect our air and water from toxic pollution and taken swift action to protect our planet from climate change. We have pushed for progress, and won. But now, these artificial intelligence data centers and their power demand threatens to undo all of the work we’ve accomplished,” Sierra Club Chief Program Officer Holly Bender said in a statement.

The findings are particularly relevant as Louisiana attracts more than $81 billion in announced data center investments, including Meta’s Hyperion development in Richland Parish, which is projected to become the world’s largest. Entergy Louisiana is seeking approval for $12.9 billion in additional natural gas generation to power the development.

The report, released Nov. 17, also comes as the Sierra Club prepares for a Nov. 18 rally in Baton Rouge under the banner “The People Vs. Meta’s Pollution,” with organizers also highlighting opposition to corporate giveaways. The demonstration precedes the Louisiana Public Service Commission’s scheduled Dec. 16 consideration of Entergy’s proposed gas-fired generating facilities.

Report Warns of Rising Emissions

The Sierra Club’s report, Artificial Intelligence, Real Pollution, projects that U.S. power sector carbon dioxide emissions could reach approximately 2.3 billion short tons annually by 2030, returning to levels comparable to 2011.

The report identifies more than 550 natural gas-fired power plants representing 351 gigawatts of generating capacity planned or under construction nationwide, with at least one-third potentially serving data centers. Including proposed on-site generation, nearly 250 gigawatts of new gas capacity could be associated with data center growth, according to the Sierra Club.

Data centers supplied through the electric grid alone could add 170 million short tons of carbon dioxide emissions annually by 2030, the report projects. It also warns that natural gas plants and backup diesel generators could increase local air pollution, including nitrogen oxides and fine particulate matter.

Louisiana’s Growing Energy Demands

The Louisiana Public Service Commission approved three natural gas-fired generating facilities in August 2025 to support Meta’s Hyperion development in Richland Parish. Entergy’s latest proposal would add seven combined-cycle natural gas generating units totaling 5,278 megawatts to support the project’s expansion, bringing approved and proposed generation capacity to approximately 7,500 megawatts.

Four of the proposed units would be located in Richland Parish, with three near Entergy’s existing Big Cajun generating site in Pointe Coupee Parish. The $12.9 billion generation proposal is part of a larger infrastructure package that also includes approximately $1.5 billion in transmission investments and at least $700 million in battery storage. The generating units are expected to enter service in 2030 and 2031.

An April 2026 study by the Union of Concerned Scientists estimated that data center growth could account for $14 billion to $26 billion in Louisiana wholesale electricity system costs through 2041, depending on the pace of development. The estimates do not establish how those costs would be distributed among utility customers.

Entergy maintains that its agreements with Meta include protections for existing customers, including advance payments, minimum monthly bills and financial guarantees intended to cover infrastructure costs associated with the development. Entergy says the arrangements are designed to prevent existing customers from subsidizing Meta’s electricity needs, while Meta estimates the agreement will deliver approximately $2.65 billion in savings to Entergy Louisiana customers over 20 years.

When Meta announced its Richland Parish development in 2024, it pledged to match its electricity consumption with 100% clean and renewable energy and support at least 1,500 megawatts of new renewable generation. A subsequent corporate sustainability agreement includes provisions for Meta to support 2,500 megawatts of additional renewable energy and storage resources, nuclear-related initiatives and assistance programs for low-income customers.

However, the three generating facilities already approved to power Hyperion and the seven additional units Entergy is seeking approval to build are all natural gas-fired, not renewable energy facilities.

Local Concerns Over Data Center Development

The Sierra Club’s concerns about Louisiana’s data center expansion predate its latest national report. The organization’s Delta Chapter collaborated with the Alliance for Affordable Energy on an analysis examining five proposed hyperscale data center projects in Louisiana, raising questions about infrastructure financing, utility agreements and potential costs to existing electricity customers. The Sierra Club has also challenged Meta’s air pollution permit for Hyperion, arguing that emissions from emergency diesel generators were undercounted and calling for stricter permitting requirements, additional air monitoring and a public hearing.

Entergy’s transmission expansion has also drawn opposition from rural landowners. As reported by Drew Hawkins of WWNO and the Gulf States Newsroom, LaSalle Parish cattle farmer Dustin McAnn discovered survey stakes on his property before learning that Entergy planned to run power lines across his pasture. The Louisiana Landowners Coalition and two other groups filed a lawsuit Nov. 9 challenging the Louisiana Public Service Commission’s expedited approval process for utility projects associated with Meta’s development.

The Sierra Club’s new report calls for data center developers to bear the costs of infrastructure needed to serve their facilities, along with greater transparency about electricity and water consumption and stronger oversight of air emissions. It also advocates expanding renewable energy generation, estimating that tripling solar and doubling wind nationally could reduce power sector carbon emissions by 25% below 2025 levels and lower annual electricity costs by more than $5 billion compared with a business-as-usual scenario.

text:
An 83 year old Congressional representative who sent an embarrassing letter to a well-meaning 10 year old constituent on the topic of electric cars and climate change, where she seems to brag about saddling his generation with debt through a recent climate rollback she voted for, is currently losing her seat

Update: This article was originally posted on May 14, but we wanted to update it with news of the election result. As of now, with 100% of votes counted, Foxx is losing by 362 votes, but has requested a recount. We’re updating this article with the most current information on the race below.

Christian Mango is ten years old, and was encouraged by his elementary school class to write a letter about a topic of his choice, and mail it to a decisionmaker. Christian chose his Congressional representative, 83 year old Virginia Foxx.

Foxx is an 11-term Congresswoman in North Carolina, one of the most gerrymandered states in the nation, and was expected to win a 12th term in the heavily republican district, having previously proudly touted an endorsement from an enemy of the US who tried to overthrow the government. Her opponent is Democrat Chuck Hubbard, a former journalist and native of the district.

Advertisement - scroll for more content

10 year old suggests EVs, climate action

For the topic of his letter, Christian chose electric cars – which is what makes this story relevant to us here at Electrek. Christian laid out several points about EVs, stating that “they’re better than normal cars. They’re better for the environment. They pay less. And there’s no gas.” (All true! well done Christian).

Christian suggested that electric cars could be incentivized with a $5,000 tax rebate – lower than the $7.5k EVs used to get, but better than the $0 they get federally today (compare to the ~$20k in ignored costs that gas cars still benefit from).

Christian went on to suggest action on climate change, stating “maybe there is still a chance for 6.5 million people to not die anymore and for the weather to get better just maybe glaciers stop melting.” Christian was probably referring to the number of people who die from air pollution globally each year (though several estimates suggest that number is actually higher, and Christian did conflate climate and weather… but we’ll give him a pass on this one, his heart is in the right place).

Christian was proud of his letter, as was his mother, Emily Mango, who said “he researched, cited facts, and made good arguments in his essay – an essay that had nothing to do with politics. He was proud of his essay.”

Congresswoman’s response sparks outrage from mother

But then he got a response, and that’s when things took a turn for the worse. Christian’s mother Emily angrily shared the response on Instagram, where it gained traction.

Emily said Foxx’s screed was “disrespectful, hostile and unkind” and called it “demoralizing and reprehensible.” She said she had to speak to her son and teach him that this response was “not okay,” and that “nobody should talk to a child like that and nobody should talk to a teacher like that.”

I’d also add that it’s full of disinformation, and that it even seems to brag about the massive debt that Foxx has imposed on Christian’s generation.

Foxx’s response filled with climate/EV disinformation

Foxx includes six links, all from propaganda publications that deny the science of climate change. 3 are from from WSJ (2 of which are opinion pieces) and 1 is from Fox, both of which are owned by the same climate denier, Rupert Murdoch. 1 is from Washington Times, a tabloid founded by a religious cult (yes, really), and 1 is from another right-wing climate denying publication, National Review.

Notably, none of the six links have anything to do with electric cars.

In the text of the response, Foxx touts republicans’ “all of the above” energy policy, which is ironic given that the party whose energy policy she touts has spent most of the last year forcing broken dirty coal plants open (which they are still doing after ruled illegal) and trying to shut down clean cheap ones. Apparently “all of the above” is code for “fossil fuels and nothing else.”

Foxx’s letter does not directly address the strengths of electric cars, despite them being the subject of Christian’s letter. Notably, EVs actually can receive energy from any generation method, whether it be wind, solar, or even coal or gas – whereas gas-powered vehicles can only use one type of energy, oil. Thus, an “all of the above” strategy should probably find EVs the preferable route for transportation.

But in apparent contradiction to Foxx’s surely sincerely held belief that we should pursue an “all of the above” energy policy – which electric cars would help to achieve – she in fact has voted against EVs when given the opportunity.

Foxx voted against EVs, for giveaways to wealthy

Foxx claims in her response that she can’t support tax credits on electric cars, because those go to “mostly people with higher incomes who are able to purchase ‘new’ electric cars.”

But she in fact voted against, and later voted to repeal, incentives which were limited to lower-income-earners and were only available on cars up to a certain MSRP cap. Further, they were available on used vehicles, not just new ones – suggesting that Foxx doesn’t know what she voted against.

Foxx was one of 218 republicans to vote in favor of a ~$4 trillion giveaway to wealthy elites. Her vote raised electric bills and threatened US energy security and surrendered US manufacturing jobs to China. Some of the money given away to wealthy elites in the bill was clawed back from energy efficiency programs that had been going to regular Americans.

Those energy efficiency programs had been instituted by the Inflation Reduction Act, the Biden-era law which established tax credits for EVs and other efficiency rebates. The Inflation Reduction Act was actually revenue positive, which is to say it reduced the national debt (by $238B), rather than adding to it, because of provisions to increase enforcement against wealthy tax cheats.

But most of the IRA was repealed by the bill that Foxx voted for, meaning the US lost out on those deficit reductions. All in all, the bill Foxx voted for would add $4 trillion to the national debt – which, incidentally, is another point Foxx touches on in her response.

And she mocks a 10 year old over the trillions in debt she voted for

In one sentence, she seems to directly mock Christian, telling him that “YOU and your classmates will be responsible for that debt” as part of a warning about the dangers of government debt.

But I read this sentence as mockery, rather than as a sincere warning, given that Foxx voted to add $4 trillion to the national debt, which she, at 83 years old, knows she will not have to pay off. Christian, who is 10, will likely spend his whole life saddled with the debt Foxx voted for.

He will also have to pay for her inaction on climate change, which will have increasingly worse effects on the world Christian will grow up into. Foxx’s generation has already felt the heat, with the massive floods that devastated her state in 2024, from a hurricane that was made 200x more likely due to climate change. Now, imagine how much worse it could get if Foxx’s policies remained in place until 72 years from now when Christian will be her age.

Foxx then closes out the letter with disparaging remarks about teachers, claiming that they are “too interested in indoctrinating you,” and warning Christian about “propaganda.” Which I guess shows where Foxx’s attitude comes from – if she has spent her 83 years never trusting anyone who knows more than her about a topic, that would certainly lead to the ignorance reflected in her letter.

Foxx – who somehow has a doctorate in education and currently sits on the Congressional education committee – could have turned this into a nice moment to teach the child who wrote her something about democracy and responsive government, but instead turned it into a moment to teach the world what’s wrong with her.

When we first wrote this article, Foxx had a projected 97% chance of winning in a district which voted for her by a 19% margin in 2024.

But that was before America (and its short memory) was reminded of how incapable republicans are of leading anything.

After a pile of economic crises caused by Donald Trump’s incompetent “leadership,” and his continued participation in an 8-month-and-counting war of choice that is spiking energy prices worldwide, bringing oil profits to record highs (and attempting to distract the news from talking about the Epstein files, which he is heavily featured in and has tried to cover up), America was once again fed up. And his incompetence took his entire party down with him.

Safe republican seats were flipped around the country in the biggest “wave” election we’ve seen in recent times, with the Democrats gaining control of both the House and Senate.

And it looks like Democrat Chuck Hubbard, a Wilkes county native and former journalist, who also ran against Foxx in 2024, will now get his chance to represent the people of North Carolina’s 5th district… assuming a recount goes in his favor.

The situation in North Carolina is particularly interesting, given that republicans had done an emergency redraw of district lines in an attempt to cheat their way to winning more seats.

Generally, district lines get redrawn after each Census, which happens on the decade mark, rather than mid-decade. But republicans saw ahead of time that they were likely to lose the House due to their unpopularity, and wanted to fudge the numbers in several states instead of going for a fair fight.

So they engaged in Gerrymandering, a process wherein district lines are redrawn to favor a particular political party. The idea is to put as many of your opponents’ votes into a few safe seats as possible, while spreading out your own votes to a wider range of seats that you win each by a small margin.

But it turns out that republicans were even more unpopular than they thought, and as a result, their Gerrymandering backfired. Those narrow margins they sought ended up flipping more seats than would have otherwise flipped, turning North Carolina almost completely blue in what analysts have called a “Dummymander“. (NC-5 itself was not one of the redrawn districts, though – it just swung 19 whole points to the Dems)

That said: the race is not over yet. The deadline to request a recount is today, and sure enough, Foxx has done so. The current margin is extremely thin, just 0.12% of votes, so things could certainly change in a recount. Foxx also vowed to run again in 2028, hoping for a less hostile political environment. She will be 85 years old at the time of that election.

title: Thoughts on the Bipartisan Affordability and Jobs Act | KRWG Public Media
description:
To some businessfolk, any safety and environmental requirements are “too much government in our lives.” However, requirements must make sense; inspections should be prompt; and two inspectors’ interpretations of rules shouldn’t contradict each other.
The trendily named Bipartisan Affordability and Jobs Act does some good, but scares New Mexicans.
It would weaken enforcement of the Clean Water Act, the Environmental Policy Act, the Endangered Species Act, and the Historic Preservation Act, and narrow the scope of environmental review.
He’ll use procedural improvements to help oil, gas, and coal – not sustainable energy projects.
Let’s urge Senator Heinrich to slow down and allow careful consideration of game-changing legislation.
text:
COMMENTARY:

In Washington or Las Cruces, speed and substance of permitting processes matter. I want to build a dojo quickly and cheaply. The mayor doesn’t want the viewing balcony to crumble, killing folks – and wants adequate ventilation and emergency egress.

To some businessfolk, any safety and environmental requirements are “too much government in our lives.” However, requirements must make sense; inspections should be prompt; and two inspectors’ interpretations of rules shouldn’t contradict each other.

Bigger projects potentially harming our environment pose more complex issues to analyze, and value conflicts to balance.

The trendily named Bipartisan Affordability and Jobs Act does some good, but scares New Mexicans. Can it deliver faster clean-energy development without making environmentally damaging projects to easy to approve and too hard to stop?

BAAJA, which NM U.S. Senator Martin Heinrich and others want to rush through without much public debate, combines critically important transmission and grid reforms with significant and concerning changes to federal environmental laws, permitting standards, and judicial remedies. We need to update an aging power grid. But many provisions reinforce the powerful position of traditional energy interests just when survival requires switching to sustainable energy sources rapidly and sensibly. BAAJA does not encourage clean energy investment and pollution reduction.

At a critical moment, the Act alters the balance of power between developers and the public, making it much harder to avoid environmental damage once a project has gained approval. Cutting “red-tape” has long been a major goal of oil and gas companies. This Act does that. But the “red-tape” includes important environmental study, analysis, and public comment. Why not streamline permitting for renewable energy/transmission, while preserving our ability to protect water, wildlife, tribal lands, and the public from clearly harmful projects?

“Project certainty” language intended to prevent arbitrary project cancellations also prevents properly addressing newly-discovered problems. These provisions could protect fossil-fuel projects long-term against environmental regulation. Agencies would be less able to respond to newly-discovered health or environmental damage, or later impose new rules science has taught us we need. Since we know developers of big projects sometimes lie, hide the ball, or make significant late changes, we need projection.

BAAJA would weaken our ability to protect water resources. It would weaken enforcement of the Clean Water Act, the Environmental Policy Act, the Endangered Species Act, and the Historic Preservation Act, and narrow the scope of environmental review. It would diminish state and tribal authority, public participation, and courts’ ability to stop projects unlawfully approved. Those are big changes we might not like. Senators’ unseemly haste will prevent us from figuring that out in a timely manner.

Improving the permit process is environmentally agnostic. It could help with a coal plant or a wind farm. Accompanied by strong environmental laws and policy, it would be great; but Trump, bankrolled by petroleum corporations, constantly attacks clean energy projects, and denies our climate is changing. He’ll use procedural improvements to help oil, gas, and coal – not sustainable energy projects. Forget that blue wave.

On Main Street, an ordinance expediting inspectors’ response times and requiring prompt rulings and quick appeals, would seem sensible. If it also cut requirements for fire escapes and sprinklers, the public might want a closer look.

Let’s urge Senator Heinrich to slow down and allow careful consideration of game-changing legislation. This could be a career-defining mistake by Heinrich. I applaud Senator Ben Ray Lujan and Representative Melanie Stansbury for refusing to be stampeded.

Womble Bond Dickinson will bring together energy executives, investors, industry leaders and legal professionals in Houston on Tuesday, November 17 for the 2026 Womble Bond Dickinson Energy Conference: “The 2030 Energy Landscape: Growth, Infrastructure & Capital.”

The daylong event at The Houstonian Hotel will examine how the global energy industry can meet rising demand driven by LNG, electrification, data centers and industrial expansion while navigating evolving investment, regulatory and geopolitical conditions.

Discussions will focus on four interconnected areas shaping the energy sector through 2030:

Energy supply and system leadership;

Infrastructure and delivery;

Capital and financing; and

Policy and global engagement.

Speakers will examine how industry, investors and policymakers can work together to build, finance and scale the energy systems needed to support continued economic growth.

Womble Vice Chair Ken Van Winkle and Jeff Whittle, Co-Leader of the firm’s Energy & Natural Resources Sector, will open the conference. Dan Pickering, Founder and Chief Investment Officer of Pickering Energy Partners, will deliver the opening keynote on the future of U.S. energy leadership.

The first panel, “Powering Growth: Grid Expansion, Utilities, Electrification & Hyperscalers,” will examine one of the energy sector’s most pressing challenges: delivering reliable, affordable power as electricity demand accelerates. Moderated by Womble partner Paul Afonso, the discussion will address grid modernization, interconnection, reliability and resilience, as well as the growing role of hyperscalers and other large energy users. Panelists include Jimmy Glotfelty, Power/Data Center Consultant and former Texas PUC Commissioner; Will Hazelip, President of National Grid Ventures US; Shannon Miller, Co-Founder and President of Mainspring Energy; Pablo Vegas, President and CEO of ERCOT; and Brandon Shaw, Interim Chief Financial Officer of JERA Americas Inc.

A lunchtime fireside chat will broaden the discussion to the infrastructure and strategic investments needed to support energy expansion. Veronica Irastorza, Senior Managing Director at FTI Consulting, will join José Luis Vittor, Womble partner and Head of the firm’s Latin America Practice, to discuss grid expansion, infrastructure readiness, supply chain resilience and cross-border energy flows. The conversation also will examine the outlook for energy investment in Latin America.

The afternoon will turn to the composition of the global energy system. Colin Graham, Co-Leader of Womble’s UK Energy Sector, will moderate “The 2030 Energy Mix: A Mid-Point in the Energy Transition or Fast Forward to the Future?” Panelists Erin Dyer, Executive Vice President and General Counsel at TotalEnergies USA; Cody Dick, Partner at Fayez Sarofim & Co.; and Seán Martyn, Executive Vice President of Business Development at HIF Global, will explore the roles of U.S. LNG, nuclear power, renewables and emerging technologies in meeting growing energy needs.

The conference’s final panel, “Capital at the Crossroads: Financing Energy & Infrastructure,” will focus on how investors and lenders are responding to changing risks, capital requirements and geopolitical conditions. Moderated by Womble Partner Mark Riedy, Head of the firm’s Energy & Infrastructure Project Finance Practice, the panel will examine project finance innovation, bankability, capital allocation and the impact of U.S. political and regulatory developments on investment decisions. Panelists include Mike Darcy, CEO of DG Fuels; Cole Folwell, Assistant Vice President at Barclays Investment Bank; Sarah Key, Director of New Ventures at KBR; and John Nisi, CEO of QuantumHPC.

Lisa Rushton, Co-Leader of Womble’s Energy & Natural Resources Sector, will deliver closing remarks.

This event offers a forward-looking look at how energy systems can be built, financed and scaled through 2030, and what those changes mean for businesses, investors and other stakeholders across the energy value chain.

text:
A handful of East Feliciana Parish residents aired concerns and calls for greater transparency about the state's effort to lure a nuclear fuel reprocessing plant, but top state energy officials cautioned them that the effort was still in its early days and could take years to reach fruition.

Some residents are part of a local group called "Feliciana Forever," formed after the parish was identified as a potential site for the complex, which could bring thousands of jobs and billions of dollars in private-sector investment to the small, rural parish with a poverty rate of 18.4%.

This summer, Louisiana became one of six finalists for a Nuclear Lifecycle Innovation Campus, a facility that would turn spent but still radioactive uranium fuel rods into a new nuclear power source but would also require the burial of leftover nuclear waste deep underground.

As part of a deal for Louisiana, state energy officials said this week they have also asked for a new U.S. Department of Energy national lab, creating an additional potential economic catalyst for the region.

But underground burial in East Feliciana Parish would also mean placing nuclear waste miles beneath Baton Rouge and other regional cities' and towns' primary drinking water source, the Southern Hills aquifer.

Some residents told Stephen Swiber, the deputy state energy secretary, and parish police jurors that too many questions remained about the project and its safety, and that they suspected the information shared so far didn't address the operation's full consequences.

Ida Sharp Herrick of Ethel told jurors that she, her neighbors and family were completely unaware of the proposal until a week ago but have tried to inform themselves and believe "a lot of this is being sugar-coated."

The underground burial of the nuclear waste, which would be shipped in from across the country, was one of the primary concerns.

One thing Herrick learned, she said, is that burial of nuclear waste in deep boreholes hasn't been tried before. State officials did not dispute this claim. The U.S. Department of Defense buries its waste underground but in large, open salt caverns.

"It seems that it's an experiment," Herrick said. "They want to use Louisiana and this area as an experiment."

Outside, as residents were filing into the Police Jury meeting room in Clinton on Monday evening, two residents who are part of Feliciana Forever held up signs that urged people to "Say no to nuclear waste" and claimed that "People aren't guinea pigs."

One sign had a picture of a guinea pig with a red slash through it.

Other residents said, based on their experience, that they didn't trust Louisiana's government to follow rules that protect the environment and public once the facility was here.

Paul Davidson, a biologist and environmental consultant who says he spent years on an advisory committee for the U.S. Strategic Petroleum Reserve and is active in black bear conservation, said he is not opposed to the concept but doesn't know enough yet.

"I just don't trust everybody that's involved in this. I'm sorry if that hurts anybody's feelings. I've been doing this for a lot of years, and I've watched state agencies turn the other cheek, not necessarily, eyes away, when violations were occurring and, you know, they seem not to care," he told Swiber, who agreed to sit in a chair facing public speakers. "Politics plays a big role in a lot of this. And you know. You're a political appointee."

Once Louisiana was named a finalist, Gov. Jeff Landry signed an agreement in late July with the Department of Energy to explore the possibility further, making commitments in that deal to back the project, to ensure local and state permitting and to defer to the federal agency in regulatory conflicts.

The federal department is expected to narrow the finalists to three states, which would have to sign host agreements and gain their own campuses. That decision was expected to come by mid-December, but Anna Johnson, a spokesperson for the state energy department, said it's likely that deadline could be pushed back.

State officials also cautioned that neither the initial agreement nor a future host agreement is a final commitment.

A key factor in the selection is the geology underlying the site, state officials explained, and further progress would require studies to see whether the geology is suitable for waste burial. In addition to needed state and federal legal changes, Johnson said the campus could be one to two decades away.

In addition to East Feliciana, Lafourche and St. Charles are among three parishes state officials initially identified as possible sites. Since then, nextdoor West Feliciana Parish, home to River Bend nuclear power plant, has thrown its hat in the ring, state officials said. A few other parishes have also expressed interest.

Though Swiber and other state officials have had private talks with local officials, the police jury meeting was the first forum with state officials and the public in one of the parishes the state is eyeing for the complex.

In Swiber's opening talk, he emphasized the project's economic potential and national importance and the safety of underground burial.

The nuclear lifecycle campus would support a federal government initiative to deal with the nation's nuclear waste problem and restart nuclear energy development as data centers and other industrial development drive energy demand.

Currently, spent fuel rods are held in cooling pools or concrete-and-steel dry casks spread across the nation's nuclear power plants. Years of public and official opposition have stalled plans to send them to the permanent underground storage site designated by Congress: Yucca Mountain, Nevada.

Swiber explained that only 5% of the fuel rods have been used once "spent," and reprocessing would capture the remaining fuel along with rare elements and isotopes for medical and commercial needs.

"So, a lot of utility comes when you crack open that dry cask and you start to treat your spent product, not as a waste stream but as a potential feedstock for the next round of energy," he said.

The nuclear lifecycle campus would likely draw several companies, like the startup Curio Energy that has been speaking with parish officials.

Swiber pointed out that in the state's negotiations, officials have also asked that Louisiana get a national lab as a condition for the deal. The federal government has 17 national labs but none are along the Gulf Coast. The labs, some affiliated with nearby universities and some outgrowths of the Manhattan Project that built the nation's first nuclear bombs, focus on energy, atomic physics and other scientific research.

"They are really innovation hubs, catalysts for activity where they are," Swiber said.

He pointed out that Oak Ridge National Lab near Knoxville, Tenn., supports 40,000 jobs.

Another condition that Louisiana is seeking, Swiber said, is that no out-of-state nuclear waste would be shipped to Louisiana until all of the waste in Louisiana was used, about 1,800 tons. Swiber said River Bend in St. Francisville has 600 tons of nuclear waste on site.

Swiber pointed out that the reprocessing effort would extract the uranium and other isotopes, leaving behind a less potent waste that would then be "vitrified." The process melts the waste at high heat with ceramic- or glass-forming material so that it becomes a solid, stable block that is then encased in a concrete-and-metal container.

text:
ANTALYA, Türkiye, November 17, 2026 – At COP31, the World Bank Group and its partners showcased a series of transformative investments and projects expected to mobilize an additional $10.7 billion in private capital, alongside more than $6.9 billion in investment to support client-led development priorities, create jobs, and strengthen resilience. The investments span agriculture, manufacturing, urban infrastructure, renewable energy, and more.

Together, these investments demonstrate how climate-smart development can support the foundations of growth and jobs. Reliable electricity enables businesses to grow. Better agriculture raises productivity and incomes. Resilient infrastructure protects investments, connects people to markets, and allows economic activity to continue when shocks occur.

The announcements build on growing World Bank Group financing and private capital mobilization for climate-related investments. In fiscal year 2026, the Group provided $48 billion in financing with climate co-benefits and mobilized a further $48 billion in private capital. The combined $96 billion is 21 percent higher than in the previous year.

Agriculture and industry

In Türkiye, a World Bank Group operation will expand farmers' access to finance and markets and strengthen agricultural value chains. It is expected to benefit 225,000 farmers and support more than 100,000 job equivalents, while mobilizing commercial financing and helping reduce emissions from agricultural production. The operation puts the Group's AgriConnect approach into practice, contributing to its goal of reaching 300 million smallholder farmers.

A separate World Bank program will give Turkish manufacturers, including small and medium-sized enterprises, long-term financing to adopt greener and more digital technologies. It will help hundreds of firms prepare and implement transformation plans. It is expected to support more than 100,000 job equivalents and to mobilize additional commercial financing.

In Afghanistan, IFC is supporting the development of an organic fertilizer facility that would turn agricultural waste into locally produced inputs. The project aims to improve soil health and farm productivity and to create local jobs in a fragile market.

Water, infrastructure, and energy

In Timor-Leste, IFC financing, IDA-PSW, and a MIGA guarantee are supporting a new solar power plant with battery storage. The plant is expected to lower energy costs, strengthen energy security, and deliver estimated annual savings of around 1.5 percent to 2.0 percent of the country's GDP. It offers a model that other small islands and Pacific economies could replicate.

A coordinated World Bank Group initiative in Türkiye will finance water, sanitation and urban transport infrastructure. It is expected to give 1.65 million people safely managed water and sanitation and improve sustainable transport for nearly 1.5 million people. It will also strengthen climate-resilient infrastructure benefiting more than 3 million people. The initiative is part of Water Forward, a multistakeholder coalition that aims to advance water security for over 1 billion people by 2030.

Opening markets

Several sustainable finance loans to Turkish banks will direct capital to social inclusion, the blue economy, climate adaptation and Türkiye’s low-carbon transition, using a range of new instruments, including a blue digitally native note.

Global supply chains

A new blended finance-supported fund will help textile, apparel and footwear manufacturers – largely SMEs in emerging markets – invest in cleaner, more competitive production. It combines IFC financing, concessional funds from the Global Environment Facility as well as technical assistance and investment from global brands to support energy efficiency, renewable energy, water savings, circularity and reduced industrial pollution. By bringing together suppliers, finance and global buyers, the initiative aims to unlock investments that have been difficult to finance, while helping manufacturers remain competitive as global supply chains shift toward more sustainable production.

text:
INDIANAPOLIS, IN – Americans for Prosperity–Indiana (AFP-IN) today praised the Indiana Department of Environmental Management (IDEM) for rescinding more than a quarter of its non-rule policy documents and urging the U.S. EPA to follow Indiana’s lead.

Under Governor Mike Braun’s Executive Order 25-17, IDEM identified 26 of its 103 non-rule policies as obsolete, duplicative, or no longer grounded in current law. Eliminating them removes roughly 176 pages of “shadow regulations” — guidance that shaped agency decisions without ever going through public comment or legislative review. IDEM has also recommended that the EPA review more than 500 federal guidance documents for consolidation or elimination.

AFP-IN State Director Cody White issued the following statement:

“Hoosier businesses, farmers, and families shouldn’t have to navigate rules that were never actually written into law. Governor Braun and Commissioner Woods are showing what accountable government looks like: review the rules, keep what works, and clear out what doesn’t. Indiana isn’t just cleaning up its own house, it’s pushing Washington to do the same, and we urge the EPA to act quickly on IDEM’s recommendations.”

IDEM Commissioner Clint Woods issued the following statement:

“The top priority of government should be to be accountable to the citizens it serves. By reviewing and removing outdated policies, Indiana is increasing transparency, reducing unnecessary bureaucracy, and ensuring agency actions remain firmly grounded in the law and worthy of the public’s trust.”

Executive Order 25-17 directs state agencies to cut regulatory requirements by 25 percent by 2029. AFP-IN will continue to support the Braun administration and General Assembly in delivering on that goal.

Only 10 applicants under the Component Champion Incentive Scheme have secured DVA certification across 37 variants, according to the report.

The certification process requires companies to demonstrate domestic value addition in their products and submit the necessary documentation to designated testing agencies.

The assessment notes that stringent DVA norms make compliance difficult, particularly as the domestic supply chain for advanced automotive technologies and EV components is still evolving.

The PLI scheme seeks to strengthen domestic manufacturing of advanced automotive technology products. However, meeting the localisation threshold requires manufacturers to build domestic sourcing capabilities across their supply chains.

The assessment highlights the need to develop a wider domestic ecosystem for advanced automotive technologies to help manufacturers meet the DVA requirement.
