text:
ANNAPOLIS, MD – Governor Moore signed a memorandum of understanding (MOU) expanding the areas of cooperation of the Maryland-Gyeongsangnam-do Sister State relationship, originally established in 1991, to increase collaboration in Nuclear Power and Small Modular Reactor (SMR) policy and supply chain development. The expanded partnership is an additional step in the Moore-Miller administration’s work to increase access to clean and sustainable energy solutions throughout the state.

The MOU between the State of Maryland and Gyeongsangnam-do will identify joint projects through business consultations and technological exchanges, while supporting investment attraction and overseas expansion. In particular, both sides will operate a joint working group consisting of 3 to 5 members each, holding meetings at least twice a year to establish priority cooperation tasks and action plans.

“This partnership with our Korean counterparts is helping Maryland lead in nuclear power, promising economic prosperity and delivering relief for our communities struggling with rising energy prices at home,” said Gov. Moore. “Together, we are advancing innovative solutions to address the growing energy demand, while growing our economy.”

The MOU was signed by Governor Park Wan-su of Gyeongsangnam-do today at the Korea SMR International Conference in Changwon, Gyeongsangnam-do. Maryland Department of Commerce Assistant Secretary John Gilstrap attended the conference, as a representative of the Moore-Miller administration, and delivered a keynote presentation. Governor Moore signed the agreement asynchronously last week.

Governor Park visited Annapolis in 2023 and Governor Moore traveled to Changwon during the 2025 Maryland Mission to Asia.

“I hope this conference leads beyond technological exchanges between overseas SMR developers and Gyeongnam nuclear companies to substantive cooperation such as joint technology development and equipment supply,” said Governor Park Wan-su. “Based on Gyeongnam’s accumulated nuclear manufacturing experience and technological capabilities, we will actively support small and medium-sized enterprises in the province to participate in the global SMR supply chain and achieve tangible orders and export results.”

“Maryland is proud to grow its partnership with Gyeongsangnam-do, South Korea while exploring new opportunities in the energy industry,” said Maryland Commerce Secretary Harry Coker, Jr. “This agreement can deliver real results—strengthening both regional economies and providing trusted collaboration while exploring clean, carbon-free innovations. We look forward to deepening our bilateral relationship and seeing what we can accomplish together next.”

The conference brought together 400 participants from Korean and international nuclear companies, research institutes, and government officials to expand global SMR industrial cooperation and overseas market entry for local nuclear enterprises. This is the second time the administration has participated in the Korea SMR International Conference. Last year, Senior Energy Advisor Connor Shinn attended the conference and presented on the Maryland Nuclear Landscape.

The Moore-Miller administration has utilized nuclear power advancements to increase access to clean, sustainable and reliable energy and address growing demand across the state. Under the governor’s leadership, the Maryland Public Service Commission continues to develop a zero emission credit procurement program to support new or expanded nuclear energy generation facilities serving the state, as established in the 2025 Next Generation Energy Act. This major new state program bolsters our strong investment in nuclear power and will be ready to receive bids for new projects in 2027.

Thanks to the administration’s investments, Maryland is home to a world-class nuclear ecosystem and has welcomed market-leading companies to our state, paving pathways for our communities to profit and supporting our state’s economy. The nuclear industry employs over 5,000 full-time Maryland employees.

Constellation Energy, the U.S. largest nuclear power operator and top U.S. producer of carbon-free electricity, is headquartered out of Baltimore. The company operates a facility out of Lusby and generates 40% of Maryland’s in-state generation capacity. Additionally, SMR technology leader X-energy is headquartered in Rockville, with a test and training facility in Frederick.

Supporting in-state generation is a key strategy to address the rising demand straining our energy grid. Last month, the Governor launched “Megawatts for Maryland,” a $200 million clean energy auction program, aiming to add hundreds of megawatts of clean, affordable power to the grid, enough to power more than 150,000 Maryland homes per year.

In addition to investments in nuclear energy, the Moore-Miller administration has made significant advances in the state’s renewable energy strategy. In August, the Governor, with the Maryland Department of General Services (DGS), announced a long-term Power Purchase Agreement that is expected to save the state approximately $300 million over the next 20 years while significantly expanding the State's use of clean, Maryland-generated solar energy. The agreement doubled the amount of renewable energy currently purchased directly by the State and provided enough renewable electricity to power nearly 15 percent of the State government's portfolio beginning in 2028.

Additionally, over the past two years, the Moore-Miller administration has helped deliver hundreds of dollars in immediate relief to families struggling with utility costs across the state, including $200 million in direct rebates last year and $100 million in direct relief through the Utility RELIEF Act. Governor Moore also issued a December 2025 executive order to support energy affordability and address anticipated shortfalls in energy generation.

The Governor also remains a driving force behind the PJM Governors’ Collaborative. In May, the Governor delivered remarks directly to PJM executives at their annual meeting, calling on the organization to take more accountability for how their actions have driven increased rates. In April, Governor Moore joined a coalition of governors from across the PJM region calling for urgent action to protect families and businesses from rising energy costs driven by explosive data center growth. Earlier this year, Governor Moore secured a win from PJM that will save Marylanders billions on their energy bills in avoided capacity costs after PJM announced it was extending the capacity market price cap through the end of the decade.

title: There Will Only Be 6 Electric Trucks Left In 2027 - CarBuzz
description:
If the Rivian R1T proves that an electric pickup can be practical, the Hummer proves that it can be the coolest, toughest thing on the road.
The Sierra EV Will Continue Alongside The Silverado EV The Silverado EV sold 5,327 units in the first three quarters of 2026, combined.
2 Slate Pickup The First Slate Deliveries Are Expected Sometime In Late 2026 The Slate Truck represents the electric pickup segment pivoting away from luxury models and supercar-challenging monsters, and towards daily drivers.
The Slate Pickup Might Change Everything We can't read the future, but the Slate pickup could be a game-changer.
The Fathom Is Bigger Than A Slate, But Smaller Than A Maverick Slate Auto thinks the future of the electric pickup is in smaller trucks, and so does Ford.
text:
Two or three years ago, electric pickups seemed like the natural next step forward. How many of us saw the Tesla Cybertruck and said, "If only someone would make one of those, but good." The instant torque and massive horsepower provided by electric powertrains seemed like just the thing for the pickup segment.

Now, with the EV tax credits off the table, and Ford and Tesla both scrapping their full-size battery-powered trucks, it's clear that big electric trucks are simply too expensive to be anything but a niche product. Meanwhile, small EVs could dominate 2027.

6 Rivian R1T

Still Going Strong, Five Years Since Its September 2021 Launch

Rivian has teased the possibility of making the Rivian R2 available as a pickup, but, officially speaking, it's only planned to sell as an SUV for the foreseeable future. That sounds like a brand that doesn't want to squander its momentum by over-diversifying the product lineup after an improvement of 45.7% in year-over-year sales for Q3. This was a period during which the rest of the EV market saw a 39.5% dip in sales.

The base Rivian R1T clears 60 mph in under five seconds, while higher trims bring supercar power to the luxury car price range. The truck tows a minimum of 7,700 lbs, and the styling is more conventional than the Cybertruck, while still having a bit of a futuristic lean. It's an easy truck to like.

Reasonable Sales Goals Have Helped To Keep Rivian In The Game

An early adopter in the electric pickup game, the Rivian R1T has managed to weather the ups and downs of the EV market as many of its peers have fallen by the wayside. The truck is just as expensive as its discontinued competitors, but seems to have held out in part due to the brand's more reasonable sales goals. Put simply, 70,000 annual sales across all models would be a good year for Rivian, but a disaster for Ford or Tesla.But if Rivian survived by staying modest, GMC took the opposite approach – and it's starting to show.

5 Hummer EV Pickup

GMC Is Holding Its Ground Five Years Since The Hummer EV's Late 2021 Launch

GMC sold 5,024 electric Hummers through the first three quarters of 2026. Like the Rivian R1T, the Hummer isn't posting six-figure sales numbers, but it doesn't need to in order to stay competitive in a niche market.

A 3X Hummer produces an incredible 1,160 hp, and it hits 60 mph in just 2.8 seconds, leaving some of the slower supercars choking on its dust. The standard model will get there in under four seconds. If the Rivian R1T proves that an electric pickup can be practical, the Hummer proves that it can be the coolest, toughest thing on the road.

The Hummer EV's Future Feels Uncertain At The Moment

GMC has reported a decline in sales, to the tune of about 62%, year-over-year. The problem with electric pickups is that you have a very dedicated, but very small customer base, and sales tend to bottom out quickly. There's no announcement of the truck being discontinued, but GM did slow production earlier this year.

4 Chevrolet Silverado EV

Hitting Dealer Lots In 2023, The Silverado EV Will Continue Production Into The New Year

Electric Silverados can tow up to 12,500 lbs, and they can carry more than a full ton in the box. All that cargo tends to cut heavily into your mileage when you're driving an EV, but the Silverado EV is the best pure work truck in the electric vehicle segment for the time being.

Chevy Finally Beat Ford In The Full-Size Pickup Game

The gas-powered Silverado has never beaten the Ford F-150 in year-end sales, but the electric variant now claims a decisive victory over the blue oval: The Silverado EV is getting a 2027 model year, and the Ford F-150 Lightning EV isn't. Ford is keeping the Lightning nameplate, but attaching it to an EREV, a hybrid comprised of an electric powertrain with an on-board gas-powered generator.

3 GMC Sierra EV

The Sierra EV Launched In August 2024, A Few Years After Its Sister Truck

Where the Silverado goes, so goes its slightly upscale sibling, the GMC Sierra. The Denali trim in particular feels nicely luxurious with real wood trim and stainless steel accents, superior sound insulation, and higher-grade materials throughout.

The Sierra EV Will Continue Alongside The Silverado EV

The Silverado EV sold 5,327 units in the first three quarters of 2026, combined. The Sierra EV sold 4,705 units in that same stretch. Both models are reporting sales losses alongside the GMC Hummer EV, in the 50% range, year-over-year. Whether these trucks are viable in the long run, who can say, but we're certain that GM is happy not to compete with Ford in the full-size electric sphere.

2 Slate Pickup

The First Slate Deliveries Are Expected Sometime In Late 2026

The Slate Truck represents the electric pickup segment pivoting away from luxury models and supercar-challenging monsters, and towards daily drivers. Even the ownership experience has been simplified, as Slate is working directly with RepairPal and independent garages to handle repairs and recalls.

The Slate Pickup Might Change Everything

We can't read the future, but the Slate pickup could be a game-changer. Where the cheapest electric pickup for 2026 starts above $60,000, the Slate will be selling for less than you'd spend on a new Nissan Altima. It's a simple, stripped-down affair with manual windows and no infotainment screen.

The Slate is remarkably low-tech, and not just for an EV. No other highway-legal vehicle for sale in the US has manual windows right now. Slate Auto essentially looked at what was wrong with the Cybertruck, and did the opposite.

1 Ford Fathom

Ford's Midsize Electric Pickup Will Go Up For Pre-Order In Early 2027

Classified as a mid-size but arguably closer in spirit to the compact Ford Maverick than to the Ford Ranger, the Ford Fathom promises more interior space than a Toyota RAV4, with total range expected somewhere around 300 miles.

The Fathom Is Bigger Than A Slate, But Smaller Than A Maverick

Slate Auto thinks the future of the electric pickup is in smaller trucks, and so does Ford. The Fathom has been in development for more than four years, so we're not saying Ford got the idea from Slate. But, both brands are clearly banking on more reasonably priced daily drivers over three-ton, 1,000-hp behemoths.

The segment seems to be leaning away from electric pickups as a premium product, and towards smaller grocery-getters, with the big boys occupying an increasingly small niche. We'll have to wait and see how that pays off, and then wonder why they weren't already building cheap electric trucks a few years ago when we had the tax credits to help out.

Halifax, Nova Scotia--(Newsfile Corp. - November 17, 2026) - Ucore Rare Metals Inc.UCU (OTCQX: UURAF) ("Ucore" or the "Company") is pleased to announce that it has received its Minor Source Air Permit (Permit No. 2360-00177-00, the "Air Permit") for the Louisiana Strategic Metals Complex ("SMC") in Alexandria, Louisiana, from the Louisiana Department of Environmental Quality ("LDEQ"). Testing at all Louisiana coal plants found unsafe groundwater contamination.

BATON ROUGE, La. — The Sierra Club, Earthjustice, and the Alliance for Affordable Energy Louisiana decried the Trump administration’s final decision today to put the State of Louisiana in charge of oversight of toxic coal ash waste. The Louisiana Department of Environmental Quality (LDEQ) has repeatedly allowed coal plants to violate federal coal ash protections.

Coal ash is generated when coal is burned, and massive quantities are stored at coal-burning power plants near Baton Rouge, Alexandria, and Shreveport.

At all three active Louisiana coal plants (Big Cajun 2, Brame Energy Center, R S Nelson), and the state’s one retired plant (Dolet Hills), monitoring data shows that coal ash is contaminating groundwater at levels above federal safe drinking water standards. These toxic chemicals include arsenic, boron, cobalt, lead, lithium, radium, sulfate, and thallium. More than 61% of Louisiana’s population relies on groundwater for all or part of their drinking water supply.

“Louisianans know all too well that we can’t trust our state regulators to hold polluters accountable, so it’s nonsensical that the Trump Administration just gave LDEQ even more authority to handle something as dangerous as coal ash,” said Darryl Malek-Wiley, a Sierra Club senior field representative in Louisiana. “It’s clear this decision is meant to favor wealthy coal-owning utilities at the expense of our health.”

“The Trump administration chose polluters over the people of Louisiana,” said Earthjustice senior attorney Mychal Ozaeta. “An alphabet soup of toxic chemicals from burning coal is contaminating groundwater in locations across the state. The right thing to do is make the polluters clean up their toxic mess, and protect sources of drinking water. Instead, the Trump administration is handing over authority to Louisiana’s state government which won’t lift a finger to clamp down on the concerning levels of contaminants poisoning the state’s groundwater.”

“Our state regulators are dangerously inadequate in their oversight and enforcement of polluting industries, which has already cost Louisiana our safe air and water. We simply don’t think LDEQ can handle even more responsibilities they won’t take seriously,” said Logan Burke, Executive Director of the Alliance for Affordable Energy.

Background:

Public interest groups submitted formal comments to EPA urging the administration to reject Louisiana’s request to handle coal ash oversight in the state.

Coal ash contains arsenic, mercury, chromium, lead, lithium, radium, and other heavy metals, which have been linked to numerous types of cancer, heart and thyroid disease, respiratory illness, reproductive failure, and neurological harm.

As an example of the state’s abysmal track record on coal ash, LDEQ has allowed power plants to close coal ash dumps with ash in groundwater, ensuring that the dumps will contaminate groundwater with toxic chemicals indefinitely. LDEQ should not be in charge of issuing permits that let coal plants continue to violate the law. These permits will shield power plants from federal enforcement and prevent Louisiana residents from stopping coal ash pollution.

LDEQ is a severely understaffed and extremely lenient environmental regulator. In addition to its coal ash failures, its air monitors are far away from Louisiana’s heaviest air-polluting facilities, and the agency has for years been criticized for approving permits for wealthy polluters, including LNG terminals and a massive Formosa plastics factory. Louisianans know all too well that LDEQ does not protect low-income communities of color, and creates a lax regulatory environment that has enabled disasters like the recent Smitty’s Supply explosion and spill.

There’s a New Push at Climate Talks: Wire the World for Electricity

With war squeezing global oil and gas supplies, leaders at COP31 are backing a plan that would mirror China’s rapid grid expansion.

Nov. 17, 2026, 5:03 a.m. ET

If the leaders of this year’s United Nations climate conference achieve one of their big goals, countries will rally behind a new global target on expanding the reach of electric power.

The implication: The rest of the world will have to look a lot more like China.

Over the past two decades, China has raced ahead of other industrialized countries, building ultrahigh-voltage power lines, constructing the world’s largest high-speed rail system and filling its roads with electric vehicles. It is sometimes called the first electrostate.

At the same time, countries across the West and in Africa are scarcely more electrified than they were a generation ago.

That disparity is one of the things the climate conference, known this year as COP31, is campaigning to change. The event’s leaders say the shift is well-suited for a year when the United States’ war in Iran has pinched the global oil and gas supply.

Advertisement

SKIP ADVERTISEMENT

“Electrification is the answer,” said Murat Kurum, the Turkish environment minister, who is leading the 12-day conference in Antalya, Turkey. “Everyone now understands that energy that you must import is energy that you do not control.”

Electrification involves replacing technologies that directly burn fossil fuels. That means swapping gas-powered vehicles for E.V.s, for instance, and trading oil-fired furnaces for heat pumps. It also entails looking for electric alternatives to generate the steam and intense heat needed by factories.

text:
JACKSON, Mich. — A public-private partnership between the Michigan Department of Labor and Economic Opportunity (LEO), the Michigan Economic Development Corporation (MEDC) and Consumers Energy designed to create and retain good-paying jobs, support Michigan manufacturers and strengthen the state’s energy supply chain reached a major milestone, demonstrating that it is delivering on its mission by successfully integrating a local manufacturer into the utility’s supply chain.

“This partnership helps manufacturers lead in the clean energy future and keeps our energy production local – making sure Michigan remains a hub of innovation and industry,” said LEO Director Susan Corbin. “By helping Michigan companies find suppliers here at home, we’re paving the way and keeping Michigan a leader in manufacturing and we’re also supporting meaningful, good-paying jobs.”

Through a competitive sourcing process and engagement with LEO’s Community and Worker Economic Transition Office and MEDC’s Supply Chain Resiliency team, Consumers Energy selected Wolverine Assemblies LLC, a Wixom-based company, to establish a network of high‑voltage distribution (HVD) laydown yards across the state. The initiative will provide critical infrastructure to support electric reliability and long‑term economic growth.

This success demonstrates how Michigan is making progress on the state’s first Economic Transition Strategy launched earlier this year to ensure workers, communities and businesses are positioned to adapt and thrive in a changing economy. By building sector-based partnerships that connect purchasing demand to supportive economic development programming for local businesses, Michigan is solving supply chain challenges and creating new market diversification opportunities for small and medium-sized businesses.

“The success between Wolverine Assemblies and Consumers Energy shows that our plan to keep Michigan’s economy strong and well-positioned for future growth and stability is working,” said Community and Worker Economic Transition Office Director Luke Forrest. “This partnership positions our manufacturers to lead in new and growing markets, keeping production local and ensuring Michigan remains a hub of innovation and industry.

The partnership, announced at the 2025 Mackinac Policy Conference, leverages the utilities’ joint commitment to spending $3.5 billion annually on technology, equipment and services from Michigan-based businesses.

This partnership also directly supports Michigan’s ability to attract and execute major infrastructure and economic growth projects by ensuring materials can be staged closer to where work is happening. The laydown yards supplied by Wolverine Assemblies will improve logistics efficiency, reduce response times and enable faster delivery of projects that power Michigan communities and businesses.

“This is exactly the kind of outcome we strive for — pairing Michigan companies with Michigan infrastructure investment,” said Marlon Merritt, Consumers Energy’s vice president of supply chain. “With MEDC’s support, we were able to connect with a local supplier that could move quickly, scale responsibly, and help us deliver value to customers while strengthening regional economies.”

Al Hall, Wolverine Assemblies’ president and CEO, expressed his gratitude for the new partnership. “We’re very excited to partner with Consumers Energy and the MEDC on this impactful project. Our team understands our key role to make this endeavor a resounding success. We will work with great urgency to exceed Consumer Energy expectations in every area, especially safety and cost effectiveness. This is a commitment not just from me, but the entire Wolverine Assemblies team, to service our customer, community and the great state of Michigan with excellence.”

Wolverine Assemblies was introduced to Consumers Energy through state‑supported engagement, including participation in the MEDC PowerUp Utilities Summit in April 2026, which connects Michigan suppliers with utility and infrastructure opportunities. The partnership demonstrates how those connections translate into real investment, real projects and real impact across the state.

“MEDC is helping Michigan utilities identify critical commodities and connect with in-state manufacturers that can help strengthen supply chain resilience,” said Bobby Chasnis, Director of Supply Chain Resiliency at the MEDC. “By helping manufacturers diversify into the energy sector, we can support utility reliability, create new business opportunities and grow Michigan’s manufacturing base.”

Together, Consumers Energy, the Economic Transition Office, MEDC and Wolverine Assemblies are demonstrating how sector-based partnerships deliver durable infrastructure, resilient supply chains and shared economic success.

title: Critical Minerals: Demand Drivers and Supply Risks - Kings Research
description:
Critical minerals are becoming increasingly important to industries supporting electrification, digital infrastructure, advanced manufacturing, and national security.
The U.S. Geological Survey (USGS) published its updated critical minerals list in November 2025, covering 60 minerals.
The IEA's Global Critical Minerals Outlook 2026 highlights the growing importance of minerals such as gallium, germanium, indium, and antimony as AI, robotics, and semiconductor technologies advance.
The IEA's Global Critical Minerals Outlook 2026 projects that recycling rates for key energy minerals could rise from approximately 10% currently to close to 20% by 2040.
What minerals are included in the US critical minerals list?
text:
Critical minerals are becoming increasingly important to industries supporting electrification, digital infrastructure, advanced manufacturing, and national security. Demand is rising as electric vehicles (EVs), battery storage systems, renewable energy installations, and artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure expand. Copper supports electricity networks, while lithium, cobalt, graphite, and nickel are essential to several battery technologies. Gallium, germanium, and other specialized materials support semiconductor manufacturing and advanced electronics.

However, the ability to secure these materials depends on more than mining capacity. Refining and processing remain concentrated in a limited number of countries, exposing manufacturers to supply disruptions, geopolitical tensions, and export restrictions. These vulnerabilities are particularly significant for materials with specialized processing requirements and limited alternative sources.

According to Kings Research, the global critical minerals market is projected to reach USD 584.95 billion by 2033 from USD 362.42 billion in 2025, registering a CAGR of 6.17% from 2026 to 2033.

For businesses and investors, the central challenge is securing reliable access to these materials while building more diversified extraction, processing, and recycling capabilities.

What Are Critical Minerals?

Critical minerals are materials considered essential to economic or national security because of their importance to key industries and their potential exposure to supply disruptions. Their classification depends on factors such as economic significance, supply concentration, import dependence, and the availability of substitutes. Governments and international organizations maintain their own assessments to reflect different industrial priorities and supply risks.

In the United States, the definition is established under the Energy Act of 2020. The U.S. Geological Survey (USGS) published its updated critical minerals list in November 2025, covering 60 minerals. Copper, silver, and uranium were among the materials added to the revised list.

The European Union and the International Energy Agency (IEA) maintain separate assessments based on their respective policy objectives and supply chain requirements. These lists help governments identify materials that require greater attention through domestic production, international partnerships, strategic stockpiling, and recycling initiatives.

Critical minerals serve a broad range of applications. Lithium, cobalt, nickel, and graphite support battery manufacturing, while rare earth elements are used in permanent magnets for electric vehicles, wind turbines, and industrial equipment. Copper is essential to power transmission, electrical equipment, and renewable energy infrastructure.

As demand for mineral extraction increases, mining companies also need advanced machinery to improve operational efficiency, handle complex extraction requirements, and increase production capacity. This creates additional demand for specialized mining equipment, including excavation, drilling, crushing, and material-handling systems.

What Is Driving Demand for Critical Minerals?

Demand is increasing as energy systems, digital infrastructure, and advanced manufacturing become more dependent on mineral-intensive technologies. Battery deployment, electricity network expansion, renewable energy installations, and semiconductor production are creating additional requirements for both established materials, such as copper, and specialized minerals used in high-performance applications.

The IEA's Global Critical Minerals Outlook 2026 highlights the growing importance of minerals such as gallium, germanium, indium, and antimony as AI, robotics, and semiconductor technologies advance. Defense and aerospace applications also depend on materials including cobalt, titanium, tungsten, and yttrium.

Batteries for electric vehicles and storage

Electric vehicles and stationary energy storage systems are major sources of demand for battery materials. Lithium, nickel, cobalt, graphite, and manganese are used across different battery chemistries, with material requirements varying according to performance, cost, and application.

According to the IEA's 2026 analysis of mineral demand, global battery demand across applications grew by more than 35% in 2025, exceeding 1.5 TWh. Energy storage systems were a major contributor to this increase as utilities, businesses, and households expanded their use of battery-based storage.

Stationary storage is becoming increasingly important for managing electricity supply from renewable sources. Batteries can store excess electricity generated during periods of high renewable output and release it when demand rises or generation declines.

These factors are supporting investment in battery technologies, particularly lithium-ion batteries, which are widely used in electric vehicles and stationary energy storage installations.

Copper for power and grids

Copper is essential to electricity generation, transmission, distribution, and consumption. Its electrical conductivity makes it a key material in power cables, transformers, motors, charging infrastructure, and renewable energy installations.

The expansion of electricity grids, wind power, solar energy, and EV charging networks is increasing copper requirements across energy infrastructure. Grid modernization is particularly important because electricity systems need additional transmission and distribution capacity to connect new generation sources with consumers.

According to the IEA's 2026 outlook, the current pipeline of mining projects points to a potential copper supply deficit of 25% by 2035. This outlook highlights the importance of developing new mining projects, improving production efficiency, and expanding recycling capacity.

Where Are Critical Minerals Refined, and How Concentrated Is Supply?

Mining capacity and processing capacity are distributed unevenly across countries. Several regions produce substantial quantities of raw minerals, while a smaller group of countries dominates refining and downstream processing. This creates supply chain exposure for manufacturers that depend on processed materials, even when mining operations are geographically diversified.

The IEA reported that the leading refining country for each key energy mineral held an average share of 72% of refined supply in 2025, excluding rare earth elements. Indonesia led nickel refining, while China led the other key energy minerals covered by the assessment.

China's position is particularly significant in rare earth processing and permanent magnet manufacturing. The country produced 94% of the world's sintered permanent magnets in 2025, according to the IEA's analysis of export controls and supply concentration.

Copper provides another example of the difference between mining and refining capacity. The USGS Mineral Commodity Summaries 2026 reports the following estimated production levels for selected countries.

China's refining output is substantially higher than its domestic mine production, reflecting its extensive processing infrastructure and access to imported raw materials. Peru, meanwhile, produces more mined copper than China. This distinction illustrates why mining diversification alone cannot ensure supply security. Countries also need the technical expertise, infrastructure, investment, and industrial capacity required to process minerals into usable materials.

The dependence on concentrated processing capabilities is particularly significant for rare earth elements, which require specialized separation and refining processes before they can be used in industrial applications. Their role in electric vehicle motors, wind turbines, and advanced electronics is increasing the importance of developing reliable processing capabilities and diversified sourcing arrangements.

How Are Export Controls Changing Critical Mineral Supply?

Export controls are becoming an important instrument in critical mineral policy. Governments are using licensing requirements, quotas, and trade restrictions to manage access to materials considered strategically important. These measures can affect manufacturers that rely on imported minerals and processed components, particularly when alternative suppliers have limited production capacity.

The IEA's Global Critical Minerals Outlook 2026 identifies export restrictions and policy changes in major producing countries as growing sources of supply uncertainty. The Democratic Republic of the Congo introduced a cobalt export quota, Zimbabwe restricted lithium exports, and Mozambique introduced restrictions affecting graphite supply.

Rare earth and battery material controls

China's export controls have drawn particular attention because of its central role in rare earth processing and permanent magnet manufacturing. According to the International Energy Agency (IEA), China's dominance across these supply chain stages creates significant vulnerabilities for downstream industries. On April 4, 2025, China introduced export controls on certain medium and heavy rare earth-related items under Announcement No. 18 of 2025. The controls covered seven heavy rare earth elements and related compounds and magnets. These restrictions disrupted international supply chains, prompting some automakers to reduce production or temporarily halt plant operations as they faced difficulties sourcing permanent magnets.

In October 2025, China introduced a broader set of export controls covering additional rare earth materials, processing equipment, technologies, lithium batteries, artificial graphite anode materials, and other related items. These measures were issued through separate announcements. Their implementation was suspended until November 10, 2026, under Announcement No. 70 of 2025, issued by China's Ministry of Commerce and the General Administration of Customs.

On November 9, 2026, China's Ministry of Commerce announced that the suspension would continue from November 11, 2026, through January 10, 2027. The announcement covers the specified October 2025 measures. The April 2025 controls under Announcement No. 18 remain outside this suspension.

The restrictions are particularly significant for manufacturers of permanent magnets, which depend on a consistent supply of processed rare earth elements. These magnets are essential components in electric vehicle motors, wind turbines, and several industrial applications. Consequently, disruptions in rare earth processing can affect manufacturers across multiple downstream industries that depend on reliable permanent magnet supplies.

Why Are Critical Mineral Prices So Volatile?

Critical mineral prices respond to changes in production, inventories, trade policy, geopolitical conditions, and industrial demand. Supply disruptions can have a pronounced effect when production or processing is concentrated among a small number of suppliers. Long project development timelines and specialized refining requirements can also limit the speed at which additional supply reaches manufacturers.

The IEA's 2026 outlook reported that base metal prices increased by approximately one-third between January 2025 and April 2026, with copper reaching record levels. Lithium prices more than doubled during 2025 and early 2026, while cobalt prices rose by approximately 130% following export restrictions in the Democratic Republic of the Congo. Tungsten prices increased sixfold over the same broader period.

These movements reflect the interaction between demand growth and supply constraints. Battery manufacturers, for example, face procurement challenges when lithium availability changes or when export restrictions affect the flow of raw materials. Changes in the cost of lithium carbonate can influence cathode production expenses and purchasing decisions across the lithium carbonate supply chain.

For manufacturers, price volatility affects budgeting, procurement planning, inventory management, and long-term supply agreements. Companies with diversified sourcing arrangements and stronger visibility into upstream suppliers are better positioned to manage these fluctuations.

How Are the United States and Its Allies Securing Supply?

Governments are pursuing domestic production, international partnerships, strategic financing, and recycling programs to reduce supply exposure. These efforts aim to strengthen access to essential materials across extraction, processing, refining, and recovery. The United States and its allies are also developing policy frameworks to encourage investment and improve coordination among trusted suppliers.

The USGS Mineral Commodity Summaries 2026 reported that the United States was fully reliant on imports for 13 of the 58 critical mineral commodities it assessed in 2025. This dependence has encouraged policymakers to prioritize domestic production and diversify sourcing arrangements.

The United States and its allies

The United States is pursuing several initiatives to strengthen its domestic supply chain. In August 2026, the Office of the United States Trade Representative (USTR) described negotiations for an Agreement on Trade in Critical Minerals. The proposed framework would establish phased-in, border-adjusted price floors for specific minerals and common standards among participating trading partners. The USTR statement outlined the proposed approach and the ongoing discussions.

The European Union is also working to strengthen domestic capabilities. Under its Critical Raw Materials Act, the bloc aims to process at least 40% of its annual consumption of strategic raw materials within the EU by 2030. It also seeks to limit dependence on any single non-EU country to 65% of annual consumption. These benchmarks are intended to encourage domestic capacity and diversify external supply.

Other initiatives involve investment support, international coordination, and the development of strategic reserves.

Policy initiatives supporting critical mineral supply chains

These initiatives demonstrate how governments are combining domestic investment with international cooperation. Their effectiveness will depend on project execution, financing, permitting timelines, processing capabilities, and the ability to establish commercially viable supply arrangements.

Can recycling ease the squeeze?

Recycling can supplement primary mineral production by recovering valuable materials from used batteries, electronic waste, and industrial products. It can also reduce the volume of waste requiring disposal and support the reuse of materials across manufacturing supply chains.

The IEA's Global Critical Minerals Outlook 2026 projects that recycling rates for key energy minerals could rise from approximately 10% currently to close to 20% by 2040. However, recycling capacity remains concentrated, with China accounting for more than three-quarters of global battery recycling pre-treatment capacity.

As battery waste volumes increase, recovering valuable materials from used batteries is becoming an important part of resource planning. Improvements in collection, sorting, and material recovery technologies can help manufacturers recover lithium, cobalt, nickel, and other useful materials for further processing. This is creating opportunities for specialized battery recycling solutions that support material recovery and reduce dependence on newly extracted resources.

Conclusion

Critical minerals are becoming increasingly important to energy infrastructure, battery manufacturing, digital technologies, and defense applications. Copper, lithium, rare earth elements, and specialized materials are supporting the expansion of these industries, while concentrated refining capacity and export controls are increasing supply exposure. Governments are responding through domestic investment, international partnerships, and recycling initiatives. For manufacturers and investors, building resilient sourcing strategies will depend on greater supply chain diversification and stronger processing capabilities.

Explore the critical minerals report by Kings Research for further analysis of industry developments, key segments, and growth opportunities.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why does the United States need critical minerals?

Critical minerals support industries such as energy, defense, electronics, transportation, and advanced manufacturing. The United States relies on international suppliers for several of these materials, creating exposure to trade restrictions and supply disruptions. Strengthening domestic production and building relationships with reliable international suppliers are therefore important policy priorities.

What minerals are included in the US critical minerals list?

The US list includes materials such as copper, lithium, cobalt, graphite, nickel, silver, uranium, and rare earth elements. The USGS updates the list based on the economic importance of minerals and their potential exposure to supply disruptions.

Which country refines the most critical minerals?

China leads refining for several key energy minerals, including lithium, cobalt, and rare earth elements. Indonesia is a major refining country for nickel. This concentration gives these countries an influential position in the supply chains serving battery manufacturing, electronics, renewable energy, and other industrial applications, according to the IEA.

Which mineral accounts for the largest share of critical minerals demand?

Copper is a major contributor because it is widely used in electricity networks, renewable energy systems, electric vehicles, and industrial equipment. Its role in power transmission and distribution makes it particularly important as electricity demand and infrastructure investment increase.

text:
KUALA LUMPUR – A joint rare earths mining and processing venture between Malaysia and France is expected to begin operations in early 2027 as the two nations agreed to deepen cooperation and elevate ties to a strategic partnership, French President Emmanuel Macron said Tuesday.

The project, which involves French company Carester and Malaysian firm Malaco Mining Sendirian Berhad, would cover the extraction and processing of rare earths in Malaysia, with reserved volumes and the possibility of refining in France, Macron said.

“Operations are due to begin in early 2027,” he said at a joint news conference after talks with Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim. “This will allow us to proceed ... involving not only extraction, but also processing here, with reserved volumes and capacity, including the possibility of refining in France, which is crucial for our entire value chain.”

The arrangement reflects Malaysia’s move to build domestic processing capabilities, while France seeks to secure and diversify supplies of critical minerals used in a wide range of products from electric vehicles, electronics and renewable energy to defense industries.

The two leaders said that they agreed to elevate bilateral ties to a broader strategic partnership, focusing cooperation on defense, energy, semiconductors and digital connectivity, among other areas.

Anwar said that Malaysia has made an exception in its policy against exporting rare earth minerals in return for collaboration with France in developing its rare earths industry. He didn’t provide further details. He said that cooperation with France demonstrated how resource-rich countries could work with foreign partners while securing technology transfer, training and industrial expertise.

“We do not export raw materials, but with France we have done so, because you are committed to that processing and working with the Malaysians as a team,” Anwar said.

Macron said that the partnership reflected a shared commitment to national sovereignty and greater independence in a world increasingly shaped by competing major powers.

Plans for defense cooperation will include a new industrial road map, support for a regional center to counter hybrid threats and Malaysia's procurement of combat search-and-rescue helicopters from Airbus, he said. For semiconductors, Macron said that Malaysian firm SkyeChip and French company SiPearl will collaborate to develop a high-performance computing platform.

More than 300 French companies operate in Malaysia, making France its second-largest European investor, he said.

Sierra Club staff & members highlight dangers of rolling back methane pollution standards.

Washington, DC — Today and tomorrow, environmental and public health experts, alongside community advocates, will testify during a virtual public hearing to the dangers and risks posed by the Trump administration’s proposed rollback of long-awaited methane pollution standards finalized in 2024. The hearing is part of a broader public comment period in reaction to the Environmental Protection Agency’s plan to reverse key components of the landmark safeguards aimed at reducing methane, and associated pollution, from both new and existing oil and gas equipment.

Soon after taking office in 2025, the Trump EPA suspended the implementation of key provisions from the Biden-era standards, delaying their enforcement by up to 18 months despite no widespread evidence of compliance difficulties. Now, this rollback would permanently eliminate some of the rule’s most important safeguards, including its ban on routine flaring at oil wells and its program to leverage third-party monitoring data to identify and stop particularly large methane releases known as super-emitter events.

The proposal would also shield low-producing wells from leak monitoring requirements and other key safeguards, despite consistent evidence showing that such wells do not pollute less than higher-producing wells. Nearly one in ten people in the U.S. live in a county with over a thousand low-producing wells. These sources represent nearly half of the sector’s methane emissions and are primarily owned by large, well-resourced and highly profitable corporations.

Sierra Club experts and members will be among many testifying against the rollback.

In reaction, Sierra Club staff providing testimony released the following statements:

Andres Restrepo, Sierra Club Senior Attorney said: “EPA’s authority and obligation under the Clean Air Act to control methane emissions from the oil and gas sector has long been settled law, and the safeguards that the Biden Administration put into place in 2024 rely on cost-effective, widely available technologies and practices that the industry itself has used for years. The Trump Administration’s current proposal to strip the 2024 rule for parts and leave a rump regulation in place has support in neither the law nor the facts. The agency is attempting to manufacture sham justifications to mask what is nothing more than the giveaway that Donald Trump openly promised to oil and gas executives in exchange for supporting his campaign. Sierra Club will use every resource at its disposal to fight back against this betrayal of our families and communities.”

Cyrus Reed, Legislative and Conservation Director of Sierra Club’s Lone Star Chapter, said: “No state produces more oil and gas than Texas, and no state has more to gain from strong methane regulations than our state. We already have poor air quality from ozone pollution, particulate matter and other pollutants like hydrogen sulfide, and rolling back the methane standards will only make matters worse. Texas voters went to the polls in record numbers for a non-presidential election, and for the most part, voted for change, in largely because of anger over rising prices, but also due to a politics that often favor entrenched wealthy interests. This rollback proposal does not respond to this call for change, but instead proposes to let bad corporate actors off the hook and increase pollution that leads to higher energy prices, harms our health, and supercharges climate disruption.”

Antoinette Reyes, Permian Basin Organizer, Sierra Club Rio Grande Chapter, said: “As the federal government moves to weaken methane protections, New Mexico is working to strengthen its own. But pollution doesn’t stop at state lines, and neither should our commitment to protecting communities. Families in the Permian Basin already face industrial air pollution, from odors and poor visibility to respiratory health concerns. Every preventable methane leak wastes a valuable energy resource, potential tax revenue, and affects the quality of the air we breathe. Proven technology exists to reduce these emissions. State action alone cannot fill the gap left by federal rollbacks. We need strong protections at every level to safeguard our health, climate, and communities.”

Sarah Corcoran, Deputy Director of the Sierra Club Pennsylvania Chapter, said: “Pennsylvania is one of the leading states in the nation for fracked gas infrastructure. We are also one of the states with the highest pediatric asthma and cancer rates — but those numbers are increasing across the nation. The Trump Administration is not doing anyone any favors by reducing these regulations, not the industry, not the environment and not the American people who will feel the health impacts of these decisions for years to come. Policies that reduce methane waste, such as controls on flaring, quicker response times, transparent communications with impacted residents and more frequent testing are commonsense and cost effective. We need stronger protections in place for methane, not looser.”

Additional Background:

Methane is a potent greenhouse gas that has more than 80 times the power of carbon dioxide over a 20-year period, driving approximately one-third of the warming our planet has experienced to date. Each year, the U.S. oil and gas sector emits large amounts of methane into our atmosphere. Methane is emitted from oil and gas sources alongside other damaging pollutants, such as smog- and soot-forming volatile organic compounds and air toxins like benzene and formaldehyde, human carcinogens.

According to EPA’s analysis, the 2024 standards are projected to avoid 58 million tons of methane through 2038, as well as 16 million tons of volatile organic compounds and 590,000 tons of air toxins.

text:
North Carolina will ban the disposal of lithium-ion batteries in landfills and most permitted incinerators starting Dec. 1. The deadline puts pressure on collection programs to provide drop-off options for loose batteries and for devices that still contain them.

The state’s Department of Environmental Quality (DEQ) is urging residents to keep batteries and electronics out of recycling bins. Discarded lithium-ion batteries can start fires in collection trucks and processing facilities.

The law was enacted both for safety reasons and to generate another domestic source for critical minerals. The US Geological Survey estimates that less than 1% of all battery materials are manufactured in the US, so recycling would allow for more element recovery and create a domestic source for lithium, cobalt and other minerals. This aligns with federal initiatives to secure US mineral independence.

Local collection plans

DEQ advises local governments to plan for batteries from households and from their own operations. The agency says a certified household hazardous waste contractor can help establish collection and handling procedures. The state has made a grant available to local governments to help fund collection infrastructure and outreach.

The city of Salisbury, for one, says it plans to add collection bins this fall for lithium-ion batteries commonly found in laptops and cellphones. The city also directs residents to a locator for sites already accepting lithium-ion batteries.

DEQ has issued separate guidance to help businesses review their battery handling practices and identify collection or recycling outlets. The law already covers certain discarded computers and televisions. Stores in the state currently have optional collection programs, but the state advises that acceptance policies may vary by location.

Collection costs

North Carolina’s battery recycling market assessment cites a concern from an unnamed recycler that local drop-off programs could receive more batteries than they had budgeted to recycle. The assessment says collection costs and fire risks during handling and storage can make small, loose batteries less attractive to recover per unit than electric vehicle batteries.

Recyclers who spoke to DEQ in preparing this assessment also cited a lack of public education on how to properly recycle batteries.

“Improper preparation, such as mixing battery chemistry types and failing to label or protect terminals, can create dangerous fire risk situations for generators as well as battery collectors, transporters and processors,” the report read. “Ensuring that lithium batteries are prepared and packaged according to safe handling, best management practices will also reduce economic losses from collection vehicle and processing equipment fires.”

The assessment recommends that the state pass an extended producer responsibility law to help fund battery collection and recycling, alongside the disposal ban.

Supporting local business

The law will also help support a burgeoning battery and mineral manufacturing and processing across the Southeast, particularly in North Carolina, regulators said. Gaston and Cleveland counties contain more than 80% of the nation’s lithium ore reserves, while Livent Corp. in Gaston County operates the nation’s largest lithium hydroxide refinery.

A Toyota battery manufacturing plant also opened in Randolph County, but several other announced projects have stalled out — momentum that lawmakers hope the new rule can help reverse. To that end, the DEQ recommends the state help ensure downstream processors have enough capacity to handle the expected increase in battery volume, and leverage grants and other government funding to support in-state development for processors and manufacturers.

text:
New analysis finds that a revolving state loan program deploying $2 billion in geothermal development financing would help unlock more than 30 GW of dispatchable geothermal power in Texas, equivalent to roughly one-third of Texas' record peak electricity demand, while supporting the local workforce and returning the state's capital investment

AUSTIN, Texas, Nov. 17, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Project InnerSpace has published 'The Texas Geothermal Development Fund: Investing in the Next Century of Energy Abundance and Deploying Texan Oil and Gas Talent to Unlock Geothermal at Scale,' an analysis examining how Texas can deploy its oil and gas industry to develop a major local source of firm, dispatchable electricity as the state's power demand reaches new highs.

Since 2022, Project InnerSpace has worked to develop a robust set of geothermal capacity and financial frameworks to assess how much geothermal energy can be deployed in countries, states, and regions around the world, and at what cost. These frameworks are being used by the InnerSpace family of entities to assess geothermal development potential on a planetary scale, and to build structures and frameworks aimed at enabling that potential. This analysis is the first of a series-of-its-kind, leveraging these frameworks into a specific model for local action — and because everything is bigger in Texas, there was no better place to start.

'The Texas Geothermal Development Fund' envisions a revolving state loan program built to accelerate geothermal development in Texas. The analysis concludes that if Texas developed such a program, a one-time $400 million investment could deploy approximately $2 billion in geothermal exploration financing over 15 years by repeatedly lending and recovering the same capital. That investment could help unlock more than 30 gigawatts of firm, dispatchable electricity in the Lone Star State, up to $235 billion in private investment, $14 billion in state and local tax revenues, and 939,000 job years (an average of 62,600 jobs per year), all while leaving approximately $450 million in the program. The broader return would be a thriving and home-grown Texas geothermal industry capable of continued organic growth without additional state support.

The barrier that the state loan program seeks to solve is early stage financing risk. Geothermal developers must spend millions drilling wells and acquiring data to prove a geothermal resource exists, and conventional lenders won't finance that risky early stage. The proposed revolving state loan program would share that cost and risk, allowing for loan repayment after a resource is proven and traditional project financing enters. After repayment, the funds revolve to support the next project. The envisioned structure involves no ratepayer charges, no generation mandates, and no changes to ERCOT's market design.

The opportunity builds on Texas' substantial geothermal resources and existing oil and gas industry and workforce. In total, the analysis finds, Texas has roughly 140 gigawatts of technical geothermal electricity potential, a number orders of magnitude larger than what the envisioned state loan program would enable — paving the way for sustained and massive future growth of the geothermal development in the state.

"Texas helped develop the drilling technologies that are making next-generation geothermal possible, yet much of the investment and development is happening in other states," said Barry Smitherman, Chairman of Texas Geothermal Energy Alliance. "We already have the workforce, equipment, and expertise to build this industry here. This program would bring those projects home, creating jobs for Texas workers, and continuing Texas' legacy of global energy leadership."

There is precedent for this type of action in Texas. In 2025, the Texas Legislature created and funded a $350 million Advanced Nuclear Development Fund, even though nuclear energy was already eligible for financing through the Texas Energy Fund. Geothermal faces a similar early-stage financing gap to nuclear, but carries the additional benefits of local workforce deployment and oil and gas industry leadership in its development.

Key Findings from the 'Texas Geothermal Development Fund' Analysis:

Capital: A $400 million revolving loan program could deploy approximately $2 billion over 15 years by recycling repayments, with developers contributing another $499 million of their own capital;

Projects: The program could de-risk approximately 55 geothermal projects;

Electricity: Successful projects emerging from the de-risking phase could catalyze over 30 gigawatts of dispatchable, baseload electricity generation in Texas;

Private Investment: The program could catalyze up to $235 billion in downstream private investment to build geothermal projects in Texas, equivalent to approximately $588 for every dollar of initial state funding;

Fiscal Returns: After 15 years, approximately $450 million would remain in the program, after program administration costs and including interest earned on cash held between rounds; the program would also generate $14 billion in state and local tax revenues;

Jobs and Economic Development: The program would create 939,000 job years (an average of 62,600 jobs per year) providing a new market for Texas-based workforce, drilling rigs, operators, oilfield-service companies, and suppliers.

"This report offers a path to a transformative, affordable, bipartisan investment in Texas's economy and its power grid. Our state's pioneering history in the oil fields can unlock a powerful new clean, dispatchable energy resource — and do so in a way that repays taxpayers," said Drew Nelson, VP of Strategy of Project InnerSpace. "The Texas Legislature will obviously weigh a number of different energy ideas during the upcoming legislative session, but few can have as big of an impact as this revolving loan program."

Project InnerSpace and Texas Geothermal Energy Alliance will present the findings in an online webinar on November 17 at 2 p.m. CT.

Read the 'Texas Geothermal Development Fund' analysis here: https://projectinnerspace.org/resources/texasgeothermaldevelopmentfund.pdf

About Project InnerSpace

Project InnerSpace is the leading independent non-profit organization dedicated to the global development of geothermal energy. We are a focused research organization, on a mission to remove the major barriers standing in the way of the exponential growth and development of geothermal energy worldwide by 2030. Project InnerSpace proudly began its work in 2022 in Texas, with publication of the 'Future of Geothermal in Texas.' To learn more about Project InnerSpace, please visit www.projectinnerspace.org.

About Texas Geothermal Energy Alliance (TxGEA)

The Texas Geothermal Energy Alliance (TxGEA) is a Texas-based, Texas-led advocacy organization created for the purpose of advancing geothermal energy in Texas. TxGEA is comprised of a broad and interdisciplinary group of entities engaged in geothermal resource exploration, well drilling, plant construction, resource production and markets. These supporters include representatives from the oilfield service sector, oil & gas operators, utilities, start-up companies working to advance geothermal relevant technologies, and leading scientists and engineers from a number of academic institutions across Texas. To learn more about TxGEA, please visit www.txgea.org.

text:
RALEIGH, N.C. — North Carolina residents will soon be prohibited from throwing lithium-ion batteries in their household trash under a new state law aimed at preventing dangerous fires.

According to the North Carolina Office of State Fire Marshal, the law takes effect Dec. 1, 2026, banning the disposal of lithium-ion batteries in household trash and municipal landfills.

The batteries are commonly found in everyday electronics, including cellphones, laptops, power tools, toys, electric shavers and other rechargeable devices.

Fire officials warn that improperly discarded lithium-ion batteries can ignite when damaged, creating serious fire hazards for garbage trucks, waste collection facilities and recycling centers.

Why are lithium-ion batteries dangerous?

The Office of State Fire Marshal says lithium-ion batteries can catch fire if they are damaged or improperly handled.

When batteries are thrown into household trash, they can be crushed or punctured during collection and processing, potentially causing fires that spread quickly.

These fires can damage equipment and facilities while putting sanitation workers and others at risk.

State officials say the new disposal restrictions are intended to reduce those dangers and improve safety throughout the waste management process.

How to properly dispose of lithium-ion batteries

With the new law taking effect Dec. 1, the Office of State Fire Marshal is encouraging residents to begin using approved battery disposal methods.

Officials recommend the following precautions:

Never place lithium-ion batteries in household trash or recycling bins.

Take used batteries to an authorized battery recycling program or household hazardous waste collection facility.

Cover battery terminals with tape before transporting them for disposal.

Place each battery in a separate bag to help prevent accidental contact.

Check with your county government for designated battery collection locations.

The agency emphasizes that lithium-ion batteries should be handled separately from regular household waste, even if they are no longer working.

Residents are encouraged to contact their local county waste management department to find an appropriate collection site.

State fire officials say properly disposing of batteries can help prevent fires, protect waste management workers and reduce the risk of damage to collection vehicles and facilities.

description:
Most of the wind turbines that make the news are either brand new or broken.
So what does it actually take to remove a wind turbine this size?
Bowling Green says the excavation will happen without blasting, and that each site gets backfilled and restored afterward.
That’s arguably a better outcome than in Casper, Wyoming, where the city landfill buried a whole lot of old turbine blades before it stopped taking them.
If the weather cooperates, Bowling Green expects the whole removal job, foundations included, to be finished by mid-December.
text:
Most of the wind turbines that make the news are either brand new or broken. A developer wants to put up a bigger one, or, like the turbine at a Missouri wind farm back in August, a tower ends up bent over in a field. It can get a bit repetitive, to be honest.

But the four turbines outside Bowling Green, Ohio, don’t fit either category. They’re just old, and they’re due to come down by crane. On a schedule, one at a time.

The city calls the site Ohio’s first commercial wind farm, and its own project page also describes it as the state’s first utility-scale wind project. The turbines started generating electricity in 2003, ran for more than 20 years, and were officially retired in 2025. Now Bowling Green is paying to remove them.

So what does it actually take to remove a wind turbine this size?

There’s a lot of turbine to take down

Each of the four is a 1.8-megawatt machine on a 257-foot tower, according to a 2016 annual report from American Municipal Power, the group that developed the wind farm as a joint venture of Ohio towns. The blades reach 132 feet out from the turbine housing. When one of them swings straight up, the whole thing stands nearly 400 feet tall.

Those are AMP’s own figures from 2016, not something anyone’s re-measured since. Then again, steel towers don’t tend to shrink.

For scale, 132-foot blades look pretty modest by today’s standards. A developer in Australia now wants a new road built just so its 213-foot blades can get around a roundabout.

The city plans to take the four turbines down one at a time over the fall. Big cranes handle the lifting. That way, the blades and nacelles are lowered to the ground, and the towers come apart in sections. If you’ve never had to think about a nacelle, it’s basically the box at the top of the tower that holds the gearbox and the generator, which is what turns spinning blades into electricity.

Then there’s the stuff you can’t see. Each turbine sits on a foundation that goes approximately 33 feet into the ground, and those get dug out too.

That might sound like overkill. But think about what a foundation’s job is here. A tall tower with three long blades catches a lot of wind, and all that sideways push is constantly trying to tip it over. The foundation is the anchor that stops it, so it has to be big, heavy, and deep.

Bowling Green says the excavation will happen without blasting, and that each site gets backfilled and restored afterward. The city doesn’t say why explosives are off the table, though I’d guess a working county landfill right next door has something to do with it. The landfill stays open to the public through all of this, and the city’s warned residents they’ll probably notice more activity and cranes.

Has anything come down yet?

The prep work started in August. According to BG Independent News, which covered the start of the job in late August, that first stage meant pulling out underground electrical infrastructure, with the turbines themselves to follow.

The city’s project page still talks about the crane work in the future tense. City council heard updates on Sept. 8 and Oct. 19, though neither said a turbine was already down. So I can’t tell you which of the four, if any, has already been lowered. What we do know is the deadline, which I’ll get to.

Why not just swap in new turbines?

You’d think the obvious move would be to put newer turbines on the same spots. Bowling Green did look at that. Back in 2020, BG Independent reported that replacing each machine with a newer model was estimated at $8.8 million apiece.

The old ones weren’t cheap to keep alive, either. In 2020, the same outlet reported that a couple of gearboxes had already failed, at up to $500,000 each to replace. Replacement parts got hard to find, which isn’t too surprising when the city has said the turbines’ model, the Vestas V80, is obsolete. In 2021, one turbine was retired early because repairs were too expensive. That cut the wind farm’s output from 7.2 megawatts, enough for about 2,500 residential customers, to 5.4 megawatts.

Even if the money had worked out, the site would be off the table. The city says the land won’t host renewable generation again, because the county needs it for future landfill space and Plain Township’s zoning rules get in the way.

It’s a bit of a shame, frankly. Still, BG Independent puts the turbines’ expected working life at roughly 20 years, and these made it past that, which is a pretty respectable run.

Nothing’s going into the landfill next door

I’ll admit I like how the city’s handling the leftovers. Bowling Green says none of the material will end up in the landfill. The plan is to recycle the metal, the wiring, and even the foundation concrete, capture oil and other fluids where it can, and check whether the major components are worth selling or reusing.

That’s arguably a better outcome than in Casper, Wyoming, where the city landfill buried a whole lot of old turbine blades before it stopped taking them.

So who’s paying for it?

The demolition costs $1.77 million, according to BG Independent. Bowling Green owns 51% of the project, so it’s covering about half, and the nine other communities that share in the wind farm split the rest. The city’s been saving for its share through utility rates, which is sensible planning for a machine you know will wear out.

$1.77 million to remove all four sounds like a lot. It’s arguably a bargain next to the $8.8 million that a single replacement was expected to cost in 2020.

Brian O’Connell, the city’s director of infrastructure and public utilities, didn’t pretend to be thrilled about it. “It’s sad to see them coming down,” he told BG Independent.

I get it. You don’t look at something that big on the horizon for two decades without getting a little attached.

Bowling Green isn’t giving up on renewables, though. The city’s renewable energy page says it’s working on a new solar project elsewhere to replace the lost wind power, and BG Independent reports two possible sites near I-75. If the weather cooperates, Bowling Green expects the whole removal job, foundations included, to be finished by mid-December.

title: Tesla Wants to Build 1 Million Cybercabs in Europe. There's Just One Problem. - Gizmodo
authors: Bruce Gil, Mike Pearl, Matt Novak
description:
