text:
The U.S. battery manufacturing industry is digesting production lines formed by the previous round of expansion, and adjusting subsequent factory construction plans. At the same time, amid the divergent growth trends of the electric vehicle and energy storage markets, it is reselecting battery products and technical routes.

In the past few years, the electrification plans of U.S. automakers, federal tax credits and state investment promotion incentives have jointly driven a wave of battery factory investment. These projects have extended from the traditional automotive industrial heartland of the Midwest such as Michigan and Ohio to southern manufacturing bases including Kentucky, Tennessee, Georgia and the Carolinas, forming the U.S. "Battery Belt".

In August 2022, the Inflation Reduction Act (IRA) promoted by the Biden administration came into effect, supporting electric vehicle consumption as well as the construction of electric vehicle and battery production capacity through purchase tax credits and local manufacturing incentives. After the Trump administration took office in 2025, policies related to clean energy took a sharp turn: the purchase tax credits were terminated early, and electric vehicle sales fell immediately. Automakers cut production lines for pure electric models, and battery companies also adjusted their investment plans accordingly.

According to statistics from the U.S. think tank Atlas, the total new investment in full electric vehicles and their supply chains across the United States plummeted from a peak of about 55 billion U.S. dollars in 2023 to about 6.5 billion U.S. dollars in 2025. In 2025 alone, formally canceled electric vehicle-related projects involved nearly 20 billion U.S. dollars in originally committed investment. From the beginning of 2025 to August 2026, the canceled projects involved a total of about 27,000 committed jobs.

Against the backdrop of overall investment contraction, completed battery factories are also facing choices over product routes: slowing demand for electric vehicles and considerable growth in the energy storage market are attracting enterprises to switch production lines to seek short-term orders to absorb idle capacity; the requirements of next-generation electric vehicles for low-cost, high-energy-density batteries are also driving subsequent technology investment.

The adjustment of Ultium Cells, a joint venture between General Motors and LG Energy Solution, is the most typical case. Its factory in Spring Hill, Tennessee, was originally built to support GM's electric vehicles, with a planned power battery capacity of over 45 GWh. In June 2026, it completed a 70 million U.S. dollar renovation to switch to producing pouch-type lithium iron phosphate (LFP) cells for energy storage systems (ESS).

Three months later, GM announced at the end of September that it would add production capacity for lithium-rich manganese-based (LMR) prismatic cells for next-generation electric vehicles at this plant. The related facility renovation is expected to start in 2026 and be completed in 2028, adding about 500 new jobs. The product portfolio of the factory covers both energy storage and automotive applications.

GM stated that the designed energy density of lithium-rich manganese-based batteries is 33% higher than that of LFP batteries, with comparable manufacturing costs, and Ultium Cells is expected to become the world's first enterprise to achieve commercial mass production of LMR prismatic cells.

This swing reflects the current situation of the U.S. battery manufacturing industry: terminal electric vehicle demand falls short of expectations, forcing completed factories to switch to energy storage production to save themselves; in order to overcome cost bottlenecks and maintain medium and long-term competitiveness, automakers still have to push ahead with continuous investment in new technology routes.

01

Policy Shift, Investment Recession

The explosive expansion of the U.S. "Battery Belt" was jointly driven by federal legislation, state government investment promotion and radical transformation of traditional automakers: U.S. auto giants are eager to restructure the local supply chain, Asian battery companies from Japan, South Korea and other regions need to be close to North American vehicle customers to provide supporting supplies, and midwestern and southern state governments are eager to use new energy bases to retain manufacturing jobs lost due to the decline of fuel vehicles.

The battery construction boom was launched between 2019 and 2022. According to public statistics, half of the 52 major battery projects in the United States had their sites selected or investment implemented before the IRA took effect in August 2022.

The IRA injected a strong stimulus to both the supply and demand sides of the boom: on the supply side, qualified locally manufactured cells are eligible for advanced manufacturing tax credits of up to 35 U.S. dollars per kWh, and module manufacturing enjoys an additional 10 U.S. dollars per kWh credit. On the demand side, new energy vehicles that meet the localization thresholds for North American assembly, critical minerals and battery components are eligible for a federal new vehicle purchase tax credit of up to 7,500 U.S. dollars. Combined with low-cost land, infrastructure expansion and employment subsidies from various states, automakers and battery companies' expectations for future electric vehicle shipment scales were pushed to the peak.

Investment expectations shifted immediately in 2025 with the Trump administration taking office. In July 2025, the U.S. Congress passed legislation to cancel compliance fines for Corporate Average Fuel Economy (CAFE) standards. Previously, increasing sales of pure electric models could raise the overall average fuel economy of automakers, reducing the fine pressure brought by selling high-fuel-consumption pickup trucks and large SUVs. Two months later, the federal tax and expenditure legislation was adjusted, and the maximum 7,500 U.S. dollar federal tax credit was completely terminated for vehicles purchased after September 30.

The buying spree before the tax credit expiration pushed the penetration rate of new pure electric vehicles in the U.S. to a high of 10.6% in the third quarter of 2025, after which the market cooled rapidly. According to data from Cox Automotive, from the fourth quarter of 2025 to the second quarter of 2026, the penetration rate of new pure electric vehicles in the U.S. hovered between 5.7% and 5.8%, with year-on-year sales declines of 36%, 27% and 20.5% respectively in each quarter.

In 2026, the United States further relaxed fuel vehicle regulations. In February, the Environmental Protection Agency revoked the motor vehicle greenhouse gas endangerment finding and related emission standards; in September, the federal government lowered fuel economy requirements and clarified that CAFE credit trading between automakers will be canceled from 2028. These adjustments have reduced the compliance pressure on automakers to sell fuel vehicles, and also weakened their motivation to meet regulatory requirements by increasing the production and sales of pure electric models.

On the other hand, the advanced manufacturing tax credit policy, as the profit pillar of battery factories, has strengthened penetrating review of foreign investors and supply chains. In February 2026, the U.S. Internal Revenue Service issued guidelines extending the review of "Foreign Entities of Concern (FEOC)" to foreign shareholders, debts, supply chains and technologies of battery enterprises. When applying for tax credits, enterprises need to verify the qualifications of investors and suppliers, trace material costs, and prove that their production, operation and technical cooperation arrangements meet the "actual control" requirements, which increases the compliance costs of financing, procurement and technology introduction.

As demand cools down, automakers and battery companies have changed their original capacity expansion plans one after another.

Large bases that are completed or nearly completed mainly adjust operations by splitting joint venture assets, transferring equity, reducing production loads and switching to energy storage production. The most typical example is the BlueOval SK project, a joint venture between Ford and SK On: Ford took over the Kentucky campus, converted the first-phase power battery plant to energy storage production and halved its capacity, while the second-phase plant is reserved for other uses; the Tennessee plant is independently owned and operated by SK On, with its production launch postponed.

Projects that have started civil construction or completed plant construction mostly choose to cut investment, capacity and job scales, and postpone equipment installation and production launch to reduce subsequent capital expenditure. For example, Ford's wholly-owned BlueOval LFP battery plant in Michigan reduced its committed investment from 3.5 billion U.S. dollars to 2.5 billion U.S. dollars, planned capacity from 35 GWh to 20 GWh, and committed jobs from 2,500 to 1,700.

Projects in the early stage of planning or capacity expansion mainly exit by canceling construction, terminating leases or selling sites. Norwegian battery company FREYR and U.S. battery company KORE Power respectively canceled their originally planned 34 GWh and 12 GWh cell projects; silicon anode battery enterprise Amprius terminated the expansion of new bases, retaining existing R&D and small-scale manufacturing facilities; U.S. battery enterprise iM3NY declared bankruptcy and sold its assets afterwards; Natron Energy, which focuses on sodium-ion batteries, closed its existing facilities and terminated new plant plans due to capital chain rupture.

The vast majority of hundreds of GWh of new capacity planned in the previous boom was not supported by real vehicle orders from the very beginning. Canceling the unimplemented capacity expansion commitments on paper is a correction and stop-loss for irrational bubbles.

In terms of capacity supply and demand, according to statistics from the International Energy Agency (IEA) in its *Global Electric Vehicle Outlook 2026*, by the end of 2025, the nominal manufacturing capacity of completed lithium-ion batteries in the United States has reached about 330 GWh (including power and energy storage). If estimated based on the annual sales of about 1 million pure electric vehicles across the country with a battery capacity of around 70 kWh per vehicle, the annual demand for power cells from local automakers is less than 80 GWh, accounting for only about a quarter of the nominal capacity.

02

Automakers Reassess Electric Vehicles

Ford officially announced a major adjustment to its electrification strategy in December 2025, listing "lower-than-expected demand, high structural costs and changes in the regulatory environment" as the three main reasons. It will comprehensively cut capital expenditure on electrification, and shift resources to fuel vehicles, hybrid models and next-generation pure electric platforms with stronger price competitiveness.

Since the second quarter of 2025, General Motors has accrued about 10.9 billion U.S. dollars in total electric vehicle-related asset impairment and restructuring expenses; when Ford announced the contraction of its electrification strategy in December 2025, it accrued more than 19 billion U.S. dollars in one-time related expenses.

In the third quarter of 2026, General Motors sold about 25,000 electric vehicles in the United States, down 62% year-on-year. Ford sold about 6,000 units, down 80% year-on-year; the much-anticipated F-150 Lightning pure electric pickup truck sold only 289 units in the single quarter, and has now been announced to discontinue production.

However, amid the recession trend, the heads of the two major U.S. automakers insisted on stating that "they have not abandoned electric vehicles".

Mary Barra, CEO of General Motors, publicly admitted in 2026 that without federal subsidies, the popularization of electrification will take longer, but General Motors will still reach that stage, and internal data shows that consumers who have bought electric vehicles are 80% more likely to repurchase electric vehicles. She said General Motors still believes that electric vehicles are the final destination, and the mission of transformation remains unchanged.

Jim Farley, CEO of Ford, set the conditions for continued investment in electric vehicles on specific cost and competitiveness. He recently stated publicly that Ford's internal disassembly and calculation found that the battery procurement cost of BYD's equivalent vehicle is about 20% lower than that of Ford's next-generation mid-size electric pickup truck Fathom. To narrow the vehicle cost gap, Ford's countermeasure is to redesign motors, reducers and inverters, improve electric drive efficiency, and achieve the same cruising range with a smaller battery pack. Farley also admitted that it is not easy to launch this vehicle according to the established scale, cost and schedule, and the mass production engineering solution has not been finally finalized.

Automakers first need to adapt to the sales scale after the withdrawal of subsidies. According to quarterly data from Cox Automotive, in the first three quarters of 2026, quarterly sales of pure electric vehicles in the United States remained at more than 200,000 units, with a market penetration rate of about 6%, roughly returning to the level between 2022 and 2023.

Subsequent product development pays more attention to the optimization of selling price and cost. In the previous round of investment, full-size pure electric pickup trucks and large SUVs occupied an important position, and some models were equipped with high-nickel battery packs of 100 kWh to 200 kWh, resulting in high vehicle costs and selling prices. These models were most affected by the tax credit policy. Automakers have turned to focus on a product system with higher cost-effectiveness and lower battery cost: for example, Ford plans to control the starting price of Fathom below 30,000 U.S. dollars and adopt LFP batteries; General Motors is promoting solutions such as LFP and lithium-rich manganese-based batteries to serve entry-level models and large electric vehicles that balance cost and cruising range respectively.

Automakers are also adjusting the proportion of investment in cell manufacturing assets. In 2025, GM sold its joint venture equity in the Lansing cell plant in Michigan to LG Energy Solution, and in August 2026, transferred the equity of the under-construction battery plant in New Carlisle, Indiana to Samsung SDI; after Ford took over the Kentucky joint venture campus, it shifted it to the energy storage market.

Through equity transfer and business divestiture, automakers transfer the depreciation pressure and capacity utilization risk of heavy-asset cell manufacturing to professional battery manufacturers and the energy storage market, and retreat to vehicle platforms and system integration.

03

Exploring Production Conversion Paths

Despite the shrinking of new investment commitments, many of the stock projects that started construction intensively in previous years crossed the acceptance nodes between 2025 and 2026 and entered the production or commissioning period. IEA data shows that the nominal manufacturing capacity of lithium batteries in the United States increased by about 50% year-on-year in 2025, reaching a nominal capacity of about 330 GWh at the end of the year. This includes about 60 GWh of cell capacity already built in the United States by multinational automakers and Asian battery giants before this boom.

The U.S. Energy Storage Association (SEIA) supply chain tracking in September 2026 shows that the operational energy storage and dual-purpose cell manufacturing capacity across the United States is 62.3 GWh per year, while the downstream energy storage module and battery pack assembly capacity reaches 107.6 GWh per year. A large number of factories are located in the module and system integration links with lower capital expenditure and shorter construction cycles, and the core cells are still highly dependent on external procurement or imports.

Fully shifting to the battery energy storage market is the most mainstream "self-rescue" channel for battery production lines originally planned to support electric vehicles. As power batteries face sluggish demand, the transformation of the U.S. power grid and the expansion of artificial intelligence data centers are driving high growth in local energy storage installations. Data from SEIA and Benchmark shows that new battery energy storage installations in the United States reached 57.6 GWh in 2025, and 30.8 GWh in the first half of 2026, of which the single-quarter installation in the second quarter reached a record 20.2 GWh. Institutions generally predict that the total new installations in 2026 are expected to be close to 70 GWh.

Huge energy storage demand has become the "receiver" of idle power production lines. In addition to the aforementioned GM Ultium Tennessee plant switching to producing pouch LFP energy storage cells in June 2026, the L-H Battery plant in Ohio, a joint venture between Honda and LG Energy Solution (originally planned for 40 GWh of automotive power cells), has taken the lead in mass-producing LFP energy storage cells in July 2026; the Lansing plant in Michigan, which is wholly owned by LG Energy Solution, started production in August 2026, also prioritizing the production of pouch LFP energy storage cells, and has scheduled the mass production of prismatic LFP energy storage cells for 2027; together with the Holland plant in Michigan that launched LFP energy storage mass production in May 2025, LG Energy Solution has densely laid out an energy storage manufacturing network in North America.

text:
Tidewater Renewables Ltd. on Nov. 12 announced its renewable diesel and renewable hydrogen (HDRD) complex in Prince George, British Columbia, achieved a record-high average throughput rate of 3,411 barrels per day during the third quarter, or 114% of design capacity, compared to 2,011 barrels per day, or 67% design capacity, reported for the same period of last year.

The company said the higher throughput during the third quarter of 2026 reflects continued robust facility reliability and sustained benefits of targeted facility debottlenecking initiatives, which collectively enabled the HDRD complex to consistently operate above nameplate capacity. Facility utilization during the third quarter of last year was adversely impacted by operational interruptions, including planned turnaround activities initiated in September 2025, severe weather-related rail logistics challenges, and softer Canadian renewable diesel demand.

“The ability to consistently run significantly above the 3,000 barrels per day design capacity of the facility has been possible due to the excellent work of our operations team, who completed a number of very low-cost debottlenecking initiatives earlier in the year,” said Jeremy Baines, CEO of Tidewater, during an earnings call. “We expect to be able to continue to run at these elevated utilization rates throughout the coming winter months, except for short periods of reduced rates to complete scheduled maintenance.”

Baines confirmed Tidewater is continuing to consider plans to develop a proposed 6,500-barrel-per-day sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) project in British Columbia, but said the company is no longer plans to make a final investment decision (FID) before the end of the year.

He explained that the Canadian government in October released a proposal to update its Clean Fuel Regulations. The proposal, in part, aims to introduce a credit multiplier for eligible low-CI fuels produced in Canada on or after Jan. 1, 2026. The proposed credit multipliers would increase the number of credits created per unit of eligible low-CI fuel, thereby increasing its compliance value under the CFS regulations. As a result, a given quantity of domestically produced low-CI fuel would create more credits than an equivalent quantity of imported low-CI fuel of equal carbon intensity.

As part of the proposal, the Canadian government plans to set the credit multiplier for SAF at 1.8. The proposal, however, is subject to a 75-day public comment period that closes in mid-January. Baines noted the government could elect to make changes to the proposal after the comment period.

“Given the ongoing regulatory uncertainty, Tidewater has made the prudent decision to extend its targeted timeline for a potential FID into the first half of 2027,” he said. “This extension will allow the corporation to actively participate in the 75-day federal CFR consultation period, continue to advocate for further regulatory amendments that will support the creation of a domestic SAF industry, and continue advancing long-term offtake agreements and committed financing required to support efficient project execution.”

In its financial report, Tidewater Renewables indicated it expects strong financial and operational strength to continue. The company said it now has more than 65% of forecasted renewable diesel production for each of 2027 and 2028 under contract. To protect its financial position, the corporation has hedged approximately 50% of renewable diesel (and attached emission credit) sales and associated feedstock purchases for the balance of 2026 and has further secured hedges for approximately 30% of anticipated 2027 renewable diesel (and attached emission credit) sales and associated feedstock purchases, at significantly higher fixed prices relative to the 2026 hedges.

The company also discussed its planned merger with Tidewater Midstream and Infrastructure. On Nov. 2, Tidewater Midstream and Tidewater Renewables announced that they entered into the arrangement agreement pursuant to which Tidewater Midstream will acquire all of the outstanding common shares of Tidewater Renewables that Tidewater Midstream does not already own, with each such Tidewater Renewables common share to be exchanged for 0.88 of a Midstream share. The transaction is expected to close in mid-December, subject to required approvals and closing conditions.

text:
The partnership will build on the Memorandum of Understanding signed by Massachusetts Governor Maura Healey and Nova Scotia Premier Tim Houston in February to strengthen regional cooperation on offshore wind development, transmission planning, workforce development and economic growth.

“We need more affordable, reliable energy, and that's going to take working with our neighbors,” said Gov. Healey in a written statement.

“Massachusetts and Nova Scotia have a strong partnership, and we're building on that relationship to explore new opportunities to bring offshore wind power to New England,” she continued, adding, “this work has the potential to lower energy costs, strengthen our energy supply and create good-paying jobs in our port communities.

“We're excited to take this next step together,” Healey said.

“We’ve worked hard to make sure clean energy is a union industry. We saw Vineyard Wind sustain thousands of good jobs along the South Coast. We need to continue to push this industry forward to support good union careers now and into the future. We look forward to continued partnership with the Healey-Driscoll Administration and Nova Scotia," said Frank Callahan, President, Massachusetts Building Trades Unions.

Connecticut, Maine, Rhode Island and Vermont are also participating; New Hampshire is the only New England state that declined to join.

The request asks about ways to move power from potential offshore wind projects to consumers, including undersea cables and overland lines through New Brunswick and Quebec.

Responses are due Dec. 31, 2026. The governments have not announced a preferred route or committed to building a particular project.

“We are becoming the starting point,” Houston said, pointing to Nova Scotia’s potential to produce 60 GWs of energy.

Massachusetts Secretary of Energy and Environmental Affairs Rebecca Tepper described the request as the “initial concrete implementation” of the regional partnership.

The effort comes as offshore wind developers in the United States continue to face federal permitting and leasing uncertainty and opposition to wind projects by the White House.

The request for information is an early step in a renewed effort to overcome those obstacles and to gather proposals and assess possible transmission options.

It is not itself an approval for construction or a final decision on which projects or routes should move forward.

The participating governments have not said what decisions they expect to make after the Dec. 31 response deadline.

text:
Hyundai Motor's global plant utilization rate fell in the first nine months of this year as vehicle production declined despite increased manufacturing capacity, corporate data showed Tuesday.

The South Korean automaker's overall plant utilization rate stood at 86.1 percent in the January-September period, down from 94.3 percent a year earlier, according to its quarterly report.

Total production capacity rose 3 percent on-year to 3.17 million vehicles, while actual output fell 6 percent to 2.73 million units.

The combined utilization rate of its eight overseas plants dropped to 80.7 percent from 88.5 percent a year earlier.

Hyundai Motor Group Metaplant America in the U.S. state of Georgia recorded the steepest decline, with its utilization rate plunging to 41.4 percent from 68.1 percent over the period.

Production at the plant also fell to 35,000 vehicles from 52,000 units, apparently affected by the expiration of U.S. federal tax credits for electric vehicle (EV) purchases.

In South Korea, the automaker's plant utilization rate fell to 93.6 percent from 101.7 percent, partly due to production disruptions caused by labor strikes.

Domestic output declined 9.8 percent to 1.25 million vehicles in the January-September period from 1.39 million a year earlier.

title: NRDC Urges Incoming Benson Administration To Prioritize Clean Transportation - Patch
description:
Among Michigan residents, transportation ranked as the second-highest household expense, behind housing.
“High gas and diesel prices have been extremely hard on Michigan families, and we need to do more to provide affordable options.
“Michigan’s next governor and legislature can increase reliable transit options, safe ways to walk and bike, and access to electric vehicles that cost less to run and maintain.
“Clean transportation is essential to Michigan’s climate future, our public health and our economy,” NRDC Michigan Policy Director for Climate and Energy Derrell Slaughter said.
“We can’t build a clean future for Michigan by cleaning up power plants alone.
text:
In a new policy brief, the Natural Resources Defense Council argues that clean transit belongs at the center of any governor’s affordability agenda “because it lowers household costs while improving access, air quality, and economic resilience.”

According to the NRDC, the average Michigan family spends $17,000 a year on car payments, fuel, maintenance and insurance, making up nearly a quarter of the state’s median $72,000 household income. Among Michigan residents, transportation ranked as the second-highest household expense, behind housing.

“High gas and diesel prices have been extremely hard on Michigan families, and we need to do more to provide affordable options. Michigan is behind on this front, and it doesn’t have to be this way,” Abby Clark, the Michigan director of government affairs at NRDC, said in a statement. “Michigan’s next governor and legislature can increase reliable transit options, safe ways to walk and bike, and access to electric vehicles that cost less to run and maintain. We can be less vulnerable to volatile gas prices and put real money back in people’s pockets.”

In the brief, the NRDC offers four policy solutions to lower transportation costs in Michigan. The first is to rewrite the state law governing how transportation tax revenue is distributed to prioritize investments to expand access to reliable public transit and safe walking and biking options and ensure tax dollars are spent on projects that will deliver the greatest impact for residents.

Its second recommendation urges state leaders to accelerate the deployment of electric vehicle charging equipment, which the NRDC says will help families save money by making the switch to an electric vehicle an easier choice. According to the U.S. Department of Energy’s Alternative Fuels Data Center, there are 5,765 public charging ports within the state.

The NRDC also advised Benson and the Legislature to mitigate the impact of high diesel prices stemming from the war in Iran by supporting existing grant programs administered by the Department of Environment, Great Lakes and Energy to reduce the price of electric trucks and help transition medium and heavy-duty vehicles to electric options.

The council also encouraged the state to lead by example by electrifying the states’ own vehicle fleets, cutting down on fuel and maintenance costs for the state government and taxpayers.

“Clean transportation is essential to Michigan’s climate future, our public health and our economy,” NRDC Michigan Policy Director for Climate and Energy Derrell Slaughter said. “We can’t build a clean future for Michigan by cleaning up power plants alone. The cars and trucks we drive every day matter just as much.”

text:
NYSE debut backs a proposed North Carolina metals-recovery plant.

Seeking to expand the recovery of gold and other valuable metals from discarded electronics, Modern Mining Technology Corp. completed a $40 million initial public offering ahead of its Nov. 13 debut on the NYSE American, raising capital to move its proprietary water-based recycling process beyond demonstration-scale operations in North Carolina.

From households to industrial facilities, computers, smartphones, appliances, and other electrical equipment eventually reach the end of their useful lives, leaving behind metals, plastics, glass, and other materials that can be recovered or must be managed as waste.

Recovering those materials involves an industry that collects and sorts discarded equipment, removes reusable components, and separates metals and other materials for further processing, offering another source of commodities that would otherwise need to be obtained through mining and primary production.

Encompassing everything from large household appliances to computers and small communications devices, electronic waste amounted to approximately 62 million metric tons worldwide in 2022, according to the United Nations' Global E-waste Monitor 2024.

Of that total, only 22.3% was documented as formally collected and recycled.

Global e-waste generation is projected to reach 82 million metric tons annually by 2030, increasing the amount of discarded material available for potential recovery.

Alongside those growing volumes, discarded electronics represent a substantial inventory of metals that have already been mined, refined, and incorporated into manufactured products.

In its 2024 report, the United Nations estimated that electronic waste generated in 2022 contained approximately $91 billion worth of metals, including $19 billion in copper and $15 billion in gold.

Within that larger waste stream, printed circuit boards require more specialized processing than the bulk metals recovered from appliances and other equipment.

Used throughout computers, servers, mobile phones, and other electronics, those boards contain copper, gold, silver, and palladium combined with plastics, fiberglass, and insulating materials, requiring additional treatment to separate the valuable metals from the surrounding components.

Even after circuit boards have been removed from discarded equipment, recovering their metal content involves separating and concentrating those materials before further refining can produce commodities suitable for sale into industrial markets, a process Modern Mining has been developing through its research, testing, and demonstration operations in North Carolina.

Recovering metals from e-waste

Tracing its metal-recovery research to a U.S. subsidiary established in 2017, Vancouver-based Modern Mining Technology was incorporated in British Columbia in 2021, with early laboratory and pilot testing in Raleigh, North Carolina, preceding the opening of its Greenville demonstration facility in November 2023.

Established to test the recovery of valuable metals from discarded printed circuit boards, the Greenville operation processes material obtained from qualified electronics recyclers, allowing Modern Mining to work with metals already incorporated into manufactured products rather than extracting them from newly mined ore.

"We start with valuable metals that are already above ground, sitting inside the electronics the world throws away every day," said Modern Mining President and CEO Jeet Basi.

To begin processing, those circuit boards are sorted and shredded before entering a water-based separation stage that concentrates their metal-bearing particles while removing much of the surrounding plastics and other nonmetallic materials.

Known as pre-concentration, this initial stage produces a metal-rich material the company calls metallic sand concentrate, which contains a mixture of recoverable metals rather than individual refined products.

Instead of relying on high-temperature smelting, Modern Mining uses water and mechanical separation methods during this stage without adding chemical reagents, with the company reporting that nearly all the water used in processing is recovered and reused.

Once separated from the nonmetallic material, the resulting concentrate can be sold to third-party processors or undergo further treatment through a second process intended to recover individual metals.

Unlike the initial separation stage, Modern Mining's proposed aqueous purification process uses controlled chemical solutions to separate and enrich gold, silver, copper, palladium, and other valuable metals for sale into domestic and international industrial supply chains.

Alongside those metal-recovery operations, the company directs separated plastics to downstream recycling facilities and waste handlers, while continuing to examine how the two processing stages could operate together as part of a larger commercial facility.

During an initial demonstration in 2023, Modern Mining processed approximately 3,000 pounds of discarded circuit boards into roughly 1,000 pounds of metallic sand concentrate, which was subsequently purchased by third-party buyers after independent testing confirmed that it met their purchasing requirements.

Continuing that work at Greenville, Modern Mining conducted additional processing campaigns using different electronic waste materials, with filings to the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission documenting 41 product-lot settlements between December 2023 and June 2026.

Despite those sales, the company remained in the development and pre-commercialization stage through the first half of 2026, recording proceeds from its pilot activities as other income rather than revenue generated through established commercial operations.

Through its combined pre-concentration and purification system, Modern Mining has established a recovery objective exceeding 90% of the economically valuable metals contained in its feedstock, although those results have not yet been demonstrated through sustained commercial-scale processing.

Continuing work at Greenville has therefore focused on equipment testing, processing improvements, and evaluating the conditions needed to increase throughput, providing the technical foundation for Modern Mining's plans to move from individual demonstration campaigns toward continuous commercial production.

Toward commercial production

To move the technology toward commercial production, Modern Mining is developing plans for a processing facility in North Carolina that would incorporate both its pre-concentration and aqueous purification systems, with engineering studies examining equipment requirements, operating capacity, plant design, and the infrastructure needed for expansion.

Under the proposed commercial design, an initial pre-concentration plant would process approximately 8,000 metric tons of electronic waste annually, while an accompanying purification plant would be capable of processing metal concentrates from as many as four pre-concentration facilities.

Over the longer term, Modern Mining intends to establish additional pre-concentration plants near major sources of discarded electronics, allowing metal-bearing materials to be separated closer to suppliers before the resulting concentrates are transported to centralized purification facilities.

Having generated income from demonstration sales but not yet established commercial revenue, Modern Mining remained dependent on outside financing to advance construction plans for its first commercial processing facility in North Carolina.

To help fund that transition, the company pursued an initial public offering in the United States and a separate Canadian offering under a prospectus filed in five provinces.

Across those offerings, Modern Mining sold 9,411,764 common shares priced at $4.25 each, with its stock beginning trading on the NYSE American under the symbol MDRN.

After commissions and offering expenses, Modern Mining expects approximately $34.8 million in net proceeds, with its SEC offering circular outlining plans to direct 50% toward capital expenditures, 30% toward working capital and general corporate purposes, 15% toward marketing, and 5% toward additional research and development.

Describing the next stage of the company's growth, Basi said the financing would support increased processing capacity, expanded operations, and further improvements to the company's recycling technology.

"With the financing complete, our focus is on execution and scaling the business," he said.

Modern Mining intends to complete the initial commercial plant's construction and equipment installation within six months of the IPO, followed by commissioning and operational improvements intended to increase throughput to approximately 20 to 25 metric tons of electronic waste daily within a year.

Between 12 and 18 months after the offering, the company is targeting sustained commercial operations and revenue.

Alongside the proposed expansion, Modern Mining intends to pursue R2 certification, an electronics recycling standard covering environmental management, worker safety, data security, and the handling of discarded equipment, while continuing research aimed at improving metal recoveries and expanding the types of electronic waste its technology can process.

Before those commercial targets can be achieved, however, Modern Mining must secure dependable supplies of printed circuit boards and other suitable electronic waste, along with customers for its recovered metals, with its latest offering circular reporting no binding feedstock supply commitments or product offtake agreements.

name: Texas Environment
title: Texas data centers are staring down a December limbo | Latitude Media
authors: Lisa Martine Jenkins, Jeff Young, Victoria Yang, Maeve Allsup, Catherine Boudreau
description:
It’s going to be a strange winter for Texas data center developers, and for the companies betting on providing them with power.
Greg Abbott’s data center audit, which stopped approving grid connections for new data centers and crypto mines of 75 megawatts or more until regulators have the chance to review them.
But no matter what happens, there are no guarantees even for the data centers who get rubber-stamped next month.
Of course, there are large loads that need power other than data centers; Texas’ manufacturing output is accelerating “sharply” this year according to the Federal Reserve Bank of Dallas.
In June, ERCOT reported that of its 474-GW pipeline of large loads that it is tracking, roughly 90% are data centers.
text:
It’s going to be a strange winter for Texas data center developers, and for the companies betting on providing them with power. They were already waiting to hear the results of Gov. Greg Abbott’s data center audit, which stopped approving grid connections for new data centers and crypto mines of 75 megawatts or more until regulators have the chance to review them.

So far, ERCOT has provisionally let some 200 projects totaling 66.4 gigawatts keep their place in line, and has already shut out over 350 projects totaling more than 300 GW. That leaves nearly 170 GW worth of projects still waiting for the Texas green light, according to a Latitude Intelligence analysis of the queue.

Clarity on the review process, known as “Batch Zero,” has long been expected in December. But then Democrat Gina Hinojosa won the election for governor, ending the GOP’s 30-year run in the governor’s mansion, and raising questions about how and if she’ll maintain Gov. Abbott’s plans.

The state is the second-largest data center market in the U.S., and in her campaign, Hinojosa blamed Abbott for that explosive growth; Abbott just a year ago declared Texas the “epicenter of AI development,” and offered incentives for qualifying data centers looking to build in the state. Hinojosa said she would block new construction until state lawmakers can pass stronger restrictions, including on water and energy use. She takes office on January 19, 2027.

Of course, Hinojosa can’t do everything on her own. Passing laws like Senate Bill 6, which rewrote the rules for how large loads connect to and operate on the grid, requires lawmaker cooperation — and after Democrats also took the statehouse this month, 2027 will be the first time in 25 years that there will be a partisan split in the legislature. But her predecessor froze the load queue via letters to the Public Utilities Commission, ERCOT, and the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality, which means that Hinojosa can do the same.

Analysts for the investment bank Jefferies said in a post-election note that they’re skeptical that the new governor will reverse changes already implemented by Abbott. Instead, they anticipate that “the most plausible policy outcome is a legislative compromise that codifies consumer protections and sets guardrails on large-scale development.”

“The pause could be long,” they added, though they “expect Texas to build significant data centers in 2028 [and beyond]. Those already underway appear to be accelerating.”

The reasoning behind the Abbott pause, as well as Hinojosa’s stated plans, includes concerns about whether data centers are driving up costs for ratepayers. But because of the peculiarities of the Texas market, the absence of new data centers could also have a direct impact on prices, both for consumers and for power producers. Wholesale power for future years already trades at prices that assume, according to Jefferies, about six GW of grid-connected data centers each year. If those facilities don’t arrive, those prices fall. That is good for bills, and bad for the companies that own power plants.

The market is already responding to the potential that data center development will slow; both NRG and Vistra stock prices fell 14% post-election.

The decisions to come

Elizabeth K. Whitney, managing principal at the government relations firm Meguire Whitney, said data centers are certainly concerned about what a blue Texas could mean for their work. But there’s a potential bright side, she added: Once the state has regulation finalized, especially rules that have been touched by leaders in both parties, that will give future facilities more certainty about the policy regime they’re building under. That’s more than they have in much of the country.

And times had been changing in Texas since long before the election, she pointed out. “If you were thinking that it would be the laissez-faire Wild West forever, your first indication probably should have been Gov. Abbott instituting his pause on new interconnections,” Whitney said.

In Abbott’s last months in office, there are a few key dates for data centers and the energy companies that power them: On Dec. 10, ERCOT will file its verification and community impact reports for the data centers in the queue, which will determine which facilities “passed” the audit. Then on Dec. 17, the state’s current PUC will meet for what may be its last time. (Public utility commissioners have staggered appointments by the governor in Texas, so it’s likely that Gov.-elect Hinojosa will reconfigure some of the group’s make-up.) Their meeting will be the first action on which facilities keep a place in the Batch Zero line. Final Batch Zero classifications are due sometime in December.

But no matter what happens, there are no guarantees even for the data centers who get rubber-stamped next month. In between mid-December and mid-January, those that make it through the Batch Zero process will be in limbo. A project that clears the audit in December will still need for ERCOT to restart approvals and for the state to lift the permit freeze — and both of those decisions will fall on Hinojosa.

Joshua Rhodes, a research scientist with the Webber Energy Group at the University of Texas at Austin, pointed out that this process was always first-of-a-kind and therefore uncertain; the partisan flip is just an added layer of confusion. “It was always a bit unclear how [the information in the audit] was going to be used,” Rhodes said. “And I think it’s probably going to be a lot more scrutinized now.”

An opportunity for influence?

Of course, there are large loads that need power other than data centers; Texas’ manufacturing output is accelerating “sharply” this year according to the Federal Reserve Bank of Dallas. But data centers are by far the biggest opportunity. In June, ERCOT reported that of its 474-GW pipeline of large loads that it is tracking, roughly 90% are data centers.

As a result Rhodes and Whitney emphasized that this window of data center limbo, and especially the months after Gov.-elect Hinojosa takes office, offers a key opportunity for energy companies looking to influence the new policy regime for what has become a major market for emerging energy technologies.

“This will be a negotiation, and that people shouldn’t assume that because a certain party or certain individuals are in power that the policy outcomes are a foregone conclusion,” Whitney said. “It’s really important to be in those rooms and be part of those discussions.”

She distinguished between a process that is focused entirely on restricting data centers, versus one focused on bolstering the grid to ready it for the influx of large loads. “Will policymakers treat the grid as something that’s relatively static, and continue to delegate operational authority to ERCOT and Texas PUC? Or will they pick up the pen and start thinking about how the grid needs to be reimagined in order to accommodate data centers?” she asked rhetorically.

Choosing the latter path, she said, could include embracing grid flexibility or grid utilization or more clean energy on the grid — and it’s on energy solutions providers to pitch those options for “the dual benefit of reducing system costs and providing flexibility, while [bringing] more affordability benefits to consumers.’”

Rhodes agreed, and emphasized that a blue Texas may require energy companies to change how they talk about their work. “In terms of influencing policy in Texas, you’ve only really had to speak Republican for the past 30 years,” he said. “But for the next little while, you’re going to have to learn how to speak Democrat too.”

text:
A new report shows that climate solutions are already working around the world, but greater effort is needed to scale them up and keep the goals of the Paris Agreement within reach

The Belém Mission to 1.5 Report, launched today at a high-level event during COP31 in Antalya, was developed at the request of Parties following COP30. Prepared jointly by the COP29, COP30 and COP31 Presidencies, the report identifies practical solutions to help countries reduce emissions, strengthen resilience and support economic growth.

The report highlights opportunities across energy, industry, agriculture, forests, oceans, health and cities, with a strong focus on clean energy and electrification. Drawing on more than 140 submissions and extensive consultation with governments, business, researchers, financial institutions and civil society, the report shows many solutions are already available and delivering results.

It finds that, with the right finance, technology, capacity building and international cooperation, countries can accelerate climate action while supporting energy security, economic diversification and jobs. The report contributes to global efforts to achieve the goals of the Paris Agreement, including limiting long-term warming and building resilience to climate impacts.

“The Belém Mission to 1.5 Report brings a message of possibility. Many solutions are already delivering results,” said Ana Toni, CEO of the COP30 Presidency. She emphasized that international cooperation can help scale up these solutions and trigger tipping points at which change becomes self-reinforcing, making their benefits available to more countries and communities while keeping 1.5 within reach and strengthening resilience. Toni also highlighted the full operationalization of the Global Implementation Accelerator, supported by a robust and open partner network to scale up practical solutions from the Action Agenda and support countries in implementing their NDCs and NAPs.

At the high-level presentation of the Belém Mission to 1.5 Report, COP31 President Murat Kurum highlighted the gaps between countries’ climate commitments, their implementation and what science requires, emphasizing that every fraction of a degree matters. “I do not see the Belém Mission as a concluding document. I see it as a working document for the period ahead,” he said, underscoring its importance in guiding climate action beyond Antalya. During the event, Kurum also announced the publication of the first draft of the COP31 cover decision, which remains under negotiation. The draft welcomes the Belém Mission to 1.5 Report and includes proposals to advance its recommendations through implementation, the second Global Stocktake and the next NDC cycle.

“The Belém Mission to 1.5 Report doesn’t simply describe the challenge – it explains the solutions. We’ve heard from countries around the world that clean energy and electrification are the key to strengthening energy security, cutting emissions and calming volatile prices,” said Chris Bowen, President of Negotiations for COP31, Australia.

“The Belém Mission to 1.5 sends a clear message: the solutions to address the climate crisis are increasingly within our reach, but commitments alone will not deliver results. Building on the historic agreements reached in Baku, we must now close the gap between ambition and implementation by turning political commitments into concrete action, which will be backed by adequate finance, technology and international cooperation. From Baku to Belém and Antalya, our shared responsibility is to ensure that multilateralism continues to prevail and delivers tangible results for people and the planet,” said Mukhtar Babayev, COP29 President, Azerbaijan.

SEOUL, Nov. 17 (Yonhap) -- Hyundai Motor Co.'s global plant utilization rate fell in the first nine months of this year as vehicle production declined despite increased manufacturing capacity, corporate data showed Tuesday.

The South Korean automaker's overall plant utilization rate stood at 86.1 percent in the January-September period, down from 94.3 percent a year earlier, according to its quarterly report.

Total production capacity rose 3 percent on-year to 3.17 million vehicles, while actual output fell 6 percent to 2.73 million units.

The combined utilization rate of its eight overseas plants dropped to 80.7 percent from 88.5 percent a year earlier.

Hyundai Motor Group Metaplant America in the U.S. state of Georgia recorded the steepest decline, with its utilization rate plunging to 41.4 percent from 68.1 percent over the period.

Production at the plant also fell to 35,000 vehicles from 52,000 units, apparently affected by the expiration of U.S. federal tax credits for electric vehicle (EV) purchases.

In South Korea, the automaker's plant utilization rate fell to 93.6 percent from 101.7 percent, partly due to production disruptions caused by labor strikes.

Domestic output declined 9.8 percent to 1.25 million vehicles in the January-September period from 1.39 million a year earlier.

title: America's auto industry is about to be left behind, and it's not their fault - AutoTalk
description:
Let’s stop the Chinese from doing what Japan and Korea have done to the American auto market.
Let’s protect the domestic market with tariffs, and so the Republicans’ theory goes, tariffs will make the imported competition more expensive and will also encourage local manufacturing.
The domestic market trap It is not unusual for brands to have a domestic market focus, or to focus on their domestic market first and their export market second.
First, China built their domestic market through manufacturer investment incentives and then drove demand through consumer incentives.
Otherwise, policies designed to protect America’s auto industry may ultimately leave it further behind.
text:
The policy dilemma

It started with good intentions, or at least the politicians thought it did. Let’s stop the Chinese from doing what Japan and Korea have done to the American auto market. Let’s protect the domestic market with tariffs, and so the Republicans’ theory goes, tariffs will make the imported competition more expensive and will also encourage local manufacturing.

But decisions on where to build plants take years, while the immediate impact of tariffs is increased prices for many vehicles. The short-term solution to this dilemma was to roll back CAFE, Corporate Average Fuel Economy, based on the logic that lower emissions vehicles cost more to manufacture. But the rolling back of CAFE standards, the earlier removal of US federal tax credits and the fuel crisis caused by the Iran conflict are likely to leave the US car industry with lasting scars. It didn’t need to be this way.

The challenge with tariffs is threefold. Firstly, they put the price up of imported cars for consumers, and more often than not for any given brand, some vehicles are manufactured locally and some are manufactured overseas. Secondly, you hit low-cost cars hard, given that low-cost cars for the American market are often manufactured in one of the neighbouring countries, either Canada or Mexico, until recently encouraged under the United States Mexico Canada Agreement (USMCA). Thirdly, rarely are cars fully made in just one country. They might have an engine made at one plant and final assembly at another. If one of those plants is overseas and one is in America, the imported component will have tariffs applied to it. And so the price of the finished vehicle is again pushed upwards.

Some US-developed electrified products like the Ford Mustang Mach-E, Chevrolet Equinox and Chevrolet Blazer are made in Mexico, which is now subject to tariffs, removing cost advantages that were needed to help build lower volume cars profitably while hitting key price points.

As a result of the removal of US federal tax credits, Ford, Stellantis and GM have been winding back their EV portfolios just as the American-made fuel crisis has encouraged more consumers to switch to EVs. At the tail end of 2025, with weak demand and a clearly signalled removal of the tax credit, product planners across the country saw that their volumes would slip. As the numbers slipped, so did the business case. The first generation of American EVs, Tesla excepted, have struggled to hit volume targets even before the removal of tax credits.

The domestic market trap

It is not unusual for brands to have a domestic market focus, or to focus on their domestic market first and their export market second. The challenge for the US domestic brands is that the vehicles they are being encouraged to sell are not products that are in demand globally. Right now, and in the short term at least, consumers want more fuel-efficient vehicles, whether that’s mild hybrid, plug-in hybrid or full electric (the latter two types being considered New Energy Vehicles). This can be seen overseas, where in markets with little protection or low tariffs, Chinese brands, who excel in electric vehicles, are gaining market share rapidly with their NEVs.

This is a perfect storm for GM, Ford and Stellantis, who need to speed up their NEV development in order to be stronger on the world stage. Yet they are being encouraged to develop and build products locally (with the cost penalties this entails) against the backdrop of weak NEV incentives locally and a less certain medium-term outlook, alongside looser emissions standards.

One only has to look at the strategic intent of the Chinese government in developing their NEV strength. First, China built their domestic market through manufacturer investment incentives and then drove demand through consumer incentives. China aligned strategic intent and desired outcomes with long-term planning (10 to 20 years). Chinese brands have developed a strength in electric vehicles just as the market needs more electric vehicles. Meanwhile, in America, brands are being encouraged to build bigger, less efficient vehicles just as the world is turning away from them.

Taken separately, tariffs, weaker fuel economy standards and the removal of EV incentives can each be defended to a point as a response to immediate political or economic pressures. Together, however, they send America’s carmakers in the wrong direction. Tariffs raise costs across an integrated North American supply chain, while weaker CAFE standards and reduced consumer incentives undermine the scale needed to make efficient and electric vehicles profitable. That may provide short-term relief, but it also reduces the incentives and capabilities to develop products for markets that increasingly value efficiency and electrification.

The danger is not simply that American consumers will have fewer affordable choices. It is that Ford, GM and Stellantis will become increasingly dependent on a protected domestic market while global competitors build scale, lower costs and improve their technology elsewhere.

If US policy is intended to protect domestic manufacturing, it must do more than restrict imports. It must help North American manufacturers build globally competitive vehicles, across the US, Mexico and Canada, and sell them at scale. Otherwise, policies designed to protect America’s auto industry may ultimately leave it further behind.

text:
On November 9, 2026, the U.S. Senate voted 73-25 to advance the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026 (BAAJA), clearing an important hurdle and setting the stage for a final vote on the Senate Floor on comprehensive federal permitting reform legislation. Sponsored by Senators Shelley Moore Capito (R-WV), Mike Lee (R-UT), Sheldon Whitehouse (D-RI), and Martin Heinrich (D-NM), the BAAJA seeks to modernize federal permitting processes, reduce regulatory delays, and provide greater certainty for infrastructure and energy projects.

A central component of the BAAJA is reforming the federal environmental review and permitting process under several core environmental statutes. The legislation proposes several changes intended to address lengthy environmental reviews, permitting delays, and litigation that can affect infrastructure and energy development. Among its most significant provisions, the BAAJA would:

Shorten judicial review window: Establish a 150-day deadline for filing certain legal challenges under the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA), Clean Water Act, and Endangered Species Act. The BAAJA would also generally limit lawsuits to parties who raised their issues in sufficiently detailed comments during the public comment period.

Limit judicial remedies: Generally limit courts from vacating federal authorizations or issuing injunctions based on NEPA violations. Instead, courts would remand matters to agencies for further consideration within a specified timeframe.

Improve permitting efficiency: Provide additional deadlines and procedural requirements for environmental review and improve coordination among federal agencies. For instance, the BAAJA would keep NEPA’s existing one-year deadline for environmental assessments and two-year deadline for environmental impact statements. If passed, however, participating federal agencies would then have 90 days, and nonparticipating agencies 120 days, to decide all outstanding authorizations for the project.

The BAAJA’s advancement is particularly notable because it represents a bipartisan agreement between Republican and Democratic lawmakers. Bipartisan agreement on significant permitting legislation is not a common achievement, making this collaboration an important development. It also reflects growing recognition that federal permitting delays affect projects across multiple sectors and that meaningful reform requires cooperation.

Following the November 9 vote, the Senate is now considering amendments, with a final vote expected during the week of November 16, 2026. The coming days will be critical in determining whether the Senate can reach agreement and advance the bipartisan permitting reform legislation.

For more information, contact Liskow attorneys Greg Johnson, Clare Bienvenu, Emily von Qualen, and Colin North, and visit Liskow’s The Louisiana Industrial Insights Hub to stay up-to-date on further developments.

"Republicans and Democrats alike recognize the need for reforms to unlock investment to build projects that are important to our states. On both sides of the aisle, we understand that our constituents need lower costs and good jobs, communities need economic investment, businesses need certainty, and America needs to build. name: Clean Energy
title: Future Energy Transition Mineral Demands and Barriers for South and Southeast Asia
authors: Seaver Wang, Peter Cook, Ryan Alimento
description:
While the global geological availability of critical minerals is likely sufficient to support energy transition efforts, geographically imbalanced energy transition mineral production and consumption raise concerns around supply chain disruption and import dependence.
This study uses a new, customizable mineral demand model for a wide set of commodities to estimate future energy transition mineral demand in the power generation and transport sectors for India, Bangladesh, and countries in ASEAN.
Results indicate that ASEAN and South Asia may become significant consumers by 2050 on par with developed economies like the United States.
South Asia faces additional nickel, rare earths, copper, polysilicon, and cobalt deficits.
Our results identify mineral supply-demand imbalances that may present future tradeoff risks between import dependence, downstream clean technology manufacturing ambitions, and public policy efforts to secure energy transition mineral supplies.
text: While the global geological availability of critical minerals is likely sufficient to support energy transition efforts, geographically imbalanced energy transition mineral production and consumption raise concerns around supply chain disruption and import dependence. While regions like Europe and the United States are actively studying such vulnerabilities, they remain relatively underexplored for emerging economies. This study uses a new, customizable mineral demand model for a wide set of commodities to estimate future energy transition mineral demand in the power generation and transport sectors for India, Bangladesh, and countries in ASEAN. Results indicate that ASEAN and South Asia may become significant consumers by 2050 on par with developed economies like the United States. In many cases, current mining in South and Southeast Asia falls short of projected regional demands. Both regions lack requisite graphite and lithium production. South Asia faces additional nickel, rare earths, copper, polysilicon, and cobalt deficits. Our results identify mineral supply-demand imbalances that may present future tradeoff risks between import dependence, downstream clean technology manufacturing ambitions, and public policy efforts to secure energy transition mineral supplies. Such results pose important implications particularly for countries like India, Vietnam, and Indonesia seeking to develop domestic solar, battery, and electric vehicle industries. This analysis highlights the need for emerging economies to proactively assess the mineral security considerations of national goals and to adopt efforts including recycling, energy efficiency, materials research and substitution, international cooperation, and mining and processing project development to alleviate supply-demand imbalances.

title: For Critical Minerals, Money Isn't the Problem. Commitment Is.
authors: Kirsten Asdal, Thomas J. Koch, Chryssa Rask, Tao Tan
description:
Washington faces what game theorists call a commitment problem.
On January 1, 2027, a Pentagon rule (DFARS 252.225-7052) barring rare-earth magnets with any Chinese content from defense supply chains is set to take effect, already a year late.
A constituency with its own money at stake becomes a commitment device that a future Congress will be hard-pressed to ignore.
Pooling demand would create both a reliable demand signal and price discovery, important indicators of bankability for would-be investors.
GPO members can include related efforts such as Project Vault, the Trump administration’s $12 billion critical minerals stockpile, to further improve price discovery.
text:
In May 2025, Ford halted its Chicago-based Explorer assembly line for a week. It wasn’t due to a strike or an equipment failure. Rather, it was China’s new licensing regime for exports of rare-earth magnets, which are used in the electric motors that operate braking and steering systems, fuel injectors, and even power seats. In ordinary times, those magnets cost perhaps a few dollars. Put another way, the inability to source a few dollars’ worth of magnets halted production of a $40,000 vehicle.

In the past few years, the United States has come to feel the costs of the Chinese Communist Party’s control of critical chokepoints in rare earths. The response of both parties has been to throw money at the problem: the Pentagon’s Office of Strategic Capital, established under President Joe Biden, was allocated $200 billion of loan authority under President Donald Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act, with $100 billion earmarked specifically for critical minerals. A steady drumbeat of deals shows the office is successfully getting funds out the door.

Capital, ironically, is the easy part. Washington faces what game theorists call a commitment problem. It is a challenge of political economy: rebuilding a supply chain can take a decade or more and require consistent government support because industry fundamentals are unprofitable, and today’s Congress cannot bind tomorrow’s. Meanwhile, the Chinese Communist Party understands perfectly well that its near-monopoly market position means that it can make the same material worthless or priceless on command, providing it a wide array of tools to put pressure on rivals, extract policy concessions, or both.

Some of that pressure is already building. A lobby exists in rare earths, but unfortunately, it is pointed in the wrong direction. On January 1, 2027, a Pentagon rule (DFARS 252.225-7052) barring rare-earth magnets with any Chinese content from defense supply chains is set to take effect, already a year late. Major defense contractors have aggressively moved to push for delays and waivers because no Western source can meet their needs. And no one can blame them as their interest is in securing supply, not in where it comes from.

There is an underappreciation in national security circles that private investors are fundamentally uninterested in funding those deals because they are unprofitable and complex relative to other opportunities. Meanwhile, the danger of relying solely on government funding is political instability for a political system that works on one-year budget and two-year electoral cycles to sustain a program that will take a decade or more to bear fruit.

Washington should intentionally create a counter-constituency that will advocate for a domestic supply chain regardless of who is in office. If Congress and executive branch agencies structure the financing so that defense contractors, automakers, and semiconductor manufacturers come to depend on a domestic supply chain, then they will defend it long after today’s officials are gone. A constituency with its own money at stake becomes a commitment device that a future Congress will be hard-pressed to ignore. There are three ways to build one.

The first mechanism makes companies dependent on a market that does not exist today but that Washington can help create. Buying rare-earth products is hard because prices vary widely by compound, purity, and source. There is no global benchmark like West Texas Intermediate or Brent for oil. Instead, buyers face a patchwork of divergent prices, each negotiated bilaterally and shielded by nondisclosure agreements, with little of it visible to the market. Investors cannot finance, and buyers cannot rely on, projects whose output has no reliable price.

Washington could borrow a model from health care. Hospitals buy many of their supplies and drugs through group purchasing organizations (GPOs), which aggregate demand and bargain collectively. The government can either contract with an existing company or industry association or charter a new organization and pair it with the Defense Logistics Agency’s long experience in bulk procurement. Pooling demand would create both a reliable demand signal and price discovery, important indicators of bankability for would-be investors.

Several start-ups are already trying to build such marketplaces, but none can aggregate demand at scale. The government can create that overnight by requiring the producers it backs to sell a portion of their offtake through the GPO. GPO members can include related efforts such as Project Vault, the Trump administration’s $12 billion critical minerals stockpile, to further improve price discovery. Companies that source through the GPO would therefore have a stake in its survival. Over time, if the GPO consistently operates at a profit, it could be spun off or even sold, much like how the Nasdaq Stock Market spun off from its parent industry association and the New York Stock Exchange de-mutualized, both in 2006.

Both the legal authority and operational precedent for that strategy already exist. Section 708 of the Defense Production Act permits companies to coordinate through “voluntary agreements,” with a limited safe harbor against antitrust claims. The Department of Energy has used it to bring nearly one hundred nuclear fuel companies into a consortium aimed at rebuilding a domestic fuel supply chain. (Russia is the only commercial supplier of high-assay low-enriched uranium.) Critical minerals look similar in that the chokepoint is held by an adversary, and the market is too thin for scattered deals to form a demand signal.

The second mechanism incentivizes companies to coinvest their own capital. Today, in deals such as the one with MP Materials, the government allocates offtake through a waterfall: defense primes first, then the broader defense industrial base, then other U.S. companies, then companies in allied countries, and finally companies in non-embargoed countries. In effect, it gives access away without asking anything in return.

We recently proposed a contingent convertible financing mechanism that would be paired with an offtake commitment and a price floor, which could dynamically change form in response to external events such as Beijing weaponizing supply. We recommended reserving a share of the offtake, say 40 percent, for vetted strategic coinvestors (including firms from allied countries) who put capital into the project alongside the government on a pro rata basis. The rest would still flow through the waterfall, and both would price through the GPO. Such a dynamic could also crowd in capital, as no company wants to sit out while a rival locks up supply.

Institutional investors are unlikely to take part, because those projects could well fail a pure financial underwriting standard. But an automaker or a defense prime or a semiconductor manufacturer might conceive of its return less in financial terms than in terms of guaranteed access to the elements it cannot do without.

U.S. allies already think that way. After China flexed its rare-earth chokepoint against Japan during a maritime dispute in 2010, a Japanese consortium of the private Sojitz Corporation, the state-owned Japan Organization for Metals and Energy Security, with support from the Ministry of Economy, Trade, and Industry, invested $250 million into Australia’s mining company Lynas in return for priority access to the offtake. Since then, Japan’s reliance on China for rare-earth elements has fallen from 90 to 60 percent.

Beijing could still try to deter coinvestors by threatening their interests in China, which is one more reason to bring them in as a group, so no single company or country stands out. A company with skin in the game becomes a fierce defender of the program.

The third mechanism gives the program’s defenders a clear record they can point to. In 2011, the energy company Solyndra, backed by $528 million of taxpayer-funded loans, declared bankruptcy. Politicians of both parties rushed to hold hearings. But by 2014, the Department of Energy’s program as a whole had turned profitable. Still, the Biden-era Loan Programs Office (now the Office of Energy Dominance Financing) managed to issue only about a quarter of its $412 billion loan authority, most of it after the 2024 election, of which $83 billion has since been canceled or restructured. Fifteen years after the event, “Solyndra fear” is still real in Washington and still hamstringing policy.

Projects are most vulnerable after vast sums of taxpayer money have been spent but before they have fully ramped up to create viable alternative sources of supply. Some could fail, whether from Chinese predatory pricing or simple execution risk. The idea is not to prevent failure at all costs but to ensure that isolated failures do not imperil an entire policy.

Washington should judge its investments the way any investor judges a fund, where wins in one project offset losses in another, and communicate it as such. Specifically, the government should systematically track those wins and losses across the whole of government rather than agency by agency, so that the program’s aggregate record is easy to point to. A simple scorecard would give its supporters the data to advocate for continuing the effort.

Today’s critical minerals lobby pushes for delays and waivers. Washington can turn that around. Pooled demand makes an industry bankable, coinvestment puts skin in the game, and portfolio perspective gives supporters ammunition. With a proper alignment of interests, defense contractors, automakers, and semiconductor manufacturers would have every reason to defend the program long after the administration that created it is gone.

A note of caution: A lobby can also outstay its welcome. The constituencies that keep subsidies alive can also keep them alive too long. Such programs should have built-in sunsets tied to output targets and performance, not fixed end dates, which would only tell Beijing how long to wait.

In the years to come, the real test will not be how Beijing acts but what Washington does in response. The questions will be whether a future member of Congress will look askance at long-term offtake agreements in a debt ceiling standoff, or whether a future U.S. trade representative will offer to quietly wind down a price floor to bank a quick win ahead of a summit. Our fear is that the absence of a constituency to answer those questions means that silence will calcify into the answer itself.

title: Why Mercedes Is Trying to Build an EV Battery Without Cobalt - Autoweek
description:
