The breakthrough so far is lithium-iron phosphate (LFP), a chemistry that produces inexpensive packs whose only downside is fairly low energy density.
Approximately 55 percent of the world’s new EVs (including many made in China) use LFP batteries.
Sam Abuelsamid, vice president of market research at Telemetry, said General Motors had originally planned to use LFP batteries for all of its entry-level models.
The 2027 Bolt is equipped with LFP cells from Chinese supplier CATL that give it ok-but-not-great 262-mile range.
text:
At a tech event in Germany last month, Stephan Bach, Mercedes-Benz senior manager of cell technologies and battery concepts, said the company is shooting for 2030 as the year it can finally equip its product line with cobalt-free batteries.

Mined cobalt (often extracted as a byproduct of nickel and copper mining) has been a sore point for EVs since they went mainstream around 2010. The metal has its good points. The typical lithium-ion battery pack contains 10 to 20 pounds of cobalt, which is there to forestall cathode corrosion, increase efficiency and range, and also keep the pack stable—reducing fire risk. The cobalt costs $100 to $400 in an average battery array.

But 70 to 74 percent of the world’s cobalt comes from the Democratic Republic of the Congo, where its extraction at artisanal sites in the southeastern part of the country is linked to horrendous working conditions, low pay, and child labor.

According to Save the Children, “The DRC sees tens of thousands of children working at mine sites daily to support families in making ends meet.” The organization cites the case of 12-year-old Muntosh (not his real name) who was six when he saw his brother die in a cobalt mine. “As his family needed the income, he continued to turn up to work and spent six years in the mines,” Save the Children said.

Children collecting cobalt in the DRC.

Finding a replacement for cobalt has not been easy, but iron-based formulations are leading the way. The breakthrough so far is lithium-iron phosphate (LFP), a chemistry that produces inexpensive packs whose only downside is fairly low energy density. Approximately 55 percent of the world’s new EVs (including many made in China) use LFP batteries. Tesla is a major proponent of LFP but the density issues mean the company’s longer-range versions of the Models 3 and Y use high-nickel cells.

Advertisement - Continue Reading Below

Tesla has promised to reduce cobalt use to “almost nothing.” The company’s supplier Panasonic isn’t there yet, but it manufactures nickel-cobalt-aluminum li-ion cells that have reduced cobalt to five to 10 percent of the cathode weight. Panasonic’s roadmap gets it out of the cobalt business.

The energy density of LFP is still an issue for carmakers. Sam Abuelsamid, vice president of market research at Telemetry, said General Motors had originally planned to use LFP batteries for all of its entry-level models.

The 2027 Bolt is equipped with LFP cells from Chinese supplier CATL that give it ok-but-not-great 262-mile range. “But GM has made such progress with lithium manganese-rich [LMR] batteries that it decided to use that chemistry, with virtually no cobalt, across the board,” Abuelsamid said. GM and its Ultium Cells joint venture with LG are investing up to $1 billion to build LMR cells in Spring Hill, Tennessee.

2027 Chevrolet Bolt.

LMR batteries use a mix of 65 percent manganese and 35 percent nickel. Reducing the nickel content lowers costs. Since importing high-tariff CATL LFP cells from China no longer made sense, GM decided to keep the expensively retooled Bolt (also affected by the loss of the federal tax credit) to a single model year. But other entry-level GM EVs, priced around $30,000, are coming.

There’s an irony here. As the EV market stalled, automakers and startups LFP companies such as Sparkx and TexPower (whose professor partners actually developed LFP) have looked at everything from powering homes to drones and energy storage as promising markets. Considering how many data centers were being built, the market looked bullish, but on November 3, 40 of 41 anti-data center ballot initiatives passed across the states, so the outlook is now cloudy.

Switching to solid-state batteries and abandoning liquid electrolyte doesn’t by itself solve the cobalt problem. “Solid-state batteries can be built with any kind of chemistry, with or without cobalt,” Abuelsamid said. As an example, Factorial Energy, partnered with Mercedes, Hyundai/Kia, Karma and Stellantis on solid-state, is working to eliminate or lessen the use of cobalt with various chemistries, including lithium nickel manganese oxide (LNMO) and LFP.

Mercedes isn’t promising to be done with cobalt by 2030, but it’s an aspirational goal, aided by development of LNMO cells that the company said could improve energy density, lower production costs, and also deliver up to 30 percent more driving range.

text:
PHNOM PENH, Cambodia (AP) — Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said Monday that Canada could turn to Chinese automakers if trade negotiations with U.S. President Donald Trump fail to preserve an integrated North American auto industry.

Carney’s comments in Cambodia came ahead of a planned meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping this week in Shenzhen, China, where Chinese auto manufacturing is expected to be discussed. The two leaders reached an agreement in January allowing tens of thousands of Chinese electric vehicles into Canada at reduced tariffs.

“We have the best auto workers in the world, and we want them fully deployed, full opportunity, in an integrated North American market,” Carney told reporters in Cambodia. “That market has become less integrated because of U.S. trade actions.”

Carney said Saturday in Manila, Philippines, that any trade agreement with Washington must leave Canada with a viable auto industry. He said Monday that negotiations with the United States remain his priority, but their outcome could determine whether Canada pursues alternatives involving European, Chinese or Japanese automakers.

Asked whether potential Chinese investment was leverage in the U.S. negotiations, Carney replied: “It’s not leverage. But action, reaction” on behalf of Canada’s auto workers and manufacturing assets.

“If they’re not fully utilized in a North American context, that provides other opportunities,” Carney said. “Canada is going to move forward either way.”

White House trade adviser Peter Navarro lashed out on social media Monday in response to Carney’s suggestion that Canada could turn to Chinese automakers.

“Are u really threatening to play China off the U.S.? This is offensive in the extreme,” Navarro wrote on X. “You should be far more worried China is going to eat Canada alive.”

The Detroit Three — Ford, General Motors and Stellantis — operate factories across Canada, the United States and Mexico, with parts sometimes crossing borders multiple times before a vehicle is completed. Trump has repeatedly pushed automakers to move production to the United States from Canada.

Carney said any Chinese investment would have to involve substantial manufacturing in Canada rather than simply assembling imported parts. He said it would require proper labor standards, manufacturing facilities and domestic supply chains that expand over time, including the use of Canadian critical minerals in electric vehicles.

“It’s not just about kit cars,” he said. “There has to be a manufacturing aspect involved.”

Under the January agreement, Canada reduced its 100% tariff on Chinese electric vehicles to 6.1%, initially allowing up to 49,000 vehicles annually, with the cap increasing over time. In exchange, China agreed to lower tariffs on Canadian agricultural products, including canola.

Carney said at the time that he expected the agreement to attract Chinese investment in Canada’s auto industry and create jobs.

The deal drew criticism from Ontario Premier Doug Ford, whose province is the center of Canada’s auto industry. Ford warned that allowing Chinese electric vehicles into Canada could threaten Canadian jobs and jeopardize access to the U.S. market.

“The federal government’s focus needs to be on protecting Canadian auto workers, not undermining them by importing even more state-subsidized cheap Chinese cars,” Ford said on social media on Monday.

Trump’s tariffs have battered Canada’s auto industry, potentially unraveling decades of cross-border integration. Canada recently threatened to sue Stellantis after the company moved its plans for Jeep Compass production from Ontario to Illinois and agreed to sell its idled Canadian assembly plant.

Carney said Saturday that he had spoken at length with Trump and senior U.S. officials and that the two countries were making progress toward a possible trade agreement, although differences remained.

Associated Press writer Rob Gillies in Toronto reported from Toronto.

text:
Brownstein Hyatt Farber Schreck is pleased to announce that Jaime Lizárraga, former commissioner of the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) and senior Democratic staffer, will join the firm’s Washington, D.C., office as a policy director in its Government Relations Department on Dec. 1, 2026. A trusted adviser to Democratic congressional leadership, Lizárraga brings more than three decades of experience shaping federal policy and helping drive major legislative and regulatory initiatives.

“Having worked alongside Jaime in Speaker Pelosi’s office, I’ve seen firsthand how deeply he was trusted by House members, the depth of his policy expertise, strategic judgment and ability to navigate complex legislative challenges. Few people have his experience at the highest levels advising House leadership through major economic crises, financial services and budget negotiations combined with his SEC experience,” said Nadeam Elshami, co-chair of the firm’s Government Relations Department. “His guidance during the change in leadership ushered in by the recent elections will be a huge asset for clients navigating the political environment.”

Before joining Brownstein, Lizárraga served for more than 14 years as a senior adviser to Speaker Nancy Pelosi, where he oversaw the speaker’s policy portfolio on financial markets, housing, small business, international finance and immigration. During his tenure, he played a key role in developing and advancing landmark legislation, including the Dodd-Frank Wall Street Reform and Consumer Protection Act, COVID-19 relief measures, the American Rescue Plan and numerous appropriations packages and economic policy initiatives. His extensive experience working with congressional leadership, committee chairs, members of both parties and executive branch officials provides clients with valuable insight into the legislative process and federal policymaking.

Lizárraga later served as a commissioner of the SEC after being nominated by President Joe Biden and unanimously confirmed by the U.S. Senate. In that role, he worked on issues involving capital formation, investor protection, corporate governance and financial market regulation, further expanding his expertise in the intersection of policy, regulation and business.

Earlier in his career, Lizárraga held senior positions with the House Financial Services Committee, the U.S. Department of the Treasury and the SEC. His experience across Congress, federal agencies and the regulatory landscape enables him to help clients anticipate policy developments, engage effectively with decision-makers and navigate complex legislative and regulatory challenges.

“Brownstein’s reputation for delivering results and its deep bipartisan relationships make it one of the premier public policy firms in Washington,” said Jaime E. Lizárraga. “I look forward to joining this talented team and helping clients navigate an increasingly complex policy environment.”

He earned a master’s degree in public affairs from the University of Texas at Austin’s Lyndon B. Johnson School of Public Affairs and a bachelor’s degree in political science from the University of California, San Diego.

Dear Chairman Capito and Ranking Member Whitehouse:

The U.S. Chamber of Commerce strongly supports the nomination of Justin Schwab to be the Assistant Administrator of the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency’s (EPA) Office of Air and Radiation and urges his swift confirmation. Mr. Schwab’s breadth of government service makes him exceptionally qualified for this critical role.

Throughout his career, Mr. Schwab has demonstrated his ability to navigate complex regulatory environments and foster collaboration. He brings a deep understanding and extensive institutional knowledge of the intricacies involved in federal environmental regulation, informed by prior experience at EPA, as well as his vital work in the current administration at both EPA and the Council on Environmental Quality. Mr. Schwab’s ability to navigate complex regulatory environments will be instrumental in ensuring balanced regulatory policy that sustains economic growth and expands opportunity.

Advancing our nation’s clean air agenda and promoting economic growth are not mutually exclusive. Mr. Schwab’s comprehensive understanding of air policy, environmental law, and administrative law will be instrumental to ensuring that EPA regulations are properly constructed within lawful bounds, providing clarity and certainty while avoiding unnecessarily prescriptive requirements and the imposition of excessive costs.

We urge quick consideration by the full Senate of Mr. Schwab’s nomination and look forward to continuing to work with him upon his confirmation.

Sincerely,

Neil L. Bradley

title: Over 400 American AI Data Centers Use As Much Electricity As Wisconsin, Michigan, or Indiana
description:
The number of hyperscale data centers, which are larger and more powerful than traditional data centers, and are often used to train and run large-scale AI models, has exploded in recent years.
That number is only expected to grow: the research firm Synergy estimates that the total capacity of U.S. data centers will double in the next three years, largely driven by the growth of hyperscale data centers.
In 40 out of 41 local ballot initiatives across the country, citizens voted to limit or prevent data center development.
Yet few studies have quantified just how much electricity each hyperscale data center uses, and what fuels generate the electricity, the researchers say.
Virginia, Iowa, and Ohio have the most emissions attributable to hyperscale data centers, while Oregon, which is home to more hyperscale data centers than Iowa and Ohio, has significantly fewer emissions due to a cleaner energy grid.
text:
America's hyperscale data centers together use as much electricity as some entire U.S. states and produce millions of metric tons of carbon dioxide over the course of a year, according to a new study published Monday in Nature Sustainability.

The number of hyperscale data centers, which are larger and more powerful than traditional data centers, and are often used to train and run large-scale AI models, has exploded in recent years. Between 2019 and 2024, the number of data centers around the world doubled from a little over 500 to over 1,100, with more than half located in the United States. That number is only expected to grow: the research firm Synergy estimates that the total capacity of U.S. data centers will double in the next three years, largely driven by the growth of hyperscale data centers.

American voters rallied against data center development in the midterm elections this November, with many citing economic and environmental concerns. In 40 out of 41 local ballot initiatives across the country, citizens voted to limit or prevent data center development. Yet few studies have quantified just how much electricity each hyperscale data center uses, and what fuels generate the electricity, the researchers say.

"Even though there were a lot of [public and scientific] statements about the environmental impact of data centers, when we started this research, we realized that there was basically very little, if none, peer-reviewed data," says Francesca Dominici, director of the Harvard Data Science Initiative and senior author of the paper.

The study provides one of the first facility-level estimates of the electricity use and carbon dioxide emissions of hyperscale data centers since the rise of AI. The researchers used satellite imagery to build a list of 403 hyperscale data centers across the U.S., and then estimated the annual electricity consumption for each facility between May 2024 and April 2025 under a range of operating scenarios. They then used data from the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency to calculate their emissions.

They found that, together, the data centers used between 68 and 99 terawatt-hours (TWh) of electricity—with the upper estimate equivalent to what some states, like Indiana, Michigan, and Tennessee, use in a year. In the lower scenario, the facilities still consumed approximately the annual electricity sold to customers in Wisconsin, roughly 70 TWh, or Minnesota, around 65 TWh.

More than half of the electricity powering the data centers comes from fossil fuels, primarily natural gas and coal. The facilities studied produced a combined estimated 25.7 million metric tons of carbon dioxide—roughly the annual emissions of Denmark.

Half of the electricity use of all the data centers studied was concentrated in just four states: Virginia, Oregon, Ohio, and Iowa, the report found. Virginia has long been known as "data center alley" due to its high number of data centers, but size and power capacity can also impact electricity consumption. The researchers identified 26 hyperscale facilities in Iowa, combined electricity consumption for which was approximately 7.2 TWh, with the average facility having substantially higher estimated electricity demand than the average facility in Virginia, where 142 hyperscale facilities account for approximately 21.4 TWh of annual electricity consumption.

However, the emissions impacts were not always the same. Virginia, Iowa, and Ohio have the most emissions attributable to hyperscale data centers, while Oregon, which is home to more hyperscale data centers than Iowa and Ohio, has significantly fewer emissions due to a cleaner energy grid.

"For the same amount of electricity consumed, the regional electricity mix associated with data centers in Wyoming produces approximately seven times more carbon dioxide than in Oregon," says Gianluca Guidi, Harvard data scientist and the study's lead author. "So these environmental impacts are not necessarily inevitable. Geography matters."

Without clean energy alternatives, U.S. data centers are projected to consume more natural gas than most countries by 2035, according to a report from BloombergNEF.

The electricity demand and carbon emissions are likely even higher than the research shows. The team did not have enough data to assess every single hyperscale data center in the U.S. at the time, and more data centers have emerged since their study concluded in April 2025.

The researchers hope to continue to quantify the environmental impacts of hyperscale data centers to better understand their impact on air pollution, water, and health, adding that, as AI continues to scale, its infrastructure growth must be done sustainably.

"We tend to imagine AI as something that is almost immaterial, but in the end, the infrastructure power is profoundly physical," says Guidi. "Behind every algorithm, there are enormous buildings, power plants, water resources, and ultimately also communities that live with the consequences."

HAMILTON, Mont., Nov. 16, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Local Bounti Corporation (NYSE: LOCL) ("Local Bounti" or the "Company"), a breakthrough U.S. indoor agriculture company currently servicing approximately 13,000 retail doors, today announced that it has entered into an agreement to purchase Revol Greens' two certified-organic controlled environment agriculture (CEA) facilities located in Texas and Minnesota. The Texas facility spans 20 acres and the Minnesota facility spans 10 acres. Together, the 30 acres of certified-organic production will add a new capability and product offering for Local Bounti. The transaction will increase the Company's total growing capacity by roughly 70%, to approximately 73 acres, and is expected to close in the coming days, subject to customary closing conditions.

"We are excited to add these two facilities to our production footprint to meet growing customer demand," stated Kathleen Valiasek, President and CEO of Local Bounti. "Our existing capacity of approximately 43 acres is sold out. Buying rather than building has two clear advantages: speed to market and cost. First, we will be adding 30 acres of certified-organic greenhouse capacity that is already growing and selling to retailers, as we work toward our goal of being Nationally Known, Locally Grown. Second, the purchase price is considerably lower than the cost to build comparable new capacity, and the additional capacity is expected to be accretive to Local Bounti's earnings.

"Specifically, the Minnesota facility will expand our growing and distribution presence into the Midwest with a new local growing facility, which aligns with our previously communicated plans to enter this market and enables us to better serve customers in the region. In Texas, the facility will complement our existing presence in the region and provide us with additional capacity to service the large and growing Southern U.S. market where we've already built a network of growing and distribution operations that spans from California to Georgia.

"These facilities use growing processes that we've used in our existing network and fit naturally with our operations, with the potential to implement our patented Stack & Flow Technology® to drive future yield increases. Further, these facilities are certified organic, adding a new organic offering to our portfolio and allowing us to meet additional customer preferences. Retailers and consumers know and trust the Revol brand, and we look forward to building on that trust as we expand our national footprint."

Dirk Aleven, Chief Executive Officer of FoodVentures and President of Revol Greens, said, "Having operated these greenhouses day to day, I know what these facilities are capable of, and Local Bounti is the right home for them. Local Bounti brings the retail relationships and operating know-how to get the most out of these greenhouses and to serve customers close to where they shop. FoodVentures and DENSO are committed to the future of controlled environment agriculture, and we are pleased to support Local Bounti as it brings these facilities into its network."

FoodVentures, a Netherlands-based developer and operator of high-tech greenhouses and a stakeholder in Revol Greens, became a consolidated subsidiary of DENSO Corporation in 2026. DENSO, one of the world's largest automotive technology suppliers, has been building its agriculture business since 2017, including through its investment in greenhouse provider Certhon.

Both facilities use Deep Water Culture, a growing process Local Bounti already operates, and produce baby leaf products similar to its existing assortment, creating opportunities to increase product velocities with existing customers and pursue new retail and distribution opportunities. Both also bring established customer relationships, including new customers as well as existing Local Bounti customers across new distribution centers and regions, and have the flexibility to support head lettuce production in the future. Identified upgrades are expected to increase production per square foot by approximately 30%, with the potential to implement the Company's patented Stack & Flow Technology® over time.

The acquisition is also expected to include the Revol brand and related intellectual property.

Local Bounti's sustainable growing methods are better for the planet, using 90% less land and 90% less water than conventional farming methods. With a mission to 'revolutionize agriculture, ensuring accessibility to fresh, sustainable, locally grown produce and nourishing communities everywhere for generations to come,' Local Bounti's food is fresher, more nutritious, and lasts longer than traditional agriculture. text:
FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE: November 16, 2026

Contact: Katie Valentine, kvalentine@cacampaign.org

“Coal is Killing Us:” Local Electeds, Health Experts, and Community Leaders Across the Country Demand an End to the Trump Administration’s Policies Propping up Coal

Events in five states highlight the toll the Trump administration’s coal policies are having on communities’ health, pocketbooks, and the safety of our climate

WASHINGTON, D.C. – This week, local leaders, health experts, and community members are coming together to demand an end to the Trump administration’s use of taxpayer dollars to prop up the coal industry. Through events in five states – Michigan, Arizona, Colorado, Georgia, and Florida – communities are speaking up about the dangerous ways coal is affecting their health, destroying the climate, and contributing to higher prices on their energy bills. The first of these events, in Phoenix, Arizona, is kicking off on Monday.

“Coal is killing us. It’s poisoning our air, wrecking our climate, and jacking up our bills at a time when costs are top-of-mind for American families,” said Climate Action Campaign Director Margie Alt. “This week, Americans across the country are stepping up and saying: No more. No more to polluted air and water, no more to skyrocketing energy bills, no more to the deepening climate crisis that coal brings, and no more corrupt dealings with fossil fuel interests.”

Since taking office in 2025, the Trump administration has deepened Americans’ reliance on coal, one of the dirtiest, costliest and most toxic fossil fuels in use today. The administration has gutted pollution standards, including critical protections against Mercury and Air Toxics and carbon pollution. Those rollbacks present a major concern for Americans’ health: The MATS protections were expected to create $300 million in health benefits over ten years.

“Coal power plants have been harming health for as long as they have existed, and health professionals have been ringing the alarm on this issue for decades,” said Brian Campbell, PhD, Executive Director of Physicians for Social Responsibility. “There is no logical reason to prolong our reliance on coal when cleaner, more affordable options are available. Our current cost of living crisis is impossible to ignore, and giveaways to fossil fuels are only making the situation more dire. Between soaring utility prices and healthcare costs, the American people have had enough of dirty energy.”

Research has shown that communities near coal plants suffer higher rates of asthma, heart disease, cancer, and premature death, so any policy that props up coal plants is putting communities’ – and especially our most vulnerable community members’ — health in danger.

"As an oncologist, Trump’s coal policies put my patients in danger," said Joan Schiller, Chair of the Steering Committee at Oncology Advocates United for Climate and Health International. "Coal-fired power plants and the pollution they produce have been directly linked to multiple kinds of cancer, and are also a major driver of climate change, which puts my already-vulnerable patients at risk in another way: via increasingly dangerous and destructive weather. We call on the administration to stop propping up this dangerous industry – for the sake of cancer patients and all Americans."

"Burning coal releases fine particles and toxic pollutants that older adults and children breathe in, driving up suffering from asthma attacks, heart and lung disease, and hospital visits,” said Paloma Greenwald, MA BSN RN, with Elders Climate Action. “We demand protections for children whose lungs are still developing, and older adults who are more likely to have exacerbations of heart and lung conditions.”

The administration also sought to bail out coal with taxpayer money, announcing in June a $700 million coal industry bailout under the little-used Defense Production Act, funding that would go towards new coal plants and a new coal export terminal. And they’ve kept dirty, expensive coal plants running far past their planned retirement dates, with the Department of Energy unlawfully issuing emergency orders to keep 6 coal-fired power plants open beyond their scheduled retirements.

“The Trump administration is abusing emergency powers to force dirty coal plants to keep running, at the expense of communities across the country,” said Michael Lenoff, Senior Attorney at Earthjustice. “The administration must follow the law and stop harming our lungs, our water, and our wallets.”

Propping up aging coal plants is expensive, and the costs continue to rise. According to a new analysis by the Environmental Defense Fund, in 2024, it was 28% more expensive to generate power using coal than it was in 2021. Household energy bills have risen 16% compared to before Trump took office.

“Trump’s coal bailout shows exactly where his priorities lie: with ultra-wealthy fossil fuel donors, not the American people,” said Climate Power Communications Director Alex Glass. “Instead of investing in American-made, affordable clean energy, Donald Trump is using taxpayer dollars to prop up an industry that is making us sicker and spiking our energy costs. This week, Americans across the country are making it clear that they are tired of footing the bill for his obsession with dirty, expensive coal.”

Trump’s relentless federal support of coal is having real impacts on American families. In Michigan, the J.H. Campbell power plant has been kept online to an estimated tune of nearly $300 million, with ratepayers in Michigan and 10 surrounding states set to pay the bill. On November 14, the U.S. Department of Energy issued yet another emergency order under the Federal Power Act, forcing the Campbell coal plant to stay open through mid-February 2027 – a move that’s in defiance of a federal appeals court decision this fall ruling that the DOE does not have the emergency authority to keep the plant running.

“The Trump administration has put dirty coal power plants slated for decommissioning on life support – effectively taking money out of consumers’ pockets and putting into the the wallets of coal barons who heavily lobbied him,” Tracey Lewis, senior legislative and policy counsel with Public Citizen’s Energy Program. “His corrupt attempt to revive an industry that was rightly on the path to oblivion does a disservice to the American economy and our health.”

Costs were a central concern of voters this midterm election, and they roundly rejected the costly energy policies of the Trump administration, including the administration’s actions to prop up coal. Clean, affordable energy like wind and solar, meanwhile, were a clear desire for voters this election cycle.

“The midterm election could not have been a clearer rejection of the Trump Administration," said Matthew Davis, LCV Vice President for Federal Policy. "People are sick and tired of rising costs, especially on their energy bills. At every turn, this administration has done everything it can to make the problem worse, propping up expensive aging coal fired power plants and undermining cheaper clean energy options. Communities are standing up to Trump and his allies for leaving us with nothing but polluted communities and a higher bill to show for it.”

“For two years, Donald Trump has been using every tool in the box to prop up the dying, deadly, and expensive coal industry,” said Sierra Club Climate Policy Director Patrick Drupp. “Last week, Americans sent a strong message that they are sick and tired of skyrocketing costs and they are through with Donald Trump’s corruption. Our communities deserve a future with affordable, clean energy that protects our public health and our environment, and we will continue to fight to deliver that future”

“Instead of investing in cleaner, safer and less expensive sources of energy, the Trump administration is doubling down on unreliable power plants that put Americans’ health at risk,” said Surbhi Sarang, Director and Senior Attorney, Clean Power with Environmental Defense Fund. “Technology is available for coal plants to reduce their pollution, but the Trump administration is ignoring these solutions and instead taking extreme actions to prop up the coal industry and allow them to pollute more at the expense of American families.”

If you’d like more information about the events kicking off this week, please email Katie Valentine, kvalentine@cacampaign.org.

text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — The Energy Department has again extended an order forcing an aging Michigan coal-fired power plant to stay open past its scheduled retirement date, defying a court order that set aside the agency's previous actions as unlawful.

Energy Secretary Chris Wright issued an emergency order late Friday extending the continued operation of the 64-year-old J.H. Campbell Generating Plant near Grand Rapids, saying the plant is needed to prevent blackouts and preserve customers' access to reliable, secure electricity.

The Energy Department said it disagrees with the September decision by a three-judge panel on the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit and has petitioned for a rehearing in front of the entire court.

The emergency order is among a series of actions by President Donald Trump and his administration to boost the struggling U.S. coal industry, including a plan announced in June to spend nearly $700 million to support ​coal-fired power plants and coal exports.

The Environmental Protection Agency, meanwhile, has repealed rules that limit planet-warming greenhouse gas emissions from power plants fueled by coal and natural gas. The agency under Administrator Lee Zeldin also is moving to prevent future administrations from regulating climate pollution from power plants.

Environmental groups slammed the latest emergency order on coal — the seventh such declaration for the Campbell plant since May 2025 — and said there is no evidence that the Michigan plant has ever been needed to avoid a grid emergency or prevented power outages. The extension order costs families in the Midwest more than $600,000 per day to keep the old, polluting plant online, they said.

“At a time when prices are soaring and Americans are struggling to make ends meet, the Trump administration’s decision to issue yet another illegal and expensive extension is punishing,” said the Sierra Club's Jessi Eidbo.

According to a Burning Money tracker compiled by the group, the administration’s orders extending the lives of fossil fuel plants in six states have cost ratepayers more than $600 million, with over half of that total stemming from the Campbell plant in Michigan.

“Instead of saving families’ money and letting the plant retire as planned, the Trump administration keeps putting its thumb on the scale for costly coal," said Ted Kelly, director of U.S. clean energy at Environmental Defense Fund, another environmental group.

Wright and other officials have said the Campbell plant and others are needed to ensure reliable electricity, and he used emergency powers to keep them operating. Environmental groups and multiple states — including Michigan, Illinois and Minnesota — went to court to try to overturn orders keeping the plants online.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit sided with the states and the groups, saying there was no real emergency under the law. A decision is pending on whether the full Appeals Court will hear the case, which could end up at the Supreme Court.

text:
Increasing the number of Eligible Electric Vehicles Continues Connecticut’s Commitment to Clean Air and Expanding Options for Moderate Income Residents Seeking Cleaner Transportation Options With Lower Lifetime Maintenance Costs

(HARTFORD) — The Connecticut Department of Energy and Environmental Protection (DEEP) announced today that it is making more used electric vehicles eligible for the Connecticut Hydrogen and Electric Vehicle Purchase Rebate (CHEAPR) program effective November 16, 2026. The CHEAPR program offers incentives to Connecticut residents who purchase or lease an eligible new or used battery electric (BEV) or plug-in hybrid electric (PHEV) vehicle from a licensed Connecticut automobile dealership or original equipment manufacturer.

DEEP has made an important change to the CHEAPR Program guidance for used vehicles. Effective November 16th, used vehicles will be eligible for the CHEAPR Rebate+Used program if the price paid at the time of purchase or lease, excluding any discounts, taxes, fees, accessories or warranties, is $35,000 or less regardless of the model year of the vehicle. Prior to this date, vehicles were required to be between 1 and 3 model years old with an original MSRP of $50,000. Prior to purchasing or leasing a used EV be sure the vehicle is on this list of eligible used vehicles. If it is not on the list, please contact cheapr@engergycenter.org and they will help get the vehicle listed if it is eligible. Private sales are not eligible for a CHEAPR incentive.

The Rebate+Used incentive provides up to a $5,000 incentive for prequalified low- and moderate-income families and residents of environmental justice communities to help offset the cost of an eligible used electric vehicle. Today’s announcement will significantly increase the number of eligible vehicles available for eligible Connecticut drivers. There remains significant interest in Rebate+ with demand slightly ahead of 2025. DEEP will continue to monitor demand for this popular program, and work with the CHEAPR board and the Connecticut General Assembly to ensure the program continues to support Connecticut drivers.

“With gasoline and diesel prices at all-time highs, it’s more important than ever that the CHEAPR program meet Connecticut drivers where they are,” said DEEP Acting Commissioner Emma Cimino. “Connecticut’s CHEAPR rebate remains a popular incentive that has helped almost 28,000 drivers get behind the wheel of an EV and benefit from lower fuel and lifetime maintenance costs.”

EVs can be CHEAPR over the long term

Cars and trucks cost us more than their up-front purchase price. These costs are called the “total cost of ownership” or “TCO” and many factors go into determining their impact. TCO includes upfront costs such as purchase price, taxes and registration fees; recurring costs such as fuel, maintenance, repairs and insurance; and end of ownership costs that reflect depreciation in the resale value of the vehicle.

While BEVs may not be right for everyone, if you tend to purchase used vehicles and hold on to them for a while, then a BEV will likely cost you less over the long run. BEVs are inherently more efficient than internal combustion vehicles because more energy goes to moving the vehicle and less is wasted as heat, and electricity is usually less expensive than gasoline when used as a transportation fuel (e.g., at Connecticut’s retail electric rate and assuming average efficiency of 3.5kWh, fueling with electricity is equivalent to paying about $2.66/gallon). EVs require less maintenance (no oil changes, water pumps, timing belts, etc.), and their brakes last longer because BEVs use regenerative braking technologies.

About CHEAPR

CHEAPR provides a cash rebate at the Point-of-Sale (POS) to Connecticut residents who purchase or lease a new eligible vehicle costing up to $50,000 from a licensed Connecticut new car dealer. DEEP launched the CHEAPR program in May of 2015 and since that time has issued over $50 million in rebates to Connecticut residents who have purchased or leased almost 28,000 new or used electric vehicles. Since the beginning of the year, CHEAPR has issued incentives for over 2,700 new EVs, including over 520 for Rebate+.

Incentive levels fall into two buckets: “Standard” and “Rebate +.” All Connecticut licensed drivers are eligible for the standard incentive. To be eligible for Rebate +, a Connecticut licensed driver must be pre-qualified and either meet income thresholds, participate in an identified list of income qualified programs, or reside in either a distressed municipality or an environmental justice (EJ) community. The Rebate + incentive is awarded in the form of a voucher, so applicants must pre-apply to ensure eligibility.

As of October 15, 2026, the Standard incentive for a new battery electric vehicle will be $1,500. The Rebate + incentive for a new battery electric vehicle will be unchanged at $3,000. As this award is issued in addition to and stackable with the Standard incentive, the new total incentive will be $4,500. The Rebate + incentive for a new plug-in hybrid vehicle will be unchanged at $1,500 and is awarded in addition to the Standard incentive, for a total incentive of $2,000. With uncertainty and added expense caused by tariffs, changes in federal policy, and auto manufacturers cancelling their investments in new technology, new electric vehicles remain out of reach for many moderate-income residents, the Rebate+ program also offers incentives for used battery electric and plug-in hybrid electric vehicles. These voucher-based incentives also remain unchanged at $5,000 and $3,000, respectively. Keep in mind that Rebate+ requires pre-approval to ensure eligibility.

About Connecticut’s Air Quality

There are over 2.7 million vehicles registered in Connecticut. Cars and trucks account for almost 70% of smog-forming emissions in Connecticut and almost 44% of our climate pollution. Air quality in Connecticut exceeded the federal health-based standards for ozone (smog) on 17 days in 2026, 22 days in 2025 and 23 days in 2024. Individuals in sensitive groups, including children, the elderly and those with pre-existing health conditions, who are exposed to unhealthy levels of air pollution are at an increased risk of developing respiratory symptoms and may experience shortness of breath or difficulty breathing. Children and people with asthma or other lung disease are most at risk for experiencing these symptoms. People experiencing severe symptoms are more likely to miss work or school and seek medical treatment.

Helping to put cleaner vehicles on our roads is one of the most effective means to combat air pollution and the associated poor health outcomes while also pushing back on federal cuts to health care and weakened fuel efficiency and emissions standards. CHEAPR helps fill the gap left by the federal government and will remain an important tool to help Connecticut consumers overcome the higher sticker price on a vehicle that will save them money on fuel and maintenance while having a more positive impact on our air quality.

DEEP monitors, tracks, and forecasts daily air quality levels across Connecticut for ozone from May 1st through September 30th each year and for fine particulate matter (PM2.5) each day of the year. On April 30, 2024, DEEP began informing Connecticut’s regulated community and the general public of the ozone season via the State of Connecticut E-mail list serve and posting air quality forecasts on the DEEP web page, available here.

That’s why I’m introducing the bipartisan AGRI-FLOOD Act to help rural communities upgrade aging flood infrastructure, restore watersheds, and strengthen early warning and real-time response systems.
Our rural communities deserve reliable water systems and the peace of mind that comes with knowing their homes and businesses are safe.
The AGRI-FLOOD Resilience and Infrastructure Act directs USDA to establish a Floodplains and Watershed Resilience Program that would provide: Infrastructure assistance.
The Agri-Flood Act is a strong bipartisan step toward strengthening resilience, modernizing critical watershed infrastructure, and supporting economic opportunity in rural communities.
text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. — Today, Congresswoman April McClain Delaney (D-MD) and Congresswoman Carol Miller (R-WV) introduced the bipartisan AGRI-FLOOD Resilience and Infrastructure Act(link is external), legislation to help rural communities prepare for severe flooding, protect farmland, and reduce taxpayer costs of disaster recovery.

The bill would establish a new U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) program to modernize aging dams and flood control systems, restore floodplains and wetlands, and improve flood risk information and emergency preparedness. Rather than reinforcing costly disaster recovery programs, this bill prioritizes prevention measures that reduce damage to rural lands and infrastructure while protecting our country’s food security and supply chains.

“Last year’s flooding in Westernport devastated families and underscored the need to better prepare our rural communities,” said Congresswoman McClain Delaney. “Our neighbors deserve to feel safe in their homes and have the tools to prepare for the next flood. That’s why I’m introducing the bipartisan AGRI-FLOOD Act to help rural communities upgrade aging flood infrastructure, restore watersheds, and strengthen early warning and real-time response systems. Investing in prevention now can save lives and spare families the heartbreak and expense of rebuilding. ”

“In West Virginia, aging dams and outdated infrastructure leave many of our communities vulnerable to devastating floods. Our rural communities deserve reliable water systems and the peace of mind that comes with knowing their homes and businesses are safe. This vital legislation will strengthen USDA watershed programs, which support a variety of resilience activities including dam repairs, road upgrades, and rural water infrastructure while cutting unnecessary government red tape that slows down critical projects. Flooding threatens lives and devastates communities. We must do everything we can to prepare for disasters before they strike and ensure West Virginia has the most up to date infrastructure,” said Congresswoman Miller.

The AGRI-FLOOD Resilience and Infrastructure Act directs USDA to establish a Floodplains and Watershed Resilience Program that would provide:

Infrastructure assistance. Financial and technical support to modernize aging dams and flood control infrastructure in rural communities.

Watershed restoration. Projects to restore floodplains, wetlands, and degraded watersheds to reduce future flood risks.

Better flood risk information. National flood risk assessments and publicly accessible flood maps to support local planning and preparedness.

Read the bill HERE(link is external)

Endorsees Quotes:

“We thank Representatives April McClain Delaney and Carol Miller for introducing the AGRI-FLOOD Act and recognizing the value of protecting both people and rivers through smart conservation investments,” said Tom Kiernan, President, American Rivers Action Fund . “Floodplain restoration and easements are a proven land-management strategy that supports landowners while conserving flood-prone land. These USDA programs provide multiple benefits — from storing floodwaters and improving water quality to creating critical wildlife habitat and helping rivers reconnect with their natural floodplains. Healthy rivers and floodplains make communities more resilient to increasingly severe floods and storms.”

“ASFPM supports the overall goals of the AGRI-FLOOD Resilience and Infrastructure Act because the legislation advances proactive flood risk reduction, watershed resilience, nature-based solutions (including restoration of wetlands), and modernization of aging flood infrastructure,” states Chad Berginnis, Executive Director of the Association of State Floodplain Managers. “We note that NRCS assisted in designing, planning, and constructing nearly 12,000 watershed dams to control flooding and prevent damage to communities since the 1950s. As these dams have aged, surrounding areas have developed, and rainfall patterns have changed, flooding has increased. Rural communities in particular, need assistance to better identify, assess, and mitigate flood risk. ASFPM looks forward to working with Congress and NRCS on this bill as it moves through the legislative process.”

“We thank Representatives April McClain Delaney and Carol Miller for introducing this important legislation to strengthen the nation’s watershed infrastructure,” said Gene Stauborn, Executive Director, National Watershed Coalition. “This bill will help prioritize rehabilitation of high hazard dams that are critical to protecting rural communities, while also generating jobs, supporting agricultural economies, and ensuring these aging structures continue to provide flood protection, water management, and public safety benefits for future generations. By reducing barriers and increasing federal support, this legislation will help local sponsors move urgently needed projects forward without delay.”

“Counties play a critical role in building flood-resilient infrastructure across our nation's rural communities,” said Matthew Chase, Executive Director of the National Association of Counties. “The AGRI-FLOOD Resilience and Infrastructure Act provides targeted technical assistance and financial support for watershed resilience and flood protection efforts, helping rural county leaders better protect our communities. Counties urge Congress to swiftly pass this bipartisan legislation.”

“ASCE strongly supports a watershed management approach that considers all residents within a watershed basin. Rural communities are adversely affected by lack of resources to reduce flood risk, implement plans to mitigate the effects of natural disasters, and ensure that water resources infrastructure is able to withstand increasingly severe weather events. The AGRI-FLOOD Resilience and Infrastructure Act will provide needed assistance to rural communities by providing financial and technical assistance for pre-disaster flood risk reduction, prioritizing projects to improve resilience of high-hazard dams that could otherwise result in loss of life in the event of dam failure, and ensure that accurate and up to date data are available to stakeholders to help improve safety preparation and response capability. ASCE is proud to support this critical bipartisan legislation.” - Marsha Anderson Bomar, President, American Society of Civil Engineers (ASCE)

“Rural communities, farmers, and local businesses are facing growing risks from flooding and aging water infrastructure. The Agri-Flood Act is a strong bipartisan step toward strengthening resilience, modernizing critical watershed infrastructure, and supporting economic opportunity in rural communities. American Sustainable Business Network supports policies that invest in resilient infrastructure solutions that are good for businesses, farmers, and communities alike.”

— Liza LaManna, Manager of Agriculture and Water Policy, American Sustainable Business Network

"As the U.S. faces increasing climate risks, we must also acknowledge that extreme precipitation events are becoming more frequent, making the prevalence of high-hazard dams unacceptable. That is why we strongly support the Agri-Flood Resilience and Infrastructure Act as a means of providing States, local governments, Tribal Nations, and territories with the resources they need to improve resilience against flooding in their communities on an expedited timeline." – Jeff Diamond, Institute for Agriculture and Trade Policy

name: Congress
title: Ezra Klein's Misplaced Hopes About the Permitting Bill - Earthjustice
description:
Regarding clean energy deployment, Rhodium projects a wide range of outcomes, from deployment of as little as 17 GW to as much as 249 GW over the current baseline.
In short, it is unconvincing to promote BAAJA, standing alone, as an affordability bill or a climate bill.
On the red tape front, Klein points to the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA) as the problem, and the Sunzia transmission line as the evergreen example of permitting dysfunction.
The bill would also allow states to take over Endangered Species Act permitting, a move that would jeopardize the survival of imperiled species while complicating the federal permitting process immensely.
Transmission reforms have bipartisan appeal: gas-fired power plants will benefit from expanded transmission capacity as much or more than clean energy generators.
text:
Ezra Klein is urging Congress to roll the dice on the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA) even though he admits in his latest column that he is “unnerved” by the differing impacts of this bill by Hill staffers and conscious that “legislation at this scale rarely plays out exactly as its architects expect.” As he recognizes, much of the 400+ page bill is “dedicated to technical changes to other laws.” Nevertheless, he remains sure that that the bill will engender better politics and a nation that can deliver all the goods we need.

Earthjustice has analyzed BAAJA, including the recent manager’s amendment, and we have detailed the ways it would change the federal energy and environmental laws that we work with every day. While we very strongly support BAAJA’s package for transmission and grid reforms, the overall deal gives President Trump more power, weakens environmental protections, undermines Tribal sovereignty, and diminishes access to the courts. Very serious changes to bedrock laws and judicial review demand equally serious consideration and debate. But there has been none here – no debates, no committee hearings, no legislative reports. Legislators cannot simply assume that a major overhaul of federal law will make our lives better, not worse.

While the title of Klein’s piece tries to try to sell BAAJA as an affordability bill, there is no modeling to suggest that it will deliver relief that people will feel any time soon, if ever. Commonly-cited modeling by the well-respected Rhodium Group projects annual savings of only $50-78 on household electricity bills in 2040. BAAJA does include important provisions that may compel data centers to cover the costs they impose on the electric grid, but that depends on the development of a new policy at the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) and subsequent implementation by states.

Regarding clean energy deployment, Rhodium projects a wide range of outcomes, from deployment of as little as 17 GW to as much as 249 GW over the current baseline. The high end assumes “continued meaningful cost declines for clean technologies with more expensive fossil fuel prices.” However, BAAJA does nothing to address the perfect storm of tariffs, high interest rates, and lost tax credits that are eroding the competitive cost advantage that renewables should enjoy relative to methane gas. Meanwhile, methane gas prices remain relatively low. For now, we appear to be living in the Rhodium scenario that assumes “much less reduction in the cost of clean resources paired with very low prices for fossil fuels.” That scenario yields only modest incremental gains in clean energy deployment and zero percent reductions in greenhouse gas emissions by 2040. Even in the mid to low emissions scenarios, Rhodium projects cumulative emissions reductions of 3% and 4% respectively by 2040. These projections are all consistent with an ongoing gas rush that BAAJA would speed up.

In short, it is unconvincing to promote BAAJA, standing alone, as an affordability bill or a climate bill. Maybe that is why Klein leans into the intertwined arguments that BAAJA would deliver (1) a victory for a better functioning democracy and (2) an all-around solution for red tape.

Regarding democracy, he states that “[t]he bill represents Democrats and Republicans deciding that the fight over what gets built should play out in elections and markets rather than in the bowels of administrative agencies and courts.” To start, it’s wrong to imply that this bill is the product of any sort of considered bipartisan agreement. Again, there has never been a single hearing on BAAJA, and the Democratic Senators who negotiated the bill did so without involving their colleagues. With the exception of Senator Whitehouse, every single Democrat on the Environment and Public Works (EPW) committee voted no on moving the bill to a vote. Its passage would represent a rush job, not a deliberate agreement about the best path forward.

Based on our litigation experience, it’s also wrong to suggest that BAAJA would move the fight for our future out of the courts and into the realm of electoral accountability. Given ambiguous and even inscrutable drafting, BAAJA would drive more not less litigation. For most parties, BAAJA would make it harder to secure meaningful relief. But for the most powerful companies, it would invite litigation to secure new, extraordinary remedies. Regardless of elections, BAAJA would constrain new presidential administrations from shifting policy and responding to new and evolving circumstances.

On the red tape front, Klein points to the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA) as the problem, and the Sunzia transmission line as the evergreen example of permitting dysfunction. Absolutely, the Sunzia project took way too long to permit, but it was proposed in 2006 and is an extreme example from a different time. Klein never acknowledges that Congress has passed a litany of changes to NEPA in recent years. The Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act of 2021 created, among other things, a federal permitting council and a permitting fast track for large projects —for better or worse. Congress also made very significant changes to NEPA in the Fiscal Responsibility Act of 2023, including more NEPA exemptions and specific timelines for action. On top of all that, the Supreme Court limited the scope of NEPA review dramatically just last year in Seven County Infrastructure Coalition v. Eagle County, Colorado.

BAAJA would not solve a live problem, but it would create a new one by eliminating any enforceable obligation to undertake the most basic environmental review and public disclosure of impacts. Further, dispensing with upfront public engagement under NEPA and the National Historic Preservation Act (NHPA) would foreclose an important opportunity to surface problems and solutions at an early stage of project development. Eliminating enforceable obligations to take these simple steps at the outset would make the federal government less transparent and accountable at a time when people very much want it to be more of both. In the Trump administration, NEPA has been a critical tool for subjecting extremely harmful federal actions to judicial scrutiny. For example, Earthjustice, the ACLU, and many state AGs have relied on NEPA to prevent ICE from converting warehouses into massive, inhumane detention centers.

At a time when meritorious lawsuits are often the only check on the Trump administration’s abuse of power, BAAJA would give it more license and immunity for illegal actions. Klein never grapples with the fundamental threat that this presents in a Trump administration helmed by Stephen Miller.

Members of Congress must be real about the ways that BAAJA would accelerate the Trump agenda over the next two years. As the President has promised, his administration would super-charge “Pipelines, Mines, and Power Plants faster than ever before” while the war on wind and solar would continue. Now that the Supreme Court has given the President the power to hire and fire commissioners of once-independent agencies at will, he can force the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission to follow through on its recent promises to “unleash natural gas” without a commensurate push for clean energy.

More broadly, President Trump would cash in on new powers to provide “project certainty” for developers of all kinds. The administration would lock in federal authorizations for polluting projects, most likely in communities that are routinely targeted for pollution. It would move fast to confer private rights to drill, mine, log, construct data centers, and otherwise exploit public lands. Klein himself recognizes the concern that “Trump would issue all manner of illegal permits to drill on public lands that will then be protected by the bill’s provisions in the future.” But while he concedes that this would be a “huge problem,” he brushes it off, stating that “the bill’s architects don’t think it’s true.” But the views of the bill’s architects don’t matter. It’s the courts that will interpret BAAJA’s ambiguous provisions. And in the end, it will be the Supreme Court that gets the final word, driven by a conservative supermajority that has been actively hostile to climate protection, energy transition, and social justice.

Then there are the glaring problems that Klein entirely fails to address. BAAJA systematically undermines Tribal sovereignty and the ability of all communities to uplift and preserve history and culture – this as the Trump administration is taking unprecedented steps to erase history and demolish cultural heritage. Speaking at a rally representing 1,200 Tribal nations and organizations, Martin Luther King III put it this way: “For sixty years, Section 106 of the National Historic Preservation Act has given communities a voice when federal projects may affect historic places. It asks federal agencies to identify what matters, consider the effects of their plans, and consult with those whose heritage may be at stake. It does not say that we cannot build. It says that before we build, we must listen.”

As state Attorneys General are warning, Tribal and state governments, including newly elected governors, would lose much of their power to protect waters and wetlands under BAAJA. This is especially troubling given the Supreme Court’s decision in Sackett v. EPA, which curtailed federal protection of wetlands very dramatically. The bill would also allow states to take over Endangered Species Act permitting, a move that would jeopardize the survival of imperiled species while complicating the federal permitting process immensely.

Klein elides all of these concerns and urges passage of BAAJA on grounds that the “single most important climate policy going forward is for Democrats to win elections so that they have the power to set climate policy in the future.” Agreed. But why would this bill be popular with voters who turned out in record numbers to reject Trump?

Maybe Klein is assuming that voters won’t notice or remember that Democrats passed this bill in the immediate aftermath of a historic wave election. That would be a mistake and a betrayal. Eviscerating laws that protect our health, our communities, and the environment will hurt people in profound ways that they will notice. Abandoning federal trust obligations and government-to-government relations will create rifts that will not be forgotten. And we can be sure that President Trump will brag incessantly (and accurately) that this deal codifies a suite of regulatory changes that he has proposed as part of his “America First Agenda.”

Building everything, from clean energy infrastructure to gas pipelines and dirty data centers, is not a prescription for sustaining the momentum of a transformative election. An overwhelming number of people have experienced what happens when the most powerful companies in the world can build whatever they want as fast as they want without transparency or guardrails. They want it to stop, and their analysis is sharp. It is not going unnoticed that BAAJA’s package for pipelines is precisely crafted to speed up gas delivery to power more and bigger data centers complexes.

Support for Democrats is at best fragile. Rather than passing a bill that will do predictable and enduring damage, Democrats should negotiate a better deal that reforms the law without dismantling it. Transmission reforms have bipartisan appeal: gas-fired power plants will benefit from expanded transmission capacity as much or more than clean energy generators. Speed-to-power is still an imperative from the perspective of AI hyperscalers. These structural incentives will remain in the next Congress and can drive the votes needed for a bipartisan deal. Democrats can and must pursue legislation that protects people and their well-being while incentivizing the infrastructure that will genuinely serve all of us.

text:
The Illinois Power Agency (IPA) and the Illinois Environmental Protection Agency (IEPA) have released the draft Mitigation Plan required under Section 9.15(o) of the Illinois Environmental Protection Act.

The Mitigation Plan serves to assess whether to allow any plants whose emission reduction deadlines may impose reliability concern to continue operating, including operating with reduced emissions or as emergency backup where appropriate.

The draft Mitigation Plan was developed with support from the IPA’s Procurement & Planning Consultant, Energy and Environmental Economics Inc. (E3), and informed by stakeholder workshops conducted in 2026.

The Climate and Equitable Jobs Act (CEJA) tasked the IPA, IEPA, and Illinois Commerce Commission (ICC) with developing a comprehensive study to assess “the current and projected status of electric resource adequacy and reliability throughout the State.” That Resource Adequacy Study was published in December of 2025 and concluded that Illinois faces a resource adequacy risk over the coming decade. Based on this finding, CEJA directed the IPA and IEPA to “develop a plan to reduce or delay CO2e and copollutant emissions reductions requirements only to the extent and for the duration necessary to meet the resource adequacy and reliability needs of the State.”

Review the Draft Mitigation Plan and Submit Comments:

Review the draft Mitigation Plan here

The IPA and IEPA are seeking stakeholder feedback on the draft Mitigation Plan through a 60-day public comment period, opening November 16, 2026, and closing January 15, 2027, at 5:00 p.m. CT.

Comments must be submitted to the IPA at IPA.ContactUs@illinois.gov

The draft Mitigation Plan is available on the IPA, IEPA, and ICC websites. Comments submitted during the stakeholder feedback period will be posted on the Agencies’ websites.

Preliminary Key Findings:

Statewide adequacy and reliability challenges persist. Updated projections show that resource adequacy needs continue across the PJM and MISO regions of Illinois.

Resource adequacy modeling demonstrates that retaining certain CEJA-limited units can support reliability during a limited number of high-risk hours without producing large amounts of energy and associated emissions throughout the year.

The majority of the reliability and customer affordability benefits associated with extending closure deadlines come from gas and oil units—not from coal units. Continued availability of CEJA-limited units preserves near-term flexibility as Illinois undertakes a substantial buildout of new energy resources, while allowing the state to continue making progress toward its decarbonization goals.

Near-term retirements of CEJA-limited units could lead to the development of new natural gas generation outside Illinois to meet the state’s reliability needs.

Retirement of CEJA-limited units without sufficient replacement capacity could increase consumers’ exposure to capacity market costs.

Extending eligible gas and oil units, but not coal units, best balances affordability, reliability, emissions reductions, and environmental justice considerations.

Proposed Recommendations:

Given a potential resource adequacy or reliability deficiency remains reasonably likely, the draft plan proposes the extension of the applicable CEJA deadlines for certain covered units (those units subject to Section 9.15(i) of the Illinois EPA Act’s zero carbon emission requirements enacted through CEJA) through at least the end of the 2032-2033 planning year.

Under CEJA, any extension should be limited to the extent necessary to address the identifiable need. The proposed extension is therefore intended to preserve near-term reliability while replacement resources are developed, and future reliability needs are reassessed.

Authorization of the extension of the applicable CEJA deadlines lies with the Illinois Commerce Commission (ICC), through the Order that will follow litigation of the Mitigation Plan.

Next Steps:

Following the close of the stakeholder feedback period on January 15, 2027, the IPA and IEPA will have 30 days to review submitted comments, make any necessary updates, and file the final Mitigation Plan with the ICC.

name: Texas Environment
title: COP31: A Post-Midterms Mood Shift at the Largest Climate Gathering Ever - The Austin Chronicle
description:
Texas Impact is on the ground in Antalya, Türkiye, at the United Nations climate negotiations known as COP31.
Texas Impact traveled to Türkiye for the UN Climate Negotiations but thanks to the online platform, people from all over the world can participate.
In partnership with other U.S. faith observer organizations Texas Impact is providing an opportunity for U.S.-based faith leaders to serve as credentialed online observers.
Two dozen online observers from all over the U.S. were selected for the cohort.
Texas Impact is Texas’ oldest and largest interfaith advocacy network.
text:
Texas Impact is on the ground in Antalya, Türkiye, at the United Nations climate negotiations known as COP31. Each day, Texas Impact staff and other U.S. faith delegates are reporting on the proceedings, and sharing conversations with global colleagues about the state of play and the urgency of the moment. Find more coverage at austinchronicle.com/COP31.

This year’s gathering is estimated to be the largest COP ever, with 92,000 registered attendees, and another 3,000 with virtual badges. In today’s daily dispatch, COP participants reflect on who’s in attendance, in person and virtually, describe a post-midterms mood shift, and check in with Niyanta Spelman, founder and board chair of Austin nonprofit Rainforest Partnership.

Texas Impact traveled to Türkiye for the UN Climate Negotiations but thanks to the online platform, people from all over the world can participate. In partnership with other U.S. faith observer organizations Texas Impact is providing an opportunity for U.S.-based faith leaders to serve as credentialed online observers. Online observers agree to monitor an assigned policy area across negotiations, side events, and other programming then contribute to Texas Impact’s coverage of the COP by writing Substack posts.

Two dozen online observers from all over the U.S. were selected for the cohort. They represent clergy and laypeople from many different faiths. They are students, professionals, and retirees. Some are experienced advocates and some are brand new to the process. This broad coalition of observers is already generating a rich conversation about the meetings, the UN process, and the role of the faith community in advocating for just climate policy.

Each online observer will plan and deliver a broader impacts activity after the negotiations to share their experience. We look forward to hearing more about their creative ways to start the climate conversation in their communities.

Here are a few of the initial Substack contributed by the online observer cohort:

Kate Burke, a retired chemical engineer, now works with climate advocacy groups the Laudato Si Movement and the Catholic Climate Covenant in her local community. She writes about the importance of methane monitoring and methane mitigation. Watching the negotiations, she notices that methane has lots of different sources requiring different solutions. Given the gas’s big impact on the climate, monitoring and mitigating methane is critical.

Read Kate’s post, An Identity Crisis.

Julian Daniel, Hunger Fellow for the Evangelical Lutheran Church in America, writes about climate-resilient agriculture. Agriculture is an important topic both because we depend on farms for food and also because of the role soils play in carbon sequestration. Given the right conditions, soils can hold two to three times as much carbon as the atmosphere. Climate smart agriculture has the potential to play a role in both mitigation and adaptation.

Read Julian’s post, Slow and Steady.

Keith Hammer speaks to the value of COP in bringing together diverse voices from around the world, including voices that are sometimes excluded from global conversations like Indigenous people, women, and young people. These sometimes marginalized voices remind us that the impacts of climate change are disproportionately endured by those with the fewest resources.

Read Keith’s post, A Great Cloud of Witnesses.

Texas Impact is Texas’ oldest and largest interfaith advocacy network. Based in Austin with members in every corner of the state, Texas Impact equips and mobilizes Texans of faith and conscience to advocate for public policies that reflect widely shared, deeply held values of love and justice. Learn more and get involved at texasimpact.org.

name: Clean Energy
title: Can AI actually help the climate? Nations want to harness the technology to cut emissions
description:
Some climate advocates welcomed the pledge as a necessary, if vague, step to address the growing emissions and environmental impacts caused by running AI data centres.

text:
Ten countries including Germany and Brazil at the COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Turkey, have pledged to do more to limit the greenhouse-gas emissions produced by the rapid development of artificial intelligence — and to use the technology to cut emissions elsewhere.

How much energy will AI really consume? The good, the bad and the unknown

“The pledge brings together two priorities that must advance together: reducing the environmental footprint of AI and expanding its contribution to climate action,” said Mehmet Fatih Kacır, Turkey’s minister of industry and technology at a launch event for the Antalya Artificial Intelligence Pledge on 16 November.

Some climate advocates welcomed the pledge as a necessary, if vague, step to address the growing emissions and environmental impacts caused by running AI data centres. And researchers say there are ways that the technology could be used to cut emissions, for instance by helping to integrate renewables onto power grids or by improving logistics.

But it remains unknown whether such emissions reductions could offset AI’s consequences for the climate. “The trillion-dollar question is whether or not those savings will outweigh those impacts we’re seeing now,” says Eric Masanet, a mechanical engineer who studies decarbonization at the University of California, Santa Barbara.

Intelligent emissions

The rapid building of AI data centres — which are used to train and operate AI systems — has drawn increasing ire from environmental quarters because of its insatiable demand for electricity. A report this month from BloombergNEF, which provides research on the clean-energy transition, estimated that electricity demand from data centres will quadruple over the next decade, making up 7% of global electricity demand in 2035, and accounting for at least 2% of global emissions.

Most of that would come from the United States, where the building of data-centres has been biggest and fastest, followed by China. In the race to train the most capable models, many big tech firms in the United States are seeking to build gas-fired power plants to satisfy data centres’ energy demands, rather than waiting for permission to connect to the public power grid.

Can AI models reliably forecast extreme weather events?

That’s the sort of approach the pledge aims to prevent. It calls on countries to take action to power AI infrastructure with “zero- and low-emissions energy” and to improve the efficiency with which data centres use power and water for cooling. Countries that join will assess progress yearly.

The other G20 countries that signed on are South Korea and Turkey, which sponsored the pledge and said it would aim to power its data centres with 60% low-carbon sources. They were initially joined by Andorra, Colombia, Luxembourg, Sierra Leone, Somalia and Uganda. More than 80 organizations endorsed the pledge, including a few large tech companies such as Nokia and Telefónica, according to a tracker from the UN’s International Telecommunications Union, one of the effort’s organizing bodies. However, none of the frontier AI firms have joined the pledge.

Given the absence of AI’s biggest emitters, some climate advocates dismissed the initiative. “The AI pledge risks giving Big Tech a green stamp without requiring it to address the real climate impacts of its infrastructure,” says Jill McArdle, a campaigner at Beyond Fossil Fuels, an advocacy group in Berlin.
