title: Environmental citizen suits—abused and unconstitutional - Pacific Legal Foundation
description:
The presentation particularly detailed PLF’s recent litigation—and wins!— in challenges to environmental citizen suits.
And that’s not the end of the incentive problems with environmental citizen suits.
And the intrinsic problems of the environmental citizen suit don’t end there: The method is also fraught with constitutional issues.
But the environmental citizen suit forces the president to prosecute cases that he may be ill-equipped to manage efficiently.
This is just the tip of the iceberg of the problems with the environmental citizen suit.
text:
Last month, Pacific Legal Foundation attorneys and researchers participated in the Mercatus Center’s Markets & Society conference—a gathering attended by economists, attorneys, policymakers, and more. PLF staff showcased the groundbreaking work of our litigators and researchers, highlighting our passion for liberty and individual rights.

One conference presentation focused on the work of our new Environment and Natural Resources practice group, whose focus is litigating to unleash human ingenuity that solves environmental issues and builds a brighter future. The presentation particularly detailed PLF’s recent litigation—and wins!— in challenges to environmental citizen suits. Under major environmental laws like the Clean Water Act and the Clean Air Act, private individuals (or more often, special interest groups) can sue Americans for alleged violations of these federal environmental laws. Although likely enacted by Congress with the best of intentions, these suits have been wildly abused and weaponized against Americans, their businesses, and their communities.

Take, for instance, the case of Amsted Graphite Materials, a graphite manufacturing company based in rural Anmoore, West Virginia. In addition to continuing its century-long tradition of producing graphite materials, Amsted was upgrading its facility to reduce its environmental impact and working with the Environmental Protection Agency and the West Virginia Department of Environmental Protection to find new ways to protect the environment. But its pursuit of innovation was forced to a screeching halt when two special interest groups filed an environmental citizen suit against Amsted, alleging that the company violated the Clean Water Act.

Businesses like Amsted have two options when facing a citizen suit: spend copious money, time, and resources fighting the allegations in court, or settle the case with the suing party. This dichotomy is the first failure of the environmental citizen suit method: Because violations of environmental legislation carry a hefty per-day fine, accused Americans are highly incentivized to simply settle the case.

The catch? The money from a settlement often doesn’t go to the government, as the civil fines for violations would if the case was concluded in court. Rather, the money can go to a third party—which, many times, ends up going to a project affiliated with the suing party. As long as the group filing the citizen suit offers to settle for less than the sued party would pay if convicted in court, the suing party has a high chance of successfully settling.

This incentive structure is inherently unfair. It places all of the power—and the financial incentives—in the hands of the suing party.

And that’s not the end of the incentive problems with environmental citizen suits. These suits can be weaponized by special interest groups in a way that doesn’t even address any environmental concerns, but instead go after paperwork errors—a far cry from what the authors of the environmental citizen suit likely envisioned. PLF is involved in just such a case—where our clients, a family-run clay supply company, was sued by two special interest groups for alleged violations of the Clean Water Act. After eight years of litigation, the groups are still pushing their suit forward—even though the only harms alleged now are paperwork violations. And these groups can pursue attorney fees, as well—even though it’s nearly impossible for the defendants to recover theirs if they win the case.

And the intrinsic problems of the environmental citizen suit don’t end there: The method is also fraught with constitutional issues. As detailed by PLF attorneys in case filings, these suits offend constitutional protections in multiple ways.

First, environmental citizen suit plaintiffs wield presidential power, but without any checks on that power. When the president directs the prosecution of an alleged crime, he is cabined by various checks on his power—if he over- or under-enforces a law, his actions are checked by the voters via elections. But not so with the private suer in a citizen suit. Unlike the president, whose power is penned in by the legislative and judicial branches, as well as by elections, the actions of plaintiffs in citizen suits are totally unmonitored by another body—let alone the American electorate. The constitutional protections that keep prosecutions fair and impartial are nowhere to be found in the environmental citizen suit, where the plaintiffs don’t face the guardrails that keep the president’s actions in check.

Additionally, environmental citizen suits steal the executive branch’s jurisdiction over prosecuting a suit. The Framers placed the power for how to prosecute a law in the executive’s hands. But the environmental citizen suit forces the president to prosecute cases that he may be ill-equipped to manage efficiently. In days of backlogged and understaffed agencies, the president should allocate resources to address society’s biggest problems first. If his attention and resources are forced away from that, then Americans are left without attention to their everyday needs, while special interest groups pocket money from exploiting sue-and-settle tactics.

This is just the tip of the iceberg of the problems with the environmental citizen suit. But American businesses like Amsted are fighting back, challenging these suits in court, represented free of charge by PLF attorneys. PLF is hopeful that the intrinsic flaws of environmental citizen suits will encourage courts to shelve this vehicle in favor of methods that preserve Americans’ constitutional protections and empower businesses and individuals alike to move toward environmentalism rooted in innovation and human ingenuity, rather than red tape and fear.

text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — The Energy Department has again extended an order forcing an aging Michigan coal-fired power plant to stay open past its scheduled retirement date, defying a court order that set aside the agency's previous actions as unlawful.

Energy Secretary Chris Wright issued an emergency order late Friday extending the continued operation of the 64-year-old J.H. Campbell Generating Plant near Grand Rapids, saying the plant is needed to prevent blackouts and preserve customers' access to reliable, secure electricity.

The Energy Department said it disagrees with the September decision by a three-judge panel on the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit and has petitioned for a rehearing in front of the entire court.

The emergency order is among a series of actions by President Donald Trump and his administration to boost the struggling U.S. coal industry, including a plan announced in June to spend nearly $700 million to support ​coal-fired power plants and coal exports.

The Environmental Protection Agency, meanwhile, has repealed rules that limit planet-warming greenhouse gas emissions from power plants fueled by coal and natural gas. The agency under Administrator Lee Zeldin also is moving to prevent future administrations from regulating climate pollution from power plants.

Environmental groups slammed the latest emergency order on coal — the seventh such declaration for the Campbell plant since May 2025 — and said there is no evidence that the Michigan plant has ever been needed to avoid a grid emergency or prevented power outages. The extension order costs families in the Midwest more than $600,000 per day to keep the old, polluting plant online, they said.

“At a time when prices are soaring and Americans are struggling to make ends meet, the Trump administration’s decision to issue yet another illegal and expensive extension is punishing,” said the Sierra Club's Jessi Eidbo.

According to a Burning Money tracker compiled by the group, the administration’s orders extending the lives of fossil fuel plants in six states have cost ratepayers more than $600 million, with over half of that total stemming from the Campbell plant in Michigan.

“Instead of saving families’ money and letting the plant retire as planned, the Trump administration keeps putting its thumb on the scale for costly coal," said Ted Kelly, director of U.S. clean energy at Environmental Defense Fund, another environmental group.

Wright and other officials have said the Campbell plant and others are needed to ensure reliable electricity, and he used emergency powers to keep them operating. Environmental groups and multiple states — including Michigan, Illinois and Minnesota — went to court to try to overturn orders keeping the plants online.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit sided with the states and the groups, saying there was no real emergency under the law. A decision is pending on whether the full Appeals Court will hear the case, which could end up at the Supreme Court.

Subject of Research: Comparative analysis of carbon neutrality strategies, energy transition policies, and decarbonization technologies in China, the United States, and Germany.
text:
A comparative study published in Carbon Neutral Systems evaluates the distinct statutory frameworks, technological roadmaps, and transition strategies deployed by China, the United States, and Germany as each economy advances toward net-zero. As the largest energy markets in Asia, North America, and the European Union, the three nations face shared climate mitigation imperatives amid divergent energy structures. While Germany relies on binding legislative targets to expand renewables and reduce fossil reliance, the United States experiences policy fluctuations driven by partisan political shifts despite strong technological capabilities. Meanwhile, China leverages coordinated institutional planning and immense manufacturing capacity to accelerate non-fossil deployment, achieving global leadership in wind power, photovoltaics, and electric mobility while managing an energy system historically rooted in domestic coal.

Structural variations stem from baseline primary energy consumption profiles and legacy power assets. China’s primary energy mix remains heavily reliant on coal, accounting for 56.20 percent of total consumption, followed by petroleum and natural gas, with nuclear and renewables comprising smaller proportions. In the United States, petroleum comprises 35.85 percent and natural gas 33.41 percent, with renewables contributing 9.12 percent. Conversely, Germany maintains a 19.63 percent renewable share alongside a minimal 0.74 percent reliance on nuclear generation. In electricity generation, fossil fuels supply 64.1 percent of China’s power, whereas Germany generates 29.2 percent from wind and 11.2 percent from solar. Hydropower supplies 12.9 percent of electricity in China, compared to 5.3 percent in the United States and 3.8 percent in Germany.

Statutory commitments and timelines further delineate each government’s pathway. In September 2020, China announced its dual carbon goals at the United Nations General Assembly, pledging to peak emissions before 2030 and achieve carbon neutrality by 2060. The United States, having peaked emissions in 2007, released its long-term climate strategy in November 2021, establishing targets to reduce net greenhouse gas emissions by 50 to 52 percent below 2005 levels by 2030, achieve 100 percent clean electricity by 2035, and reach net-zero by 2050. Germany, which recorded its emissions peak in 1990, enacted its Climate Protection Law in November 2019 and revised statutory targets in July 2021, mandating a 65 percent reduction by 2030 relative to 1990 levels, an 88 percent cut by 2040, and net-zero emissions by 2045.

To contextualize these domestic trajectories, the authors reviewed global tracking metrics and analytical emissions methodologies. Oxford Net Zero statistics indicate that as of May 2024, six nations—Benin, Bhutan, Comoros, Gabon, Guyana, and Suriname—had self-proclaimed carbon neutrality, while over 150 jurisdictions have formulated net-zero targets. Among these, forty-two countries have enacted binding legal frameworks, fifty reference targets in policy documents, ten have issued declarations, and fifty-four maintain goals under active discussion. Methodological tools for sectoral emissions analysis include environmentally-extended input-output analysis, index decomposition analysis, computable general equilibrium models, and integrated assessment models. Additionally, orbital surveillance satellites including Japan’s GOSAT, the American OCO-2, China’s TANSAT, and Europe’s Sentinel-5P measure atmospheric carbon dioxide and trace gases, providing empirical observations to calibrate climate models and monitor regional emissions.

China’s domestic policy implementation is anchored by its 1 plus N policy framework, combining central guidance with customized regional and sectoral action plans. Thirty-one provincial jurisdictions have issued carbon peaking policies, exemplified by Shanghai’s plan to lower energy intensity by 14 percent by 2025 and achieve a 25 percent non-fossil share by 2030. At the national level, the State Council issued guidelines in August 2024 to accelerate green transformation across industrial sectors, spatial planning, and transportation. Furthermore, the National People’s Congress enacted the Energy Law of the People’s Republic of China in November 2024, providing statutory backing for clean energy. Sectoral roadmaps include a hydrogen development strategy targeting 50,000 hydrogen fuel cell vehicles and an annual renewable hydrogen output of 100,000 to 200,000 tons by 2025.

Driven by massive capital investment, China’s renewable generation capacity has expanded at an exceptional rate. By late 2023, China’s total renewable capacity reached 1.52 terawatts, surpassing fossil fuels to exceed 50 percent of total installed capacity. By July 2024, combined solar and wind capacity reached 1.206 terawatts, achieving international capacity goals six years ahead of schedule. In solar photovoltaics, China maintained 649 gigawatts of cumulative capacity by 2023, compared to 174.8 gigawatts in the United States and 35.5 gigawatts in Germany, adding 263 gigawatts in 2023 alone. Similarly, China’s cumulative wind capacity reached 440 gigawatts by 2023, adding 74 gigawatts in 2023, compared to 147.5 gigawatts in the United States and 69.5 gigawatts in Germany. Furthermore, China’s utility-scale wind and solar pipeline reached 1.1 terawatts, with 339 gigawatts actively under construction.

China’s manufacturing scale has established dominant positions across clean mobility and battery supply chains. In 2023, China recorded 8.1 million electric vehicle sales, capturing a 38 percent market share, compared to 0.7 million in Germany at 24 percent, and 1.47 million in the United States at 9.3 percent. Chinese automakers manufactured over half of all electric vehicles sold globally in 2023 and exported 1.2 million electric cars out of 4 million total vehicle exports. In battery manufacturing, Chinese output exceeded 650 gigawatt-hours in 2023, representing nearly 80 percent of global production, while domestic companies produced 89.4 percent of cathodes, 93.5 percent of anodes, 87.4 percent of electrolytes, and 85 percent of separators. Forecasts indicate domestic electrification will reduce China’s oil demand from a peak of 800 million tons before 2028 to 200 million tons by 2060.

United States federal initiatives emphasize power transformation, infrastructure modernization, and clean financing through the two-trillion-dollar American Jobs Plan. Targets include deploying 30 gigawatts of offshore wind capacity by 2030, acquiring 100 percent zero-emission federal vehicle fleets by 2035, and achieving net-zero emissions across federal buildings by 2045. In 2023, domestic energy-related carbon dioxide emissions fell 4.1 percent, aided by a 7 percent power sector decline as coal gave way to gas and solar, alongside mild winter temperatures. Concurrently, technological breakthroughs in horizontal drilling and hydraulic fracturing have expanded domestic fossil fuel output. In 2023, United States crude oil extraction increased by 8 percent and natural gas rose by 4 percent, establishing the nation as the leading global exporter of liquefied natural gas, shipping over 60 percent of monthly exports to Europe.

The decentralized American governance model introduces policy instability, as state regulatory differences and federal administrative shifts create recurring climate disruptions. Historical shifts include withdrawal from the Kyoto Protocol in 2001, departure from the Paris Agreement in 2017, re-entry in 2021, and proposals to repeal clean energy tax credits and exit the Paris accord in 2026. Analyses project that abandoning core federal climate policies could raise domestic emissions by over 4 billion tons by 2030 relative to 2005 baselines. Trade measures, including a 10 percent tariff on Chinese imports in February 2025, further complicate clean energy supply chains. Nonetheless, the United States maintains substantial capacity in carbon capture and storage, recording 22.5 million tonnes of annual capacity in 2023, compared to 3.5 million tonnes in China, which operated 67 carbon capture projects by August 2024.

Germany’s Energiewende transition relies on statutory mandates but faces structural strain following European energy disruptions. The Climate Action Act imposes binding sector emission limits, supported by a fuel carbon pricing mechanism enacted in 2021 that established a fee of 45 euros per ton on fuels for 2024. In 2023, German emissions dropped 10.1 percent to 674 million tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalents, with energy falling 20.1 percent and industry dropping 7.7 percent to 155 million tonnes, while transport reached 146 million tonnes, exceeding annual limits by 13 million tonnes. Following the loss of Russian pipeline gas, Germany restructured imports, sourcing 35 percent from Norway and 30 percent from the Netherlands, while continuing open-pit lignite mining, which yielded 130.8 million tonnes in 2022.

Decarbonizing heavy manufacturing and deploying carbon capture technologies remain vital cross-sector priorities. Traditional blast furnace steelmaking requires approximately 300 kilograms of coke and 200 kilograms of pulverized coal per ton of pig iron, prompting European plants in Germany, Austria, and Sweden to advance direct hydrogen reduction. In cement production, which generates 0.8 tons of carbon dioxide per ton of product, substituting 60 percent carbide slag can lower emissions by 40 percent. Beyond industrial retrofits, expanding biological and artificial carbon sinks is necessary to offset residual emissions. Germany’s Action Plan on Nature-Based Solutions outlines 69 measures to restore natural sinks, while emerging methods like underground biochemical synthesis of natural gas from captured carbon dioxide offer options to unite economic utilization with permanent geological sequestration.

Achieving mid-century net-zero objectives ultimately requires international cooperation to address the technological and economic barriers of power grid modernization. Global operational power storage reached 289.2 gigawatts by late 2023, with pumped hydro providing 67 percent and lithium-ion batteries 31.6 percent, underscoring storage needs for intermittent renewables. While Germany demonstrates regulatory consistency and high renewable electricity penetration, its consumers bear elevated energy prices and its industry remains dependent on imported battery components. Conversely, China commands unmatched clean energy manufacturing capacity but must decarbonize an industrial base reliant on coal, whereas the United States combines leading innovation and carbon capture infrastructure with recurring policy shifts. Aligning carbon trading markets, expanding joint research, and sustaining open technology supply chains remain essential to achieving global climate targets.

text:
Data centers are the backbone of the digital age. In these facilities, packed with processors, vast quantities of data that enable online services and artificial intelligence (AI) are computed, stored, and distributed. The recent AI boom has sparked a construction frenzy for data centers. Keeping them running around the clock requires huge amounts of energy, used both to power the machines themselves and to cool them. But how much? And what is their carbon footprint?

Only the companies that operate data centers know the answer to those questions. There is no public, transparent information. The industry’s opacity means the figures in circulation are estimates produced by the scientific community. A team of researchers led by Harvard University published the results of their own investigation in the journal Nature on November 16, focused on hyperscalers (the name given to the largest data centers). The study concentrates on the U.S., the country with the largest share of data centers — around half of the global total.

The numbers are huge: hyperscalers consumed between 68 and 99 terawatt-hours (TWh) of electricity. To put that in context, the highest estimate exceeds the annual consumption of a country like Chile (83.2 TWh), according to data from the Department of Energy’s statistical agency (EIA), and approaches the consumption of states such as Indiana, Michigan, or Tennessee. That is roughly 1.8% of total U.S. electricity consumption. The researchers also conclude that four states — Iowa, Ohio, Oregon, and Virginia — account for more than half of the detected energy use.

As for emissions, the team’s calculations place them at about 25.7 million metric tons of CO₂, an amount two to three times higher than a previous estimate for 2018.

The interesting part of the study is how they constructed their estimate. “There is barely any public data. The Department of Energy, for example, only provides aggregated energy consumption data for the whole country. That does not allow us to know how individual data centers behave,” says the study’s lead author, Gianluca Guidi, a postdoctoral fellow in the department of biostatistics. Because there are no public registers to check how many of these facilities exist in the U.S. or where they are located, the researchers opted for a combination of methods. First, they tried to obtain information from the operators themselves, a laborious task (company by company and state by state) that is not always successful.

Second — and here is the novelty — they cross-checked and expanded that information through direct observation: they analyzed satellite imagery to detect rooftops or plots typical of hyperscalers, which have a very particular architecture (they look like industrial warehouses but feature easily identifiable cooling systems and are often close to energy infrastructure). They estimated each data center’s installed capacity based on the square meters occupied by the facility.

Using this method, they located and mapped 403 hyperscalers in the U.S., with an average installed capacity of 40 megawatts (MW) and an average footprint of about 2,000 square meters. The authors stress that this number is an undercount, since it resulted from observations made between May 2024 and April 2025. Therefore, the consumption and emissions data are necessarily conservative. “The data center boom has not slowed since April 2025. New facilities have been built, existing campuses have been expanded and the demand for AI computing continues to grow. That means the electricity consumption and carbon footprint we report could already be considerably higher,” says Guidi.

Conservative estimates

The estimate of hyperscaler volume does not account for the activity carried out. AI training and inference processes, for example, consume far more energy than data hosting or other cloud services. In other words, a smaller data center dedicated to AI can consume more than a larger one that performs other activities. Because operators do not usually disclose what their centers are used for, the researchers overcame this obstacle by outlining three possible scenarios — low, moderate, and high consumption.

The next step was to estimate energy consumption based on each facility’s size, and emissions by taking into account the energy mix used in each locality. The authors note that energy use rose substantially in the early 2000s but remained steady through the 2010s despite industry growth (which can be explained by improvements in hardware efficiency and cooling systems). Demand has grown again in recent years, driven by the computing required to support commercial generative AI models.

The study also finds that roughly 54% of the electricity supplying hyperscalers during the observed period was generated from fossil fuels, mainly natural gas (38%) and coal (15%), and that about one quarter of the electricity came from regions with grids dirtier than the national average.

The researchers observed substantial regional differences in emissions, which vary greatly because of differing local energy mixes. Many facilities were concentrated in areas where electricity is largely generated by coal-fired plants, amplifying their carbon footprint. “Decisions about where data centers are located and how they are powered are crucial for the environment and public health, and they must be made based on reliable data,” says one of the study’s authors, Francesca Dominici, the Clarence James Gamble professor of biostatistics, population and data science and director of Harvard’s Data Science Initiative.

That view is shared by Shaolei Ren, who was not involved in the study and is an associate professor of electrical and computer engineering at the University of California, Riverside and an AI sustainability specialist. “This work illustrates why the location of data centers matters environmentally, in contrast to more aggregated analyses,” he says. Ren sees the study’s findings as a starting point for more detailed research. “If we had more information on how specific facilities actually operate, we could better identify where the biggest opportunities lie. In my own work I’m particularly interested in linking energy and carbon emissions to water use, air quality, and health impacts,” he adds.

Although the method developed by the Harvard team is interesting, it may have some gaps. “The paper assumes that all hyperscalers are connected to the grid, when that is not the case,” says Ana Valdivia, a professor of artificial intelligence, government and policy at the University of Oxford, whose recent research focuses on assessing AI’s environmental impact. “My critique of this approach is that many data centers, such as xAI’s in Tennessee, are not finding grid connections and are developing their own generation. That means the results underestimate actual data because they do not account for those that generate their own energy,” says the researcher, who did not participate in the study published in Nature.

The shift in the balance of political power in Washington following the Democratic Party midterm victories on November 3, 2026, will help determine which US policies can be funded and sustained over the next two years. Since US President Donald Trump took office in January 2025, energy and international development have seen sharp policy pivots, including the curtailment of clean energy incentives, withdrawal from multilateral climate initiatives, and expanded support for legacy energy technologies.

With the Democratic Party taking control of both chambers of Congress in January, there are questions as to how US energy and development cooperation policies may evolve. This could matter for US partners, especially those in emerging markets and developing economies (EMDEs), because changes to these policies may affect access to energy supplies and technology, financing for infrastructure and minerals projects, and even the terms on which firms can access the US market.

Three possible policy trajectories could shape the direction of US global energy and development cooperation: continuity, change, and stasis. Which trajectory emerges in each policy area will depend on where authority lies between the executive and Congress, the extent of bipartisan support or political polarization, and the incoming Congress’s willingness to influence policy through oversight, appropriations, or legislation. The presidential veto could, however, limit the scope for legislative reversal. The following questions examine how these scenarios could unfold across different policy areas.

What areas are likely to see policy continuity?

Some policies are likely to follow their current course because the White House can continue to pursue them through executive action and/or because their objectives have bipartisan support. These include bilateral energy partnerships, international development finance, multilateral energy and climate initiatives, and foreign assistance.

Will the nature of US bilateral energy partnerships change?

The Trump administration is likely to continue promoting its “energy dominance” agenda in ways that shape US energy technology exports associated with fossil fuel production, nuclear power, and geothermal energy. The Department of Energy’s Energy Dominance Financing Program is likely to continue supporting the expansion of domestic energy infrastructure and critical minerals projects, while deprioritizing renewable energy. Nevertheless, solar energy’s share of US electricity generation continued to rise and is expected to reach nearly 10 percent in 2027, from 7 percent in 2025.

For US partners, this means that Washington will likely continue promoting American liquefied natural gas (LNG) exports, along with nuclear and geothermal technologies through bilateral agreements and commercial diplomacy. These priorities were reflected in the March 2026 Indo-Pacific Energy Security Ministerial and Business Forum, which highlighted LNG exports and advanced nuclear energy cooperation, and in a September 2026 agreement between the US Trade and Development Agency and Thailand to support a feasibility study of US small modular reactor technologies.

Will US development and export finance remain available to partner countries?

It is likely that US development and export finance will remain available for select projects because the agencies responsible have underlying bipartisan support for their activities. Congress reauthorized the US International Development Finance Corporation (DFC) in December 2025 through 2031. Financing for the Lobito Corridor Railway Project in Angola, backed by a $553 million DFC loan, reached financial close in December 2025, for example.

The US Export-Import Bank’s (EXIM) authority for new business is scheduled to expire on December 31, 2026. Congress has demonstrated bipartisan support for EXIM, although proposals differ in their approaches to reauthorization, financing capacity, and priorities. A bipartisan Senate bill introduced in February 2026 proposes a 10-year reauthorization of EXIM, compared with five years under a March House discussion draft. Another bipartisan bill introduced in August seeks to expand civil nuclear export financing under EXIM’s China and Transformational Exports Program. Separately, Senate Democrats’ June proposal would raise EXIM’s exposure ceiling, the maximum amount that the bank can lend, from $135 billion to $205 billion and expand financing for export-oriented domestic manufacturing, including critical minerals, batteries, and advanced energy technologies. The incoming Congress’s ability to influence these proposals will depend on the outcome of reauthorization and White House support for subsequent changes.

How could US engagement with multilateral energy and climate initiatives evolve?

Several energy initiatives at multilateral development banks (MDBs) where the United States is a major shareholder have a basis for continuity because borrower countries support them. At the October IMF-World Bank Annual Meetings, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent applauded electrification expansion efforts by Mission 300, launched by the World Bank and African Development Bank in 2024, and endorsed a technology-neutral approach to energy financing. The World Bank has since approved financing for a regional gas project in West Africa and is advancing nuclear energy cooperation in partnership with the International Atomic Energy Agency, and expansion of engagement in critical minerals (the lender announced $19 billion in planned minerals financing and private capital mobilization for fiscal years 2026–30). Washington will likely continue encouraging similar shifts at other MDBs. The Asian Development Bank has already revised its energy policy to allow support for nuclear power.

US financial contributions to MDBs could continue, although funding levels remain contested. The current administration reduced its proposed contribution to the World Bank’s International Development Association’s 21st replenishment (IDA21) from $4 billion to $3.2 billion, requesting $866.7 million for FY2027, while a House-passed bill proposes just $504 million, well below the annual amount needed to fulfill the commitment. The administration also did not pledge funding for the African Development Fund’s latest replenishment (AfDF-17) and proposed canceling $197 million in previously appropriated funds. Given congressional Democrats’ previous support for IDA21 and earlier AfDF contributions, the incoming Congress could seek higher funding if FY2027 appropriations remain unresolved. However, competing domestic spending priorities and negotiations with the White House could constrain any increases.

US disengagements from major multilateral climate initiatives are unlikely to be reversed because they were done through executive orders. These include the Trump administration’s departure from the Paris Agreement, the Green Climate Fund, the Just Energy Transition Partnerships, and international organizations such as the International Renewable Energy Agency. The separate withdrawal from the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change is due to take effect on February 27, 2027, although Congress could hold hearings to question and examine the implications of this withdrawal.

Could Congress restore US foreign assistance agencies and programs that supported international energy and climate-related projects?

Congress may examine the role of the US DOGE Service in cutting foreign assistance and closing associated agencies that implemented projects in international energy- and climate-related areas. These include the US African Development Foundation and the Inter-American Foundation, policy institutes such as the United States Institute for Peace, and most notably, the US Agency for International Development (USAID), which, according to the Government Accountability Office, terminated about 6,780 of 7,510 awards between January 2025 and March 2026. However, reconstituting USAID’s operating capacity during the next Congress appears unlikely.

What are the areas for potential policy change?

There are also areas where partisan disagreement or the economic issues that figured in the election give the incoming Congress reason to act. Congressional tools such as oversight, appropriations, or legislation could materially alter policy or its implementation. The main cases are federal support for critical minerals projects, US military operations against Iran, and broad tariffs and the trade negotiations they underpin.

How could congressional scrutiny affect US support for critical minerals projects?

Government equity stakes and other critical minerals incentives taken by the Trump administration could face greater scrutiny over the selection of beneficiary firms and deal terms. Even before the election, Democratic lawmakers signaled interest in investigating these transactions, which amounted to at least $10 billion according to CFR. Pending financing proposals could face additional scrutiny over project selection and financing terms. In Tanzania, Lifezone Metals is negotiating an investment in the Kabanga nickel project with the DFC-backed Orion Critical Mineral Consortium, with a final investment decision expected in early 2027. Congressional examination of US overseas minerals financing could introduce further disclosure requirements and uncertainty over the timing of support.

Furthermore, the role of US-government-backed individuals in mining projects could be investigated. Vulcan Elements, a US rare-earth magnet manufacturer backed by 1789 Capital, where Donald Trump Jr. is a partner, has already faced congressional inquiries over a $620 million conditional Pentagon loan commitment, and scrutiny that could intensify under the incoming Congress. However, the underlying bipartisan support for securing critical minerals supply chains makes a broad reversal less likely.

How could congressional action on Iran affect energy supplies and prices in emerging markets?

The Iran war’s inflationary impacts on energy prices for US consumers contributed to voters’ cost-of-living concerns in the midterm elections. The incoming majorities in Congress could renew efforts to constrain military action through war powers legislation or seek conditions on future fiscal appropriation, following the Senate’s narrow rejection of an Iran war powers resolution in September 2026. Some Democratic lawmakers are already pushing to restrict funding for military operations against Iran ahead of the December 11 government funding deadline. However, the party remains divided over how to pursue these restrictions. Countries around the world will be tracking the role of Congress in these military and diplomatic developments associated with the Strait of Hormuz due to the inflationary impacts, especially in fuel-importing EMDEs across Asia and Africa.

Could the incoming Congress constrain US tariff policy?

The tariffs on US trade partners could face greater scrutiny, in part, because of their implications for consumer prices. After the Supreme Court ruled that the International Emergency Economic Powers Act did not authorize the original reciprocal tariffs, the administration relied on other statutory authorities. In July, the US Trade Representative imposed Section 301 duties of 10 percent or 12.5 percent on imports from 60 economies, subject to exemptions. While the House Ways and Means and Senate Finance committees could scrutinize executive-led negotiations, specific legislation narrowing executive tariff authority could face a veto by the White House.

What are the areas of possible policy stasis?

Other areas face competing priorities and/or political polarization making further progress unlikely even where congressional action could materially change the course. This applies to federal support for US renewable energy technology exports and the bilateral agreements on reciprocal trade (ARTs), whose implementation also depends on decisions by US trading partners.

What is the outlook for US renewable energy technology exports?

The outlook for US clean technology exports is likely to remain subdued due to the stalling of domestic developments. The 2025 tax law shortened eligibility for certain wind and solar deployment credits and ended federal EV consumer credits for vehicles acquired after September 30, 2025, although manufacturing credits for eligible solar and battery components continue. But progress in renewable energy deployment around the world continues. Africa installed about 4.5 GW of solar capacity in 2025, up 54 percent year-on-year, and Asia added 513.3 GW of renewable energy capacity, up 21.6 percent from the previous year. Disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz have incentivized fuel-importing countries – from Ethiopia and Kenya to Bangladesh and Pakistan– to diversify their energy sources. For US exporters, however, expanding global demand may not translate into greater market share amid strong competition from lower-cost Chinese manufacturers.

text:
At a November 9, 2027, press conference, Senator Ron Wyden, D-Ore., told reporters that the incoming congress, driven by the “blue wave” of Democratic officeholders, would revisit clean energy credits that were affected by the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA).

Wyden plans to “push hard to restore the incentives” as reported by Tax Notes. While specific proposals were not discussed, the effort could include restoring the investment and production tax credit for wind and solar projects beyond the end of the 2027 cliff imposed by the OBBBA as well as other extensions and expansions. These efforts are subject to President Trump’s veto power, so the outcome remains to be seen.

Industry participants should continue to monitor news out of the Senate Finance Committee as this process develops.

What This Means for You

Developers, investors, and tax credit buyers with exposure to wind and solar projects impacted by the OBBBA’s 2027 phase-out should track the composition and priorities of the incoming congress, particularly developments out of the Senate Finance Committee. Because any restoration effort remains subject to a potential presidential veto, stakeholders should avoid making project or financing decisions premised on an assumed legislative outcome and should instead continue planning around the credit timelines currently in effect under the OBBBA while monitoring for further detail on any specific legislative proposals.

text:
Check out the latest transportation project updates across the Austin metro.

Austin's light rail system takes first step toward 3-mile airport connection

The Austin Transit Partnership is kicking off planning for an extension of Austin Light Rail to Austin-Bergstrom International Airport.

Austin Light Rail is a signature piece of the multibillion-dollar Project Connect transit initiative approved by city voters with a permanent property tax increase in 2020. After cost increases resulted in scaled-down plans in 2023—including the removal of an anticipated airport connection—the rail network is now expected to connect Central, South and East Austin over 9.8 miles of track with 15 stations.

The Nov. 10 announcement from ATP officials said the roughly 3-mile extension from the Yellow Jacket station will be a "mostly elevated structure" ending at a station at the expanded ABIA. According to ATP, the new round of planning will take up to a year.

Read the full story.

EV chargers and e-bikes: $1.47M Bastrop CARTS expansion planned

The Capital Area Rural Transportation System is planning a $1.47 million expansion of its Bastrop park-and-ride station at 310 Hospital Drive.

An Oct. 19 filing with the Texas Department of Licensing and Regulation shows the project will cover 28,000 square feet.

As reported in July, work will include adding electric vehicle charging stations and a bike-share pod. Landscaping and other site improvements to the current station are also expected, according to the filing.

Read the full story.

Austin commits $1M to Dean Keeton transit lane at I-35

The city is committing $1 million for the construction of a new dedicated transit lane down the center of Dean Keeton Street near I-35, as part of the Texas Department of Transportation's highway expansion through Central Austin.

City Council voted to spend $1 million on the transit lane associated with TxDOT's multibillion-dollar Capital Express Central project. The lane will run through a redesigned, at-grade intersection over the interstate that will be built as part of the highway initiative.

The new transit lane will be placed in the center of the reconstructed Dean Keeton Street to accommodate service like Capital Metro's existing Rapid Route 837, which connects East Austin to downtown.

Read the full story.

Park Lane temporarily closed in downtown Round Rock

Park Lane, which typically provides access to Lake Creek Park, will be closed for the next few weeks, the city of Round Rock announced Nov. 7.

The road closure comes as the city continues to add and enlarge drainage culverts along McNeil Road and the Union Pacific railroad tracks. City Council first approved contracts totaling $110,583 for the project in 2024.

The city directed drivers to use Deerfoot Drive to access Lake Creek Park.

Read the full story.

Austinites soon to be able to fly nonstop to Arkansas

Austinites will soon be able to fly directly to Fayetteville, Arkansas, beginning in March.

Delta Air Lines announced the new nonstop destination on Nov. 3. This is the latest domestic expansion for Austin-Bergstrom International Airport and the first nonstop connection between Central Texas and the state of Arkansas, according to an ABIA news release.

Read the full story.

Williamson County breaks ground on new phase of Ronald Reagan Boulevard

Williamson County officials broke ground on a new segment of the Ronald Reagan Boulevard expansion in Georgetown on Oct. 7.

This portion of the project will add two new southbound lanes from Williams Drive to CR 245. The existing road will become the northbound lanes, separated by a median, according to a county news release.

The 2.4-mile project will cost approximately $27 million and is anticipated to be completed by summer 2028, the release states.

title: Ferguson proposes $10M investment in Tri-Cities for jobs, economic growth | Northwest
description: RICHLAND — Gov. Bob Ferguson will ask the Washington Legislature to make a $10 million investment in the Tri-Cities in the upcoming legislative session.
text:
Gov. Bob Ferguson announces plans Friday to request $10 million in his state capital budget for infrastructure development for the Northwest Advanced Clean Energy Park at Richland. He's surrounded by local municipal, business and labor leaders for the announcement at a press conference in Pasco.

RICHLAND — Gov. Bob Ferguson will ask the Washington Legislature to make a $10 million investment in the Tri-Cities in the upcoming legislative session.

He made his first announcement about a request for the state’s next capital budget Friday afternoon in the Tri-Cities, an indication, he said, of the importance of the proposed investment.

A decade after the Department of Energy transferred 1,641 acres of unneeded Hanford nuclear site land to the Tri-Cities community, the $10 million could help kickstart development there of the Northwest Advanced Clean Energy Park just north of Richland. The money, if approved by the Legislature, would be used by the city of Richland to provide infrastructure for industrial use of the land. Water, sewer and electrical service as well as roads are needed to develop the land.

“This investment will support thousands of good-paying jobs in the trades and advanced industries, and unlock billions in private investment,” Ferguson said after the announcement at the pipefitters Local 598 union hall in Pasco. “We as a state can make big things happen with strategic investments, including building the infrastructure needed to cement the Tri-Cities’ position as a green energy hub,” he said.

The Tri-Cities already has commitments for two projects on the former Hanford land. Atlas Agro North America has deals to purchase land along Horn Rapids Road to build the world’s first full-scale, low-carbon plant to produce fertilizer. The combined investment value of the plant and a proposed data center alongside it is about $2 billion.

The second project is the Ruby Flats Solar Farm on land leased by Energy Northwest to Tucci Energy Services for a 127.5-megawatt project. It would use 600 acres of former Hanford site land.

Customers of the city of Richland and the Franklin and Snohomish public utility districts will use the electricity produced. Construction could start when the transmission connection is finalized with the Department of Energy Hanford office.

In addition, General Matter, which had representatives at the Pasco announcement Friday, is interested in 425 acres of former Hanford land for a $4.5 billion project to produce fuel for small advanced nuclear reactors. It already has signed a separate agreement with the Department of Energy to use Hanford’s Fuels and Materials Examination Facility to support its development of new nuclear fuels and materials.

Washington state's capital budget is separate from the operations budget, which is facing a multibillion-dollar shortfall for the next two-year budget. And although the state's capital budget is healthy, demand for money for capital projects across the state is high.

Ferguson’s staff has already received about 200 requests for capital investments for his proposed budget to be announced in December and staff expect to receive many more during the legislative session.

But an investment in infrastructure for the Tri-Cities area Northwest Advanced Clean Energy Park should have appeal to values held across the state, Ferguson said. It brings a combination of clean energy projects, large numbers of new jobs and billions of dollars invested to grow the state’s economy, he said.

“This clean energy park has the ability to bring manufacturing, clean manufacturing, to Washington state on a very, very large scale,” added Rep. Stephanie Barnard, R-Pasco. Barnard is on the House Capital Budget Committee and the founder of the Legislative Nuclear Energy Caucus which is being expanded to become the Innovative Energy Caucus.

Ferguson said he would be heavily invested in persuading legislators in one-on-one conversations that infrastructure to advance the clean energy park is a key priority for him.

“I think this will be looked back on someday as a historical moment where folks say, ‘Hey, they did it right back then’ ... and use it as an example how to build things, how to grow an economy, how to create jobs,” Ferguson said.

The majority of the land at the 580-square-mile Hanford nuclear site is planned to be used for conservation and preservation as Hanford environmental cleanup is completed. The 1,641 acres was designated by DOE for industrial use with the goal of helping replace thousands of Hanford jobs that will disappear as cleanup is complete.

Hanford was used from World War II through the Cold War for production of nearly two-thirds of the plutonium for the nation’s nuclear weapons program. Cleanup at a cost of more than $3 billion a year continues on extensive radioactive and chemical contamination and waste left by the weapons program on parts of the site.

text:
RIYADH, SAUDI ARABIA, November 16, 2026 /EINPresswire.com/ — Muhammad Abdulwahid

The Saudi company “Al Marasem Engineering Consultants” contributes to urban planning and urban design projects that combine the development of existing city centers with the planning of new communities, at a time when the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia is reshaping its urban environment within the targets of Saudi Vision 2030. The company’s work, which is headquartered in Dammam and has a branch in Hail, includes participating in the master plan design for the “New Dammam” project and preparing the urban design for the central area of Hail, in addition to the “West Al-Aziziyah” project in Dammam and projects for parks, roads, and infrastructure.

These works highlight the role of local consulting firms in translating development objectives into actionable designs, and developing engineering expertise that addresses the needs of residents and investors, while respecting local identity and sustainability requirements. “New Dammam” is considered one of the most prominent projects in which “Al Marasem” participated in preparing its master plan design, according to company data, as it is being developed by the real estate developer “Adel” in partnership with “Alinma Investment”, spanning an area of approximately 32 million square meters.

The master plan includes eight residential neighborhoods and 49 parks, in addition to water bodies and marine canals covering an area exceeding five million square meters, as well as commercial and entertainment areas. This layout aims to connect neighborhoods with the waterfront, public spaces, and economic activities within an integrated urban environment. The project won the “Master Plan in Saudi Arabia” award at the Arabian Property Awards for the 2026–2027 cycle, part of the International Property Awards program, during a ceremony held in London on November 5, 2026. This honor grants the project an international presence and highlights the importance of integration among the developer, consulting entities, and partners. It also enables participating Saudi firms to build upon a large-scale planning experience and strengthen their expertise in designing urban communities.

In Hail, northern Saudi Arabia, the central area development project presents a different model, focusing on the rehabilitation of the downtown area and improving the connection between historic souqs, public squares, and circulation paths. “Al Marasem” prepared the urban design for the project, which covers an area exceeding 750 thousand square meters, combining pedestrian and bicycle paths, green spaces, and fountains, with the aim of enhancing the experience of residents and visitors and offering more opportunities for social and commercial activities.

The transformation is evident on Afnan Street, where spaces once used for vehicle parking have been converted into a pedestrian promenade connecting to Barzan Souq, along with reorganizing uses and providing spaces for seating and promenading. The project connects the souq and its surroundings to historic landmarks, including Al-Qishlah Palace and Aerif Castle, within an experience that preserves the presence of heritage in everyday life. Hail Region Municipality received the Prince Abdulaziz bin Saad “Basmah” Award for the year 2023 for the central area development project and the Quality of Life Program initiative supporting it, in local recognition of the project’s significance.

The experience reflects a design philosophy that places human needs at the core of planning decisions by facilitating walkability, improving facility connectivity, and providing spaces for gathering and leisure. These elements allow urban centers to maintain their social and economic function as their usage requirements evolve. Combining both projects highlights the broad scope of consulting work, ranging from dealing with the existing historic fabric to planning new urban extensions. Each path requires solutions that take into account site characteristics and balance resident movement, economic activities, and public space requirements.

The services of “Al Marasem” encompass planning, surveying, GIS, architectural and structural design, studies, supervision, and project management. The diversity of specializations enables addressing site needs within a vision that integrates infrastructure, services, and public spaces. According to the company, its professional direction is founded on innovation and sustainability, leveraging national talent and multidisciplinary engineering teams. The importance of this approach lies in building expandable local knowledge, transferring expertise across projects, and expanding the participation of Saudi engineers in designing their built environment.

These projects open avenues for “Al Marasem” to deepen its expertise in city development, whereas the long-term impact of design is tied to the projects’ capacity to serve residents, maintain the quality of facilities, and adapt to future needs. From this perspective, the accumulation of national expertise serves as a foundation for enhancing the competitiveness of the Saudi engineering consulting sector and its international presence.

text:
The Tesla Cybertruck fell so that the Cybercab may live, and soon "select customers" will know if the sacrifice was worth it. Elon Musk has been making promises about consumer-ready autonomous vehicles for a while, and now deliveries are set to begin by the end of 2026 on Tesla's new autonomous two-door driving pod. However, those planning on plunking down the $29,990 for the new ride should be aware that there are currently some heavy limitations and additional costs (though Tesla owners really shouldn't be surprised by hidden costs).

Along with Tesla announcing the end of Cybertruck production, the long-promised autonomous Cybercab is now available to purchase, but only through a Tesla invitation. Originally announced in a post on X, individuals are being invited to purchase the Cybercab for "personal use," though it currently comes with a $299-per-month subscription fee for its autonomous features alongside a $1,000 nonrefundable deposit. Deliveries are set to begin in December 2026 for the sub-$30,000 vehicle, though those on the invite list can only receive delivery in select Texas cities such as Austin, Dallas, Fort Worth, Houston, and San Antonio.

As of now, the Cybercab, which doesn't have pedals or a steering wheel, is only capable of operating essentially in the same geofenced areas as Tesla Robotaxis. Per Car and Driver, Elon Musk has shared in a post on X his plans to expand Cybercab availability as it clears regulatory approval. Tesla is also trying to get the subscription price down to the same as Full Self-Driving, which is around $115 a month.

Despite raising the price of the Cybertruck by over $5,000 back in August 2026, Tesla CEO Elon Musk still announced in a November 2026 post on X that the company would begin "winding down" Cybertruck production at its Texas Gigafactory starting in mid-2027. According to Musk, this is so the company can increase production of its autonomous Cybercab, and Tesla is also hoping to expand Robotaxi services to a "dozen or so states" by the end of 2026.

First announced for the 2024 model year, the Cybertruck didn't have the best 2026, as reports from USA Today indicate only 11,586 Cybertrucks were sold in the first nine months of 2026 — a total trending downward from the 16,097 sold in the first nine months of 2025. The article also mentions sales of the Cybertruck falling 28% in 2026, according to data from Cox Automotive. Though the Cybertruck itself had numerous problems it faces throughout its history, the elimination of certain U.S. federal EV tax credits also did the vehicle few favors.

As Tesla looks ahead, the company envisions an autonomous future, though time will tell how Cybercabs fare in a consumer space. Those wanting to get a head start have a number of hurdles to overcome, including the additional subscription charges and limited geo availability. If you're in a big Texas city, the initial price may catch your eye, but the extra costs certainly won't let you forget you're in the future.

text:
TRUMP AND EVs PART 2

YESTERDAY’S PART 1 DETAILED A FAILED BROMANCE and the degrees of EV popularity around the world. Today, Automotive News’ Molly Boigon continues her “How the U.S. is Becoming an Outlier in the Global EV Race.”

The U.S. Reverses EV Push. “In 2020,” Boigon recounts, “the U.S. government and its automakers were closely watching the success of a paradigm-shifting startup: Tesla. During the course of that year, Tesla’s stock price rose more than 650 percent, reaching a market value of $658 billion—more than Ford Motor Co., General Motors and what was then Fiat Chrysler Automobiles combined.”

Boigon continues, “The Inflation Reduction Act, signed into law by then-President Joe Biden in 2022, revamped policies to grant a $4,000 tax credit for used EVs and a $7,500 credit for new EVs, part of an effort to drum up consumer interest.” But demand did not grow as expected and policies shifted. President Donald Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act eliminated the EV tax credits after Sept. 30, 2025.”

She observes, “The loss of federal tax credits has contributed to slowing U.S. EV sales, but consumer preferences, geography and the mix of available vehicles have also held back adoption. North America is expected to account for just 5 percent of global battery-electric vehicle production in 2026, according to Mobility Global’s September forecast.”

Boigon quotes Riley Keehn, senior consultant at SBD Automotive specializing in government regulatory affairs: “You have a government that says, ‘We want to maintain our competitiveness in vehicle technology, but we are going to walk back the federal funding.’ That makes it “very hard for OEMs to want to make a strong long-term commitment one way or the other.”

Meanwhile, Back in Beijing…. Boigon reports, “China has become the clear leader in EV sales and manufacturing after investing in supply chains, and establishing consistent industrial policies and incentives to spur production. China’s ‘governmental push’ has ‘catapulted the entire global electric vehicle industry forward by increasing battery range [and] improving battery technology to make it less expensive,’ said Sam Fiorani, vice president of global vehicle forecasting for AutoForecast Solutions. ‘It has really pushed the industry forward, and because of that, the acceptance rate in China is astounding.’ ”

“In 2020,” Boigon observes, “EVs and plug-in hybrids made up 6 percent of sales in China. In 2025, they were 53 percent, according to the International Energy Agency.”

Other Chinese Advantages. Boigon observes, “China also has several other advantages, notably access to raw materials crucial for EV production. The Chinese government has invested heavily in developing processing capacity and other parts of the supply chain, such as battery manufacturing. Finally, companies in China have deep experience in manufacturing consumer electronics, transferable skills for EV assembly.”

What U.S. Automakers Must Compete With. “From 2010 through 2024,” Boigon observes, “Chinese carmakers received twice as much government support in absolute terms and four times more support relative to revenue than 38 other countries, including the U.S., Germany and South Korea, according to a June 2026 Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development report on industrial subsidies.”

In the Meantime, Back in D.C. Confronting all of these challenges, Duffy and (climate-change-denying) Trump prattle on about “The Biden-Buttigieg administration previously broke the law by setting standards that went far beyond the requirements mandated by Congress—all to artificially juice supply for electric vehicles that American consumers didn’t ask for.”

Imagine that! Going “far beyond the requirements mandated by Congress”! ds

name: American Energy
title: Over 400 American AI Data Centers Use As Much Electricity As Wisconsin, Michigan, or Indiana
description:
The number of hyperscale data centers, which are larger and more powerful than traditional data centers, and are often used to train and run large-scale AI models, has exploded in recent years.
That number is only expected to grow: the research firm Synergy estimates that the total capacity of U.S. data centers will double in the next three years, largely driven by the growth of hyperscale data centers.
American voters rallied against data center development in the midterm elections this November, with many citing economic and environmental concerns.
Yet few studies have quantified just how much electricity each hyperscale data center uses, and what fuels generate the electricity, the researchers say.
Virginia, Iowa, and Ohio have the most emissions attributable to hyperscale data centers, while Oregon, which is home to more hyperscale data centers than Iowa and Ohio, has significantly fewer emissions due to a cleaner energy grid.
text:
America’s hyperscale data centers together use as much electricity as some entire U.S. states and produce millions of metric tons of carbon dioxide over the course of a year, according to a new study published Monday in Nature Sustainability.

The number of hyperscale data centers, which are larger and more powerful than traditional data centers, and are often used to train and run large-scale AI models, has exploded in recent years. Between 2019 and 2024, the number of data centers around the world doubled from a little over 500 to over 1,100, with more than half located in the United States. That number is only expected to grow: the research firm Synergy estimates that the total capacity of U.S. data centers will double in the next three years, largely driven by the growth of hyperscale data centers.

American voters rallied against data center development in the midterm elections this November, with many citing economic and environmental concerns. In 40 out of 41 local ballot initiatives across the country, citizens voted to limit or prevent data center development. Yet few studies have quantified just how much electricity each hyperscale data center uses, and what fuels generate the electricity, the researchers say.

“Even though there were a lot of [public and scientific] statements about the environmental impact of data centers, when we started this research, we realized that there was basically very little, if none, peer-reviewed data,” says Francesca Dominici, director of the Harvard Data Science Initiative and senior author of the paper.

The study provides one of the first facility-level estimates of the electricity use and carbon dioxide emissions of hyperscale data centers since the rise of AI. The researchers used satellite imagery to build a list of 403 hyperscale data centers across the U.S., and then estimated the annual electricity consumption for each facility between May 2024 and April 2025 under a range of operating scenarios. They then used data from the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency to calculate their emissions.

They found that, together, the data centers used between 68 and 99 terawatt-hours (TWh) of electricity—with the upper estimate equivalent to what some states, like Indiana, Michigan, and Tennessee, use in a year. In the lower scenario, the facilities still consumed approximately the annual electricity sold to customers in Wisconsin, roughly 70 TWh, or Minnesota, around 65 TWh.

Half of the electricity use of all the data centers studied was concentrated in just four states: Virginia, Oregon, Ohio, and Iowa, the report found. Virginia has long been known as “data center alley” due to its high number of data centers, but size and power capacity can also impact electricity consumption. The researchers identified 26 hyperscale facilities in Iowa, combined electricity consumption for which was approximately 7.2 TWh, with the average facility having substantially higher estimated electricity demand than the average facility in Virginia, where 142 hyperscale facilities account for approximately 21.4 TWh of annual electricity consumption.

However, the emissions impacts were not always the same. Virginia, Iowa, and Ohio have the most emissions attributable to hyperscale data centers, while Oregon, which is home to more hyperscale data centers than Iowa and Ohio, has significantly fewer emissions due to a cleaner energy grid.

“For the same amount of electricity consumed, the regional electricity mix associated with data centers in Wyoming produces approximately seven times more carbon dioxide than in Oregon,” says Gianluca Guidi, Harvard data scientist and the study’s lead author. “So these environmental impacts are not necessarily inevitable. Geography matters.”

The electricity demand and carbon emissions are likely even higher than the research shows. The team did not have enough data to assess every single hyperscale data center in the U.S. at the time, and more data centers have emerged since their study concluded in April 2025.

text:
A Michigan-based battery maker is going public in what's expected to be a $1 billion deal.

Novi startup Our Next Energy Inc. on Monday, Nov. 16 said it's merging with a "blank check" company to speed its way to public trading. The deal is set to close in the first half of 2027.

ONE will trade using the Nasdaq ticker symbol ONEE.

ONE is combining with Wen Acquisition Corp., which was created to pool money from investors and then identify a promising startup with which to merge. The process, called a special purpose acquisition, allows ONE to go public quickly by attaching to a shell company that is already public.

ONE was worth $600 million before the deal, and Wen brings $300 million in investments. The companies expect another $100 million after going public, including $30 million already promised by two unnamed global steel and defense investors.

ONE workers make battery cells in a Van Buren Township plant that are then put into packs and energy storage systems in Novi.

The startup was founded in 2020 to supply lithium-iron-phosphate-based batteries for electric vehicles. The formula is significant because it relies on a higher ratio of iron, a cheaper metal, to reduce battery costs.

ONE has since shifted its focus to supply batteries for railroads, the U.S. military and power grids after the Trump administration in the past two years gutted vehicle emissions rules that had pushed the auto industry toward EVs under the Biden administration.

ONE is hoping to capitalize on federal policies from both the Trump and Biden eras promoting U.S.-based battery production amid growing national security concerns over China's global dominance in the field.

The battery maker said in the Monday announcement that the Van Buren Township plant is "America’s only source" of large-format lithium-iron-phosphate cells built using domestic cell technology.

"Over the last five years, LFP has grown from roughly 20% to 60% of the global battery market, yet China produces approximately 99% of the world’s LFP cells," ONE founder and CEO Mujeeb Ijaz said in a statement. "We built ONE to close that gap with a secure American and allied supply chain. We believe our combination with Wen will give us a public platform to scale ONE into this $40B addressable market with access to growth capital as we scale our operations to meet rising demand.”

ONE says it already has multiyear agreements worth $200 million with five defense contractors and train companies including Canadian National.

The Michigan Economic Development Corporation in 2022 awarded ONE roughly $236 million in state support, including a $200 million performance-based grant through the state's Critical Industry Program.

The Michigan Strategic Fund Board in September reduced the Critical Industry Program grant by $50 million after ONE cut projected staffing from 2,112 to 1,606 new jobs in response to its pivot from EVs.

Ijaz in September thanked Michigan economic development officials for "continued support" as the company took on a "challenging turnaround."

Ijaz at the time said ONE had begun a second shift at its Van Buren Township facility and planned to expand the production line. He said the company’s battery technology was operating in more than 100 locomotives in North America and Canada, with a 50% improvement in diesel fuel economy for Class 1 locomotives.

As of September, the company employed 156 people in Michigan. The company laid off 29 employees in January after its largest electric vehicle customer "suddenly and unexpectedly cancelled its contract," the company told state employment officials.

title: Digging Deeper: How Geothermal Energy Can Strengthen America's Grid
description:
In many cases, geothermal development may also benefit from existing energy infrastructure, workforce expertise, and supply chains developed through decades of leadership in American energy production.
Utility regulators and state policymakers can help ensure geothermal resources are fully considered in utility planning processes and resource procurement decisions.
The Time to Act Is Now Geothermal energy is no longer a niche technology with limited potential.
Rapid technological innovation, growing electricity demand, and increasing focus on grid reliability are creating a major opportunity for geothermal deployment in the U.S.
Now is the time for Congress and states to act boldly to accelerate geothermal deployment and unlock one of America’s most promising energy opportunities.
text:
As America enters a new era of electricity demand growth, corporate energy buyers are increasingly investing in geothermal projects to power their growing operations.

Notably, recent technological advancements in geothermal have enabled much larger projects that can scale up to meet the demands of large energy customers, while also opening new areas of the U.S. to geothermal development. Together, these advances are making geothermal an increasingly attractive resource for CEBA members.

The U.S. needs more reliable, resilient, and affordable energy resources. New and growing economic sectors, including advanced manufacturing, electrification, and artificial intelligence, are increasing electricity demand.

Geothermal Is Built for Reliability

One of geothermal energy’s greatest strengths is its ability to provide consistent, around-the-clock electricity.

As reserve margins tighten and electricity demand continues to climb, reliable generation resources are becoming increasingly valuable to maintaining grid stability and supporting economic growth. Geothermal facilities operate with extremely high capacity factors and provide dependable power all day, rain or shine.

That reliability matters enormously to large electricity customers. Data centers, advanced manufacturers, and major retailers all depend on a stable supply of electricity to operate continuously and efficiently.

More Affordable Electricity

Affordability was a top issue for voters during the recent midterm elections, making access to lower-cost electricity increasingly important for both American businesses and households.

Across many regions, electricity prices are facing upward pressure from growing demand, transmission constraints, infrastructure costs, and fuel market volatility. Expanding reliable generation resources is essential to maintaining affordable electricity over the long term.

Geothermal energy offers important cost-stabilizing advantages as well. Once operational, geothermal facilities can provide stable generation with predictable operating costs over very long time horizons. Because geothermal resources do not depend on fuel deliveries or global fuel markets, they can provide long-term price stability benefits that help reduce exposure to volatility.

Accelerating geothermal deployment can also help reduce stress on constrained electricity systems by adding additional firm generation capacity closer to growing load centers.

In many cases, geothermal development may also benefit from existing energy infrastructure, workforce expertise, and supply chains developed through decades of leadership in American energy production. That overlap creates exciting opportunities to accelerate deployment while supporting domestic jobs and economic growth.

America Has a Big Opportunity to Lead

Even more exciting is the rapid advancement of enhanced geothermal systems and closed-loop geothermal technologies. These innovations are expanding geothermal’s potential far beyond traditional hydrothermal regions in Western states and creating opportunities for deployment in other parts of the country.

The U.S. could be on the verge of unlocking an entirely new category of reliable, domestic, carbon emissions-free energy production.

And the excitement around geothermal extends well beyond electricity generation alone.

That creates opportunities not only for new electricity generation, but also for domestic manufacturing growth, workforce development, technology exports, and energy leadership.

As countries around the world search for reliable and scalable energy solutions, America has an opportunity to lead the development of technologies that could shape the future of global energy systems.

Policies Help Unlock Geothermal’s Potential

Despite growing excitement and technological progress, geothermal deployment still faces important barriers.

Drilling risk is widely viewed as the geothermal industry’s greatest financial and geological challenge. Without direct visibility into the resource, exploration risks “dry holes” (inadequate water, heat, or permeability), compounded by high upfront costs and mechanical hazards.

Project developers also often encounter lengthy permitting timelines, financing challenges, transmission constraints, and regulatory frameworks that do not fully recognize the reliability and resiliency benefits geothermal provides.

In addition to passing BAAJA, Congress can help accelerate deployment by passing federal legislation focused on:

Establishing a federal drilling risk-sharing or “appraisal risk” program, including cost-share grants or co-financing of deep exploratory drilling

Streamlining permitting and environmental review processes for geothermal projects while maintaining strong environmental protections

Expanding support for demonstration projects and commercialization of advanced geothermal technologies

Improving access to federal financing tools and loan programs

Supporting transmission infrastructure upgrades needed to connect new generation resources

Modernizing electricity markets to appropriately value firm, dispatchable carbon emissions-free resources

Strengthening partnerships between the federal government, national laboratories, universities, utilities, and private industry

Preserving long-term policy certainty that enables durable private sector investment

The geothermal industry is advancing quickly, but long-term policy support and regulatory clarity will be essential to scaling deployment.

States also have a major opportunity to accelerate geothermal development. Utility regulators and state policymakers can help ensure geothermal resources are fully considered in utility planning processes and resource procurement decisions. States can also modernize permitting frameworks, support workforce development programs, encourage pilot projects, and create pathways for innovative procurement structures.

Importantly, states should recognize geothermal not simply as another energy resource, but as a technology that can help strengthen reliability, improve resiliency, and support long-term economic competitiveness.

The Time to Act Is Now

Geothermal energy is no longer a niche technology with limited potential.

Rapid technological innovation, growing electricity demand, and increasing focus on grid reliability are creating a major opportunity for geothermal deployment in the U.S.

The momentum is real. The technology is advancing. Now is the time for Congress and states to act boldly to accelerate geothermal deployment and unlock one of America’s most promising energy opportunities.
