text:
Staying silent on the climate crisis is pushing the world closer to disaster, the prime minister of Barbados, Mia Mottley, has said, urging people around the world to force a confrontation with politicians who are failing to do what is needed.

Taking action on methane emissions could be the emergency brake that gives the world time to decarbonise, Mottley said. She is urging people to sign a global petition to cut the powerful greenhouse gas.

She hopes to gather 1.5bn responses to her petition, in an echo of the 1.5C temperature limit countries have pledged to protect. “We have to let them know the good news: that if we can control methane, we can reduce temperature [rises] by 0.3C to 0.5C,” she said during an interview at the Cop31 UN climate summit, which is taking place in Antalya, Turkey. “We can buy time to continue decarbonising.”

Mottley, a charismatic leader who has challenged former colonial powers over slavery reparations, gained global recognition five years ago when she criticised rich countries for failing poor and vulnerable people on the climate crisis.

“Ordinary people have to be able to say what their view is with respect to living on this Earth,” she said. “I hope that by calling on ordinary people to speak out where leaders have failed to lead, we can see the kind of momentum that will cause all of us to reflect on what we’re doing as countries, and prioritise – in ways that do not compromise other aspects of our development – the efforts that are needed [on the climate].”

The “cancer of indifference” to the climate crisis, she said, would push the world closer to the brink. “We need to break [the climate crisis] down into ordinary simple language, so people understand what is at stake, either by their silence, their inaction, or indeed by their actions.

“This [petition] is not to undermine any government. It is really for us to get a sounding as a global community about how ordinary people feel about their future, how ordinary people want to embrace their future, or be sensitive to the realities of what might be their future if they continue to be inactive or silent.”

Mottley is frustrated by the chasm between leaders’ promises to act on greenhouse gas emissions, and the reality of continued reliance on fossil fuels. “We are on a train track, and all we are doing is jumping on and off, when the train is coming, and at some point the train is going to hit us,” she said. “Is this good enough management?”

The Cop31 talks are now entering their second week, with a draft text expected on Monday for a “cover decision”, a final document drawing together the main outcomes from the discussions and a series of resolutions to take stronger action on the climate.

These could include: a pledge to derive 35% of global energy from electricity by 2035; recognition that the world will “overshoot” the target of limiting heating to 1.5C above preindustrial levels; and measures to make it easier for the poorest and most vulnerable countries to access the financial assistance they have been promised.

Discussions on methane are still on the table, and though no new comprehensive treaty of the kind called for by Mottley will be signed at Cop31, the final outcome could reinforce efforts to reduce emissions the gas.

Durwood Zaelke, president of the Institute for Governance and Sustainable Development, a thinktank, said it was essential to address the release of methane, a greenhouse gas 80 times more powerful than carbon dioxide at heating the atmosphere, which comes from coalmines, oil and gas extraction sites, animal husbandry and landfill facilities.

“There is one way, and one way only, to slow warming in the near-term, and that’s to cut methane emissions, according to the best available science,” he said. “It’s clear that voluntary measures are not enough. We need a binding international agreement to cut methane.”

Mottley also endorsed a proposal put forward by Ngozi Okonjo-Iweala, director-general of the World Trade Organization, after the Nepal glacier collapse in August: that when disasters strike, banks should waive the fees they charge on the remittances sent by overseas workers back to their families.

In many developing countries, remittance money sent home by migrants is a key source of income, but banks charge substantial fees for the service. Okonjo-Iweala estimates that if the banks had waived these fees for two months on money sent home by Nepalese migrants after the glacier collapse, an additional $126m to $144m could have been raised, more than double the $49m in immediate relief from the US and others.

Banks and fossil fuel companies should understand their social obligations, Mottley said. “I hope we can have a greater sensitivity from the financial community as to what is required of them. You can’t be making trillions of dollars in profits and not be standing up where major disasters happen like this.

title: Solar lease holdouts still see value in privately-owned residential projects
description:

Some residential solar installers are still strictly pursuing and installing privately-owned solar projects.
Nickels Energy Solutions (NES), a residential solar contractor working in Central New York believes a privately-owned PV system is still the better deal for the customer.
NES is still building a steady pipeline of residential solar projects in New York.
Every state has policy enabling solar projects, but not necessarily cost incentives for individual projects.
text:
The One Big Beautiful Bill Act drastically reduced the lifespan of federal subsidies available to certain segments of the solar market, and among the first to go was the investment tax credit for residential projects. The ITC is a historic renewable energy subsidy that provides a 30% tax credit against the total cost of an eligible project, and it is currently available to the commercial and utility-scale solar segments.

After 2025, homeowners hoping to install solar on their house couldn’t subsidize the project’s cost with this federal subsidy if it was privately owned. However, a loophole in the tax credit language has allowed leased or “third party-owned” (TPO) solar projects to still receive the ITC (25D) on residential solar projects. In this scenario, it matters who owns the solar project, not necessarily where it’s built. The project can be subsidized because it is owned by a commercial company, and not the homeowner.

Some residential solar installers are still strictly pursuing and installing privately-owned solar projects. Nickels Energy Solutions (NES), a residential solar contractor working in Central New York believes a privately-owned PV system is still the better deal for the customer.

“We don’t have the same offers as some of the bigger companies,” said Kevin Nickels, VP of sales with NES. “If you can offer leases, it’s like the ‘haves and have-nots.’ I don’t have that loophole or that trick up my sleeve, so it forces me to get the project sold, while I’m as sharp as I can be with margins to make it somewhat competitive.”

TPO solar transactions are typically arranged at a lower up-front cost than a wholly owned solar project. Lease contract lengths vary by provider, and financiers have surety in these transactions because the projects will be built with products from an approved vendor list (AVL). Products on an AVL can qualify for a domestic content subsidy, another tax credit in addition to the ITC, because they are manufactured using a certain percentage of domestic components.

These are premium products vetted for AVLs. But it can also mean that installers are paying premium prices for components in building TPO solar projects.

Nickels believes that, while a privately owned residential solar project will cost more at the start, the combination of expensive components and interest rates for financing over a lease term — with factors like rate increases — can cost a customer more in the long run.

“I don’t think all leases are bad,” he said. “I just don’t think it’s what’s best for the industry or the homeowner.”

Selling residential solar in 2026

Rudy Wright, owner of Wright-Way Solar of Tyler, Texas, has shifted the company’s focus from building new projects to servicing existing systems. As the ITC exited the residential solar market, so did many of the lenders financing these projects. Without lending options, Wright-Way’s installation output has slowed down, and those clients who can afford solar are paying with cash or using a home equity loan to cover the cost.

Despite that, Wright said he isn’t very interested in building leased solar projects.

“I do think it cost me some of those entry level clients, but every time I analyzed the financing end of it, I felt like I was benefitting my company and the industry more than the customer,” Wright said. “I haven’t seen the angle where bringing a pre-purchase agreement or bringing a lease agreement has enough ironclad return for the customer.”

Tyler is a unique market for solar because many of Wright-Way’s customers are trying to make their properties more resilient, and less reliant on the grid, by installing solar and storage, and not just seeking cost savings for their energy use. Wright has installed solar plus storage systems on Texan ranches at a scale close a small commercial project.

That promise of resilience is still enough reason for some people to commission a solar project in Texas, where the state’s independent electrical grid operator has faltered and experienced dangerous outages in recent years.

“Folks realize money in the bank doesn’t do you any good if the power goes out,” Wright said.

NES is still building a steady pipeline of residential solar projects in New York. Nickels said that has been possible in part because many of its clients are upper-middle class; but New York also maintains an incentive program for solar projects, NY-Sun, which includes a 25% state tax credit for residential systems.

“The OBBBA caught a lot of states flat-footed,” Nickels said. “Without federal support, it puts a lot of pressure on what the state is offering.”

Some states’ solar subsidy programs have stepped in where federal support has diminished since the OBBBA was passed. The North Carolina Clean Energy Technology Center maintains the Database of State Incentives for Renewables & Efficiency, which analyzes which states currently have policies and incentives supporting clean energy developments. Every state has policy enabling solar projects, but not necessarily cost incentives for individual projects.

While traditional residential solar projects have lost a significant subsidy, the reality is that energy costs have risen in response to new grid demands from hyperscale data centers and oil scarcity from the United States’ war in Iran. Sure, a privately owned residential solar project won’t receive the ITC, but it can still stabilize energy costs without them.

“We lost a big incentive, but the rate increase is proportional,” Nickels said.

[Financial News] mPlus Corp., a company specializing in rechargeable-battery assembly equipment, is stepping up its push into the next-generation battery market after securing an order worth around ₩20 billion for solid-state battery equipment from a global company. The deal is drawing attention because it marks an expansion of the company’s equipment business, previously centered on electric vehicles (EVs) and energy storage systems (ESS), into solid-state battery mass-production processes.

According to industry sources on the 16th, mPlus Corp. recently secured an order worth around ₩20 billion from a global company for solid-state battery assembly and electrode-line equipment. The equipment is expected to be used to build the global company’s solid-state battery production line.

The equipment to be supplied incorporates technologies developed in-house by mPlus Corp., including notching, stacking and precision dispensing. The company is also developing Roll Press technology needed for solid-state battery manufacturing. It plans to use these technologies to expand the range of equipment it can supply for solid-state battery production.

Solid-state batteries are next-generation batteries that replace liquid electrolytes with solid ones to improve safety and energy density. However, their complex manufacturing processes make securing reliable mass-production technology a key challenge for commercialization. As a result, technological competition is intensifying not only among battery manufacturers but also among makers of equipment for key manufacturing processes.

With this order as a springboard, mPlus Corp. plans to focus on securing global customers and diversifying its business.

It has also recently been pursuing entry into the market for defense and special-purpose battery equipment, targeting European battery companies. The strategy is to broaden its order base to include solid-state and special-purpose batteries, in addition to equipment for EVs and ESS.

Industry observers expect order opportunities for related equipment makers to grow as the solid-state battery market moves beyond research and development and begins preparing for commercialization. In particular, they say that a track record of supplying initial production lines could be a factor in gauging competitiveness in future orders for mass-production facilities.

A company representative said, "This order is significant because it gives us a track record of supplying a global customer in the solid-state battery assembly-equipment sector," and added, "We also expect opportunities for additional orders as our customers expand mass production."

Meanwhile, mPlus Corp. is expanding its business portfolio to include pouch-type, prismatic and solid-state battery assembly equipment, as well as autonomous mobile robots (AIMR) and control systems.

title: 5 Ways Utilities Can Build Trust Into Energy Programs
description:
Practical strategies for creating stronger customer relationships and more effective energy programs Energy efficiency programs can offer meaningful benefits to households facing high energy burdens.
Trust should inform every stage of program design and delivery, from the first introduction to installation and ongoing support.
So, how can you earn the trust of customers who may be hesitant to participate?
Over time, those CBO partners became the program's strongest source of enrollment leads, demonstrating the value of building relationships with organizations that already have community trust.
RI's Benefication Lab brings energy efficiency and clean energy technologies directly into communities.
text:
This Solutions Spotlight article was contributed byResource Innovations.

Practical strategies for creating stronger customer relationships and more effective energy programs

Energy efficiency programs can offer meaningful benefits to households facing high energy burdens. But customers may be hesitant to participate if they question the offer: Is it really free? What's the catch? Can I trust the people coming to my home? Without confidence in the program, the utility, or the people delivering the service, customers may decide it's not worth the risk.

Reaching priority communities takes more than marketing and outreach. It requires understanding the local relationships, experiences, and barriers that shape participation. Trust should inform every stage of program design and delivery, from the first introduction to installation and ongoing support.

So, how can you earn the trust of customers who may be hesitant to participate? Start with these five strategies.

1. Go Where Trust Already Lives

There is no universal formula for establishing credibility. An organization trusted in one community may not have the same standing in another, and your utility's relationship with customers can vary based on their experiences and perceptions.

That’s why you should work with organizations already connected to the communities you want to reach. Community-based organizations (CBOs), community action agencies, and other local partners understand the needs and barriers facing the people they serve.

Resource Innovations (RI) has seen the value of this approach through its work with community action agencies and CBOs across an Illinois utility's service territory. RI helped partners identify local barriers, develop targeted outreach strategies, and strengthen their capacity to deliver energy efficiency services. Over time, those CBO partners became the program's strongest source of enrollment leads, demonstrating the value of building relationships with organizations that already have community trust.

Treat these organizations as program partners, not simply outreach or enrollment channels. Strong partnerships require clear roles, adequate resources, and fair compensation. You should also ensure that administrative requirements, reporting demands, enrollment targets, and cost-effectiveness pressures do not make sustained participation impractical for smaller organizations.

Investing in these relationships can help you reach customers who might otherwise be overlooked while building local capacity for effective, sustained program delivery.

2. No Surprises, Just Clear Answers

Customers unfamiliar with your program need to understand what they're signing up for, what they’ll receive, who will provide the service, and what’s expected of them.

This is especially important when you offer free or subsidized products and services. Customers may wonder whether your offer is legitimate, what information they must provide, how you’ll use their data, and whether any costs or obligations apply.

Answer these questions early and in straightforward, accessible language. Explain eligibility, benefits, installation expectations, potential disruptions, and next steps. Make sure your program materials, outreach conversations, and customer experience reinforce the same expectations so customers can make informed decisions.

3. One Program, One Clear Message

For customers, every interaction is part of the same program. They hear about your program from a community organization, speak with a utility representative or call center, and later interact with a contractor or installation crew. Although these groups may work independently, customers experience every handoff as part of one program.

In priority communities, inconsistent information or unfamiliar representatives can create uncertainty and undermine confidence. Set communication standards and make sure everyone involved has the training, tools, and information to answer questions, explain requirements, and communicate across cultures and languages.

During a ZIP-code-based outreach effort in Southern California, RI coordinated with the local public utility to introduce the program before field teams arrived. Flyers, emails, and other materials included the utility's name, giving customers advance notice and a familiar source to verify the program and its representatives.

When you coordinate communication across your utility, community partners, and field teams, customers are more likely to recognize legitimate program representatives and receive consistent information at every stage.

4. Show, Don’t Just Tell

As your energy programs expand beyond familiar efficiency measures to include heat pumps, induction cooking, solar, battery storage, and other newer or less familiar technologies, customers need to understand what these solutions mean for their homes and daily lives. Financial incentives can make new technologies more appealing, but your customers also need clear information about how they work, what installation involves, and what to expect after installation.

Build education into your program design. Materials in customers’ preferred languages, instructional videos, technical guidance, and hands-on opportunities can address the information needs and experiences of the communities you serve.

RI's Benefication Lab brings energy efficiency and clean energy technologies directly into communities. In partnership with one of the Midwest's largest electric utilities, RI has taken the Lab to local events, where customers and community partners can see heat pumps, EV charging, and demand response in action and ask questions.

These firsthand experiences make unfamiliar solutions more approachable, helping customers understand their options and make informed decisions.

5. Keep Showing Up

Trust is ultimately tested after customers enroll. Make sure the process is as clear and reliable during delivery as it was during outreach. Customers need to understand what they are receiving, who is providing it, what information is being collected, and what happens next.

Your support shouldn’t end after installation. Customers adopting newer technologies may need help understanding equipment, navigating controls, maintaining systems, or adjusting how they use energy. Provide clear points of contact and reliable ways for customers to ask questions and resolve issues.

Following through shows customers that your commitment extends beyond enrollment and installation. It helps them receive the value they were promised and can shape their willingness to participate in future programs.

A Better Experience Starts With Trust

A program can offer the right incentives, services, and technologies, but will customers feel comfortable taking part? To answer that, consider the experience your program creates for the people you want to reach:

Is the value of participating clear?

Do customers know who they can turn to with questions or concerns?

Does the experience reflect the needs and expectations of the communities you serve?

Looking at your programs from the customer perspective can help uncover opportunities to make participation more welcoming, accessible, and worthwhile. Sometimes, small changes can make a meaningful difference in how customers experience your programs.

title: What Governor Becerra Needs to Know About Just Land Transition
description:
We need the next Administration to become a partner and a leader to implement a just land transition.
UCS developed principles and outlined several next steps for how various decisionmakers can pursue a just land transition.
Coordinate across agencies involved in a just land transition A just land transition is a systemic transformation governed by a suite of agencies at the state, regional, and local level.
The Department of Conservation administers the Multibenefit Land Repurposing Program to fund local block grants to assist in local cropland repurposing.
Planning for and executing a just land transition will be challenging.
text:
The next Governor has the opportunity to lead California into a new future where agriculture is a thriving component of local economies that provides food and good jobs to nearby communities and improves public health. In this future, beneficial farming and soil practices are incentivized, communities have equitable access to clean, reliable, and sustainable sources of water, and rural communities are leaders in a systemic transformation that prioritizes public health, the environment, resilience, and self-determination.

Agriculture is a vital part of California’s rural economy. But conventional irrigated agricultural practices have contributed to groundwater declines and subsidence in the Central Valley, contaminated drinking water wells, and exposed communities to pesticides, dust, and poor air quality, among other public health concerns. These problems can be addressed by employing better agricultural practices, converting marginal lands to other uses, prioritizing nature-based solutions, and most importantly: ensuring that impacted communities are leading in a just land transition.

The state can do better for Californians and resolve the systemic inequities that have plagued rural communities. We need the next Administration to become a partner and a leader to implement a just land transition.

The next Governor will not be starting from scratch. California passed landmark legislation to sustainably manage groundwater throughout the state and doubled down to support a $10 billion Climate Bond, including over $200 million for multibenefit cropland repurposing. The Fifth California Climate Change Assessment, released in October, provides new tools for California communities to better understand and prepare for climate change impacts. California needs a Governor committed to building on this progress.

Cropland repurposing is a multibenefit solution

California’s challenges on water and agricultural policy represent major barriers for public health and equity, and while work has begun in earnest to tackle these issues, more needs to be done.

California’s groundwater basins are overdrafted due to a combination of overpumping and climate change impacts. Up to one million acres of irrigated agriculture may need to be repurposed in the San Joaquin Valley to achieve groundwater sustainability. Surface water is also stressed: recent research by scientists at UCS and UC Merced found that climate change has reduced April snowpack by 36% and warm season streamflow by 13%. At the same time, irrigation demand has increased by 4.3% in the western United States. In California’s Central Valley, our research found that human-caused climate change accounts for 20% of observed groundwater loss. Conversely, extreme wet periods cause destructive flooding to Central Valley communities, especially those without adequate flood protections.

A just land transition is a multibenefit solution to these challenges that will help rural California communities tackle longtime pollution and water equity issues, while also better preparing them to face climate events in the future.

But what does it mean to pursue just cropland transition? Rather than allowing the status quo to persist, and irrigated cropland to go out of production based on market forces alone, a just land transition takes strategic action to ensure that frontline communities are centered and included in cropland repurposing decisions, ultimately reshaping the agricultural system from an extractive to a just economy.

UCS developed principles and outlined several next steps for how various decisionmakers can pursue a just land transition. Ensuring frontline communities are leaders and decisionmakers in the cropland repurposing that occurs inside and around their communities is paramount to implementing these principles.

Where and how this transition happens is critical to maximizing community benefits and minimizing economic losses from unmitigated cropland retirement. Repurposing cropland within a one-mile buffer of rural disadvantaged communities in the Central Valley can significantly reduce water use, pollution from pesticides and nitrate leaching, and greenhouse gas emissions. Investments in multibenefit cropland repurposing can help recover a portion of revenues and jobs lost in the agriculture sector.

Beyond reducing harm of extractive practices and mitigating adverse economic impacts of cropland retirement, multibenefit cropland repurposing presents an opportunity to build capacity and climate resilience in rural disadvantaged and vulnerable communities. California is facing a future of weather whiplash, with increased dry and wet periods. In addition to the challenge of remedying historical groundwater overdraft, communities will continue to face periods of drought and flood. Repurposing cropland and employing nature-based solutions can produce numerous benefits tailored to the needs of different communities. Managed aquifer recharge and floodplain restoration, for example, can produce water supply benefits, helping to restore depleted aquifers while reducing flood risk for California communities. Sustainable agricultural practices are also part of the solution by reducing water use, building soil health, and reducing pollution and runoff. Incorporating solar through agrivoltaics and ecovoltaics can also build out renewable energy resources, provide local energy security, deliver shade, and save water. Prioritizing multibenefit opportunities for cropland repurposing can result in reduced groundwater demands and more widespread adoption of nature-based solutions that reduce flood risk and replenish aquifers. Together, these strategic multibenefit cropland repurposing efforts lead to a just land transition that can help address historic inequities while increasing resilience ahead of future climate disasters.

Three opportunities to advance just cropland transition in the next administration

Focus public resources on improving systems inside and around communities.

We know that investing in cropland repurposing in buffer zones can produce benefits for nearby communities and reduce economic losses from retired cropland. While California took numerous steps to increase planning and investment around sustainable groundwater management, including demand management and cropland repurposing, additional steps must be taken to ensure those benefits reach communities most impacted by land use transitions.

During the Newsom Administration, over 90 groundwater subbasins adopted Groundwater Sustainability Plans that will guide local implementation of measures to achieve sustainable management of California’s aquifers. The Legislature also established and funded the Multibenefit Land Repurposing Program (MLRP) to fund cropland transition in high and medium priority groundwater subbasins, with over $200M in additional funding provided through the Climate Bond.

Both MLRP and Proposition 4 included strong standards that prioritize funding for projects that directly benefit disadvantaged and vulnerable communities. However, more could be done to expand applicability of best practices and target investment to ensure that all rural disadvantaged and vulnerable communities are resourced to strategically implement cropland repurposing solutions in and around these communities.

Ensure decision-making processes are inclusive and equitable: communities must be included in planning and decision-making

A cornerstone of a just land transition is that communities must be included in decision-making processes.

Efforts have been made to create greater guidance and accountability about how to conduct community engagement and what it means to prioritize community needs. In 2025, the MLRP guidelines were amended to include language defining “meaningful community benefits.” Proposition 4 further requires that 40% of bond investments provide direct and meaningful benefits for disadvantaged and vulnerable communities. Public funding that prioritizes meaningful community engagement and outcomes is progress. However, we will look to the next Administration to ensure that a consistent definition of community benefits is applied across bond-funded programs, track expenditures, and provide oversight to program implementation. Looking beyond the Climate Bond, we would also encourage the Administration to carry this forward by including community decision-making processes and community benefits as requirements of future funding allocations.

Coordinate across agencies involved in a just land transition

A just land transition is a systemic transformation governed by a suite of agencies at the state, regional, and local level. For example:

Both the Department of Water Resources and the State Water Resources Control Board hold oversight authority to ensure that the Sustainable Groundwater Management Act (SGMA) is appropriately administered.

Local Groundwater Sustainability Agencies are responsible for developing and implementing plans to achieve the groundwater sustainability goals set out by SGMA.

The Department of Conservation administers the Multibenefit Land Repurposing Program to fund local block grants to assist in local cropland repurposing.

Local government agencies hold land use and permitting authority that shape cropland repurposing opportunities and benefits within their jurisdictions.

Each agency plays a critical role in guiding just land transition actions. Their cooperation is critical to ensure a swift, strategic, and coordinated transition that maximizes equity and opportunity and minimizes harm.

Transformational change is possible

With the leadership of Governor Becerra, California can enact meaningful change to develop a healthy and sustainable agricultural economy centered around healthy communities and the environment. Cropland repurposing can support communities pursuing a healthy environment, climate resilience, and groundwater sustainability. To advance this solution, we encourage the Becerra Administration to (1) focus public investments on public benefit projects near communities, (2) include communities in planning and decision-making, and (3) coordinate agencies at every level throughout California that are involved in achieving a just land transition.

Planning for and executing a just land transition will be challenging. The Union of Concerned Scientists looks forward to working with Governor Becerra and his administration with our science and evidence-based advocacy.

text:
Young people of faith from around the nation, including Texas, are in Washington, D.C., meeting with members of Congress today.

The students attended the Ignatian Family Teach-In for Justice 2026 conference, where they discussed immigration, climate change and artificial intelligence.

Robbie McCoy, an undergraduate student at the University of the Incarnate Word, said their meetings with lawmakers center around a proposed federal moratorium on artificial intelligence.

"The rate that we have progressed with development with AI data centers in such a wide variety of states, we are now calling for that to be temporarily paused while we reassess future developments and what their potential environmental harm could be," McCoy explained.

Texas is one of the nation’s leading states for data center development, with 123 data center campuses and 36 more under construction. Residents across the state have criticized lawmakers for allowing so many data centers to open in both rural and metropolitan areas. Outgoing Governor Greg Abbott issued a moratorium on rural data centers earlier this year. Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa has said all construction should be halted until the state puts more protections and guidelines in place.

McCoy pointed out as more facilities have opened, residents are experiencing negative effects, from job losses to quality-of-life issues.

"A lot of these are right next to residential communities, next to schools, and we're hearing from constituents, they're voicing concerns, rightly so, about how is this going to impact my kids? This is already impacting my life," McCoy observed.

If passed, the legislation would immediately prohibit construction or expansion of qualifying AI data centers until Congress passes additional laws establishing protections for workers, consumers, communities and the environment. It would also restrict the export of computer chips and other technology used to operate AI systems to countries that don’t have comparable AI regulations.

title: Will Latin America Capitalize on the U.S. Data Center Backlash?
description:
Reading Time: 5 minutes Two weeks ago, voters in Texas, Georgia and Ohio—which together account for about 40% of planned U.S. data center capacity—elected governors who campaigned on restricting the development of data centers.
Abundant energy resources mean little if electricity cannot reach a data center when needed.
In Chile, residents’ objections and an environmental court ruling prompted Google to abandon an original design for the Cerrillos data center.
In the state of Querétaro, Mexico, community groups have shown significant dissatisfaction with the data center boom and promised benefits that have yet to materialize.
Tags: AI, data centers, Latin America, Technology
text:
Reading Time: 5 minutes

Two weeks ago, voters in Texas, Georgia and Ohio—which together account for about 40% of planned U.S. data center capacity—elected governors who campaigned on restricting the development of data centers. Voters across the country overwhelmingly backed limits on data centers in local ballot measures, providing the most recent and clearest rejection thus far, rooted in concerns about rising electricity costs, environmental impact, and the livability of the communities involved. While the country leads the global race for AI supremacy, Americans are increasingly voicing a “not in my backyard” stance on the infrastructure powering it.

Before the elections, lawmakers in states including Georgia, Michigan, Pennsylvania, and Vermont proposed moratoriums on new data center developments, while a Virginia bill proposing a statewide pause on local approvals carried over to the 2027 legislative session. Around the U.S., communities are questioning the electricity, water, land, and infrastructure demands of these massive facilities, even as developers promise new jobs, tax revenues, and local infrastructure investments.

Could this growing opposition create an opportunity for Latin America?

The answer is yes, but success is far from guaranteed. Latin America has repeatedly struggled to convert its abundant natural resources into sustained investment and economic development. Bolivia’s once-booming gas industry and Venezuela’s now-diminished oil sector are recent examples of missed opportunities. This time, countries will need to transform their energy resources, available land, and geographic advantages into reliable electricity, predictable regulation, less red tape, and a compelling proposition for investors and local communities.

The scale of the opportunity is considerable. According to the International Energy Agency, global data center electricity consumption could more than double from approximately 415 terawatt-hours in 2024 to 945 TWh by 2030, approaching 3% of global electricity demand. In Latin America, this expansion will require enormous investments in power generation, transmission, distribution, storage, and digital infrastructure.

However, data center demand varies widely. AI model training, which involves processing vast amounts of information, may offer greater geographic flexibility than applications that require extremely low latency to serve U.S. users. Connectivity, data sovereignty, cybersecurity, technology restrictions, and customer requirements will also shape investment decisions.

Latin America’s opportunity is therefore less about relocating existing American facilities and more about capturing a meaningful share of future global investment. The maquila industry in the 80s and 90s was based on lower labor costs, favorable customs arrangements, and proximity to the U.S. For the data center ecosystem, affordable, reliable, and, in most cases, clean energy, along with high-quality connectivity and access to fiber-optic and multiple submarine cables, would bring more value than cheap labor alone.

Three priorities

As the region experiences an AI boom, with Chile and Brazil at the forefront, three priorities could determine its success. Delivering reliable power and connectivity is a critical first step. Abundant energy resources mean little if electricity cannot reach a data center when needed. AI campuses require exceptionally reliable power, often at scales that exceed the capabilities of existing local grids. Countries should identify locations where generation, transmission, connectivity, and land availability can be developed together, rather than treating each as a separate investment decision.

This is where Latin America’s energy resources could provide a competitive advantage. Natural gas can provide reliable generation, while abundant solar, wind and hydroelectric resources can support competitive electricity costs and reduce emissions. Battery energy storage systems can complement these resources, provide flexibility and improve grid reliability. The optimal mix will vary by country, but the objective should be the same: deliver reliable, competitively priced electricity while strengthening the broader power system.

Second, countries should establish predictable rules while protecting existing electricity customers. Data center developers need regulatory certainty, enforceable contracts, transparent permitting, and realistic infrastructure timelines. Governments must also ensure that the costs of serving these large new customers do not fall disproportionately on households and existing businesses.

Third, the region should create lasting benefits for local economies. The opportunity should extend well beyond construction spending and property taxes. Governments and developers can work together to strengthen local supply chains, train technical workers, support universities and research institutions, and expand access to computing infrastructure for local businesses.

Community engagement must begin early, with transparent discussions about water consumption, environmental impacts, land use and noise. Local communities should see measurable improvements in infrastructure, economic opportunities and public services.

The risks are already visible in the region. In Chile, residents’ objections and an environmental court ruling prompted Google to abandon an original design for the Cerrillos data center. In Brazil’s Ceará state, federal prosecutors filed a suit to prevent a data center from beginning operations until a consultation with the Anacé Indigenous people and an environmental impact study had been completed. In the state of Querétaro, Mexico, community groups have shown significant dissatisfaction with the data center boom and promised benefits that have yet to materialize.

Routes to competitiveness

Brazil combines a large domestic market, substantial renewable generation and an established digital economy, positioning it to serve both domestic demand and selected international computing workloads. Mexico benefits from proximity to the U.S., strong industrial integration and access to North American natural gas, although electricity and water constraints could limit development in some locations.

Argentina offers an intriguing combination of Vaca Muerta’s natural gas resources—255 trillion cubic feet of technically recoverable gas—renewable energy potential, and available land, particularly for large-scale AI computing facilities. However, regulatory predictability, financing conditions, and infrastructure execution will be decisive. Chile brings experience in renewable energy, battery storage, and attracting data center players, although transmission constraints and water availability require careful consideration.

Other markets, including Colombia, Panama, Paraguay, Uruguay and the Dominican Republic, could develop more targeted propositions based on connectivity, location, energy resources, or specific customer needs. Venezuela may eventually offer opportunities given its substantial energy resources, but significant institutional and infrastructure challenges remain.

Multilateral institutions such as the Inter-American Development Bank and CAF could help governments improve investment frameworks. IFC has financed ODATA’s expansion in Brazil, IDB Invest is considering providing up to $300 million for Scala Data Centers in Brazil, and CAF is exploring financing options for data center and technological infrastructure projects in Argentina.

Competing through certainty and reliability

Governments should act now to identify competitive locations, coordinate electricity and digital infrastructure investments, accelerate permitting, and establish clear rules to protect consumers and communities.

Some countries are already responding. The U.S. Department of State recently announced an agreement between Crusoe, a U.S. technology infrastructure company, and Araico, a Paraguayan developer, to build high-performance AI cloud computing infrastructure powered by hydroelectricity from the Itaipu dam. Brazil recently enacted tax incentives for data centers while considering additional rules on electricity infrastructure, environmental protection, and consumer costs. Mexico is debating requirements addressing electricity and water consumption, while Argentina is considering incentives for large AI infrastructure investments. These initiatives illustrate both the growing regional interest and the need to balance investment promotion with reliable infrastructure and public acceptance.

The region cannot afford to miss another investment opportunity because its natural advantages failed to translate into execution. More importantly, attracting data centers should not be the end goal. The goal is to use this wave of investment to modernize electricity grids, develop technological capabilities, and create lasting economic opportunities for its citizens.

text:
SamsungSDI has secured an additional supply volume of LFP (lithium iron phosphate) batteries for energy storage systems (ESS) worth 3 to 4 trillion won from U.S.-based Jupiter Power, signaling a major step in expanding its medium- and long-term order book. After already securing production volumes through 2028, the company has also landed large-scale, long-term contracts starting in 2029, broadening its growth foundation in the U.S. ESS market.

As of the 16th, SamsungSDI's cumulative U.S. power ESS order book has grown to over 76 GWh (gigawatt-hours), including an additional 16 GWh contract with Jupiter Power. The existing order volume of more than 60 GWh secured by the end of October this year alone is sufficient to keep the U.S. SPE (Star Plus Energy) and Ulsan production lines running at full capacity through 2028. This new contract covers supply over three years starting in 2029, marking another achievement for SamsungSDI in securing long-term supply volumes.

To meet growing ESS demand, SamsungSDI is accelerating the expansion of its local production capacity in the United States. In early October, the company began mass production of prismatic LFP batteries for ESS at its SPE plant in Indiana, and started shipping battery cells from mid-October. The produced cells will undergo module and battery box processes before being delivered to customers as finished SBB (Samsung Battery Box) products starting in December.

SamsungSDI is working to expand supply capacity by converting existing electric vehicle (EV) battery production lines into ESS LFP battery facilities. It is additionally converting two of the four production lines at its U.S. SPE Plant 1. The company also plans to utilize the U.S. Synergy Cells plant, acquired through the full buyout of its joint venture stake with GM (General Motors) in August, as an ESS production hub. Synergy Cells is currently optimizing designs to convert existing EV facilities into high-capacity LFP battery production lines for ESS. Mass production is scheduled to begin from late 2028 to early 2029, followed by phased expansion of production lines.

This expansion of the ESS business is also closely tied to efforts to capture the battery market for AI (artificial intelligence) data centers. SamsungSDI is accelerating its market push by leveraging its status as the world's only company capable of supplying all three essential battery solutions for data centers: BESS (battery energy storage systems), UPS (uninterruptible power supplies), and BBU (battery backup units). As a result, performance has shown signs of recovery. SamsungSDI's cumulative operating profit for the first three quarters of this year reached 456 billion won, turning profitable compared to an operating loss of 1.4232 trillion won in the same period last year.

Building on its improved performance, SamsungSDI is strategizing to accelerate its next-generation all-solid-state battery business. All-solid-state batteries use solid electrolytes instead of liquid ones, offering enhanced safety. The company is developing the technology with a target of commercialization in the second half of next year. Since September, it has been supplying all-solid-state battery cell and pack samples for humanoid robots to multiple customers for performance evaluation. It is currently at the stage of refining product specifications for next year's mass production through iterative performance improvements and verification based on customer requirements. The company is also working in parallel to establish a stable supply chain for key materials such as cathode materials and solid electrolytes.

A SamsungSDI official stated, "This order reflects recognition of our global technological competitiveness by securing large volumes early on," adding, "We will continue to lead the market with products that combine the performance and safety required by customers."

General Motors (GM) announced its largest clean energy investment to date, with the automotive giant signing a deal for 276 MW of energy, serving as the primary customer for two new solar facilities in Michigan developed by NorthStar Clean Energy.

According to GM, the new projects represent a combined investment of approximately $550 million, and are expected to generate roughly 539,000 megawatt-hours of electricity annually.

The new agreements follow an announcement earlier this year by GM that it had secured enough renewable energy to match 100% of electricity consumption across its U.S. facilities in 2025, becoming the first U.S. automaker to reach the milestone.

Under the new deal, GM will serve as the primary customer through a virtual power purchase agreement (VPPA) for the Branch Solar project in Branch County and Lake Iris Solar project in St. Clair County.

According to GM, the facilities are expected to generate electricity equivalent to the combined annual electricity consumption of three of the company’s Michigan assembly plants, Factory ZERO, Flint Assembly and Lansing Delta Township Assembly.

GM said that it plans to apply renewable energy credits generated by the projects toward emissions associated with electricity purchased for its manufacturing operations. The company added that it has reduced its Scope 1 and 2 greenhouse gas emissions by 52% since 2018.

Casandra Garber, Chief Sustainability Officer, GM, said:

“For GM, long-term renewable energy helps us manage costs, strengthen the operations behind the vehicles, batteries, and technologies we build, and advance our zero-emissions vision. It’s a practical example of how sustainable business and economic growth can reinforce each other.”

title: Texas turns blue, but here's where the next 4 big battles are coming
description:
After November’s election verdict, Texas isn’t doomed to become California overnight — but not for a lack of trying.
Inauguration Day in 2027, all statewide executive offices were held by Republicans — now the opposite will be the case.
Democrats took the state House of Representatives, but Republicans still hold the state Senate.
Democrat Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa will bring Texans an entirely new set of priorities and a vastly different style of governance.
Regulation and lawsuit climate Texas last passed major tort reform in 2003 and has seen its national lawsuit-climate ranking slip since then.
text:
Hinojosa is already moving against Elon Musk’s Starbase expansion in Cameron County.

After November’s election verdict, Texas isn’t doomed to become California overnight — but not for a lack of trying.

As in much of America (Florida excepted), Texas saw major midterm losses for a Republican Party that has dominated the Lone Star State for the past quarter century. Inauguration Day in 2027, all statewide executive offices were held by Republicans — now the opposite will be the case.

Democrats took the state House of Representatives, but Republicans still hold the state Senate. Republicans also retain a one-vote margin on the state Supreme Court, and the state’s powerful Railroad Commission (the agency that regulates the oil and gas industry, gas utilities, pipeline safety and surface coal and uranium mining) will have a 2-to-1 Republican majority.

Democrat Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa will bring Texans an entirely new set of priorities and a vastly different style of governance. She began her career as a labor attorney, including working for a powerful government union. In 2005, she was on the legal team that pursued lawfare against then-Republican House Majority Leader Tom DeLay on money-laundering charges.

DeLay was driven from office, convicted in 2010 and fully acquitted in 2014 — the process is the punishment. Before her election to the Texas House in 2016, Hinojosa served on the board of trustees for the Austin Independent School District, a district that has struggled with declining enrollment and the threat of state takeover after campuses received five consecutive failing accountability ratings.

How might Texas under Hinojosa’s leadership fare? Here are four things to watch.

Taxes and spending

For decades, Texas has benefited from lower taxes and a smaller, less intrusive government than peer-state rivals such as California, Illinois and New York. The population has soared as millions of Americans — and foreign nationals — sought opportunity. That is unlikely to change overnight. What is likely is incremental slippage as other states, notably Florida and Tennessee, work to attract talent and investment.

Regulation and lawsuit climate

Texas last passed major tort reform in 2003 and has seen its national lawsuit-climate ranking slip since then. Hinojosa’s ascent likely means a gradual strengthening of the state’s trial bar at the expense of economic growth.

Ironically, it will likely also increase the cost of living — with affordability an explicit promise of the incoming Democratic leadership. Further, Texas’s innovative Business Court and the Fifteenth Court of Appeals, both created in 2023, saw all three Republican members of the Fifteenth Court lose to Democrats. This flip may tilt the landscape against larger employers when interpreting the scope and power of state regulatory actions.

Hinojosa has already moved against billionaire Elon Musk’s plans to expand SpaceX’s Starbase site in Cameron County. Given the governor-elect was part of the lawfare posse that destroyed DeLay, will Hinojosa and her lieutenants resist the urge to go after Musk personally at the risk of harming job creation and innovation in Texas?

Culture and higher education

Here is where Hinojosa’s victory may have a significant long-term effect. She is positioned to reverse strictures that banned the use of so-called diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI) in hiring and curriculum, especially in the university system. Her appointments to higher-education governing boards could reverse many of the commonsense gains made under outgoing Republican Gov. Greg Abbott, including the 2023 ban on DEI offices and related practices.

Border security

Here Hinojosa’s campaign promises could have an immediate and dramatic effect. Texas has worked alongside the federal government under Republican President Donald Trump, and in spite of the federal government under former Democrat President Joe Biden, to secure its roughly 1,254-mile border with Mexico.

The state’s effort — with National Guard soldiers and Department of Public Safety troopers — aims to protect Texans’ health and welfare by interdicting transnational human smuggling and drug-cartel operations, which include the use of increasingly sophisticated and deadly drones.

The federal government has some 12,000 to 19,000 Border Patrol, Customs, DEA and active-duty military personnel deployed along the border in Texas at any given time. The state of Texas, through Operation Lone Star, has augmented that with up to 5,500 Guard soldiers and 1,600 DPS troopers for a total of up to 7,000 personnel — meaning Texas provides about one out of every two people guarding the long Rio Grande frontier.

Ending Texas’s border effort removes thousands of state law-enforcement and surveillance personnel from the border. The result could be more deadly fentanyl, more human trafficking, and more dangerous illegal aliens successfully crossing into Texas and causing death and injury. All of this could be avoidable, and it is unlikely that the voters who gave Hinojosa her margin of victory were fully aware of this portion of her platform.

Texas’s long-run advantages in taxes, regulation and energy will not vanish on inauguration day. But the direction of travel for the next four years is now clear, and the four areas above will show how quickly — and how far — the state embraces California-style dysfunction.

text:
German automaker BMW Group has begun production of high-voltage batteries at its new Plant Woodruff manufacturing facility in South Carolina, US.

The company’s sixth-generation (Gen6) high-voltage battery packs, assembled at the new facility, will be integrated into the all-electric BMW iX5 at BMW’s nearby vehicle Plant Spartanburg.

BMW did not state a capacity for Plant Woodruff but said that the two production facilities in South Carolina will produce 450,000 vehicles annually. Spartanburg produces vehicles of all fuel types.

The iX5 is BMW’s first all-electric vehicle to be assembled in the US, though the company aims to have six EV models assembled in the US available by 2030. The Woodruff facility will assemble batteries for future models too.

BMW is already assembling Gen6 batteries at facilities in Hungary, Germany and China, and has plans for a fifth site in Mexico to begin production in 2027. All of the battery plants have been constructed close to BMW’s existing vehicle assembly facilities.

Raymond Wittmann, member of the Board of Management of BMW AG responsible for production, said: “With the opening of our Woodruff plant, we are expanding our global Gen6 network: high-voltage battery assembly is now in place in Europe, Asia and North America. This creates a key prerequisite for producing fully electric Neue Klasse vehicles on three continents.”

Plant Woodruff will employ 300 people and deploy a further 250 robots in the assembly line.

The battery assembly facility will use battery cells from AESC, a lithium-ion EV battery manufacturing joint venture established by Nissan and Tokin Corporation in 2007, with Chinese OEM Envision Energy becoming a partner in 2018.

In 2022, BMW and AESC announced a production and supply partnership that saw AESC commit to investing in a dedicated new 30GWh battery manufacturing plant in South Carolina near BMW’s facilities.

However, in 2025, AESC paused construction as a result of the increased overhead caused by import tariffs. It also repurposed an existing EV battery facility in Tennessee to produce industrial energy solutions. Although AESC is still supplying cells for Plant Woodruff, it is unclear where those cells are shipped from.

text:
They are counting on you not to read our coverage of the Cop31 climate talks. Fossil fuel companies, climate science deniers, petrostates, far right populists … They want you to think the negotiations are too intractable, the progress too halting, the issues too complex, too tortuous, too pointless, TL;DR.

But as the UN’s 31st annual climate conference got underway in Antalya, Turkey this week, our journalists have been going to great lengths to help you understand why the talks remain urgent, crucial and – hopefully – consequential. As well as helping you follow the agreements reached and progress made during the two week summit, they have also been highlighting what’s at stake.

Covering a Cop is gruelling work. The negotiations are by definition difficult: representatives from almost every country in the world attempt to thrash out consensus agreements and roadmaps for confronting humanity’s greatest threat. There are also practical hurdles, with 70,000 registered delegates at this year’s summit, packed venues and tangled schedules. On Tuesday morning, the Guardian’s live blog from the conference also chronicled the odyssey of our journalist Graham Readfearn as he struggled for three and a half hours just to get to the venue on one of the special Cop31 buses that got caught in the Antalya traffic.

Graham’s quest wasn’t a metaphor – it was just one of many practical challenges reporters face when covering a Cop (which stands for Conference of the Parties to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change). These challenges are that much harder for smaller media organisations from poorer nations that are particularly vulnerable to the impacts of the climate emergency.

I asked some of our journalists ​why it’s such an important conference to cover and the challenges they face reporting from it.

Ajit Niranjan

European environment correspondent

“The hardest thing about covering Cop is satisfying the many different audiences who turn to our coverage during this chaotic fortnight. For the tens of thousands of people attending the summit, we offer a close-up view of the diplomatic spats (and rare breakthroughs) that have sweeping consequences for humanity and the other species with which we share this planet. And for the average Guardian reader, who cares about the climate but may not need the minutiae of UN diplomacy, we mix key takeaways from the negotiations with the most riveting, heartbreaking, terrifying and encouraging stories about the climate crisis. It’s a rare moment during the year when climate change is in the spotlight, and we want to serve as many readers as we can.”

Adam Morton

Executive editor, news, politics and sport, Guardian Australia, and previously climate and environment editor

“Getting across a summit that can draw 100,000 people to attend countless events and backroom meetings is challenging enough, but perhaps the hardest thing about covering Cop is working through the exhaustion that hits after two weeks of long days chasing ministers and bureaucrats across a vast convention centre as they haggle over acronyms that are impenetrable to normal people.

By the end of the final weekend it is not unusual to have gone 48 hours with little to no sleep, as delegates work through the night, well past the scheduled deadline, to try to reach an agreement. Power naps on any available surface can become a necessity. Covering a Cop is a great reporting assignment - sometimes deeply frustrating, sometimes exhilarating - but the exercise of being present and alert to translate what the end result means in tangible terms for readers across the globe is an endurance test.”

Fiona Harvey

Environment editor

“The annual Cop summits might seem futile, and they certainly have long stretches of tedium. Logistically, they’re a nightmare, as tens of thousands of delegates descend on a new location each year to spend a fortnight in white air-conditioned conference halls and cramped negotiating rooms. Oh, and the food is always terrible.

Every day at a Cop is a flurry of text messages, emails, calls, sprints down corridors desperately trying to doorstep world leaders, and forlorn attempts to update yourself on which press conferences have been cancelled, which meetings rearranged, what rumours have been scotched and which of those flying about might still be true.

On the futility side, it’s true that after three decades of Cops the climate crisis has not gone away, and global greenhouse gas emissions have continued to rise. But that’s not the whole story. The world is moving away from fossil fuels, albeit far too slowly, and those impeding that progress need to be held to account. In many countries, voters can do that, but a huge slice of the world’s emissions and fossil fuel production come from autocratic states where elections are not free and fair. Cop is one of the few places where those countries can be questioned and exposed on their failings and attempts at obstruction.

Cops are also, at their best, engines for progress - countries encourage each other to do the right thing. As John Kerry [the former US secretary of state] told me, just ahead of Cop31, when I asked him whether Cops were worth it: ‘I’d rather have it [Cop] taking place, and having people listen to each other and exchange information and views, than live in a completely dark, motionless pit where nothing happens.’”

Graham Readfearn

Environment and climate correspondent, Guardian Australia

“I can’t pick the one thing that’s hardest. They are sprawling in scale, cut across geopolitics, science, diplomacy, social affairs and so many other big issues. I’m based in Australia, so there’s always a long flight to take and some jet lag to deal with while at the same time trying to be on top of your game from day one. It’s exhausting, relentless and exhilarating. If none of my colleagues have mentioned the acronyms, then TBH they should have. You need to know your LDCs from your NDCs and your HACs from your WEOGs. The big challenge is to know enough to then be able to translate what’s happening into a language the reader understands, and to be able to tell the difference between a development that’s genuinely going to be consequential and something that’s just part of the Cop noise. And I never eat or sleep properly.”

Damien Gayle

Environment correspondent

“The most challenging thing about covering Cop is cutting through the forests of jargon to find your way to the story that actually means something to the outside world. It’s all too easy to get caught up with the excitement of Cop. For two weeks it is like a world in itself – part summit, part trade fair, part festival. Those participating believe it is the most important place anywhere, and that the fate of the world hangs on every intricacy. And it is important. But it still needs to be kept in perspective.”

text:
Falling Sticker Prices Meet Real Questions

The price of the new car in the month of March 2026 is about $58,000 based on current reports. It was noted after the year 2025 that the price had increased to $63,000.Are the costs of buying cars going down? Do you have any proof of that? Whether or not it is to be believed depends greatly on the person intending to purchase a vehicle. Therefore, all the necessary steps should be undertaken to distinguish facts from myths regarding current car prices.

Check the VIN Before the Bargain

Less expensive vehicles can lunge for impulsive decisions. But take a moment to get the VIN number. Since 1981, every car made has a one-of-a-kind 17-digit code that serves as its fingerprint. It provides information about the vehicle’s model year, its trim level, and factory of origin. EpicVIN transforms that code into an accessible account. A report will show you the general specifications of the vehicle, recall news, odometer figures, and the number of accidents along with the previous owners. Battery packs avoid water. A cheaper used electric vehicle that has a hidden flood title is nothing but a sleazy investment.

Why the Federal Subsidy Vanished and Prices Followed

Let’s think about autumn 2025. Many people were visiting showrooms. The reason was that the federal tax credit for electric vehicles, which clients could get when buying a new car, was ending on the 30th of September, 2025. The same was true for the used EV tax credit. The share of new cars was equal to 11.4% in September and decreased to 5.8% in October. The parking lots were full but dealers could hear nothing from the phones.

Experts were predicting a hike in prices. However, dealers were out of position and offered discounts. Currently, tax credits do not exist but, nevertheless, the average price of a new electric car is cut down by 12.3% per half a year. Moreover, there were situations when car makers reduced prices without waiting for Congress to change tax credits. For example, the price of a Chevrolet Equinox EV dropped by 13.4% from October to March.

It is time to consider the sales statistics and they do not seem to be optimistic. Compared to the last year, EV sales have decreased by 36% in late 2025 and by 27% in early 2026.

The Cheapest Models Right Now

Entry prices finally dip below $30,000. Look at the leaders.

Destination fees are not part of the cost. The Leaf carries a destination fee of $1,495 above the MSRP price. Study all the stickers in the windows.

The Bolt has LFP battery packs and NACS charging port. 10%-80% charging should take up to 25 minutes. According to Nissan, the Nissan Leaf can charge via 27,500+ Tesla Superchargers without the need for an adapter. Tesla Model 3 should be part of the comparison because of the vast number of chargers and the mileage of 321 miles.

Hyundai and Kia Join the Fight

However, Korean manufacturers are different; the first price tag for the Hyundai Ioniq 5 is pegged at around $36,600. Further down the line, Hyundai plans to price the upcoming Ioniq 5 lineup of 2026 without any discounts.

Kia cars are value-oriented. These vehicles like Kia Niro EV and Hyundai Kona Electric fall under the subcompact crossover segment, with no premium pricing. A good case is the price of the 2025 version of Hyundai Kona Electric SE, which is priced at $32,975. This is a good option for people who need cargo space.

What Actually Makes an EV Cheaper

The battery is key in pricing. The most expensive piece of the car is the battery. The already high price is compounded by the fact that the company produces the car with LFP battery technology that is cheaper. In terms of battery design, car engineers work to get rid of unnecessary battery parts.

The following factors drive down battery costs.

Cheaper battery technology.

Use of a single electric vehicle platform.

Use of lower cost approaches instead of leasing.

The benefits of mass production in the future.

In the case of a bakery, one oven can bake ten loaves, but three ovens may bake forty loaves significantly quicker. The economy of scale principle works the same for the car industry, as it becomes more profitable with every car produced. Consequently, although the volume of car sales by the company, which occurred in 2026, does not live up to the anticipated projections, it is imperative to monitor sales figures moving forward, given the contradiction that EV has not experienced any decrease in performance.

The Hybrid Twist

Not every shopper wants a plug-in vehicle. Hybrid sales increased almost by 27% last year. Hyundai sold 33% more hybrids in August than it did in the same month last year. One Toyota dealership from New York told NPR that their hybrid supply lasts only 12 days. Why this haste? Plug-in hybrid vehicles can travel short distances electrically, but they still have the gasoline option. Regular hybrids do not have a plug option. Gasoline prices are very close to $4.50 this fall, and that helps the argument stay heated.

A friend compared the prices of a Kona Electric and a hybrid last month. In comparison, the Kona was less expensive, but the worry of charging led him to select the hybrid. It is logical because nobody should purchase a vehicle that brings up unnecessary stress in life.

Gas Car or EV on Price

As per statistics released by the industry, the average transaction price of electric vehicles was over $54,000 in the month of August while the average price of gas-powered vehicles was around $50,000. Though gas-powered vehicles have an upper hand regarding sticker prices, this gap is constantly decreasing.

Additionally, in terms of operating costs, gas simply cannot compete with electric vehicles since they need to spend money on fuel for every mile driven along with other costs related to maintenance and other operations of gas-powered vehicles.

Charging Costs and Habits

Home charging is a modern approach to managing expenses. It is also handy since the charging can be performed when you are sleeping at night. You can wake up and find your vehicle battery fully charged and not be bothered by the need to wait for charging at a gas station. However, public charging is costly in terms of $ per kw/h and is still good regarding traveling. There can be great variations in charging times; a DC fast charger will charge the battery of a Bolt car within 25 minutes, while using a normal wall socket takes an entire night.

Use this list before buying:

Confirm a spot for a home unit

Map public stations along your commute

Check the warranty on the battery

Compare the full price with destination fees

Run the VIN on any used model

Used Is Where the Savings Hide

The typical price of a used electric vehicle (EV) in March 2026 is $35,276. Some cars, such as the Kia Niro EV and Hyundai Kona EV, tend to have much lower prices. Newly released electric vehicles lose their value very quickly, so buyers are recommended to be careful. Make sure to check the car’s battery and history of ownership. The good thing is that looking at the VIN is a very quick and cheap process that may save you a lot of money.

Premium Brands and Pickups

Rivian is developing relatively pricey adventure vehicles such as the R1S. Even the larger battery-enabled pickup is costly. The inexpensive trucks will become available sometime later. The cheapest vehicles that will be produced first will include smaller hatchback and SUV cars using much smaller batteries.

What Comes Next

Price decline is not supposed to occur quickly. Prices have dropped without the influence of the government. Car makers have started showing real prices. The decrease in battery price will make cheaper cars accessible for customers.

Consumers are in control today. Compare vehicles. Ask for the total price. Don’t pay hidden charges.

Conclusion

The reasons for the accessibility of electric cars include reduced prices of batteries, affordable car models, and actions taken by car manufacturers. The tax incentives may either continue to operate or be terminated in some cases. It is necessary to conduct a complete analysis of the range, possibilities of charging, and the price of the car. It is advisable to check the history of the car on EpicVIN before signing a deal.

FAQ

Will electric cars be priced below $25,000 soon? There are vehicles sold below $30,000 already. Further price reductions would depend on battery costs and the amount produced.

Is the price of hybrid vehicles lower than that of electric vehicles? Generally, hybrid vehicles are cheaper initially. However, fuel efficiency is subject to driving style.

Are electric vehicles prone to depreciation faster than those using an internal combustion engine? The newly released electric vehicles have suffered depreciation, which is good news for the used car industry.

Is it possible to charge an electric car from a power outlet? Yes, electric vehicles can be recharged in this manner but the process is relatively slow. Charging overnight should suffice for short trips taken in the vehicle.

text:
The Tennessee Valley Authority is retaining veteran utility executive Mike Skaggs as its CEO while restructuring its leadership to separate strategic oversight from day-to-day operations.

The utility’s board of directors announced the decision Nov. 12, citing Skaggs’ leadership in stabilizing the organization, rebuilding stakeholder relationships and strengthening strategic planning.

Skaggs, who came out of retirement in April 2026 to serve as interim president and CEO, will remain at the helm following what TVA described as a strong fiscal year.

Under the new structure, Skaggs will oversee long-term strategy, major capital investments and initiatives requiring board approval.

He has more than four decades of utility industry experience, including more than 25 years at TVA. Before retiring in 2022, he served as chief operating officer, overseeing generation, transmission and power supply.

Skaggs is a registered professional engineer, holds a bachelor’s degree in mechanical engineering from Texas Tech University, and completed senior reactor certification at TVA’s Watts Bar Nuclear Plant.

In the transition, Chief Financial Officer Tom Rice, a second-generation TVA employee, will assume the additional role of president, effective Monday, Nov. 16.

Rice has served as CFO since January 2025, overseeing financial and commercial operations that brought in more than $14 billion in reported annual revenue. His previous leadership roles include senior vice president of finance, treasurer and chief risk officer.

Rice holds a bachelor’s degree in economics from King University and an MBA from the University of Tennessee, Knoxville. He also completed the MIT/INPO Reactor Technology Course for Utility Executives.

Rice’s promotion puts him in charge of daily operations as TVA plans for a more than $13 billion spending program through fiscal 2029.

The utility’s most recent Integrated Resource Plan identifies a need for 11 GW to 32 GW of additional generation capacity by 2040, with natural gas and storage addressing near-term needs and advanced nuclear playing a potential longer-term role.

The investment covers both generation and transmission, including more than $1 billion annually to maintain and strengthen existing assets.

In August, TVA approved plans for 1,550 MW of natural gas generation targeted for completion in 2032. The utility estimates additional project spending could reach $3.1 billion, subject to environmental reviews and other requirements.

The Clinch River nuclear site is another component of TVA’s long-term generation strategy. In September, the Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) approved a construction permit for a proposed GE Vernova Hitachi BWRX-300 small modular reactor at the site. TVA has not made a final decision to build the reactor.

TVA has spent $381 million on SMR-related work through Sept. 30, including activities associated with Clinch River. However, the utility has not made a final decision to build the reactor.
