text:
Early-stage startup investor Plural says it has closed on its largest fund to date — just over $1.1 billion, or 1 billion euros — to lead early-stage investments across Europe.

With the announcement, Plural joins a select group of European venture firms that have raised funds of a billion dollars or more in recent years. Others include Balderton Capital, Atomico and Index Ventures, which is co-headquartered in London and San Francisco. It also follows a Q3 that marked Europe’s strongest venture funding quarter in years.

“Our common theme is ambition. We go after the founders that are building the most ambitious things we can humanly find,” Sten Tamkivi, a co-founder of the firm, said in an interview with Crunchbase News. “Our stated objective remains to have a GDP-level impact on Europe with the companies that we back.”

Plural’s portfolio is a mix of energy, compute, defense, robotics, health and software. The firm first backed fusion energy company Proxima Fusion in its 2023 pre-seed round and has also invested in energy storage company Ore Energy. In defense and aerospace, its investments include European defense tech company Helsing and hypersonic flight and missile company Hypersonica, whose Series A it led in 2026. Plural also led the 2024 Series B for The Exploration Co., which develops space transportation.

In robotics and manufacturing, Plural has backed Monumental, which develops bricklaying robots; Sunrise Robotics, which builds robots for manufacturing; CircuitHub, which manufactures circuit board assemblies; and Upside Robotics, which develops agricultural robots. In compute, its investments include optical AI accelerator company Olix and photonic networking company Oriole Networks. More recently, Plural led the pre-seed round for Callosum, which is building a routing layer for heterogeneous compute.

Its investments have shifted year to year and fund to fund based on where the most ambitious founders are pulling the firm, said Tamkivi.

“Europe has agonized maybe a little bit too much about, ‘Hey, we missed this wave in the models, and the big labs are in the U.S. and China,’ and so forth. But if you look at the rest of the pyramid, we’re doing well,” he said.

The latest fund is the firm’s third and is double the size of its fund 2, raised in 2024, and 4x its first fund, closed in 2022.

Plural’s portfolio companies have had a breakout year, raising more than $3 billion in follow-on capital so far in 2026.

The team has six equal partners, all prior founders and operators based in London, Tallinn and Paris. Plural was founded by Taavet Hinrikus, co-founder of Wise, and Tamkivi co-founder of Teleport, both early employees at Skype, as well as Ian Hogarth, co-founder of Songkick, and Khaled Helioui, former CEO of Bigpoint.

The team has two other partners: Carina Namih, co-founder of HelixNano, and Pierre-Dimitri Gore-Coty, a former Uber executive.

Each partner aims to make one to three new investments per year, leaving bandwidth to work hands-on with founders.

The firm’s entry point is seed and Series A, where it likes to lead. “We’re still early-stage investors, so two-thirds of this money that we raise goes into early stage. What we’ve tagged on top is that now we have more capital to follow through in our winners, and double down and triple down,” Tamkivi said, adding: “there’s more reserves to do that.”

text:
Working together to create a new prosperity for civilization

ANTALYA, Turkey, Nov. 16, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Envision Energy joined Tsinghua University and the Global Alliance of Universities on Climate (GAUC) at two high-level events during COP31, highlighting how technological innovation, academic partnerships, and youth leadership can help translate climate commitments into lasting impact.

On November 10, Hongwen Zhou, Founding Partner and Executive Director of Envision, delivered a video address at the opening of the GAUC Pavilion in the COP31 Blue Zone. Supported by the Tsinghua–Envision Sustainability Fund, the Pavilion provides an international platform for universities, industry, and young climate leaders to exchange knowledge and advance climate action.

Zhou emphasized that the energy transition is about more than replacing energy sources. By connecting clean electricity, green fuels, and artificial intelligence, countries with abundant renewable resources can transform their natural advantages into new industries and economic opportunities. A successful green transition must go beyond emissions reductions to provide reliable and affordable energy, strengthen climate resilience, and enable more people to share in the prosperity brought by technological progress.

"Climate action is a responsibility that extends across generations," Zhou stressed. Building future energy systems requires investment not only in infrastructure, but also in people capable of creating knowledge, advancing innovation, and building partnerships across borders.

On November 9, Bella Zhang, Vice President of Strategy & Innovation at Envision Energy, delivered special remarks at GAUC's High-Level Event at the China Pavilion, the Pavilion's first side event at COP31. The gathering featured Li Gao, China's Vice Minister of Ecology and Environment; Francesco La Camera, Director-General of the International Renewable Energy Agency (IRENA); and Francesco Corvaro, Italy's Special Envoy for Climate Change, alongside representatives from international organizations, academia, industry, and youth communities.

Bella highlighted two fundamental shifts shaping the global energy transition: from individual technologies to integrated systems, and from regional solutions to global opportunities. At Envision, this approach is known as "Technology Fusion"—bringing renewable energy, energy storage, green fuels, and AI together to shape future energy systems. As these systems become increasingly interconnected, solutions require collaboration across engineering, economics, policy, and local development.

These ambitions underpin Envision's long-term strategic partnership with Tsinghua University, launched in 2024 with an initial 11-year commitment. Through the Tsinghua–Envision Sustainability Fund, the partners connect real-world industrial challenges with academic research, promote international collaboration, and invest in future climate leaders. Their cooperation also includes sustainable development centers in Brazil and Indonesia, linking research and talent development with regional priorities.

"Talent is infrastructure," Bella emphasized, highlighting the importance of empowering young people to think across disciplines, collaborate across cultures, and turn knowledge into action.

Through its participation at COP31, Envision reaffirmed its commitment to working with Tsinghua, GAUC, and global partners to shape future energy systems and create a new prosperity for civilization.

description:

Panamint says this will be "the largest brownfield renewable energy project in North America."
Solar Power Leads U.S.
Key Takeaways Energy investment company Panamint Capital has secured financing for phase one of what it calls "the largest brownfield renewable energy project in North America," already in progress in central Texas.
Total project valued at $2.4 billion will achieve 958 MW of solar capacity with 201 MW of BESS.
text:
Reports related to this article:

Written by Paul Wiseman for IIR News Intelligence (Sugar Land, Texas)

Summary

U.S. largest brownfield solar/BESS project being built on reclaimed coal mine land at Panamint's Twin Oaks Power Station and Calvert Mine complex in Robertson County

Sunny Side Up

A financing package is now secured for phase one of energy infrastructure investor Panamint Capital's Big Rooter Power, a 958-megawatt (MW) solar PV project under construction in central Texas. It accounts for $769 million of a total $1.8 billion loan to fund construction that is already underway at the 403-MW Big Rooter West.

Phase two will fund construction at the 555-MW Big Rooter East, expected to cost just over $1 billion. Panamint is looking to secure funding for Big Rooter East in first-quarter 2027. Industrial Info Resources is tracking both projects here.

Co-locating Coal and Solar

The company will save significant infrastructure costs by building these solar farms on reclaimed coal mine land at its 10,000-acre Twin Oaks Power Station and Calvert Mine in Robertson County, Texas, between Bryan-College Station and Waco.

The campus combines power generation, surface mining, energy storage, data center capacity, and high voltage transmission. Panamint says this will be "the largest brownfield renewable energy project in North America." Although it lists the possibility of locating a data center on the site, the company has announced no plans for one at this time.

While nationwide there are many wind and solar plants located on retired or soon-to-be-retired coal plant sites, this one is unique, being the only solar facilities to locate next to a coal mine with no plans for a shutdown.

In fact, the company is looking at expanding the coal plant. Canary Media quotes Panamint CEO Apolka Totth as saying they are "looking at expanding the mine and building a rail terminal."

In addition to this property, Panamint also owns the 49-MW-capacity Sunnyside coal-waste-fired cogeneration plant in Utah, which Industrial Info Resources is also tracking.

Solar Power Leads U.S. Grid Supply Growth

The U.S. Energy Information Administration noted earlier this year that solar power is, and will continue to be, the fastest growing source of grid power in the U.S. The EIA expects its output to expand from 290 billion kilowatt hours (BkWh) in 2025 to 424 BkWh by 2027.

With almost 70 GW of new capacity expected to come online in 2026 and 2027, that's a 49% increase in solar operating capacity compared with the end of 2025, the EIA says.

Texas leads that growth. "Much of the utility-scale solar generation capacity additions will come online in Texas. We expect that solar electricity generation supplied to the grid managed by the Electric Reliability Council of Texas (ERCOT) will grow from 56 BkWh in 2025 to 106 BkWh by 2027."

Key Takeaways

Energy investment company Panamint Capital has secured financing for phase one of what it calls "the largest brownfield renewable energy project in North America," already in progress in central Texas. Finalizing of phase two is expected in first-quarter 2027.

A financing package accounts for $769 million of a total $1.8 billion loan to fund construction that is already underway.

Total project valued at $2.4 billion will achieve 958 MW of solar capacity with 201 MW of BESS.

title: PLI schemes generate ₹22.66 lakh crore in production, but job creation lags - Business Line
description:
The 14 schemes have attracted investments of ₹2.40 lakh crore and generated production worth ₹22.66 lakh crore as of March 2026.
Electronics manufacturing emerges as the strongest performer Electronics manufacturing has emerged as the clearest success story.
It has also laid the foundation for the ₹40,000-crore Electronics Component Manufacturing Scheme.
The automobile and auto components scheme has attracted ₹44,326 crore against an outlay of ₹25,938 crore, with electric vehicle production rising.
The report also called for standardised data collection across ministries to measure additional production, employment and revenue more accurately.
text:
The Centre’s Production Linked Incentive (PLI) schemes are beginning to deliver results, with electronics, pharmaceuticals, white goods and food processing emerging as the stronger performers. However, employment generation and domestic value addition remain uneven, while some capital-intensive sectors are struggling to translate investment commitments into commercial production, according to a NITI Aayog assessment prepared with IIM Ahmedabad.

The 14 schemes have attracted investments of ₹2.40 lakh crore and generated production worth ₹22.66 lakh crore as of March 2026. While investment achievement is 76 per cent of the full-tenure target and production 64 per cent, employment generation stands at just 28 per cent, with 8.49 lakh jobs created against a target of 30.19 lakh.

The report offered a cautiously positive assessment, saying that “directionally, the scheme is starting to bear fruit; however, in terms of quantitative impact, progress remains varied across sectors and is not yet out of the woods.” It also noted that 42 per cent of the aggregate implementation period remains, making it premature to judge some sectors solely against their final targets.

Electronics manufacturing emerges as the strongest performer

Electronics manufacturing has emerged as the clearest success story. The report described the large-scale electronics manufacturing scheme as “one of the strongest performers”, particularly in mobile manufacturing, citing significant growth in production, exports and employment among domestic and global companies. It has also laid the foundation for the ₹40,000-crore Electronics Component Manufacturing Scheme. The next challenge is to move beyond assembly and deepen domestic component manufacturing, the report said.

About the textile PLI scheme, which has an outlay of ₹10,683 crore, the Ayog said initial evidence suggests investment remains below aggregate targets and employment trends remain inconclusive.

White goods, covering air-conditioners and LED lights, have also performed strongly. The report said the scheme has contributed to a “more competitive and self-reliant domestic white goods ecosystem”. Domestic value addition has increased from 20 per cent to 55 per cent, with components such as compressors and printed circuit board assemblies increasingly manufactured locally. Pharmaceuticals, food processing, drones and medical devices have also shown encouraging progress across multiple parameters.

The automobile and auto components scheme has attracted ₹44,326 crore against an outlay of ₹25,938 crore, with electric vehicle production rising. Solar manufacturing capacity has expanded from 8 GW to nearly 116 GW, with around 24 GW directly attributable to PLI-supported projects.

ACC battery scheme lags behind targets

However, the advanced chemistry cell battery scheme remains a major concern. Against a target of 50 GWh of domestic capacity, only 1.4 GWh had been developed by March 2026, with commercial production yet to begin. The report says the scheme “so far has not performed as per expectation”, citing dependence on foreign technology, inadequate domestic supplies of critical materials, imported machinery and project delays. IT hardware and textiles are also yet to demonstrate their full potential.

“The larger success of PLI is that it has worked differently across different sectors, according to the needs of each industry. In mobile phones, it has helped create global manufacturing scale. In Pharmaceuticals Drugs, it has strengthened India’s position in high-value manufacturing and strategic inputs. In White Goods, it is deepening component localisation. In Food Processing, it is generating employment across wider value chains. At the same time, perhaps its most important long-term contribution is the emergence of entirely new strategic manufacturing priorities. Solar PV and ACC batteries, which did not historically occupy a comparable position in India’s manufacturing landscape, are now central to India’s industrial, energy-security and clean-energy strategy,” the report said.

NITI Aayog calls for demand-side incentives

It said the next phase of PLI needs a change in approach. The assessment argued that production incentives alone cannot build sustainable manufacturing competitiveness. It recommended that future schemes should not rely solely on “supply-side interventions” but also incorporate “demand-side incentives for downstream firms and consumers to purchase from PLI firms”.

The report also called for standardised data collection across ministries to measure additional production, employment and revenue more accurately. It emphasises that sector-specific constraints must be addressed rather than applying uniform benchmarks to industries with widely different investment and technology cycles.

The broader objective, it said, is to help Indian manufacturers move up the value chain, from assembly towards deeper domestic value addition, advanced technologies and globally competitive production.

Published on November 16, 2026

title: Morrisey outlines record $113B energy investment - The Inter-Mountain
description:
Patrick Morrisey praised more than $12 billion in potential investments in West Virginia, mostly from energy projects.
"This is going to be good-paying jobs for West Virginia," Morrisey said.
"Does anyone think we’re not going to get the 50 gigawatts of energy by 2050 now?"
By expanding supply across diverse energy, Morrisey said he aims to lower the per-unit cost of electricity for West Virginia families while guaranteeing ratepayer protection, so infrastructure costs do not shift to taxpayers.
We need West Virginia citizens to benefit from all of this dynamic, economic development."
text:
CHARLESTON - During his inaugural address at the Governor’s Energy Summit last year, Gov. Patrick Morrisey praised more than $12 billion in potential investments in West Virginia, mostly from energy projects.

One year later, Morrisey announced the total has increased to more than $113 billion.

Morrisey made the announcement Thursday morning on the second day of the annual Governor’s Energy Summit put on by the state Office of Energy and Department of Commerce at the Charleston Coliseum and Convention Center, soon to be renamed the Vandalia Health Center.

According to Morrisey, Columbus-based American Electric Power - the parent company of Appalachian Power and Wheeling Power - has agreed to spend $17 billion towards adding 3 gigawatts of natural gas-fired electric power in West Virginia.

The proposal, which could involve three separate plants spread out across the state, could see more than 2,000 construction jobs created and more than 100 permanent jobs. Appalachian Power already agreed to commit an additional $7.5 billion to upgrade West Virginia's coal-fired power plants through 2050, extending their reasonable useful life.

"This is going to be good-paying jobs for West Virginia," Morrisey said. "We’re talking about construction workers. We’re talking about electricians. We’re talking about welders, sheet metal workers, and the kind of jobs that make good money for our state. And when you get those paychecks in, they don’t just stop at the job site. They support our local restaurants, our retail establishments when you go out and buy new clothes for your kids, and the small businesses throughout our communities."

Morrisey said that takes the total amount of proposed economic development investments in West Virginia from $12.9 billion between October 2025 and July 2026 to $113.6 billion with approximately 21,030 jobs that could be created should all the projects become reality.

"I knew coming into this job, we had to bring capital and private investment in, and a level the states had never seen before. And that’s what we’ve been working on," Morrisey said. "People are talking about our state, from an investment perspective, that they’ve never talked about in the past. Let’s keep going. Let’s keep making progress."

Morrisey announced more than a year ago his 50 by 50 initiative to increase the number of gigawatts produced by West Virginia from 16 to 50 by the year 2050. The American Electric Power investment could add 3 gigawatts to the 27.6 gigawatts of electric generation announced since the initiative was launched.

"Does anyone think we’re not going to get the 50 gigawatts of energy by 2050 now?" Morrisey said. "I don’t think so ... We’re on our pathway to get the 50 by 50."

House Bill 5381, introduced on behalf of Morrisey and passed by the Legislature earlier this year, created the Comprehensive Energy Policy and Development Plan Act of 2026, which tasks the Office of Energy with creating a long-term strategy to bolster electrical grid stability and energy security through 2050.

The new law calls for a diverse, "all-of-the-above" energy policy, including the use of coal, natural gas, nuclear and alternative energy. The bill mandates a five-year Comprehensive Energy Plan, with the first version due by Dec. 1. The policy must include four pillars: reliability focused on stable baseload generation, efficiency driven by technological innovations, affordability focused on low-cost energy sources and independence focused on domestic energy production.

By expanding supply across diverse energy, Morrisey said he aims to lower the per-unit cost of electricity for West Virginia families while guaranteeing ratepayer protection, so infrastructure costs do not shift to taxpayers.

"We know how important that is: affordability. Whether it’s groceries, whether it’s housing, whether it’s healthcare or paying the power bills, families are being squeezed," Morrisey said. "That’s why we have to change that. While other states retire their reliable power plants and restrict new generation, West Virginia is taking a different approach. ... If we do it the right way, the cost per unit will be lower and lower. And that will ensure, one mechanism among many, that West Virginians are going to be paying some of the lowest power prices in America."

Morrisey also sees growing the number of gigawatts produced by the state as an incentive for more data center projects to come to West Virginia. One of the largest investments since Morrisey first took office is the Nscale Monarch Compute Campus in Mason County, which has partnerships with Anthropic, the makers of Claude. The potential investment for phase one of the project, which will create up to 2 gigawatts of compute capacity, is estimated at more than $69 billion.

House Bill 2014, the Power Generation and Consumption Act introduced on behalf of Morrisey and passed by the Legislature in 2025, streamlines development of data center and microgrid projects, offers regulatory exemptions within designated microgrid districts, establishes a special valuation for property taxes and a new tax distribution framework for high-impact data centers, and creates a fund for electric grid stabilization.

According to the formula in the Power Generation and Consumption Act, 50% of property tax collections from these projects would go to a personal income tax reduction fund, 30% would go to the county or counties where the data centers are, 10% would go to all 55 counties on a per capita basis and 5% would go to the state Economic Enhancement Grant Fund. Morrisey said his 50 by 50 initiative and data center growth could go hand-in-hand in phasing out the state’s personal income tax.

"I see a pathway by 2038 where we can get to not only the 50 by 50 framework, but we have a chance ... to get our state income tax down near zero," Morrisey said. "As we’re growing our energy resources, parts of (the Power Generation and Consumption Act) will feed into reductions to the state income tax. That’s important for us to know. We need West Virginia citizens to benefit from all of this dynamic, economic development."

Morrisey also praised the recent launch of the West Virginia New Home Energy Rebate Program, receiving over 1,400 applications in its first month, coupled with a $1 million commitment from Google to fund home repairs so families in six counties can access rebate programs.

text:
Thanks for your recent articles on the new pipelines threatening Louisiana, given the serious safety issues that they raise (“Trump push to build pipelines is playing out in Louisiana,” Nov. 9).

As a nearly 50-year member of the League of Women Voters, I am shocked at the deliberate efforts by state and national officials to downplay such issues and to exclude the public from vital information.

My family (Wimberly and Knighton) has been in Red River and Bienville parishes in Northwest Louisiana since the Louisiana Purchase. So I was disturbed to hear that a disaster worse than Satartia, Mississippi’s 2020 carbon dioxide pipeline burst could happen in Louisiana’s earthquake zone near Coushatta, if two planned CO2 pipelines are built to cross each other there.

The LBP/PBS documentary “Going Underground” describes the need for hybrid-electric emergency vehicles to respond to CO2 leaks, especially in the five-mile area around these pipelines, where lives are threatened and combustion vehicles will not operate in the absence of oxygen.

Louisiana officials should have already addressed this issue for the area along Highway 190, where a CO2 pipeline crosses Louisiana from Mississippi to Texas.

Private corporations and foreign investors benefit from the generous Federal 45Q tax subsidy encouraging CO2 for enhanced oil recovery and carbon capture injection, which our nation cannot afford.

Plus, our state is allowing the taking of private property for CO2 pipelines when there is no public purpose, which is and should remain unconstitutional. The Louisiana Legislature has not respected the will of the public on eminent domain or local control for CO2 projects.

text:
What happens when the world, as expected, hurtles dangerously past agreed temperature thresholds? At UN climate talks, countries are being urged to turn to technology to reverse this fate by sucking carbon directly from the atmosphere.

A renewed push by proponents of carbon dioxide removal (or CDR), where heat-trapping carbon dioxide is taken from the atmosphere and stored deep underground, in oceans or in products such as carbonated drinks, is seeking to gain recognition in the final text of Cop31, the climate summit currently under way in Antalya, Turkey.

There is a smaller but significant group of CDR promoters who have a pavilion, called Think Negative, at the sprawling summit venue, where plans for a dramatic increase in carbon removal is talked up as a way to help bring back the world from imminent “overshoot” of internationally agreed temperature thresholds.

Meanwhile, a record 700 lobbyists at this Cop are advocating for a distinct but related process called carbon capture and storage (or CCS), where carbon is captured at the source of a polluting facility and put underground, according to the Center for International Environmental Law (CIEL). This is more delegates than the from the smallest 50 national delegations combined.

CCS has less support from environmentalists over its costs, mixed track record, and potential to prolong fossil fuel reliance. But on Friday, for the first time, both CCS and CDR were included in a text that will inform the basis of a final deal at the climate talks.

The UN has acknowledged the world will soon surge past a 1.5C rise in global temperatures since the pre-industrial period, which will unleash ever worsening heatwaves, floods, droughts and other deadly impacts, as countries continue to release greenhouse gases by burning fossil fuels.

Even with reduced emissions the planet’s fever will not fall below this level for thousands of years without the sort of rapid removal of CO2 as envisaged by the CDR advocates, who want to create a new global agency to coordinate carbon removals. They have also pressed Turkey and Australia, which are jointly presiding over the Cop31 talks, to include CDR in the summit’s final outcome.

“CDR still sounds unreal to people but we spent a whole year trying to make it into the agenda of Cop31,” said Göker Avci, a decarbonization strategist at CDR Türkiye. “We spoke with the presidency about making it into the final decision and they have started to realize the potential.”

There are various forms of carbon removal, such as directly sucking it from the air, crushing up rocks that can lock away carbon or, more naturally, through protecting and seeding forests and mangroves.

CDR remains relatively small scale, with around 2bn tons of carbon removed a year, almost all of it via reforestation. Technological efforts to vacuum CO2 from the air has removed just 2 million tons, with leading companies in this area badly underperforming and struggling financially. With a lack of investor cash, which is instead flowing to areas such as artificial intelligence, CDR remains nascent and under-resourced.

Despite this, countries have long relied on the theoretical promise of carbon removal in their climate plans. That promise will quickly have to become reality if the world is to bend the temperature curve back to safe levels, rather than just flatline it – the UN recently estimated that an enormous 320bn tons of CO2 will have to be removed this century in order to get back under 1.5C.

“CDR’s really been missing from the discussion and debate even though it’s been in all the models for decades,” said Injy Johnstone, a net zero expert at the Max Planck Insitute. “It’s the only solution that we have to actually balance out those emissions and it return from the state of overshoot.”

“Really these efforts shouldn’t have to be led by the entrepreneurs kind of doing their thing on the ground, we have to get more vocal about it and actually also start to put in place these kinds of procedures,” she added about the attempt to set up an international framework for CDR.

Although CDR is still largely missing from the equation, environmentalists have warned about the risks of depending on it. Large, potentially harmful, changes to land use and the oceans would be needed to remove and store enough carbon, they argue, while the reliance on cleaning up the atmosphere removes pressure on reducing emissions in the first place.

“The focus should always be on cutting emissions now, it’s very dangerous to assume that we can put more emissions into the atmosphere and then assume we will have technology in the future to just remove them again,” said Rachel Kennerley, carbon capture campaigner at the Center for International Environmental Law.

“These are hypothetical technologies and part of the problem we’re seeing here is that we’re seeing the normalization of this overshoot peak and return pathway. That return element is at the moment hypothetical. I mean, I think it’s impossible.”

CDR is often confused for carbon capture and storage (or CCS), where emissions are captured directly at source and buried. Kennerley said that CCS is a “greenwashing exercise” used by large oil and gas companies to extend the age of fossil fuels.

But the two processes are similar in some aspects, given they both ultimately end up having to store large amounts of carbon underground. “I think they fulfill similar kind of diversionary roles from mitigation,” said Kennerley. “I think they’re both allowed for prolonging fossil-fuel use, basically.”

Kennerley added that the exceedance of 1.5C should be kept as small as possible with the elimination of fossil fuel use, with reforestation then slowly eating up the excess CO2 to the point, over many hundreds of years, the temperature dips back down.

But advocates claim the scale of the climate emergency is such that CDR will be the only viable option to bring down the temperature. “It’s the only tool we have,” said Johnstone. “We need this, we need this fast, and we need to be really seeing it on a scale that rivals the global energy industry in terms of its kind of footprint in the world.”
